title: Kourovka Notebook Problem 21.83
statement: Conjecture: Metabelian groups are permutation-stable.
background:
Source: Kourovka Notebook, New Problems, 21st issue, 2026. Original problem number: 21.83.

Discussion and literature:
The function $d_n(\sigma,\tau)=(1/n)\cdot|\{x\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\mid \sigma(x)\ne\tau(x)\}|$ is a distance on the symmetric group $S_n$. For a finitely generated group $G$, an almost-homomorphism is a sequence of set-theoretic maps $f_n:G\to S_n$ satisfying $d_n(f_n(g)f_n(h),f_n(gh))\to 0$ as $n\to\infty$ for all $g,h\in G$. An almost-homomorphism $\{f_n\}$ is said to be close to a homomorphism if there is a sequence of group homomorphisms $\rho_n:G\to S_n$ such that $d_n(\rho_n(g),f_n(g))\to 0$ as $n\to\infty$ for all $g\in G$. The group $G$ is said to be permutation stable if every almost-homomorphism of $G$ is close to a homomorphism.

A. Lubotzky

title: Kourovka Notebook Problem 21.112
statement:
A nonempty class $\mathcal X$ of finite groups is said to be complete if $\mathcal X$ is closed under taking subgroups, homomorphic images, and extensions. The symmetric boundary of a complete class $\mathcal X$ other than the class of all finite groups is defined as the largest integer $n$ such that $S_n\in\mathcal X$. For every positive integer $n\ne 3$, let $f_+(n)$ and $f_-(n)$ be respectively the maximum and the minimum of $\operatorname{BS}(\mathcal X)$, where $\mathcal X$ runs over all complete classes of symmetric boundary $n$.

(a) Find $f_+(n)$ for $n=4,5,6$.

(b) Is it true that $f_-(n)=n$ for all $n\ne 3$?
background:
Source: Kourovka Notebook, New Problems, 21st issue, 2026. Original problem number: 21.112.

Discussion and literature:
Every positive integer $n\ne 3$ coincides with the symmetric boundary of some complete class. It is proved (mod CFSG, D. O. Revin, Algebra i Analiz, 37, no. 1 (2025), 141--176 (Russian)) that, for every complete class $\mathcal X$, there exists a nonnegative integer $m$ with the following property: for every finite group $G$ and each conjugacy class $D$ of $G$, if every $m$ elements of $D$ generate a subgroup belonging to $\mathcal X$, then $\langle D\rangle\in\mathcal X$. The smallest such $m$ is called the Baer--Suzuki width of $\mathcal X$, denoted by $\operatorname{BS}(\mathcal X)$. It is also proved (mod CFSG, ibid.) that, for a complete class $\mathcal X$ of symmetric boundary $n$, the value of $\operatorname{BS}(\mathcal X)$ is at least $n$ and is bounded above in terms of $n$.

It is known that $f_+(1)=2$, $f_+(2)=3$, and $f_+(n)=2(n-1)$ for $n\geqslant 7$.

This is known to be true for $n=1,2,4$. D. O. Revin, N. Y. Yang

title: Kourovka Notebook Problem 21.120
statement:
A pro-p group is (relatively) strictly finitely presented if it is the pro-p completion of a group that is finitely presented (respectively, finitely presented in some finitely-based variety of groups). A pro-p group is finitely axiomatizable if it is determined up to isomorphism by a single sentence in the first-order language of group theory.

(b) In particular, is every finitely generated free pro-p group finitely axiomatizable?

title: Kourovka Notebook Problem 21.121
statement:
Let $p$ be a prime number. A group $\Gamma$ is called $p$-Jordan if there exist constants $J$ and $e$ such that any finite subgroup $G\subset\Gamma$ contains a normal abelian subgroup of order coprime to $p$ and of index at most $J\cdot |G(p)|^e$. (For example by the results of Brauer--Feit and Larsen--Pink, for any field $K$ of characteristic $p$ the group $\operatorname{GL}_n(K)$ is $p$-Jordan with $e=3$.) Let the $p$-Jordan exponent $e(\Gamma)$ of the group $\Gamma$ be the infimum of all constants $e$ for which the above bound holds for some constant $J=J(e)$.

a) Is it true that this infimum is always attained?

b) Is it true that $e(\Gamma)\leqslant 3$ for any $p$-Jordan group $\Gamma$?
background:
Source: Kourovka Notebook, New Problems, 21st issue, 2026. Original problem number: 21.121.

Discussion and literature:
C. Shramov

statement:

title: Kourovka Notebook Problem 21.150
statement: Let $G$ be an extension of a normal elementary abelian subgroup $A$ by an elementary abelian group $B\cong G/A$ such that $A$ contains an element $a$ with $C_B(a)=1$. Is it true that the rank of the subgroup $Z(\langle a,B\rangle)\cap\langle a,B\rangle'$ is at most the rank of $B$?
background:
Source: Kourovka Notebook, New Problems, 21st issue, 2026. Original problem number: 21.150.

Discussion and literature:
V. I. Zenkov

No, not always. Let $A=\mathbb F_3[x,y]/I^3$ be the additive group of the quotient of the polynomial algebra $\mathbb F_3[x,y]$ by the ideal $I^3$, where $I$ is the ideal generated by $x,y$. Let $B$ be the group of automorphisms of $A$ generated by multiplication by $1+x$ and $1+y$. Let $G=A\rtimes B$. For $a=1\in A$ we have $C_B(a)=1_B$. For $H=\langle a,B\rangle$ we have $Z(H)\cap H'=\langle x^2,xy,y^2\rangle$, which has rank 3, while the rank of $B$ is 2. (P. Monticone, Letter of 21 March 2026; see also https://kourovkanotebookorg.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/solution_21_150-3.pdf).

title: Kirby Problem 1.1
statement:
Is the crossing number additive under connected sum:
$c(K_{1}\#K_{2}) = c(K_{1}) + c(K_{2})$?
background:
Source: Kirby's Problems in Low-Dimensional Topology notes. Original problem number: KP-1.1.

Literature notes:
This is Problem 1.65 in [Kir97]. Many special cases are known.
The most famous case is due to Kauffman [Kau87], Murasugi [Mur87], and
Thistlewaite [Thi87], who showed the conjecture for alternating knots (and more
generally adequate knots, defined in [LT88]). Lackenby [Lac09] has shown in the
general case that if $K_{1},..., K_{n}$ are knots, then

$$
\frac{c(K_{1}) + \cdots + c(K_{n})}{152} \leq c(K_{1}\# \cdots \#K_{n}).
$$

References cited:
- [Kir97] R.C. Kirby. Problems in low–dimensional topology. In W. Kazez, editor, Geometric Topology. American Math. Soc./International Press, Providence, 1997.
- [Kau87] Louis H. Kauffman. State models and the Jones polynomial. Topology, 26(3):395– 407, 1987. doi:10.1016/0040-9383(87)90009-7.
- [Mur87] Kunio Murasugi. Jones polynomials and classical conjectures in knot theory. Topology, 26(2):187–194, 1987. doi:10.1016/0040-9383(87)90058-9.
- [Thi87] Morwen B. Thistlethwaite. A spanning tree expansion of the Jones polynomial. Topology, 26(3):297–309, 1987. doi:10.1016/0040-9383(87)90003-6.
- [LT88] W. B. R. Lickorish and M. B. Thistlethwaite. Some links with nontrivial polynomials and their crossing-numbers. Comment. Math. Helv., 63(4):527–539, 1988. doi:10.1007/BF02566777.
- [Lac09] Marc Lackenby. The crossing number of composite knots. J. Topol., 2(4):747–768, 2009. doi:10.1112/jtopol/jtp028.

title: Kirby Problem 1.2
statement:
(a) Show that if $P$ is a nontrivial satellite operator and $K_{P}$ is a nontrivial
satellite of a knot $K$, then

$$
c(K_{P}) \geq c(K),
$$

where $c$ denotes the crossing number.
(b) More generally, show that if $P$ is a satellite operator then

$$
c(K_{P}) \geq c(K) \cdot w(P)^{2},
$$

where $w(P)$ denotes the geometric winding number.
background:
Source: Kirby's Problems in Low-Dimensional Topology notes. Original problem number: KP-1.2.

Literature notes:
(1) Part (a) is Problem 1.67 in [Kir97]. Part (b) appears as the Satellite
Crossing Number Conjecture in [BM24a].
(2) Note that a special case of this problem is whether

$$
c(K_{1}\#K_{2}) \geq c(K_{1}),
$$

which is a weaker form of Problem 1.1.
It is reasonable to expect equality in part (a) only when $P$ is the core
of the solid torus.
Lackenby [Lac14] has shown the inequality

$$
c(K_{P}) \geq c(K)/10^{13}.
$$

Kalfagianni-Lee [KL23a] have shown that if $K$ is a nontrivial adequate
knot that has an adequate diagram with writhe 0, then

$$
c(\operatorname{Wh}_{\pm}(K)) = 4c(K) + 2,
$$

where $\operatorname{Wh}_{\pm}(K)$ denote the Whitehead doubles of $K$. Kalfagianni-McConkey
[KM24] have shown that if $K$ is adequate, then the cable knot $K_{p,q}$ sat-
isfies

$$
c(K_{p,q}) \geq q^{2} \cdot c(K) + 1
$$

for any coprime $p, q$.
Here $q$, denotes the longitudinal winding of the
cabling pattern. A recent preprint of Baker–Motegi claims that the more
general conjecture is true if one puts sufficiently many full twists in a
pattern with geometric winding number at least 2 [BM24a].

References cited:
- [Kir97] R.C. Kirby. Problems in low–dimensional topology. In W. Kazez, editor, Geometric Topology. American Math. Soc./International Press, Providence, 1997.
- [BM24a] Kenneth L. Baker and Kimihiko Motegi. The stable crossing number of a twist family of knots and the satellite crossing number conjecture, 2024. arXiv:2404.05308.
- [Lac14] Marc Lackenby. The crossing number of satellite knots. Algebr. Geom. Topol., 14(4):2379–2409, 2014. doi:10.2140/agt.2014.14.2379.
- [KL23a] Efstratia Kalfagianni and Christine Ruey Shan Lee. Jones diameter and crossing number of knots. Adv. Math., 417:Paper No. 108937, 35, 2023. doi:10.1016/j.aim.2023.108937.
- [KM24] Efstratia Kalfagianni and Rob Mcconkey. Crossing numbers of cable knots. Bulletin of the London Mathematical Society, 56(11):3400–3411, 2024. doi:10.1112/blms.13140.

title: Kirby Problem 1.3
statement:
How does unknotting number behave under connected sum and
mutation?
(a) Does the connected sum of $n$ nontrivial knots have unknotting number at
least $n$?
(b) Is unknotting number invariant under mutation?
background:
Source: Kirby's Problems in Low-Dimensional Topology notes. Original problem number: KP-1.3.

Literature notes:
(1) Problem 1.69 (B) from [Kir97] asks if unknotting number is additive; a
recent preprint [BH25] claims an example where it fails to be additive,
where the knots in question are the $(2, 7)$ torus knot and its mirror.
(2) Question (a) is [Kir97, Problem 1.69 (A)], and is still open. It has a
positive answer for $n = 2$ by Scharlemann [Sch85b].
(3) With regard to Question (b), Gordon–Luecke [GL06] show that having
unknotting number one is invariant under mutation.

References cited:
- [Kir97] R.C. Kirby. Problems in low–dimensional topology. In W. Kazez, editor, Geometric Topology. American Math. Soc./International Press, Providence, 1997.
- [BH25] Mark Brittenham and Susan Hermiller. Unknotting number is not additive under connected sum, 2025. arXiv:2506.24088.
- [Sch85b] Martin G. Scharlemann. Unknotting number one knots are prime. Invent. Math., 82(1):37–55, 1985. doi:10.1007/BF01394778.
- [GL06] C. McA. Gordon and John Luecke. Knots with unknotting number 1 and essential Conway spheres. Algebr. Geom. Topol., 6:2051–2116, 2006. doi:10.2140/agt.2006.6.2051.

title: Kirby Problem 1.4
statement:
Let $P$ be a nontrivial satellite pattern with winding number
$w(P) \neq 0$. Then for any nontrivial knot $K$ and its satellite $K_{P}$ , one has

$$
u(K_{P}) \geq w(P) + 1.
$$
background:
Source: Kirby's Problems in Low-Dimensional Topology notes. Original problem number: KP-1.4.

Literature notes:
(1) This problem appears as [HLP22, Conjecture 1.10].
(2) One might guess that $w(P)^{2}$ is a lower bound. However, it can be shown
that

$$
u((T_{2,3})_{2,1}) \leq 3,
$$

where $K_{p,q}$ denotes the $(p, q)$ cable of the knot $K$.
(3) It follows from [ST88] that if $w(P) \neq 0$, then

$$
u(K_{P}) \geq 2.
$$

Problem 1.4 would be a generalization of this result. More recently, Hom,
Lidman and Park [HLP22] have claimed that if $K$ is a nontrivial knot,
then

$$
u(K_{p,q}) \geq p.
$$

In the above, $p$ indicates the winding number of the satellite operation.

References cited:
- [HLP22] Jennifer Hom, Tye Lidman, and JungHwan Park. Unknotting number and cabling, 2022. arXiv:2206.04196.
- [ST88] Martin Scharlemann and Abigail Thompson. Unknotting number, genus, and companion tori. Math. Ann., 280(2):191–205, 1988. doi:10.1007/BF01456051.

title: Kirby Problem 1.5
statement:
Is there a relationship between genus and unknotting number
for specific classes of knots? Here are two instances of classes of knots for which
there might be an interesting answer.
(a) Conjecture (Murasugi-Przytycki). For every positive fibered knot $K$, the
genus of $K$ equals its unknotting number.
(b) Question (Stoimenow). For every alternating fibered knot, is the genus
greater than or equal to the unknotting number?
background:
Source: Kirby's Problems in Low-Dimensional Topology notes. Original problem number: KP-1.5.

Literature notes:
(1) There are examples of knots where the genus of a knot is greater than the
unknotting number, and vice versa. However, there could be an inequality
in some particular classes of knots. In part (a) there is evidence for an
inequality one direction; in a different setting, part (b), the evidence points
to an inequality in the other direction.
(2) The conjecture in (a) appears at the end of [MP89]. By work of Rudolph
[Rud93, Rud99] it is now known that genus $\leq$ unknotting number for
a positive knot. For a positive braid closure, manipulations with braid
group relations [BW84] allow one to construct an unknotting sequence of
length = genus, so that genus = unknotting number for a positive braid
knot. However, such arguments are not available for the slightly more
general case of a positive fibered knot.
(3) A Knotinfo [LM23b] search shows that this holds for alternating fibered
knots of at most 13 crossings, with strict inequality holding in all but 13
of the 2106 such knots.

References cited:
- [MP89] Kunio Murasugi and Józef H. Przytycki. The skein polynomial of a planar star product of two links. Math. Proc. Cambridge Philos. Soc., 106(2):273–276, 1989. doi:10.1017/S0305004100078099.
- [Rud93] Lee Rudolph. Quasipositivity as an obstruction to sliceness. Bull. Amer. Math. Soc. (N.S.), 29(1):51–59, 1993. doi:10.1090/S0273-0979-1993-00397-5.
- [Rud99] Lee Rudolph. Positive links are strongly quasipositive. In Proceedings of the Kirbyfest (Berkeley, CA, 1998), volume 2 of Geom. Topol. Monogr., pages 555–562. Geom. Topol. Publ., Coventry, 1999. doi:10.2140/gtm.1999.2.555.
- [BW84] Michel Boileau and Claude Weber. Le problème de J. Milnor sur le nombre gordien des nœuds algébriques. Enseign. Math. (2), 30(3-4):173–222, 1984.
- [LM23b] Charles Livingston and Allison H. Moore. Knotinfo: Table of knot invariants, November 2023. https://knotinfo.org.

title: Kirby Problem 1.6
statement:
Suppose that $V_{1}$ and $V_{2}$ are $S$–equivalent Seifert forms. Does
there exist a fixed knot $K$ bounding Seifert surfaces $F_{1}$ and $F_{2}$ for which the as-
sociated Seifert forms are $V_{1}$ and $V_{2}$?
background:
Source: Kirby's Problems in Low-Dimensional Topology notes. Original problem number: KP-1.6.

Literature notes:
(1) A Seifert form of a knot is a bilinear integral form $V$ for which $V - V^{*}$ is
unimodular (with $V^{*}(\alpha, \beta) = V (\beta, \alpha)$). Every Seifert form $V$ arises as the
Seifert form of a Seifert surface $F$ for some knot $K$. If $K$ bounds Seifert
surfaces $F_{1}$ and $F_{2}$, then the associated Seifert forms are $S$–equivalent.
See [Tro73] or [Kaw96, Chapter 5] for more details.
(2) One way to think about this problem is as a comparison of two flavors
of $S$–equivalence: that of $S$–equivalence of Seifert forms, versus that of
$S$–equivalence of knots, with two knots being $S$–equivalent if they possess
Seifert forms that are $S$–equivalent [Kea04, NS03]. It is shown in [NS03]
that two knots are $S$–equivalent if and only if they are related by a finite
number of doubled-delta moves. These moves do not preserve the knot
type in general: for example, it is shown in [NS03] that a knot is $S$–
equivalent to the unknot if and only if it has Alexander polynomial is
equal to 1.

(3) Consider the notation, defined for a Seifert form $V$ and for a knot $K$:
$[V]_{S} = \{$ $\widetilde{V} |$ $\widetilde{V}$ is a Seifert form $S$–equivalent to $V\},$
$[K]_{S} = \{$ $\widetilde{K} |$ $\widetilde{K}$ is a knot $S$–equivalent to $K\}.$
Since for a given knot $K$, any two of its Seifert forms $V_{1}$ and $V_{2}$ are $S$–
equivalent, it follows that $V_{1}, V_{2} \in [V]_{S}$, where $V$ is any Seifert form of
$K$. Thus, the set of all Seifert forms of $K$ maps to a subset of the $S$–
equivalence class of any one of its Seifert forms. Given this, the question
asked in this problem, can be rephrased as follows.
Question. For a given $S$–equivalence class $[V]_{S}$ of a Seifert form $V$ ,
does there exist a fixed knot $K$ such that the obvious map
$\{$ $\widetilde{V} |$ $\widetilde{V}$ is a Seifert form of $K\} \longrightarrow [V]_{S}$
is surjective?
The key here being the existence of a single knot $K$ for which the
indicated map is surjective, as every element of $[V]_{S}$ arises as the Seifert
form of some knot; cf. [AFMW23, page 20].
(4) In [AFMW23], the authors pose the genus-one version of this problem as
Problem 7.7, and claim a complete answer under the additional hypothesis
that Seifert surfaces be disjoint.
They find a necessary and sufficient
condition for a pair of $2\times2$ matrices to be Seifert forms for a pair of disjoint
Seifert surfaces of the same knot, and they give an explicit construction
realizing infinitely many pairs of disjoint Seifert surfaces with the same
boundary for any pair satisfying the condition.

References cited:
- [Tro73] H. F. Trotter. On S-equivalence of Seifert matrices. Invent. Math., 20:173–207, 1973. doi:10.1007/BF01394094.
- [Kaw96] Akio Kawauchi. A survey of knot theory. Birkhäuser Verlag, Basel, 1996. Translated and revised from the 1990 Japanese original by the author.
- [Kea04] C. Kearton. S-equivalence of knots. J. Knot Theory Ramifications, 13(6):709–717, 2004. doi:10.1142/S0218216504003408.
- [NS03] Swatee Naik and Theodore Stanford. A move on diagrams that generates S-equivalence of knots. J. Knot Theory Ramifications, 12(5):717–724, 2003. doi: 10.1142/S0218216503002639.
- [AFMW23] Menny Aka, Peter Feller, Alison Beth Miller, and Andreas Wieser. Seifert surfaces in the four-ball and composition of binary quadratic forms, 2023. arXiv:2311.17746.

title: Kirby Problem 1.7
statement:
Show that the sequence of absolute values of the coefficients of
the Alexander polynomial of a link are:
(a) concave $($ Fox’s trapezoidal conjecture $)$, or
(b) for an alternating link, log concave $($ Stoimenow’s strong Fox conjecture $)$.
(c) For a positive link, is the sequence of the coefficients of the Conway poly-
nomial strongly log concave?
background:
Source: Kirby's Problems in Low-Dimensional Topology notes. Original problem number: KP-1.7.

Literature notes:
(1) Let $K$ be a link with Alexander polynomial (up to a factor of $t^{r}$, $r \in \frac{1}{2}\mathbb{Z}$)

$$
\Delta_{K}(t)=\sum_{i=0}^{n} a_i t^i,
$$

with $a_{0}, a_{n} \neq 0$, and Conway polynomial

$$
\nabla_{K}(z)=z^{c(K)-1}\sum_{i=0}^{m} c_i z^{2i}
$$

defined by $\nabla_{K}(t - t^{-1}) = t^{-n}\Delta_{K}(t^{2})$, where $c(K)$ denotes the number
of components of $K$. Recall that $a_{i} = (-1)^{n}a_{n-i}$; that for a non-split
alternating link, $a_{i}a_{i+1} < 0$, $0 \leq i < n$; and that for a positive link,
$c_{i} > 0$, $0 \leq i \leq m$.
For the Strong Fox Conjecture (3) below, recall that a sequence of
positive numbers $(a_{i})_{0\leq i\leq n}$ is called log concave if $a_{i-1}a_{i+1} \leq a_i^{2}$
for all $i$ with $0 < i < n$. That is, the sequence $(\log(a_{i}))$ is concave. For the final
conjecture (4), recall that a sequence of positive numbers $(c_{i})_{0\leq i\leq m}$ is
called strongly log concave if $c_{i-1}c_{i+1} < c_i^{2}$ for all $i$ with $0 < i < m$.
(2) (Fox’s trapezoidal conjecture [Fox62, Problem 12]) Let $K$ be an alternating knot
with Alexander polynomial as above. Then

$$
|a_{0}| \leq |a_{1}| \leq \cdots \leq |a_{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}|
\geq |a_{\lfloor n/2\rfloor+1}| \geq \cdots \geq |a_{n}|.
$$

Moreover, if $|a_{i}| = |a_{i+1}|$ for some $i < n/2$, then

$$
|a_{i}| = |a_{i+1}| = \cdots = |a_{n-i}|.
$$

(1)
See for example [Mur85, AJK24] for some progress on Fox’s conjecture.
(3) (Strong Fox Conjecture) Let $K$ be an alternating link with Alexander
polynomial as above. Then the sequence of absolute values of the coeffi-
cients $(|a_{i}|)$ is log concave. The equality $a_{i-1}a_{i+1} = a_i^{2}$ for some $i < n/2$
holds only if $a_{i-1} = -a_{i} = a_{i+1}$. Moreover, the length of this ‘trapezoid
top’, i.e. the length of the longest string of equalities as in Equation (1) is
bounded above by the absolute value of the signature. Conjecture (3) first
appeared in [Sto05]. It is called the Strong Fox Conjecture in [Ban22].
Log-concavity is a ubiquitous phenomenon appearing in many fields of
mathematics, for example, [AHK17] and [Sta89].
The Strong Fox Conjecture was proved for 2-bridge knots by Ban-
field [Ban22] and for special alternating links by Hafner–Meszaros–Vidinas
[HMV24]. The conjecture, including the statement regarding equality,
was verified by Stoimenow [Sto16, Section 9.2] for alternating knots of
genus at most 4 and for certain plumbed links [Sto21, Theorem 5.1]
(4) Conjecture (Stoimenow): Let $K$ be a positive link with Conway poly-
nomial as above. Then the sequence of coefficients $(c_{i})$ is strongly log
concave.
Conjecture (4) was proved for special alternating links by Stoimenow
[Sto05, Theorem 1].

References cited:
- [Fox62] Ralph Fox. Some problems in knot theory. In M. K. Fort, Jr., editor, Topology of 3-manifolds and related topics (Proc. The Univ. of Georgia Institute, 1961). Prentice-Hall, Englewood Cliffs, N.J., 1962.
- [Mur85] Kunio Murasugi. On the Alexander polynomial of alternating algebraic knots. J. Austral. Math. Soc. Ser. A, 39(3):317–333, 1985.
- [AJK24] Soheil Azarpendar, András Juhász, and Tamás Kálmán. On Fox’s trapezoidal conjecture, 2024. arXiv:2406.08662.
- [Sto05] Alexander Stoimenow. Newton-like polynomials of links. Enseign. Math. (2), 51(3-4):211–230, 2005.
- [Ban22] Ian M. Banfield. Christoffel words and the strong Fox conjecture for two-bridge knots, 2022. arXiv:2212.04561.
- [AHK17] Karim Adiprasito, June Huh, and Eric Katz. Hodge theory of matroids. Notices Amer. Math. Soc., 64(1):26–30, 2017. doi:10.1090/noti1463.
- [Sta89] Richard P. Stanley. Log-concave and unimodal sequences in algebra, combinatorics, and geometry. In Graph theory and its applications: East and West (Jinan, 1986), volume 576 of Ann. New York Acad. Sci., pages 500–535. New York Acad. Sci., New York, 1989. doi:10.1111/j.1749-6632.1989.tb16434.x.
- [HMV24] Elena S. Hafner, Karola Mészáros, and Alexander Vidinas. Log-concavity of the Alexander polynomial. Int. Math. Res. Not. IMRN, 2024(13):10273–10284, 2024. doi:10.1093/imrn/rnae058.

- [Sto21] A. Stoimenow. Independence polynomials and Alexander-Conway polynomials of plumbing links. J. Combin. Theory Ser. A, 183:Paper No. 105487, 18, 2021. doi: 10.1016/j.jcta.2021.105487.

title: Kirby Problem 1.8
statement:
Which multi-variable Laurent polynomials arise as the multi-
variable Alexander polynomial of a link in the 3-sphere or, more generally, a ho-
mology 3-sphere?
background:
Source: Kirby's Problems in Low-Dimensional Topology notes. Original problem number: KP-1.8.

Literature notes:
(1) A link in a homology sphere $Y$ has a covering corresponding to the ho-
momorphism $\pi_{1}(Y \setminus L) \twoheadrightarrow\mathbb{Z}^{n}$ arising from the isomorphism $H_{1}(Y \setminus L) \cong$
$\mathbb{Z}^{n}$, where $n$ is the number of components of the link $L$.
The homol-
ogy of this covering gives rise to a multi-variable Alexander polynomial

$$
\Delta_{L}(t_{1},\dots,t_{n}) \in \mathbb{Z}[t_{1}^{\pm 1},\dots,t_{n}^{\pm 1}],
$$

well defined up to multiplication by units, which are all of the form
$\pm t_{1}^{\nu_{1}}\cdots t_{n}^{\nu_{n}}$.
(2) The problem has been solved for the single-variable Alexander polynomial
of knots. If $K$ is a knot in a homology sphere, then:

$$
\bullet \Delta_{K}(t) = \Delta_{K}(t^{-1})
$$

$\bullet \Delta_{K}(1) = 1$.
Moreover, any polynomial satisfying these two properties is realized by a
knot in the 3-sphere (or any homology sphere) [Sei35, Lev65, Rol90].
Torres [Tor53] found analogous (necessary but not sufficient–see [Hil81,
Pla86]) properties of the multi-variable Alexander polynomial of a link.
It is perhaps surprising that while there is no known characterization of
the Alexander polynomial of two-component links, Bailey found a charac-
terization [Bai77] (discussed in [Pla86]) of their Alexander modules. A
general reference for the ideas here is Hillman’s book [Hil12].
(3) The problem can be refined by focusing on specific families of links.
Question (i). Which polynomials arise for a given family of knots
or links?
Some partial results are known.
$\bullet$ Torus links. If $T_{p,q}$ is the $(p, q)-$ torus link, let $d = \gcd(p, q)$. Then

$$
\Delta_{Tp,q}(t_{1}, t_{2},..., t_{d}) = [(t_{1}t_{2}... t_{d})^{pq/d} - 1]^{d}[(t_{1}t_{2}... t_{d}) - 1]
$$

$$
[(t_{1}t_{2}... t_{d})^{p/d} - 1][(t_{1}t_{2}... t_{d})^{q/d} - 1].
$$

See [Rol90] for knots and [EN85, Theorem 12.1]; compare [Ore21,
Corollary 8.2] for links with $d > 1$.
$\bullet$ Two-bridge links. Many authors have found necessary (but still in-
sufficient) conditions on the Alexander polynomial of a 2-bridge knot
or link. Results of Koseleff and Pecker [KP15] subsume most earlier
results. Given a 2-variable polynomial, Hoste [Hos20], gives an al-
gorithm to decide if the polynomial is the Alexander polynomial of
a 2-component, 2-bridge link.
$\bullet$ Alternating links. The Alexander polynomials of alternating knots
have special properties [Cro59, Mur58], and their coefficients are
conjectured to have various concavity properties. See Problem 1.7
for an extensive discussion of these. It would be of interest to extend
such properties to the case of alternating links.
(4) Similarly, any 3-manifold with $H_{1}(X) \cong \mathbb{Z}^{n}$ has an associated multi-
variable Alexander polynomial $\Delta_{X} \in \mathbb{Z}[H_{1}(X)] \cong \mathbb{Z}[t_{1}^{\pm1},\ldots,t_{n}^{\pm1}]$.
Question (ii). Which Laurent polynomials arise as the multi-variable
Alexander polynomial of a 3-manifold?

title: Kirby Problem 1.9
statement:
If Dehn surgery on a knot $K$ gives a lens space, then $K$ is a
Berge knot.
background:
Source: Kirby's Problems in Low-Dimensional Topology notes. Original problem number: KP-1.9.

Literature notes:
(1) This appears as [Kir97, Problem 1.78]. Let $(\Sigma; H_{1}, H_{2})$ denote the genus-
two Heegaard splitting of $S^{3}$ (cf. Section 3.3). A knot $K \subset S^{3}$ is a Berge
knot if it lies on $\Sigma$ and there are properly embedded disks $D_{i} \subset H_{i}$
such that $|K \cap D_{i}| = 1$. These knots are also called doubly primitive;
see [Gor09, Section 3.2].
(2) The conjecture, often referred to as the Berge Conjecture, is known for
small order lens spaces [Gor09]. For example, if surgery on $K$ gives $L(p, q)$
with $|p| \leq 5$, then $K$ is the unknot or the trefoil [KMOS07]. In general,
if a lens space were to arise as surgery on a non-Berge knot, that lens
space must also arise as surgery on a Berge knot [Gre13b]. The putative
knot necessarily has the same knot Floer homology as that corresponding
Berge knot.
(3) From its description, any Berge knot is necessarily a tunnel number one
knot. The Berge conjecture has been verified for all tunnel number one
knots in the preprint [LMP25] and all non-hyperbolic knots [Mos71,
BL89].
(4) If surgery on a non-torus knot produces a lens space, then it must be an
integral surgery by the Cyclic Surgery Theorem [CGLS87]. The size of
the surgery coefficient is also heavily constrained. If $S^{3}_{p}(K) = L(p,q)$ for a
nontrivial, non-trefoil knot $K$, then
$2g(K)-1 \leq |p|-2\sqrt{4(|p|+1)/5}$ [Gre13b].
If $K$ is a counterexample to the Berge conjecture, then $|p| < 4g(K) - 1$
[Bak06].
(5) Using Heegaard Floer homology, it is also known that a knot with a lens
space surgery must be fibered and, after possibly mirroring, strongly quasi-
positive [Ni07, Hed10]. The knot Floer homology of the dual knot $\widetilde{K}$
in $L(p,q)$ has smallest possible knot Floer homology,

$$
\dim \widehat{\mathrm{HFK}}(\widetilde{K}) = \dim \widehat{\mathrm{HF}}(L(p,q))
$$

[Ras07, Hed11, Gre13b]. Such a knot is called Floer
simple, and one proposed strategy is to prove that Floer simple knots are
one-bridge with respect to the standard genus one Heegaard splitting of
$L(p, q)$ [BGH08], as Berge proved that such knots are necessarily doubly
primitive [Ber18].

- [Gor09] Cameron Gordon. Dehn surgery and 3-manifolds. In Low dimensional topology, volume 15 of IAS/Park City Math. Ser., pages 21–71. Amer. Math. Soc., Providence, RI, 2009.

- [Gre13b] Joshua Evan Greene. The lens space realization problem. Ann. of Math. (2), 177(2):449–511, 2013. doi:10.4007/annals.2013.177.2.3.
- [LMP25] Tao Li, Yoav Moriah, and Tali Pinsky. Tunnel number one knots satisfy the Berge conjecture. Geom. Topol., 29(6):3271–3343, 2025. doi:10.2140/gt.2025.29.3271.
- [Mos71] Louise Moser. Elementary surgery along a torus knot. Pacific J. Math., 38:737–745, 1971. http://projecteuclid.org/euclid.pjm/1102969920.

title: Kirby Problem 1.10
statement:
(Generalized Property R Conjecture). Let $L \subset S^{3}$ be an $n$-
component link such that 0-framed Dehn surgery on $L$ results in $\#^{n}(S^{1} \times S^{2})$. Is
there a sequence of handleslides converting $L$ into an $n$-component unlink?
background:
Source: Kirby's Problems in Low-Dimensional Topology notes. Original problem number: KP-1.10.

Literature notes:
(1) An $n$-component link $L \subset S^{3}$ whose 0-surgery is $\#^{n}(S^{1} \times S^{2})$ is called
an R-link. An R-link is said to have generalized property R if it can be
converted by handleslides to an unlink. (Note that all framings and linking
numbers are zero.)
Gabai proved [Gab87a] that the only 1-component R-link is the
unknot, solving the Property R Conjecture. The Generalized Property
R Conjecture (GPRC) posits that all R-links have generalized property
R [Kir97, Problem 1.82] and was studied in [GST10].
(2) There are two ways to weaken the GPRC that are of interest. Let $L \sqcup L'$
denote the split union of links $L$ and $L'$.
Conjecture (Stable GPRC). If $L$ is an R-link, then there is an
unlink $\operatorname{U}$ such that $L \sqcup \operatorname{U}$ can be converted by handleslides to an unlink.
Many potential counterexamples to the Stable GPRC are given in
[GST10, MZ22].
(3) A Hopf pair is a canceling 1-handle/2-handle pair, which can be repre-
sented in the Kirby calculus by a Hopf link with a dotted-circle component
and a 0-framed component [GS99, Section 5.4].
Conjecture (Weak GPRC). If $L$ is an R-link, then there is an un-
link $\operatorname{U}$ and a split union $H$ of Hopf pairs such that $L \sqcup \operatorname{U} \sqcup H$ can be
converted by handleslides to the split union $\operatorname{U}' \sqcup H'$ of an unlink and a
split union of Hopf pairs.
A sufficient condition for a 2-component link to satisfy the Weak
GPRC is given in [MZ22, Theorem 1.1].
(4) There are connections between these conjectures and other important
problems. Given an R-link $L$, one can construct a homotopy 4-ball $B_{L}$
by attaching 0-framed 2-handles to $S^{3} \times I$ along $L$ and capping off with
a 4-dimensional 1-handlebody. Turning this handle-decomposition upside
down gives a balanced presentation $P_{L}$ of the trivial group.
Any homotopy 4-sphere that can be built without 1-handles is $B_{L}\cup B^{4}$
for some R-link $L$. If an R-link L satisfies the Weak GPRC, then $B_{L}$ is
diffeomorphic to $B^{4}$. So, the Weak GPRC implies the Smooth Poincaré
Conjecture in dimension 4 for homotopy 4-spheres built without 1-handles.

The Andrews–Curtis Conjecture (ACC–see Problem 5.10) posits that
any balanced presentation of the trivial group can be converted to the
trivial presentation through balanced presentations. If the GPRC is true,
then so is the ACC. There is also a stable version of the ACC that is
implied by the Stable GPRC [GST10, MZ22].
If $L$ is an R-link, then $L$ bounds a collection of homotopy-ribbon disks
in the homotopy 4-ball $B_{L}$. Thus, such links provide potential counterex-
amples to the Slice-Ribbon Conjecture (Problem 1.50) but are ribbon if
they satisfy the Stable GPRC [AT16b]; see [MZ25, Proposition 5.2]. If
$K$ is a fibered, homotopy-ribbon knot, then the closed monodromy of $K$
admits an extension across a handlebody [CG83a]. Any such extension
gives rise to a link $L$ lying on the fiber of $K$ such that $L$ and $K \cup L$ are
both R-links, and $K \cup L$ is ribbon if $L$ (equivalently, $K \cup L$) satisfies the
Stable GPRC.

title: Kirby Problem 1.11
statement:
(Cabling conjecture). Let $K \subset S^{3}$ be a knot and $r \in \mathbb{Q}$. If
$r$-framed Dehn surgery on $K$ is not prime, then $K$ is a nontrivial cable of a knot
$J \subset S^{3}$ and $r$ is the slope of the cabling annulus.
background:
Source: Kirby's Problems in Low-Dimensional Topology notes. Original problem number: KP-1.11.

Literature notes:
(1) The conjecture is due to González-Acuña and Short [GAnS86]. If $K =$
$J_{p,q}$ is a cable knot, then there is an annulus in $S^{3}\setminus\nu(K)$ that has boundary
equal to two parallel curves of slope $pq$. This annulus is called the cabling
annulus and $pq$ is referred to as the slope of the cabling annulus. Using a
cut and paste argument, one can show that

$$
S^{3}_{pq}(K)=S^{3}_{q/p}(J)\#S^{3}_{p/q}(\operatorname{U}),
$$

where $\operatorname{U}$ is the unknot. Therefore, if $p \neq 1$, then $S^{3}_{pq}(K)$ is not prime.
(2) Many special cases of the conjecture are known.
Gordon and Luecke
[GL87] prove that if $r$ is a reducible slope, then $r$ is an integer and the
surgery contains a lens space summand.
The conjecture is known for
satellite knots [Sch90], strongly invertible knots [EMn92], alternating
knots [MT92] and symmetric knots [LZ94, HS98, HM97b].
(3) Greene [Gre15] has shown that if $r$-framed surgery on $K$ gives a connected
sum of nontrivial lens spaces, then $K$ is a $(p, q)$-cable of either the unknot
or a torus knot and that $r = pq$.
(4) Dunfield [Dun20] observed that a similar conjecture may hold for knots
in $S^{1} \times S^{2}$. He conjectures that there are no hyperbolic knots in $S^{1} \times S^{2}$
that have non-prime Dehn surgery.
(5) A weaker version of the cabling conjecture is the two summands conjecture,
which says that if $S^{3}_{r}(K)$ is non-prime, then it cannot have more than two
prime summands.
Note that it follows from work of Howie [How02],
Sayari [Say09] and Valdez-Sánchez [VS99] that $S^{3}_{r}(K)$ can never contain
more than three irreducible summands.

- [LZ94] E. Luft and X. Zhang. Symmetric knots and the cabling conjecture. Math. Ann., 298(3):489–496, 1994. doi:10.1007/BF01459747.
- [HS98] Chuichiro Hayashi and Koya Shimokawa. Symmetric knots satisfy the cabling conjecture. Math. Proc. Cambridge Philos. Soc., 123(3):501–529, 1998. doi:10.1017/S0305004197002399.
- [HM97b] Chuichiro Hayashi and Kimihiko Motegi. Dehn surgery on knots in solid tori creating essential annuli. Trans. Amer. Math. Soc., 349(12):4897–4930, 1997. doi: 10.1090/S0002-9947-97-01723-6.

title: Kirby Problem 1.12
statement:
This problem presents several variations on the Cosmetic
Surgery Conjecture, discussed in turn below.
(a) $($ Cosmetic Surgery Conjecture $)$ Two surgeries along inequivalent slopes are
never purely cosmetic.
(b) $($ Oriented knot complement conjecture $)$ If $K_{1}$ and $K_{2}$ are knots in a closed,
oriented 3-manifold $N$ whose complements are homeomorphic via an orientation-
preserving homeomorphism, then there exists a homeomorphism of $N$ tak-
ing $K_{1}$ to $K_{2}$.
(c) Let $K \subset S^{3}$ be a nontrivial knot, then $K$ admits no purely cosmetic surg-
eries.
(d) If $K \subset S^{3}$ is not the torus knot $T_{2g+1,2}$, then $K$ admits no chirally cos-
metic surgeries with inequivalent slopes.
background:
Source: Kirby's Problems in Low-Dimensional Topology notes. Original problem number: KP-1.12.

Literature notes:
(1) This is an update to [Kir97, Problem 1.81], contributed by S. Bleiler.
Parts (a) and (b) appear as Conjectures 6.1 and 6.2 of [Gor91] respec-
tively.
(2) For the rest of this problem, $M$ denotes an irreducible oriented 3-manifold
with torus boundary that is not the solid torus. Two fillings along dis-
tinct slopes $r_{1}$ and $r_{2}$ are called purely cosmetic if there is an orientation-
preserving homeomorphism between $M(r_{1})$ and $M(r_{2})$, and chirally cos-
metic if there is an orientation-reversing homeomorphism between these
fillings. (The terminology would be purely or chirally cosmetic surgery if
$M$ is a knot complement.) Two slopes are said to be equivalent if there
exists a homeomorphism (either preserving or reversing the orientation)
of $M$ taking one slope to the other.
(3) When [Kir97, Problem 1.81] was written, several examples of chirally cos-
metic surgeries on inequivalent slopes were known. More recently, Ichihara
and Jong [IJ18], with help from Masai, found a hyperbolic one-cusped
manifold admitting a pair of chirally cosmetic surgeries with inequivalent
slopes, such that the resulting manifold is also hyperbolic. This gives a
counterexample to [Kir97, Problem 1.81B].
Dunfield found that the manifold $o9_{39009}$ from Burton’s census [Bur14]
had Dehn fillings $(-1, 3)$ and $(-3, 2)$, which are isometric by an orienta-
tion reversing isometry, but where the core curves of the Dehn fillings are
geodesics of different lengths. This provides a counterexample to [Kir97,
Problem 1.81C].
(4) There are different versions of the Cosmetic Surgery Conjecture (a) in
the literature. A stronger version of the conjecture, which is still open,
asserts that if there exist purely cosmetic surgeries on $M$, then there is
an orientation-preserving homeomorphism of $M$ sending one slope to the
other. This version would imply that $M$ does not admit purely cosmetic
surgeries if $M$ is hyperbolic. If there exist two slopes that are related
by an orientation-reversing homeomorphism, and the surgeries on these
two slopes are amphichiral, then this would be a counterexample to the
stronger version of the conjecture, but not to the version of the conjecture
stated in this problem.

(5) Lackenby [Lac97] proved that, for “most” surgeries on null-homotopic
knots in manifolds with $b_{1} > 0$, the original manifold, the knot, and the
slope are determined by the resulting manifold from the surgery.
When $M$ is hyperbolic, there is an explicit constant $C = C(M)$,
satisfying that if the normalized lengths of two inequivalent slopes $r_{1}, r_{2}$
are both greater than $C$, then this pair is not (purely or chirally) cosmetic
[FPS22, FPS25].
Using code that is publicly available on GitHub [FPS24], Conjec-
ture (a) has been verified for all the 59,107 one-cusped manifolds in the
SnapPy census. This code can also be used to investigate Conjecture (c)
above for knots in $S^{3}$.
(6) If $M$ is the irreducible complement of a null-homologous knot in a 3-
manifold of the form $Z\#S^{1} \times S^{2}$, then the slopes of any pair of cosmetic
surgeries must be $\{\pm r\}$ [Ni13]. A similar result holds when $M$ is the
complement of a knot in a closed 3-manifold whose Thurston norm is
strictly smaller than that of $M$ [Ni11].
(7) The Cosmetic Surgery Conjecture (a) is equivalent to the Oriented Knot
Complement Conjecture (b), which is an analogue of the Knot Comple-
ment Theorem [GL89].
In [Kir97, Problem 1.81D], the homeomorphism of $N$ is required to be
orientation-preserving. Since our definition of equivalent slopes does not
require the homeomorphism to preserve orientation, we do not require
the homeomorphism of $N$ to be orientation-preserving in the problem
statement here.
Gordon and Luecke [GL89] proved Conjecture (b) for $N = S^{3}$ and
$S^{1} \times S^{2}$. It also holds for certain L-spaces [Gai18, Rav22]. Cremaschi–
Yarmola proved it for knots in an orientable circle bundle over a genus
$g \geq 2$ surface [CY24].
(8) When $M$ is the complement of a knot $K \subset S^{3}$, the Cosmetic Surgery Con-
jecture is equivalent to saying that if $K$ admits purely cosmetic surgeries
with slopes $r_{1}, r_{2}$ then $K$ is amphichiral and $r_{1} = -r_{2}$. The conclusion
that $r_{1} = -r_{2}$ was proved in [NW15]. Conjecture (c) is stronger than
this special case of Conjecture (a), because there may exist an amphichi-
ral knot in $S^{3}$ such that a nonzero surgery on it is also amphichiral. This
would be a counterexample to Conjecture (c), but not to Conjecture (a).
Futer–Purcell–Schleimer [FPS25] verified Conjecture (c) for knots
with up to 19 crossings.
Hanselman [Han23] proved that if $K$ admits a pair of purely cosmetic
surgeries, then the pair of slopes is either $\{\pm2\}$ or $\{\pm 1/q\}$ for an integer $q$
that is explicitly determined from the knot Floer homology of $K$, and the
former case happens only when $g(K) = 2$. Daemi-Lidman-Miller Eismeier
[DLME24] subsequently announced that they have eliminated the case
of $\{\pm 1/q\}$. As a result, any pair of purely cosmetic slopes must be $\{\pm2\}$,
and the knot has genus 2 and trivial Alexander polynomial.
(9) Although [Kir97, Problem 1.81 (B)] has been disproved, no such examples
have been found for knots in $S^{3}$. This is the motivation for Conjecture
(d).

(10) There are many known constraints on chirally cosmetic surgeries; see
[IIS22] for an overview. Ozsváth and Szabó [OS11] proved that if $K$
admits a pair of (purely or chirally) cosmetic surgeries with slopes $r_{1}, r_{2}$,
then either $r_{1}, r_{2}$ have opposite signs or the surgery is an L-space. Futer–
Purcell–Schleimer [FPS25] have shown that Conjecture (d) holds for all
hyperbolic knots with up to 15 crossings.
(11) Somewhat weaker versions of Conjecture (b), in which the knots are re-
quired to be null-homotopic, may be found in [Kir97, Problem 1.80 (B)
and (C)]. Using standard arguments in Heegaard Floer homology, one can
verify the conjecture in [Kir97, Problem 1.80(C)] when $Y$ is an L-space.
See, for example, [Gai18, Rav22].
(12) A list of problems about (mostly chirally) cosmetic surgeries on knots in
$S^{3}$ can be found in [Ito22].

title: Kirby Problem 1.13
statement:
Let $K$ be a null-homotopic knot in a 3-manifold $Y$ , and let
$Y_{0}(K)$ be the manifold obtained by 0-surgery on $K$.
(a) Conjecture: Let $F$ be a Seifert surface for $K$, and let $\widetilde{F} \subset Y_{0}(K)$ be the
closed surface obtained by capping off $\partial F$ with a disk. If $Y_{0}(K)$ is a surface
bundle over $S^{1}$ with fiber in the homology class $[\widetilde{F}]$, then $K$ is a fibered
knot with fiber in the homology class $[F]$.
(b) Conjecture: If $F$ is taut in the exterior of $K$ in $Y$ , then $\widetilde{F}$ is also taut in
$Y_{0}(K)$.
background:
Source: Kirby's Problems in Low-Dimensional Topology notes. Original problem number: KP-1.13.

Literature notes:
(1) Conjecture (a) is an updating of [Kir97, Problem 1.80C], and is due to
Boileau. Conjecture (b) is due to Gabai.
(2) Let $M$ be a compact, oriented, connected 3-manifold, let $F \subset M$ be a
properly embedded connected surface. We say that $F$ is taut if it realizes
the Thurston norm in the homology class $[F] \neq 0 \in H_{2}(M, \partial M),$ or if $F$
is a sphere.
(3) In the original version of Conjecture (a), the surgery slope can be any
rational number, and there is no restriction on the homology class of the
fiber. However, there are simple counterexamples to the original question
[Ni09]. More precisely, there exist nonfibered null-homotopic knots such
that every integral surgery on the knot yields a manifold that fibers over
$S^{1}$.
(4) It is known that $Y_{0}(K)$ does not contain a homologically essential 2-sphere
if $Y \setminus K$ does not contain such 2-spheres and $K$ is nontrivial [Gab87a,
Lac97, HL22, Ni23b].
Conjecture (a) and Conjecture (b) are known for knots in $S^{3}$ [Gab87b],
L-spaces [Ni07, AN09], and certain reducible manifolds [Gab87b, Ni13].
They are also known for knots obtained from the unknot by crossing
changes of the same sign [Ni24].

title: Kirby Problem 1.14
statement:
For which nonzero $r \in \mathbb{Q}$ is it true that for every nontrivial
knot $K \subset S^{3}$ there is a homomorphism

$$
\pi_{1}(S^{3}_{r}(K)) \to \operatorname{SU}(2)
$$

with nonabelian image?
background:
Source: Kirby's Problems in Low-Dimensional Topology notes. Original problem number: KP-1.14.

Literature notes:
(1) If this statement is true for some $r \in \mathbb{Q}$, then it’s true for $-r$; hence,
we assume $r > 0$. Kronheimer–Mrowka proved [KM04] that there is a
homomorphism with nonabelian image for all $r \in (0, 2]$. Work of Baldwin–
Sivek [BS23a] together with announced results of Baldwin–Li–Sivek–Ye
[BLSY24], and Farber–Reinoso–Wang [FRW24] proves the same for all
$r \in (2, 5)$ with prime power numerators.
(2) Let $r = p/q > 0$ with $p$ and $q$ relatively prime, and assume that $\Delta_{K}(\zeta^{2}) \neq$
0 for any $p$th root of unity $\zeta$. Then it is further known [BS23a] that if
$\pi_{1}(S^{3}_{r}(K))$ only admits abelian $\operatorname{SU}(2)$-representations, then $K$ is fibered,
strongly quasipositive, and $r \geq 2g(K) - 1.$
(3) Note that for most $r \in \mathbb{Z}$, there is a torus knot whose $r$–surgery is $\operatorname{SU}(2)$-
abelian. Problem 3.51 deals with a related problem about the characteri-
zation of rational homology spheres whose fundamental groups have only
Abelian $\operatorname{SU}(2)$ representations.

References cited:

- [BS23a] John A. Baldwin and Steven Sivek. Instantons and L-space surgeries. J. Eur. Math. Soc. (JEMS), 25(10):4033–4122, 2023. doi:10.4171/jems/1280.
- [BLSY24] John A. Baldwin, Zhenkun Li, Steven Sivek, and Fan Ye. Small Dehn surgery and $\mathrm{SU}(2)$. Geom. Topol., 28(4):1891–1922, 2024. doi:10.2140/gt.2024.28.1891.
- [FRW24] Ethan Farber, Braeden Reinoso, and Luya Wang. Fixed-point-free pseudo-Anosov homeomorphisms, knot Floer homology and the cinquefoil, 2024. doi:10.2140/gt.2024.28.4337.

title: Kirby Problem 1.15
statement:
(a) Are there integral homology spheres with arbitrarily large (integral) Dehn
surgery number? Are there irreducible examples? Does the connected sum
of $n$ nontrivial homology spheres have Dehn surgery number at least $n$?
(b) Given a 3-manifold $Y$ with a smooth orientation-preserving $\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}$ sym-
metry $\varphi$, Sakuma [Sak01] (generalizing [PS01]) proved that $Y$ admits a
surgery description compatible with the symmetry. Define the equivariant
(integral) Dehn surgery number of $(Y, \varphi)$ as the minimal number of con-
nected components of any such link. Do there exist $(Y, \varphi)$ whose equivari-
ant (integral) Dehn surgery number is arbitrarily larger than the (integral)
Dehn surgery number?
(c) Following the remarks below, we can consider the following specific case:
Does there exist a manifold with a 2-fold symmetry whose equivariant
(integral) Dehn surgery number is larger than the (integral) Dehn surgery
number?
background:
Source: Kirby's Problems in Low-Dimensional Topology notes. Original problem number: KP-1.15.

Literature notes:
(1) Any oriented connected closed 3-manifold $Y$ is obtained by (integral) Dehn
surgery on a link in the 3-sphere, and the minimal number of connected
components of any such link is called the (integral) Dehn surgery number
of $Y$ .

(2) Part (a) is a version of Problem 3.102 from [Kir97], asked by Auckly. The
integral Dehn surgery case is interesting to consider from the perspective
of 4-manifolds bounded by $Y$ , as it is related to the minimum number of
handles needed to describe the 4-manifold.
There are many examples of integral homology spheres with Dehn
surgery number at least 2, the earliest due to [GL87], hyperbolic examples
due to [Auc97], and Seifert fibered examples due to [HKL16b].
(3) Regarding part (b), it should be possible to show that the equivari-
ant surgery number does not agree with the surgery number. Consider
$Y=S^{3}_{2}(4_{1})$, which is a Seifert fibered space (see, for example, [BW01,
Theorem 1.1(4))]). Since $Y$ is Seifert fibered, it has a $\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}$ action, for
all $n$, while $4_{1}$ does not. It remains to be shown that there is no other
knot $K$ for which some $2/q$-surgery is $Y$ ; a plausible approach is to use
the mapping cone formula for Heegaard Floer homology.
Finding the examples as in part (b) for which the equivariant surgery
number is arbitrarily larger than the Dehn surgery number is, as in part
(a), more challenging.
(4) Lastly, we point out that this problem is closely related to Problem 3.39.

- [HKL16b] Jennifer Hom, Çağrı Karakurt, and Tye Lidman. Surgery obstructions and Heegaard Floer homology. Geom. Topol., 20(4):2219–2251, 2016. doi:10.2140/gt.2016.20.2219.

title: Kirby Problem 1.16
statement:
(a) Given a knot $K \subset S^{3}$ determine all knots $K' \subset S^{3}$ for which the branched
double covers of $S^{3}$ along $K$ and $K'$ are homeomorphic.
(b) Find a set of moves on links in $S^{3}$ so that two links are related by these
moves if and only if they have the same branched double cover.
background:
Source: Kirby's Problems in Low-Dimensional Topology notes. Original problem number: KP-1.16.

Literature notes:
(1) These are Problems 3.25 and 1.22 in [Kir97], respectively.
See Prob-
lem 1.17 for a related problem about alternating links. Let $\Sigma(K)$ denote
the branched double cover of $S^{3}$ along $K$.
(2) It follows from the Orbifold Geometrization Theorem that there are finitely
many $K'$ with $\Sigma(K') \cong \Sigma(K)$. See [Pao05] for a discussion.
(3) Mecchia and Zimmerman showed that if $\Sigma(K)$ is hyperbolic, then there are
at most eight other $K'$ with $\Sigma(K') \cong \Sigma(K)$ [MZ04]. Kawauchi showed
that this bound is sharp, exhibiting infinitely many 9-tuples of distinct hy-
perbolic knots in $S^{3}$ with homeomorphic branched double covers [Kaw06].
However, his construction is very non-explicit, and it would be interest-
ing to have some explicit constructions. Mecchia further described how
hyperbolic knots with the same double branched cover can be understood
in terms of isometries of the cover [Mec01]
(4) If $K$ is a 2-bridge knot and $\Sigma(K') \cong \Sigma(K)$ then $K' = K [\mathrm{HR}85$].
(5) If $K$ and $K'$ are related by Conway mutation then $\Sigma(K') \cong \Sigma(K)$. There
are also non-mutant knots with the same branched double covers, includ-
ing $T(3, 7)$ and $P(-2, 3, 7).$ In this example, the Khovanov homologies
have the same total rank, but Watson [Wat10] gives non-mutant knots

with homeomorphic branched double covers the total rank of whose Kho-
vanov homologies differ, showing that the rank of Khovanov homology is
not an invariant of branched double covers. See also [Pao01].
(6) Higher order cyclic branched covers are generally much better knot in-
variants. For example, work of Zimmerman [Zim98] shows that if $n \geq 3$
and $K \subset S^{3}$ is hyperbolic, then the $n$-fold cyclic branched cover of $K$
distinguishes $K$ from other knots so long as $K$ does not admit peri-
odic symmetries of order $n$, and the latter condition is satisfied whenever
$n > 2g(K) + 1$. See [Pao05] for further discussion.
(7) Extending work of Montesinos [Mon85], Piergallini constructed a com-
plete set of moves relating links with the same simple, irregular 3-fold
branched covers [Pie91].

- [MZ04] Mattia Mecchia and Bruno Zimmermann. The number of knots and links with the same 2-fold branched covering. Q. J. Math., 55(1):69–76, 2004. doi:10.1093/qjmath/55.1.69.

- [HR85] Craig Hodgson and J. H. Rubinstein. Involutions and isotopies of lens spaces. In Knot theory and manifolds (Vancouver, B.C., 1983), volume 1144 of Lecture Notes in Math., pages 60–96. Springer, Berlin, 1985. doi:10.1007/BFb0075012.

title: Kirby Problem 1.17
statement:
Can an alternating link and a non-alternating link have home-
omorphic branched double covers?
background:
Source: Kirby's Problems in Low-Dimensional Topology notes. Original problem number: KP-1.17.

Literature notes:
(1) The answer is conjectured to be no in [Gre13a, Conjecture 1.4] since
Greene shows that two alternating links have homeomorphic branched
double covers if and only if they are Conway mutants. Note that Viro
proved that mutant links have homeomorphic branched double-covers
[Vir76, Theorem 1], and Menasco proved that mutation preserves the
property of being alternating [Men84, Proof of Theorem 3(b)].
(2) The problem is related to Problems 1.22 and 3.25 of [Kir97] which ask
for a kind of classification of pairs of knots with homeomorphic branched
double covers.
(3) If a Seifert-fibered space is the branched double-cover of a pair of distinct
links, then the pair consists of either a non-alternating torus link and
a non-alternating Montesinos link, or else two mutant Montesinos links
[MR02, Introduction].
(4) Dunfield investigated knots with at most 16 crossings whose branched
double-covers are hyperbolic and of small enough volume to appear in the
Hodgson-Weeks census of closed hyperbolic 3-manifolds. He reports 3765
non-alternating knots with such branched covers but only 178 alternating
knots, and no manifold occurs as the branched double-cover of both kinds
of knots (private correspondence from 2013).
(5) While there exist many constructions of pairs of non-mutant links with
homeomorphic branched double-covers, these constructions typically ap-
pear to produce non-alternating examples (cf. [MW86, MZ04]).

title: Kirby Problem 1.18
statement:
(a) $($ Meridional Rank Conjecture $)$ Is the meridional $\operatorname{rank} \mu(L)$ of every link
$L$ equal to its bridge number $b(L)$?
(b) Given two knots $K_{1}, K_{2} \subset S^{3}$ such that $\pi_{1}(S^{3}\setminus K_{1})$ and $\pi_{1}(S^{3}\setminus K_{2})$ have
the same finite quotients, does $\mu(K_{1}) = \mu(K_{2})$? In particular, is it possible
to explicitly detect the meridional $\operatorname{rank} \mu(K)$ of a knot $K \subset S^{3}$ from the
finite quotients of $\pi_{1}(S^{3}\setminus K)$?
(c) Given two links $L_{1}, L_{2} \subset S^{3}$, if there exists a surjective homomorphism
$\pi_{1}(S^{3}\setminus L_{1}) \twoheadrightarrow\pi_{1}(S^{3}\setminus L_{2})$ that sends the meridians of $L_{1}$ to the meridians
of $L_{2}$, do the bridge numbers satisfy $b(L_{1}) \geq b(L_{2})$?
(d) Given two knots $K_{1}, K_{2} \subset S^{3}$, if there exists a surjective homomorphism
$\pi_{1}(S^{3}\setminus K_{1}) \twoheadrightarrow\pi_{1}(S^{3}\setminus K_{2})$ (which may not send meridians to meridians):
(i) Do the meridional ranks satisfy $\mu(K_{1}) \geq \mu(K_{2})$?
(ii) Do the bridge numbers satisfy $b(K_{1}) \geq b(K_{2})$?
(e) Let $K \subset S^{3}$ be a hyperbolic knot. Is every subgroup of $\pi_{1}(S^{3}\setminus K)$ generated
by at most $b(K) - 1$ meridians free? See [BJW18].
background:
Source: Kirby's Problems in Low-Dimensional Topology notes. Original problem number: KP-1.18.

Literature notes:
(1) Problem 1.11 of [Kir97] poses Question (a) for knots, and was proposed
by Cappell and Shaneson.
(2) The meridional $\operatorname{rank} \mu(L)$ of a link $L$ is the minimal number of merid-
ians needed to generate the fundamental group of its complement. It is
bounded above by the bridge number $b(L)$.
(3) Question (b) has a negative answer for links: let $W_{n}$ denote the result
of applying $|n| \geq 2$ twists to the Whitehead link $W_{0}$. Then $W_{n}$ and $W_{0}$
have homeomorphic exteriors, but $\mu(W_{0}) = b(W_{0}) = 2$, while $\mu(W_{n}) =$
$b(W_{n}) = 3$.
Note that the homeomorphism between the exterior of $W_{n}$ and $W_{0}$ dis-
cussed above does not send meridians to meridians. Under the meridian-
preserving hypothesis, the epimorphism of groups in Question (c) implies
$\mu(L_{1}) \geq \mu(L_{2})$, so a negative answer to Question (c) implies a negative
answer to the Meridional Rank Conjecture.
(4) In the case of knots, Question (d) represents a strengthening of Question
(c).
(5) Different answers to the two items under Question (d) would imply a nega-
tive answer to the Meridional Rank Conjecture. Note that there are many
epimorphisms between knot groups that are not meridian-preserving [GAn75].
For closed orientable manifolds, the answer to the analogous question with
respect to the Heegaard genus is negative if one does not assume the epi-
morphism to be induced by a non-zero degree map (see [BF18]). The
non-zero degree condition, in the knot complement case, implies that the
epimorphism is meridian preserving.
(6) In Question 4 the bridge number is defined using bridge trisections (see [MZ17a,
JMMZ22] and [AAD $^{+}23$, Question 6.1]; cf. Problem 4.111) or, equiva-
lently, using Morse position.
By [JP25], the meridional rank of 2-spheres in $S^{4}$ can collapse un-
der connected sum; therefore, either additivity of bridge number or the
equality of bridge number and meridional rank (or both) fails for 2-knots.
(7) Problem 4.117 describes a four-dimensional analog of the Meridional Rank
Conjecture.

References cited:
- [BJW18] Michel Boileau, Yeonhee Jang, and Richard Weidmann. Meridional rank and bridge number for a class of links. Pacific J. Math., 292(1):61–80, 2018. doi:10.2140/pjm.2018.292.61.
- [Kir97] R.C. Kirby. Problems in low–dimensional topology. In W. Kazez, editor, Geometric Topology. American Math. Soc./International Press, Providence, 1997.
- [GAn75] F. González-Acuña. Homomorphs of knot groups. Ann. of Math. (2), 102(2):373– 377, 1975. doi:10.2307/1971036.
- [BF18] Michel Boileau and Stefan Friedl. Epimorphisms of 3-manifold groups. Q. J. Math., 69(3):931–942, 2018. doi:10.1093/qmath/hay007.
- [MZ17a] Jeffrey Meier and Alexander Zupan. Bridge trisections of knotted surfaces in $S^{4}$. Trans. Amer. Math. Soc., 369(10):7343–7386, 2017. doi:10.1090/tran/6934.
- [JMMZ22] Jason Joseph, Jeffrey Meier, Maggie Miller, and Alexander Zupan. Bridge trisections and classical knotted surface theory. Pacific J. Math., 319(2):343–369, 2022. doi:10.2140/pjm.2022.319.343.

title: Kirby Problem 1.19
statement:
Let $Y = Y_{1}\#Y_{2}$ be a connected sum of 3-manifolds with $Y_{i} \neq$
$S^{3}$, for $i = 1, 2$. Let $\Phi: Y \to Y$ be a Dehn twist around the connected sum separating
2-sphere, and assume $Y_{1}$ and $Y_{2}$ are such that $\Phi$ is not isotopic to the identity. Does
there exist a knot $K \subseteq Y$ such that $K$ and $\Phi(K)$ are not ambiently isotopic?
background:
Source: Kirby's Problems in Low-Dimensional Topology notes. Original problem number: KP-1.19.

Literature notes:
Aceto-Bregman-Davis-Park-Ray [ABD $^{+}20$] studied the analogous
question for knots in prime 3-manifolds. They showed that the Gluck twist on $S^{1} \times$
$S^{2}$ (see Section 4.1 for the definition) can be detected by a knot that is equivalent
but not isotopic to its image under the Gluck twist. They also showed that for
irreducible 3-manifolds, diffeomorphisms that preserve free homotopy classes of
loops are isotopic to the identity. Hence the key remaining question is whether
Dehn twists around connected sum spheres can be detected by knots that are
equivalent but not isotopic.

References cited:
- [ABD+20] Paolo Aceto, Corey Bregman, Christopher W. Davis, JungHwan Park, and Arunima Ray. Isotopy and equivalence of knots in 3-manifolds, 2020. arXiv:2007.05796.

title: Kirby Problem 1.20
statement:
(a) Are there any null-homologous Floer minimal knots with irreducible com-
plements other than the Borromean knots $B_{g}, g \geq 0$, in any 3-manifolds?
It is reasonable to make the following more concrete conjectures.
(b) Conjecture (Ni): If $b_{1}(Y) < 2$, then the only null-homologous Floer mini-
mal knot in $Y$ is the unknot.
(c) Conjecture (Ni): If the Thurston norm of $Y$ is not identically zero, then $Y$
does not contain any null-homologous Floer minimal knot with irreducible
complement.
(d) Conjecture (Hedden, Rasmussen): The only Floer minimal knots in lens
spaces are simple knots.
background:
Source: Kirby's Problems in Low-Dimensional Topology notes. Original problem number: KP-1.20.

Literature notes:
(1) Let $Y$ be a closed, oriented, connected 3-manifold, and let $K \subset Y$ be a
rationally null-homologous knot. It is known that

$$
\operatorname{rank}\widehat{\mathrm{HFK}}(Y,K) \geq \operatorname{rank}\widehat{\mathrm{HF}}(Y).
$$

We say $K$ is Floer minimal if equality in the above inequality holds.
Clearly, unknots are Floer minimal. Moreover, the Borromean knot [OS04c,
Figure 16]$B_{g} \subset \#^{2g}(S^{1}\times S^{2})$ is Floer minimal. If the $p$-surgery on a knot
$L \subset S^{3}$ is an L-space and $p \geq 2g(L)$, then the dual knot in the L-space is
Floer minimal [Hed11, Ras07].
It is known that the only null-homologous Floer minimal knot in $Y$
is the unknot, when $Y$ is an L-space [NW14], and when $Y$ fibers over $S^{1}$
with fiber of genus $> 1$ [Ni14].
(2) When $Y$ is the lens space $L(p, q)$, there is a standard genus-1 Heegaard
diagram with $p$ intersection points. Any two base points $z, w$ will specify a
Floer minimal knot. Such knots are called simple.
Hedden [Hed11] and
Rasmussen [Ras07] proved that Conjecture (d) would imply the Berge
Conjecture (Problem 1.9 and [Kir97, Problem 1.78]).

References cited:
- [OS04c] Peter Ozsváth and Zoltán Szabó. Holomorphic disks and knot invariants. Adv. Math., 186(1):58–116, 2004. doi:10.1016/j.aim.2003.05.001.
- [Hed11] Matthew Hedden. On Floer homology and the Berge conjecture on knots admitting lens space surgeries. Trans. Amer. Math. Soc., 363(2):949–968, 2011. doi:10.1090/S0002-9947-2010-05117-7.
- [Ras07] Jacob Rasmussen. Lens space surgeries and L-space homology spheres, 2007. arXiv: 0710.2531.
- [NW14] Yi Ni and Zhongtao Wu. Heegaard Floer correction terms and rational genus bounds. Adv. Math., 267:360–380, 2014. doi:10.1016/j.aim.2014.09.006.
- [Ni14] Yi Ni. Some applications of Gabai’s internal hierarchy. Adv. Math., 250:467–495, 2014. doi:10.1016/j.aim.2013.10.001.
- [Kir97] R.C. Kirby. Problems in low–dimensional topology. In W. Kazez, editor, Geometric Topology. American Math. Soc./International Press, Providence, 1997.

title: Kirby Problem 1.21
statement:
(a) For a given positive integer $g$, are there only finitely many L-space knots
of genus $g$?
A related but more general question is:
(b) Question (Hedden): For which knots $L \subset S^{3}$ are there only finitely many
knots $K \subset S^{3}$ with
$\widehat{\mathrm{HFK}}(S^{3},K) \cong \widehat{\mathrm{HFK}}(S^{3},L)$?

(c) In some special cases, one expects stronger results saying that a class of
knots is characterized by its knot Floer homology. We state 3 conjectures,
ordered by their strength.
(i) For a knot $K \subset S^{3}$, if
$\widehat{\mathrm{HFK}}(S^{3},K) \cong \widehat{\mathrm{HFK}}(S^{3},T_{2g+1,2})$, then
$K = T_{2g+1,2}$.
(ii) For a knot $K \subset S^{3}$, if
$\widehat{\mathrm{HFK}}(S^{3},K) \cong \widehat{\mathrm{HFK}}(S^{3},T_{p,q})$, then $K$ is an
iterated torus knot.
(iii) Conjecture (Ni): For an L-space knot $K \subset S^{3}$, if all roots of $\Delta_{K}(t)$
lie on the unit circle, then $K$ is an iterated torus knot.
background:
Source: Kirby's Problems in Low-Dimensional Topology notes. Original problem number: KP-1.21.

Literature notes:
(1) A knot $K \subset S^{3}$ is called an L-space knot if there exists a positive integer
$p$ such that $S^{3}_{p}(K)$, the $p$-surgery on $K$ is an L-space (see Problem 3.48).
(2) The answer to Question (a) is “yes” when $g \leq 2$ [Ghi08, FRW24].
If $K$ is an L-space knot, then $K$ is fibered and strongly quasipositive
[Ni07, Hed10],

$$
\widehat{\mathrm{HFK}}(S^{3},K,g(K)-1) \cong \mathbb{Z}_{(-1)}, \tag{2}
$$

where $\mathbb{Z}_{(-1)}$ means a copy of $\mathbb{Z}$ supported in the Maslov grading $-1$
[OS05b]. (The condition (2) implies that the monodromy of the fibra-
tion is freely isotopic to a diffeomorphism without fixed point [BHS25,
Ni23a, GS22a].) However, these properties are not enough to guaran-
tee the finiteness. For each $g \geq 2$, Misev [Mis21] constructed infinitely
many strongly quasipositive fibered knots with the same Seifert form as
the torus knot $T_{2g+1,2}$. By taking cables of these knots, the condition (2)
can also be satisfied.
(3) The finiteness in Question (b) does not hold for all knots $L$: see [HW18,
Acknowledgements], [MS15], and [Wan22, Theorem 1.3]. In particular,
Hedden and Watson showed that, given any non-trivial band sum of two
unknots, altering the number of twists in the band gives rise to an infinite
family of distinct knots with the same knot Floer homology [HW18,
Theorem 1].
(4) Conjecture (i) in part (c) is known for $g = 1, 2$ [Ghi08, FRW24]. Con-
jecture (iii) would yield a positive answer to Problem 1.22; see [BBG19a].

References cited:

- [FRW24] Ethan Farber, Braeden Reinoso, and Luya Wang. Fixed-point-free pseudo-Anosov homeomorphisms, knot Floer homology and the cinquefoil, 2024. doi:10.2140/gt.2024.28.4337.
- [Ni07] Yi Ni. Knot Floer homology detects fibred knots. Invent. Math., 170(3):577–608, 2007. doi:10.1007/s00222-007-0075-9.
- [Hed10] Matthew Hedden. Notions of positivity and the Ozsváth-Szabó concordance invariant. J. Knot Theory Ramifications, 19(5):617–629, 2010. doi:10.1142/S0218216510008017.
- [OS05b] Peter Ozsváth and Zoltán Szabó. On knot Floer homology and lens space surgeries. Topology, 44(6):1281–1300, 2005. doi:10.1016/j.top.2005.05.001.
- [BHS25] John A. Baldwin, Ying Hu, and Steven Sivek. Khovanov homology and the cinquefoil. J. Eur. Math. Soc. (JEMS), 27(6):2443–2465, 2025. doi:10.4171/jems/1415.

title: Kirby Problem 1.22
statement:
If $K$ is a hyperbolic $L$-space knot, show that its branched cover
$\Sigma_{2}(K)$ is not an $L$-space.
background:
Source: Kirby's Problems in Low-Dimensional Topology notes. Original problem number: KP-1.22.

Literature notes:
This is a conjecture of A. Moore. The corresponding statement
for higher order covers $\Sigma_{n}(K)$ was shown by Boileau-Boyer-Gordon [BBG19a] for
$n \geq 4$ and by [FRW24] for $n = 3$. Boyer-Gordon-Hu [BGH25, Corollary 7.3] have
announced that $\Sigma_{n}(K)$ has a left-orderable group for each $n \geq 2$, so in particular, a
positive solution would be in accordance with the $L$-space conjecture, Problem 3.48.

References cited:

title: Kirby Problem 1.23
statement:
Let $K$ be a cubic graph embedded in the plane, and let $\mathrm{Tait}(K)$
be the number of Tait colorings of $K$.
(a) Is $\dim J^{7}(K) = \mathrm{Tait}(K)$?
(b) Is $J^{5}(K)$ nonzero when $K$ is bridgeless?
background:
Source: Kirby's Problems in Low-Dimensional Topology notes. Original problem number: KP-1.23.

Literature notes:
(1) Part (a) is Conjecture 1.2 in [KM19a].
(2) A Tait coloring of a cubic (also called trivalent) graph is a labeling of the
edges of the graph by three colors such that edges of all of the colors are
incident at each vertex. In [KM19a], Kronheimer–Mrowka used gauge
theory to assign to a web $K \subset \mathbb{R}^{3}$ a finite-dimensional vector space $J^{7}(K)$
over $\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}$, and proved that $J^{7}(K)$ is zero if and only if $K$ has an embedded
bridge.
They also proposed a combinatorial counterpart $J^{5}(K),$ which
Khovanov–Robert [KR21] showed is well-defined for planar webs $K \subset \mathbb{R}^{2}$.
Work of Kronheimer–Mrowka [KM19b] and Khovanov–Robert [KR21]
implies that

$$
\dim J^{5}(K) \leq \mathrm{Tait}(K) \leq \dim J^{7}(K)
$$

for any planar web $K$.
The Four Color Theorem is equivalent to the
statement that every bridgeless cubic planar graph has a Tait coloring,
and a new proof would therefore follow from an affirmative answer to
either of the questions in this problem.
(3) Boozer [Boo23] gave numerical evidence suggesting that the inequality
$\dim J^{5}(K) \leq \mathrm{Tait}(K)$ may sometimes be strict.
In [Boo25], he also
announced that $J^{5}$ and $J^{7}$ do not coincide as functors.

References cited:
- [KM19a] P. B. Kronheimer and T. S. Mrowka. Tait colorings, and an instanton homology for webs and foams. J. Eur. Math. Soc. (JEMS), 21(1):55–119, 2019. doi:10.4171/JEMS/831.
- [KR21] Mikhail Khovanov and Louis-Hadrien Robert. Foam evaluation and KronheimerMrowka theories. Adv. Math., 376:Paper No. 107433, 59, 2021. doi:10.1016/j.aim.2020.107433.
- [KM19b] Peter B. Kronheimer and Tomasz S. Mrowka. A deformation of instanton homology for webs. Geom. Topol., 23(3):1491–1547, 2019. doi:10.2140/gt.2019.23.1491.
- [Boo23] David Boozer. Computer bounds for Kronheimer-Mrowka foam evaluation. Exp. Math., 32(4):615–630, 2023. doi:10.1080/10586458.2021.1982078.
- [Boo25] David Boozer. The combinatorial and gauge-theoretic foam evaluation functors are not the same. Math. Ann., 392(1):47–56, 2025. doi:10.1007/s00208-024-03064-8.

title: Kirby Problem 1.24
statement:
(Jones Unknot Detection).
(a) Is there a nontrivial knot with the same Jones polynomial as the unknot?

(b) Does there exist a nontrivial knot whose colored Jones polynomials are all
trivial?
(c) Is there a nontrivial knot with trivial HOMFLYPT polynomial? (A knot
with trivial HOMFLYPT polynomial would have trivial Jones polynomial.)
background:
Source: Kirby's Problems in Low-Dimensional Topology notes. Original problem number: KP-1.24.

Literature notes:
(1) Question (a) was first proposed by V. Jones; see [Kir97, Problems 1.88(a)
and (c)] and [AALM00].
(2) Computer calculations by Sikora and Tuzun [TS21] have shown there is
no nontrivial knot with up to 24 crossings with trivial Jones polynomial.
(3) As observed in [MM01], a positive answer to Question (b) would follow
from the Volume Conjecture stated in Problem 1.27.
(4) By tabulating links, Thistlethwaite found links with two or more com-
ponents with trivial Jones polynomials [Thi01]. This was extended in
[EKT03] to infinite families of links with trivial Jones polynomials. But
these examples do not have trivial HOMFLYPT polynomials.
(5) Kronheimer and Mrowka have proven that a knot has trivial Khovanov
homology if and only if it is trivial [KM11].

References cited:
- [Kir97] R.C. Kirby. Problems in low–dimensional topology. In W. Kazez, editor, Geometric Topology. American Math. Soc./International Press, Providence, 1997.
- [AALM00] Vladimir Igorevič Arnol’d, Michael Atiyah, Peter Lax, and Barry Mazur. Mathematics: Frontiers and perspectives. American Mathematical Society Providence, RI, 2000.
- [TS21] Robert E. Tuzun and Adam S. Sikora. Verification of the Jones unknot conjecture up to 24 crossings. J. Knot Theory Ramifications, 30(3):Paper No. 2150020, 6, 2021. doi:10.1142/S0218216521500206.
- [MM01] Hitoshi Murakami and Jun Murakami. The colored Jones polynomials and the simplicial volume of a knot. Acta Math., 186(1):85–104, 2001. doi:10.1007/BF02392716.
- [Thi01] Morwen Thistlethwaite. Links with trivial Jones polynomial. J. Knot Theory Ramifications, 10(4):641–643, 2001. doi:10.1142/S0218216501001050.
- [EKT03] Shalom Eliahou, Louis H. Kauffman, and Morwen B. Thistlethwaite. Infinite families of links with trivial Jones polynomial. Topology, 42(1):155–169, 2003. doi:10.1016/S0040-9383(02)00012-5.

title: Kirby Problem 1.25
statement:
(a) Conjecture: The noncommutative $A$-ideal of a knot $K$ is exactly the an-
nihilator of the colored Jones polynomial $($ the infinite dimensional vector
whose entries are the colored Jones polynomials of $K)$.
(b) $($ AJ Conjecture $)$ Let $A(K; L, M)$ be the $A$-polynomial of the knot $K$, and
$\alpha(K, q; M, L)$ a polynomial of minimal degree in $L$ and co-prime coeffi-
cients that annihilates the colored Jones polynomial $J_{n}(K; q)$. Then

$$
\alpha(K, -1; M, L) = A(K; L, M)
$$

up to a factor depending on $M.$
background:
Source: Kirby's Problems in Low-Dimensional Topology notes. Original problem number: KP-1.25.

Literature notes:
(1) The version of Conjecture (a) for $\mathfrak{s}\mathfrak{l}_{2}$ appears in [FGL02]; the full version
is stated in [Sik08]. The AJ conjecture (b) is due to Garoufalidis [Gar04].
(2) The noncommutative $A$-ideal of $S^{3} - K$ is the left ideal in the Kauffman
bracket skein algebra of the torus that annihilates the empty skein in
the knot complement. [FGL02] shows that a series built from the colored
Jones polynomial $J_{n}(K; q)$ annihilates the noncommutative $A$-ideal, which
leads to recursive relationships satisfied by $J_{n}(K; q)$.
The noncommutative $A$-ideal is computed for $3_{1}$ [Gel02], $(2, 2p + 1)$
torus knots [GS03], and $4_{1}$ [GS04]. Demonstrating the nontriviality of
the noncommutative $A$-ideal remains a significant unresolved problem.
(3) The $A$-polynomial of a knot $K$ [CL98] is the defining polynomial for
the character variety formed by $\operatorname{SL}_{2}(\mathbb{C})$-representations of $\pi_{1}(\partial(S^{3} - K))$
that extend to $\pi_{1}(S^{3} - K)$.
See [GL05] for details on the definition
of $\alpha(K, q; M, L)$, which comes from linear recursion relations satisfied
by $J_{n}(K; q)$.
The AJ Conjecture is proved for certain 2-bridge knots

[Lê06, LZ17] and pretzel knots [LT15], and a diagrammatic approach is
suggested in [DG20]. See also [Guk05] for the physics context of the AJ
conjecture.
(4) The two Conjectures are closely intertwined, and the AJ Conjecture is an
important step towards understanding the relationship between classical
and quantum invariants.

title: Kirby Problem 1.26
statement:
(Jones Slope Conjecture). For a knot $K$, the Jones slopes $js(K)$
are the set of cluster points in

$$
\left\{\frac{4}{n^{2}}\deg_{+}\bigl(J_{n}(K;q)\bigr)\right\}_{n\in\mathbb{N}}
\cup
\left\{\frac{4}{n^{2}}\deg_{-}\bigl(J_{n}(K;q)\bigr)\right\}_{n\in\mathbb{N}},
$$

where deg $^{+}$ denotes the highest degree and deg $^{-}$ the lowest degree.
background:
Source: Kirby's Problems in Low-Dimensional Topology notes. Original problem number: KP-1.26.

Literature notes:
(1) The Jones slopes of a knot $K$ are a subset of the boundary slopes of
incompressible surfaces, boundary-incompressible orientable surfaces in
$S^{3} - K$.
(2) This conjecture was originally stated by Garoufalidis [Gar11]. There is a
stronger version of the conjecture due to Kalfagianni and Tran [KT15].
Garoufalidis proved his conjecture for up to 10 crossings [Gar11], and the
Slope Conjecture or its stronger form has been proved for various fami-
lies of knots [FKP11, GvdV16, LvdV16, Lee22, BMT21, BMT20,
MT17, LYL19, GLVDV20].

title: Kirby Problem 1.27
statement:
(Kashaev–Murakami–Murakami Volume Conjecture). For a
link $L \subset S^{3}$,

$$
\frac{1}{2\pi}\operatorname{Vol}_{\mathrm{hyp}}(S^{3}-L)
=\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{1}{n}\log\left|J_{n}\bigl(L,e^{2\pi i/n}\bigr)\right|.
$$
background:
Source: Kirby's Problems in Low-Dimensional Topology notes. Original problem number: KP-1.27.

Literature notes:
Here, $J_{n}(L, q)$ is the $n^{th}$ colored Jones polynomial of $L$ in the vari-
able $q$, and $\operatorname{Vol}_{hyp}(S^{3} - L)$ is the hyperbolic volume of the link complement. This
problem was originally proposed for a complex-valued invariant for triangulated
links in $S^{3}$ [Kas97], which was later shown to be determined by the colored Jones
polynomial of the link complement [MM01]. Note that this conjecture would imply
that the collection of colored Jones polynomials would characterize the unknot; see
Problem 1.24(b). The conjecture has been verified for some knots, including knots
with up to seven crossings [Oht16, OY18, Oht17], torus knots [KT00], White-
head doubles of $(2, b)$ torus knots or links [Zhe07], Whitehead chains, [vdV08],
and certain cables of $4_{1}$ [LT10, MT25].
Note that there is also a stronger complexified version involving the Chern–
Simons invariant. See [Mur07, MMO $^{+}02$].

title: Kirby Problem 1.28
statement:
Let $L$ be a link in the thickened annulus $S^{1} \times I \times I$.
(a) Wrapping conjecture: $w(L)$ is equal to the maximal nonzero annular de-
gree of the annular Kauffman bracket of $L$.
(b) Categorifed wrapping conjecture: $w(L)$ is equal to the maximal nonzero
annular grading of the annular Khovanov homology of $L$.
background:
Source: Kirby's Problems in Low-Dimensional Topology notes. Original problem number: KP-1.28.

Literature notes:
(1) The wrapping number $w(L)$ of $L$ is the minimum number of times $L$
intersects a meridional disk.
(2) The wrapping number $w(L)$ is less than or equal to the maximal nonzero
annular degree of the annular Kauffman bracket of $L$, as well as the maxi-
mal nonzero annular grading of the annular Khovanov homology of $L$. The
problem is asking whether these upper bounds are necessarily achieved;
that is, whether either of these invariants detects the wrapping number.
(3) The wrapping conjecture is due to Hoste–Przytycki [HP95a], who proved
it for any annular link with a $\pm$-adequately wrapped diagram.
(4) The categorified wrapping conjecture is due to Grigsby, who proved with
Ni that it holds for string links [GN14]. This conjecture would follow
from the wrapping conjecture since the graded Euler characteristic of an-
nular Khovanov homology is equal to the annular Kauffman bracket. It is
known via spectral sequences relating annular Khovanov homology with
Floer-theoretic invariants [GW10, Xie21, XZ25] that annular Khovanov
homology is nontrivial in the annular grading given by the generalized
Thurston norm of the meridional disk. The difficulty is that the general-
ized meridional Thurston norm can be arbitrarily smaller than the wrap-
ping number; see Martin’s work for this and related progress [Mar23].

References cited:
- [HP95a] Jim Hoste and Józef H. Przytycki. The $(2,8)$-skein module of Whitehead manifolds. J. Knot Theory Ramifications, 4(3):411–427, 1995. doi:10.1142/S021821659500020X.
- [GN14] J. Elisenda Grigsby and Yi Ni. Sutured Khovanov homology distinguishes braids from other tangles. Math. Res. Lett., 21(6):1263–1275, 2014. doi:10.4310/MRL.2014.v21.n6.a4.
- [GW10] J. Elisenda Grigsby and Stephan M. Wehrli. Khovanov homology, sutured Floer homology and annular links. Algebr. Geom. Topol., 10(4):2009–2039, 2010. doi: 10.2140/agt.2010.10.2009.
- [Xie21] Yi Xie. Instantons and annular Khovanov homology. Adv. Math., 388:Paper No. 107864, 51, 2021. doi:10.1016/j.aim.2021.107864.
- [XZ25] Yi Xie and Boyu Zhang. Instanton Floer homology for sutured manifolds with tangles. J. Differential Geom., 130(3):701–769, 2025. doi:10.4310/jdg/1749496718.
- [Mar23] Gage Martin. Annular Khovanov homology and meridional disks. J. Knot Theory Ramifications, 32(2):Paper No. 2250088, 14, 2023. doi:10.1142/S0218216522500882.
