title: Kirby Problem 1.29
statement:
Is the first inequality below true? If so, is the second?
(a) $(\operatorname{Vol}$-Det Conjecture $)$ For any alternating hyperbolic knot $K \subset S^{3}$,
vol $(K) < 2\pi \log \det(K),$
where vol is the hyperbolic volume of $K$ and det is the determinant.
(b) For any hyperbolic knot $K \subset S^{3}$,
vol $(K) < 2\pi \log \operatorname{rank} \mathrm{Kh}(K),$
where Kh is the reduced Khovanov homology of $K$?
background:
Source: Kirby's Problems in Low-Dimensional Topology notes. Original problem number: KP-1.29.

Literature notes:
(1) The proposed inequalities relate quantum topology and hyperbolic geom-
etry in the style of the Volume Conjecture [Kas97, MM01] (see Problem
1.27), but may be more approachable.
(2) A correlation between determinant and volume for alternating hyperbolic
knots was first noticed by Dunfield, and Champanerkar, Kofman and Pur-
cell conjectured in [CKP16] that (1) holds. They moreover showed that
the bound is sharp, and conjectured the second more general inequal-
ity (b).
(3) Burton verified (a) for several families of knots including 2-bridge knots,
closed alternating 3-braids, and an infinite family of alternating 4-braids
[Bur18].
(4) Champanerkar, Kofman and Lalin proved (a) for other infinite families of
alternating knots using number theoretic methods in [CKL19], and gave
related conjectures involving other volume-type quantities and the Mahler
measures of certain graph-theoretic polynomials. See also [CK25].

References cited:
- [Kas97] Rinat M Kashaev. The hyperbolic volume of knots from the quantum dilogarithm. Letters in mathematical physics, 39(3):269–275, 1997.
- [MM01] Hitoshi Murakami and Jun Murakami. The colored Jones polynomials and the simplicial volume of a knot. Acta Math., 186(1):85–104, 2001. doi:10.1007/BF02392716.
- [CKP16] Abhijit Champanerkar, Ilya Kofman, and Jessica S. Purcell. Geometrically and diagrammatically maximal knots. J. Lond. Math. Soc. (2), 94(3):883–908, 2016. doi:10.1112/jlms/jdw062.
- [Bur18] Stephan D. Burton. The determinant and volume of 2-bridge links and alternating 3-braids. New York J. Math., 24:293–316, 2018. http://nyjm.albany.edu:8000/j/2018/24 293.html.
- [CKL19] Abhijit Champanerkar, Ilya Kofman, and Matilde Lalı́n. Mahler measure and the vol-det conjecture. J. Lond. Math. Soc. (2), 99(3):872–900, 2019. doi:10.1112/jlms.12200.
- [CK25] Abhijit Champanerkar and Ilya Kofman. Geometric bounds for spanning tree entropy of planar lattice graphs, 2025. arXiv:2505.05688.

title: Kirby Problem 1.30
statement:
Does the Khovanov homology of every nontrivial knot contain
2-torsion?
background:
Source: Kirby's Problems in Low-Dimensional Topology notes. Original problem number: KP-1.30.

Literature notes:
This is a conjecture due to Shumakovitch [Shu14] originally posted
in 2004. It has been verified for some infinite families of knots [Shu14, AP04,

PS14, DM25a, DM25b]. Moreover, Gujral–Wang have shown [GW25] that if
$K$ is a knot with no 2-torsion in its Khovanov homology, and $J$ is obtained from
$K$ by a proper rational tangle replacement, then
rankKh $(K) \leq$ rankKh $(J),$
where Kh refers to reduced Khovanov homology. It follows in particular that Shu-
makovitch’s conjecture holds for knots with unknotting number 1.
If proven, the conjecture would offer an alternative proof that Khovanov ho-
mology detects the unknot.

title: Kirby Problem 1.31
statement:
(a) Compute the Khovanov homology for all torus knots $T(m, n)$.
(b) Compute the Khovanov–Rozansky $\mathfrak{g}\mathfrak{l}(N)$ homology for all torus knots.
background:
Source: Kirby's Problems in Low-Dimensional Topology notes. Original problem number: KP-1.31.

Literature notes:
(1) The data for the Khovanov homology of $T(m, n)$ is available at [LM23b]
for small $m, n$. Khovanov–Rozansky homology data is available at [Lew23a,
Lew23b].
(2) The homology is known to have a lot of torsion [MPS $^{+}18$]. Comput-
ing Khovanov homology with $\mathbb{Z}_{2}$ coefficients and $\mathfrak{g}\mathfrak{l}(N)$ homology with
$\mathbb{Z}_{N}$ coefficients might be easier than rational coefficients [GOR13]. On
the other hand, an open conjecture [PS14, MPS $^{+}18$] states that the
Khovanov homology of $T(m, n)$ for $m$ prime and $n > m$ has $m$-torsion.
(3) The triply graded Khovanov–Rozansky homology of torus knots (with in-
teger coefficients) is computed in [Mel22]. By [Ras15] there is a spectral
sequence from triply graded homology to Khovanov (resp.
Khovanov–
Rozansky) homology, but the differentials are not known explicitly.
(4) By [Sto09], there is a well-defined limit of the Khovanov homology of
$T(m, n)$ as $m \to \infty$, also known as $T(n, \infty)$. Rozansky [Roz14] shows
that the Khovanov homology of $T(n, \infty)$ provides a categorified equivalent
of the Jones–Wenzl projector [Wen87]. The triply graded homology of
$T(n, \infty)$ is computed in [Hog18], and precise conjectures for the Khovanov
homology of $T(n, \infty)$ are discussed in [GOR13, GL15].
(5) In contrast, the Heegaard Floer homology of $T(m, n)$ is well known [OS05b].

title: Kirby Problem 1.32
statement:
(a) Recover the Jones polynomial of links $L \subset \mathbb{R}^{3}$ by counting solutions to
the Kapustin–Witten equations on $\mathbb{R}^{3} \times \mathbb{R}_{+}$ with Nahm pole boundary
conditions;
(b) Recover the Khovanov homology of links $L \subset \mathbb{R}^{3}$ by counting solutions to
the Haydys–Witten equations on $\mathbb{R} \times \mathbb{R}^{3} \times \mathbb{R}_{+}$ with Nahm pole boundary
conditions;

(c) Use the Kapustin–Witten or Haydys–Witten equations to construct invari-
ants of links in other 3-manifolds.
background:
Source: Kirby's Problems in Low-Dimensional Topology notes. Original problem number: KP-1.32.

Literature notes:
(1) Khovanov homology [Kho00] is a link invariant defined combinatorially,
whose Euler characteristic is the Jones polynomial. It has many properties
similar to Floer homologies (e.g., functoriality under cobordisms) and, as
such, it is natural to ask if it has an interpretation in terms of gauge
theory. Such an interpretation was proposed by Witten in [Wit12], and
is summarized in points (a) and (b) of the problem.
(2) The Kapustin-Witten (KW) equations are a set of gauge invariant PDE’s
in four dimensions introduced in [KW07].
The Nahm pole boundary
conditions for these equations are described in [Wit12]; they have a more
special form along the link $L \times \{0\} \subset \mathbb{R}^{3} \times \{0\}.$ Gaiotto and Witten
[GW12] sketched an approach to showing that the count of solutions to
the KW equations with Nahm pole boundary conditions gives the coeffi-
cients of the Jones polynomial. However, there is still work to be done to
make this mathematically rigorous.
(3) The Haydys-Witten (HW) equations were introduced in [Wit12] and
[Hay15]. Witten conjectured that, if one forms a complex whose gen-
erators are the KW solutions and whose differentials count HW solutions
(with appropriate limits and boundary conditions), then its homology is
Khovanov homology.
(4) Part of the appeal of these gauge-theoretic ideas is that they may pro-
vide a definition of the Jones polynomial/Khovanov homology manifestly
independent of the link diagram. Moreover, we can write the same equa-
tions with $\mathbb{R}^{3}$ replaced by another 3-manifold, leading to part (c) of the
problem. Optimistically, the counts of KW solutions could give the class
of the link $L$ in the Kauffman bracket skein module of the 3-manifold
[Prz91, Tur88], or be related to the $\widetilde{Z}$ invariants predicted by physi-
cists [GPV17, GPPV20]; see Problem 3.68.
More ambitiously, the
count of HW solutions should give analogues of Khovanov homology for
links in 3-manifolds.
At the moment, Khovanov homology is only de-
fined in a combinatorial, concrete way for links in $S^{3}$, interval bundles
over surfaces [APS04], $\mathbb{R}$ P $^{3}$ [Man07, Gab13], and connected sums of
$S^{1} \times S^{2}$ [Roz10, Wil21]. If indeed the Haydys-Kapustin-Witten pro-
gram can be carried through, it would also be important to compare
the result with the Khovanov lasagna skein modules of Morrison-Walker-
Wedrich [MWW22].
(5) Mathematicians have made progress on understanding the analytic prop-
erties of the KW and HW equations; see [MW14], [MW20], [Tau13],
[LT20], [He19], [HM19a], [Tau18], [Tau19].
Some of the compact-
ness results (e.g. [Tau18, Theorem B]) only hold when the 3-manifold
has positive Ricci curvature, which suggests that part (c) should first be
attempted under this assumption.

title: Kirby Problem 1.33
statement:
Describe topological necessary or sufficient conditions for a
link to have KR-parity. For example:
(a) Are all links with KR-parity positive? Quasipositive?
(b) Do all algebraic links have KR-parity?
background:
Source: Kirby's Problems in Low-Dimensional Topology notes. Original problem number: KP-1.33.

Literature notes:
(1) We say that a link has KR-parity if its triply graded Khovanov–Rozansky
homology is concentrated in homological degrees of the same parity. The
motivation for this property comes from the work of Hogancamp and
Elias [EH19], who developed a recursive procedure for computing the
Khovanov–Rozansky homology of some links; their procedure relies on
the link having KR-parity.
(2) By [Mel22, HM19b] all torus links have KR-parity.
(3) If a link has KR-parity, then all coefficients in the HOMFLY polynomial
$P(a, q)$ should have the same sign (depending on conventions, one might
need to change the variable $a$ to $-a$).
(4) There are examples of positive links that do not have KR-parity, for ex-
ample the knot $10_{139}$ which is the closure of the braid $\sigma_{1}\sigma_{2}(\sigma_{1}\sigma_{2}\sigma_{2}\sigma_{1})^{2}$.
(5) Let $\mathrm{FT}_{i}$ denote the full twist on the first $i$ strands.
It is conjectured
[GHSR20, OR23, Tur24] that the closure of the braid
$\mathrm{FT}_{2}^{d_{2}}\mathrm{FT}_{3}^{d_{3}}\cdots \mathrm{FT}_{n}^{d_{n}}$
has KR-parity as long as all $d_{i} \geq 0$.

References cited:
- [EH19] Ben Elias and Matthew Hogancamp. On the computation of torus link homology. Compos. Math., 155(1):164–205, 2019. doi:10.1112/s0010437x18007571.
- [Mel22] Anton Mellit. Homology of torus knots. Geom. Topol., 26(1):47–70, 2022. doi: 10.2140/gt.2022.26.47.
- [HM19b] Matthew Hogancamp and Anton Mellit. Torus link homology, 2019. arXiv:1909.00418.

title: Kirby Problem 1.34
statement:
(a) Khovanov and Rozansky [KR08b] used braid presentations to define a
triply graded link homology theory whose Euler characteristic is the HOM-
FLYPT polynomial. Find a description of this homology in terms of arbi-
trary planar diagrams of the link, and determine whether some flavor of
this theory is functorial with respect to link cobordisms.
(b) Do the same for Cautis’ link homologies from [Cau17], which are also
defined in terms of braid presentations.
background:
Source: Kirby's Problems in Low-Dimensional Topology notes. Original problem number: KP-1.34.

Literature notes:
(1) There are several versions of the HOMFLYPT link homology in [KR08b]:
unreduced, middle, reduced, and totally reduced; see [Ras15]. Reduction
refers to choosing a basepoint and taking a mapping cone in the chain
complex, which results in a smaller homology.
Only the totally reduced theory (where a basepoint is chosen on each
link component) has a chance at functoriality. For the original unreduced
theory, the homology of the unknot is the product of the exterior and
polynomial algebras on one generator each, and this is infinite-dimensional
over the ground field (i.e., over the homology of the empty link); thus, it
cannot admit a functorial extension unless suitably modified. The totally
reduced theory assigns finite-dimensional homology groups to all links and
has a chance at being functorial for link cobordisms (decorated by paths).
A similar kind of functoriality appears in knot Floer homology [Zem19b].

(2) The definition of HOMFLYPT homology in [KR08b] starts with a com-
plex associated to a braid diagram. If one constructs the same complex
from an arbitrary planar diagram, the resulting homology does not behave
well with respect to the Reidemeister II(b) move; see [Web07, Section 3.1]
and [Abe17].
(3) HOMFLYPT homology can also be interpreted as the Hochschild homol-
ogy of the Rouquier complexes formed from Soergel bimodules [Kho07].
Functoriality of Rouquier complexes under braid cobordisms was proved
in [EK10].
(4) In [Cau17], Cautis used categorical $\mathfrak{s}\mathfrak{l}_{n}$ actions to define triply-graded link
invariants that categorify the HOMFLYPT polynomial of links colored by
arbitrary partitions. He also defined a finite dimensional categorification
of the $\mathfrak{s}\mathfrak{l}(n)$ link polynomial colored by symmetric powers of the standard
representation. See also [QRS18] for a combinatorial definition of Cautis’
homology, and [RW20] for the equivariant version.

- [Zem19b] Ian Zemke. Link cobordisms and functoriality in link Floer homology. J. Topol., 12(1):94–220, 2019. doi:10.1112/topo.12085.
- [Web07] Ben Webster. Khovanov-Rozansky homology via a canopolis formalism. Algebr. Geom. Topol., 7:673–699, 2007. doi:10.2140/agt.2007.7.673.
- [Abe17] Michael Abel. HOMFLY-PT homology for general link diagrams and braidlike isotopy. Algebr. Geom. Topol., 17(5):3021–3056, 2017. doi:10.2140/agt.2017.17.3021.

title: Kirby Problem 1.35
statement:
(a) Is symplectic Khovanov homology isomorphic to Khovanov homology, over
$\mathbb{Z}$?
(b) Give a construction of odd symplectic Khovanov homology $\mathrm{Kh}^{\mathrm{odd}}_{\mathrm{symp}}(K)$.
background:
Source: Kirby's Problems in Low-Dimensional Topology notes. Original problem number: KP-1.35.

Literature notes:
Symplectic Khovanov homology, introduced in [SS06], is a can-
didate Floer-theoretic construction of Khovanov homology. Abouzaid and Smith
[AS19] showed that it is isomorphic to ordinary Khovanov homology over $\mathbb{Q}$ (or
more generally over fields of characteristic 0), but their proof does not work with
integer coefficients.
It is not obvious from the construction how to produce a version similarly
related to odd Khovanov homology.

- [AS19] Mohammed Abouzaid and Ivan Smith. Khovanov homology from Floer cohomology. J. Amer. Math. Soc., 32(1):1–79, 2019. doi:10.1090/jams/902.

title: Kirby Problem 1.36
statement:
Categorify the ($\mathfrak{s}\mathfrak{l}(2), \mathfrak{s}\mathfrak{l}(N)$, HOMFLYPT) skein algebras for
surfaces.
background:
Source: Kirby's Problems in Low-Dimensional Topology notes. Original problem number: KP-1.36.

Literature notes:
(1) The skein algebra of a surface, introduced by Przytycki-Sikora [PS00b]
and Turaev [Tur91], encodes curves on the surface up to the Kauffman
bracket skein relations.
(2) The skein algebra of the annulus is categorified by the annular Khovanov
(or Khovanov–Rozansky) homology [GW10, GLW18, QR18].
(3) There are several constructions of Khovanov-type invariants of links in
thickened surfaces [APS04, QW21]. However, it is not known if any of
these can support a categorical analogue of the skein product.

(4) The HOMFLYPT skein algebra of the torus is closely related to the elliptic
Hall algebra [MS17b]. Categorification of the elliptic Hall algebra is an
important problem in geometric representation theory [Neg22].

title: Kirby Problem 1.37
statement:
(a) For every link $L \subset \mathbb{R}^{3}$, every simple Lie algebra $\mathfrak{g}$, and every coloring
of the components of $L$ with irreducible representations of $\mathfrak{g}$, construct
a bigraded link homology theory that is functorial under link cobordisms,
and whose Euler characteristic is the Reshetikhin–Turaev link invariant
associated to $\mathfrak{g}$ and $L$.
(b) For each of the theories above, define an odd version $($ with the same mod
2 reduction $)$ or explain the obstruction to its existence.
background:
Source: Kirby's Problems in Low-Dimensional Topology notes. Original problem number: KP-1.37.

Literature notes:
(1) Link homologies corresponding to $\mathfrak{s}\mathfrak{l}(n)$ with its standard vector represen-
tation were constructed by Khovanov [Kho00] for $n = 2$ and Khovanov–
Rozansky [KR08a] for all $n$. Generalizations to exterior products of the
standard representations of $\mathfrak{s}\mathfrak{l}(n)$ were constructed in [Wu14], [Yon11],
[QR16], and were proved to be functorial under link cobordisms in [ETW18].
(2) Webster [Web17] has a categorification of the Reshetikhin–Turaev link
invariants for any simple Lie algebra $\mathfrak{g}$ and any labeling of the link com-
ponents by irreducible representations of $\mathfrak{g}$. His homology is bigraded.
For most $\mathfrak{g}$ and labelings by irreducible representations, his homology of
the unknot is infinite-dimensional over the ground field and thus cannot
extend to a functorial link homology theory.
Such a theory should at
least assign a commutative Frobenius algebra to the unknot, necessarily
finite-dimensional over the ground field. (A naive guess is that Webster
homology extends to a functorial theory, possibly up to overall scaling, if
and only if all representations are minuscule.) It is also possible that a
good functorial theory would be more complicated algebraically, e.g. be
defined over a dg ring, or have more interesting gradings.
(3) The odd version of Khovanov homology was defined by Ozsváth, Ras-
mussen, and Szabó in [ORS13]; it is isomorphic to Khovanov homology
over $\mathbb{Z}/2$ but different over $\mathbb{Z}$. The odd version appears naturally in re-
lation to Floer homologies of the double branched cover of the link; see
[OS05c], [Sca15]. Its functoriality (up to sign) was studied by Migdail
and Wehrli [MW24].
(4) Mikhaylov and Witten [MW15] studied odd Khovanov homology from
the perspective of physics. They argued that there should be odd versions
for the link homologies associated to $\mathfrak{s}\mathfrak{o}(2n + 1)$, but not for $\mathfrak{s}\mathfrak{u}(n)$; except
for $n = 2$, when $\mathfrak{s}\mathfrak{u}(2) = \mathfrak{s}\mathfrak{o}(3)$. The odd link homologies for $\mathfrak{s}\mathfrak{o}(2n+1)$ for
$n \geq 2$ have not yet been constructed mathematically.
(5) Ellis and Lauda [EL16] gave an odd categorification of quantum $\mathfrak{s}\mathfrak{l}(2)$,
using a covering Kac-Moody algebra. They pointed out that the theory
of covering Kac-Moody algebras only exists in finite type for $\mathfrak{s}\mathfrak{o}(2n + 1)$.

(6) Khovanov, Putyra and Vaz [KPV24] constructed odd analogues of So-
ergel bimodules and Rouquier complexes, and pointed out an obstruction
to defining an odd HOMFLYPT homology.

title: Kirby Problem 1.38
statement:
What is the structure of the smooth knot concordance group?
(a) Is there a torsion element of the smooth concordance group $\mathcal{C}$ having order
other than two? Is there a torsion element in $\mathcal{C}_{TS}$, the smooth concordance
group of topologically slice knots, having order other than two?
(b) Is there a knot $K$ having concordance order two in $\mathcal{C}$ that is not concordant
to a strongly negatively amphichiral knot?
(c) Do there exist infinitely divisible elements in $\mathcal{C}$, that is, does there exist $K$
such that for infinitely many $n \in \mathbb{N}$, there is a $J$ such that $[K] = n[J]$?
background:
Source: Kirby's Problems in Low-Dimensional Topology notes. Original problem number: KP-1.38.

Literature notes:
(1) This is [Kir97, Problem 1.32]. Fox and Milnor’s original work on the
concordance group shows there exist elements of order two [FM66]; Hed-
den, Kim, and Livingston [HKL16a] show the existence of an infinite
subgroup of topologically slice knots of order two.
Many elements of
infinite order are known; for example, $\mathcal{C}_{TS}$ contains subgroup isomor-
phic to $\mathbb{Z}_{\infty}$ [End95], and in fact a direct summand isomorphic to $\mathbb{Z}_{\infty}$
[DHST21, OSS17b].
(2) Any infinitely divisible element of $\mathcal{C}$ must be sent to zero under any integer-
valued homomorphism from the concordance group, such as the Ozsváth-
Szabó $\tau$-invariant or the Rasmussen $s$-invariant.

References cited:
- [Kir97] R.C. Kirby. Problems in low–dimensional topology. In W. Kazez, editor, Geometric Topology. American Math. Soc./International Press, Providence, 1997.
- [FM66] Ralph H. Fox and John W. Milnor. Singularities of 2-spheres in 4-space and cobordism of knots. Osaka Math. J., 3:257–267, 1966. http://projecteuclid.org/euclid.ojm/1200691730.
- [HKL16a] Matthew Hedden, Se-Goo Kim, and Charles Livingston. Topologically slice knots of smooth concordance order two. J. Differential Geom., 102(3):353–393, 2016. http://projecteuclid.org/euclid.jdg/1456754013.
- [End95] Hisaaki Endo. Linear independence of topologically slice knots in the smooth cobordism group. Topology Appl., 63(3):257–262, 1995. doi:10.1016/0166-8641(94) 00062-8.
- [DHST21] Irving Dai, Jennifer Hom, Matthew Stoffregen, and Linh Truong. More concordance homomorphisms from knot Floer homology. Geom. Topol., 25(1):275–338, 2021. doi:10.2140/gt.2021.25.275.
- [OSS17b] Peter Ozsváth, András I. Stipsicz, and Zoltán Szabó. Concordance homomorphisms from knot Floer homology. Adv. Math., 315:366–426, 2017. doi:10.1016/j.aim.2017.05.017.

title: Kirby Problem 1.39
statement:
(a) Do the algebraic knots freely generate a subgroup of the smooth concor-
dance group $\mathcal{C}$?
(b) Do the algebraic knots freely generate a subgroup of the topological con-
cordance group $\mathcal{C}^{\mathrm{TOP}}$?
background:
Source: Kirby's Problems in Low-Dimensional Topology notes. Original problem number: KP-1.39.

Literature notes:
(1) This question is originally due to Rudolph [Rud76], although it is not
specified whether $\mathcal{C}$ or $\mathcal{C}^{\mathrm{TOP}}$ is intended. Litherland showed that torus
knots are independent in the smooth concordance group [Lit79]; his proof
yields the topological version as well. Litherland’s theorem uses Levine-
Tristram signatures, but various authors have shown that there exist con-
nected sums of algebraic knots and their mirrors that are algebraically
slice but not smoothly slice [LM83, HKL12] implying that Litherland’s
strategy is not sufficient to answer the question above.
(2) This problem is especially interesting in light of its connection to the slice-
ribbon conjecture (Problem 1.50): a result of Miyazaki shows that non-
trivial linear combinations of iterated torus knots are not ribbon [Miy94,
Corollary 8.4], so the slice-ribbon conjecture implies Rudolph’s conjec-
ture.
Indeed, Baker [Bak16] and Abe-Tagami [AT16a] observed that
the slice-ribbon conjecture implies a stronger form of Rudolph’s conjec-
ture, to wit, that the set of prime fibered strongly quasi-positive knots is
linearly independent in the smooth concordance group. Large families of
knots satisfying both Rudolph’s conjecture and this strengthening were
exhibited by Conway, Kim, and Politarczyk [CKP23].
(3) In a related direction, Baker showed that the slice-ribbon conjecture im-
plies that if two fibered knots supporting the tight contact structure on
$S^{3}$ are concordant, then they are in fact isotopic [Bak16, Corollary 4].
Abe and Tagami observed that it would then follow that the set of fibered
knots supporting the tight contact structure on $S^{3}$ is linearly indepen-
dent in the smooth concordance group and contains the algebraic knots
[AT16a, Observation 1.3]. This can be thought of as a generalization of
Rudolph’s question.

References cited:
- [Rud76] Lee Rudolph. How independent are the knot-cobordism classes of links of plane curve singularities? Notices Amer. Math. Soc, 23:410, 1976.
- [Lit79] R. A. Litherland. Signatures of iterated torus knots. In Topology of low-dimensional manifolds (Proc. Second Sussex Conf., Chelwood Gate, 1977), volume 722 of Lecture Notes in Math., pages 71–84. Springer, Berlin, 1979.
- [LM83] Charles Livingston and Paul Melvin. Algebraic knots are algebraically dependent. Proc. Amer. Math. Soc., 87(1):179–180, 1983. doi:10.2307/2044377.
- [HKL12] Matthew Hedden, Paul Kirk, and Charles Livingston. Non-slice linear combinations of algebraic knots. J. Eur. Math. Soc. (JEMS), 14(4):1181–1208, 2012. doi:10.4171/JEMS/330.
- [Miy94] Katura Miyazaki. Nonsimple, ribbon fibered knots. Trans. Amer. Math. Soc., 341(1):1–44, 1994. doi:10.2307/2154613.
- [Bak16] Kenneth L. Baker. A note on the concordance of fibered knots. J. Topol., 9(1):1–4, 2016. doi:10.1112/jtopol/jtv024.
- [AT16a] Tetsuya Abe and Keiji Tagami. Fibered knots with the same 0-surgery and the slice-ribbon conjecture. Math. Res. Lett., 23(2):303–323, 2016. doi:10.4310/MRL.2016.v23.n2.a1.
- [CKP23] Anthony Conway, Min Hoon Kim, and Wojciech Politarczyk. Nonslice linear combinations of iterated torus knots. Algebr. Geom. Topol., 23(2):765–802, 2023. doi:10.2140/agt.2023.23.765.

title: Kirby Problem 1.40
statement:
A satellite operator $P \subset S^{1} \times D^{2}$ induces an operation $P$ on
the concordance group $\mathcal{C}$ [Gor75].
(a) Let $P$ be a winding number one satellite operator with $P(\operatorname{U}) \simeq \operatorname{U}$.
If
$P(K) \simeq \operatorname{U}$, does this mean that $K \simeq \operatorname{U}$?
(b) Is the Whitehead doubling operator injective on $\mathcal{C}$? Can we exhibit any
(winding-number-zero) operator that is injective on $\mathcal{C}$?
(c) Conjecture (Hedden; see [HPC21]). The only homomorphisms on $\mathcal{C}$ in-
duced by satellite operators are the zero map, the identity, and the invo-
lution induced by orientation reversal.
(d) Conjecture (Hedden, Pinzón Caicedo) Let $P$ be a non-constant satellite
operator with winding number zero. Does $\\langle \\operatorname{im} P \\rangle$ necessarily have infinite
rank? Some special cases are:
(i) Does there always exist a fixed knot $K$ such that $\langle\{P(nK)\}_{n\in\mathbb{Z}}\rangle$ has
infinite rank?
(ii) If $\{nK\}_{n\in\mathbb{Z}}$ is any rank-one subgroup of $\mathcal{C}$, does $\langle\{P(nK)\}_{n\in\mathbb{Z}}\rangle$ have
infinite rank?
background:
Source: Kirby's Problems in Low-Dimensional Topology notes. Original problem number: KP-1.40.

Literature notes:
(1) Satellite operators are defined in the Introduction to this section.
(2) The overall conjecture (d) is easily verified in the case of non-zero winding
number. It was shown in [HK12b] that Whitehead doubling has infinite
rank, with many other patterns treated in [HPC21]. The authors subse-
quently posed the general conjecture, as well as subconjecture (i).
(3) In a positive answer to [DHMS24], subconjecture (i) was announced
for the Whitehead doubling operation. Indeed, $K$ was taken to be the
(right-handed) trefoil; this was previously unknown. The authors gave
a general class of patterns (as well as a flexible Floer-theoretic condi-
tion on $K$) for subconjecture (i) to hold; they subsequently made the
stronger subconjecture (ii). Roughly speaking, the latter indicates that
any (non-constant, winding number zero) pattern expands rank in the
knot concordance group.

References cited:
- [Gor75] C. McA. Gordon. Knots, homology spheres, and contractible 4-manifolds. Topology, 14:151–172, 1975. doi:10.1016/0040-9383(75)90024-5.
- [HPC21] Matthew Hedden and Juanita Pinzón-Caicedo. Satellites of infinite rank in the smooth concordance group. Invent. Math., 225(1):131–157, 2021. doi:10.1007/s00222-020-01026-w.
- [HK12b] Matthew Hedden and Paul Kirk. Instantons, concordance, and Whitehead doubling. J. Differential Geom., 91(2):281–319, 2012. URL: http://projecteuclid.org/euclid.jdg/1344430825.
- [DHMS24] Irving Dai, Matthew Hedden, Abhishek Mallick, and Matthew Stoffregen. Rankexpanding satellites, Whitehead doubles, and Heegaard Floer homology. J. Topol., 17(4):Paper No. e70008, 40, 2024. doi:10.1112/topo.70008.

title: Kirby Problem 1.41
statement:
This problem is concerned with the stable 4-genus $g_{s}(K)$ of a
knot $K$, defined below.
(a) Is there a knot $K$ such that $g_{s}(K) \in \mathbb{Q}\setminus\mathbb{Z}$?
(b) Is there a knot $K$ such that $g_{s}(K) \notin \mathbb{Q}$?
(c) Is there a knot $K$ such that $0 < g_{s}(K) < 1/2$?
(d) [Liv10, Question 1] Does $K$ represent a torsion element in the concor-
dance group if and only if $g_{s}(K) = 0$?
background:
Source: Kirby's Problems in Low-Dimensional Topology notes. Original problem number: KP-1.41.

Literature notes:
(1) The stable 4-genus of a knot $K$ is defined by

$$
g_s(K)=\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{g_4(nK)}{n}.
$$

(2) One instance under which the stable 4-genus $g_{s}(K)$ of a knot $K$ may
become strictly less than $g_{4}(K)$, is when for some $m \geq 2$, the knot $mK$
has $g_{4}(mK) < mg_{4}(K)$, for in this case

$$
g_s(K)=\lim_{\ell\to\infty}\frac{g_4(\ell mK)}{\ell m}
\leq \lim_{\ell\to\infty}\frac{\ell g_4(mK)}{\ell m}
=\frac{g_4(mK)}{m}<g_4(K).
$$

Examples of such knots are exhibited in [Liv10]. For instance, for $m = 2$,
an infinite family of knots $K$ is presented with $g_{4}(K) = 1$ and $g_{4}(2K) \leq 1$,
leading to $g_{s}(K) \leq \frac{1}{2}$. Thus, the strict inequality $g_{s}(K) < g_{4}(K)$ may
point to interesting phenomena with regards to oriented surfaces in the
4-ball bounded by connected sums of $K$.
(3) Positive answers to the first two parts of this problem automatically imply
the inequality $g_{s}(K) < g_{4}(K)$, but the problem goes beyond by asking how
“exotic” $g_{s}(K)$ can become.
In [Liv10], it is shown that for any $\epsilon > 0$, there exists a knot $K_{\epsilon}$ with
stable 4-genus near $\frac{1}{2}$, in the sense of this double inequality:

$$
\frac{1-\epsilon}{2}\leq g_s(K_{\epsilon})\leq \frac{1}{2}.
$$

Similarly, in [Ilt22] it is shown that if $K_{n}$ denotes the twist knot with $n$
full twists, where $n$ is such that the Pell equation $x^{2} - (4n + 1)y^{2} = -1$
has integral solutions in $x$ and $y$, then

$$
\frac{1}{2}-\frac{6}{2n+7}\leq g_s(K_n)\leq \frac{1}{2}.
$$

The above bounds can be interpreted as suggesting that $\frac{1}{2}$ may have a
special significance with regards to the stable 4-genus, motivating part (c).
(4) The lower bound of $0 < g_{s}(K)$ is required in part (c) of the question to
exclude knots $K$ that represent torsion elements in the concordance group;
any such knot will have stable 4-genus equal to 0. This leads to part (d),
which suggests a connection with torsion in the concordance group (See
Problem 1.38).

References cited:
- [Liv10] Charles Livingston. The stable 4-genus of knots. Algebr. Geom. Topol., 10(4):2191– 2202, 2010. doi:10.2140/agt.2010.10.2191.
- [Ilt22] Damian Iltgen. A lower bound on the stable 4-genus of knots. Algebr. Geom. Topol., 22(5):2239–2265, 2022. doi:10.2140/agt.2022.22.2239.

title: Kirby Problem 1.42
statement:
Do there exist algebraically concordant Seifert forms $V_{1}$ and
$V_{2}$ for which there do not exist concordant knots $K_{1}$ and $K_{2}$ with Seifert forms $V_{1}$
and $V_{2}$, respectively?
background:
Source: Kirby's Problems in Low-Dimensional Topology notes. Original problem number: KP-1.42.

Literature notes:
(1) Seifert forms $V_{1}$ and $V_{2}$ are algebraically concordant if $V_{1} \oplus -V_{2}$ is meta-
bolic. This problem is open regardless of whether one works with topo-
logical or smooth concordance of knots.

(2) As an example, the Seifert forms

$$
V_1=\begin{pmatrix}3&2\\1&3\end{pmatrix}
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
V_2=\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\1&9\end{pmatrix}
$$

are algebraically concordant: the set of vectors $\{(0, -3, 6, -1), (2, -1, 0, 1)\}$
is a basis for a metabolizer of $V_{1} \oplus -V_{2}$. Does there exist a pair of con-
cordant knots $K_{1}$ and $K_{2}$ having these Seifert forms? Conjecture 1.11
of [Liv01] posits that any knots $K_{1}$ and $K_{2}$ having as Seifert forms these
particular $V_{1}$ and $V_{2}$, respectively, cannot be concordant.

References cited:
- [Liv01] Charles Livingston. Examples in concordance, 2001. arXiv:math/0101035v1.

title: Kirby Problem 1.43
statement:
Does knot Floer homology give a categorification of the Fox–
Milnor condition?
background:
Source: Kirby's Problems in Low-Dimensional Topology notes. Original problem number: KP-1.43.

Literature notes:
(1) Fox and Milnor [FM66] prove that if $K$ is slice in $B^{4}$, then the Alexander
polynomial factors as

$$
\Delta_{K}(t) = f(t)f(t^{-1}).
$$

Given that the Euler characteristic of knot Floer homology is the Alexan-
der polynomial, one might expect that the knot Floer homology of a slice
knot $K$ factors as

$$
\widehat{\mathrm{HFK}}(K) \simeq V \otimes V^{*}
$$

where $V$ is a bigraded vector space, and $V^{*}$ denotes its dual. This is
false, since the knot Floer homology of the Kinoshita-Terasaka knot has
rank 33. One precise conjecture would be that there is a natural spectral
sequence from such a vector space of the form $V \otimes V^{*}$ to $\widehat{\mathrm{HFK}}(K)$.
(2) Note that Gilmer [Gil84] proved that if there is a ribbon concordance
from $K_{1}$ to $K_{0}$, then

$$
\Delta_{K_1}(t) = \Delta_{K_0}(t) \cdot f(t)f(t^{-1}).
$$

One could ask if this relation, or similar relations, also admit meaningful
lifts to knot Floer homology.
(3) One could similarly ask for categorifications of restrictions on the Alexan-
der polynomial coming from symmetries on the three-manifold or the knot.
For example, the Alexander polynomial of the preimage $\widetilde{K}$ of a knot $K$
in its $n$-fold branched cover $\Sigma_{n}(K)$ is

$$
\Delta_{\widetilde K}(t) \doteq \prod_{i=1}^{n} \Delta_K(\xi_n^i t^{1/n}),
$$

where $\xi_n$ is a primitive $n$th root of unity. Similarly, let $K$ be a $q$-periodic
knot with quotient $\overline K$, and let $\lambda$ be the linking number of $\overline K$ with the
axis of periodicity $\overline A$. Let $\overline L=\overline K\cup\overline A$. Murasugi [Mur71] shows that the
Alexander polynomial of $K$ is

$$
\Delta_K(t) \doteq \Delta_{\overline K}(t)\prod_{i=1}^{q}\Delta_{\overline L}(t,\xi_q^i),
$$

implying in particular that $\Delta_{\overline K}(t)$ divides $\Delta_K(t)$ and that

$$
\Delta_K(t) \doteq (1+t+\cdots+t^{\lambda-1})^{q-1}\Delta_{\overline K}(t) \pmod{q}.
$$

where the equivalences above are up to a factor of $\pm t^{\pm i}$. Work of Hendricks
shows that knot Floer homology recovers this last condition [Hen15], but
a precise categorification of the first two remains unclear.

References cited:
- [FM66] Ralph H. Fox and John W. Milnor. Singularities of 2-spheres in 4-space and cobordism of knots. Osaka Math. J., 3:257–267, 1966. http://projecteuclid.org/euclid.ojm/1200691730.
- [Gil84] Patrick M. Gilmer. Ribbon concordance and a partial order on S-equivalence classes. Topology Appl., 18(2-3):313–324, 1984. doi:10.1016/0166-8641(84)90016-6.
- [Mur71] Kunio Murasugi. On periodic knots. Comment. Math. Helv., 46:162–174, 1971. doi:10.1007/BF02566836.
- [Hen15] Kristen Hendricks. Localization of the link Floer homology of doubly-periodic knots. J. Symplectic Geom., 13(3):545–608, 2015. doi:10.4310/JSG.2015.v13.n3.a2.

title: Kirby Problem 1.44
statement:
(a) If $K \in \mathcal{F}_{n}$ for all $n$, is $K$ topologically slice?
(b) If $K \in \mathcal{T}_{n}$ for all $n$, is $K$ smoothly slice?
background:
Source: Kirby's Problems in Low-Dimensional Topology notes. Original problem number: KP-1.44.

Literature notes:
(1) Let $\{\mathcal{F}_{n}\}_{n\in \frac{1}{2}\mathbb{N}}$ denote the solvable filtration of $\mathcal{C}$ due to Cochran-Orr-
Teichner [COT03], and let $\{\mathcal{T}_{n}\}_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ denote the bipolar filtration of $\mathcal{T}$ due
to Cochran-Harvey-Horn [CHH13].
(2) It is known that $\mathcal{T} \subseteq \bigcap_{n} \mathcal{F}_{n}$. The solvable filtration subsumes several
topological concordance invariants, e.g. a knot $K$ is in $\mathcal{F}_{0}$ if and only if
Arf $(K) = 0$; it is in $\mathcal{F}_{0.5}$ if and only if it is algebraically slice; and if $K$ is
in $\mathcal{F}_{1.5}$ then all its Casson-Gordon sliceness obstructions vanish [COT03].
Likewise, the bipolar filtration [CHH13] subsumes many smooth concor-
dance invariants, e.g. if a knot $K \in \mathcal{T}_{0}$ then $\tau(K) = \upsilon(K) = \Upsilon(K) =$
$\nu^{+}(K) = 0$, referring to invariants from Heegaard Floer homology.
It
is not known whether $s(K) = 0$, referring to the $s$-invariant from Kho-
vanov homology. However $s^{\#}(K) = 0$ [KM13b] (see also [Gon21]) and
$\widetilde{s}(K) = 0$ [DIS $^{+}25$].

References cited:
- [COT03] Tim D. Cochran, Kent E. Orr, and Peter Teichner. Knot concordance, Whitney towers and L2-signatures. Ann. of Math. (2), 157(2):433–519, 2003. doi:10.4007/annals.2003.157.433.
- [CHH13] Tim D. Cochran, Shelly Harvey, and Peter Horn. Filtering smooth concordance classes of topologically slice knots. Geom. Topol., 17(4):2103–2162, 2013. doi:10.2140/gt.2013.17.2103.
- [KM13b] P. B. Kronheimer and T. S. Mrowka. Gauge theory and Rasmussen’s invariant. J. Topol., 6(3):659–674, 2013. doi:10.1112/jtopol/jtt008.
- [Gon21] Sherry Gong. On the Kronheimer-Mrowka concordance invariant. J. Topol., 14(1):1–28, 2021. doi:10.1112/topo.12175.
- [DIS+25] Aliakbar Daemi, Hayato Imori, Kouki Sato, Christopher Scaduto, and Masaki Taniguchi. Instantons, special cycles and knot concordance. Geom. Topol., 29(8):4189–4298, 2025. doi:10.2140/gt.2025.29.4189.

title: Kirby Problem 1.45
statement:
(a) For arbitrary $n \geq 2.5$ and $g > 1$, does there exist a knot in $\mathcal{F}_{n}$ with
topological slice genus at least $g$?
(b) For arbitrary $n \geq 0$ and $g > 1$, does there exist a knot in $\mathcal{T}_{n}$ with smooth
slice genus at least $g$?
(c) Could the $L^{(2)}$-signature invariants used to obstruct membership in deeper
levels of the solvable/bipolar filtration be used to give bounds on the slice
genus?
background:
Source: Kirby's Problems in Low-Dimensional Topology notes. Original problem number: KP-1.45.

Literature notes:
(1) The problem originates from Cha [Cha08, Remark 5.6].
(2) The filtrations $\mathcal{F}_{n}$ and $\mathcal{T}_{n}$ of the smooth concordance group $\mathcal{C}$ and the
subgroup $\mathcal{T}$ of topologically slice knots, respectively, are defined in Prob-
lem 1.44.
(3) For (a), an affirmative answer for the $n = 0, 1$ cases can be shown using
Levine-Tristram and Casson–Gordon signatures respectively. Similar, an
affirmative answer to the $n = 2$ case was established by Cha–Miller–Powell
in [CMP21]. Unlike (a), question (b) is open even in the case $n = 0$.
(4) A knot is closer to being slice if it has low slice genus. Similarly it is closer
to being slice if it lies deeper in the solvable/bipolar filtrations. There-
fore the question is asking whether these two methods of approximating
sliceness are related.
(5) We note that there are many examples of highly solvable/bipolar knots
that are not known to have low slice genera–that is, the issue in part (c)
is not a lack of potential examples but rather a lack of obstructions.

References cited:
- [Cha08] Jae Choon Cha. Topological minimal genus and L2-signatures. Algebr. Geom. Topol., 8(2):885–909, 2008. doi:10.2140/agt.2008.8.885.

title: Kirby Problem 1.46
statement:
(a) Determine the topological slice genera of torus knots. In particular, does
the topological slice genus of a torus knot equal half the absolute value of
its maximal Levine–Tristram signature?
(b) Is a two-bridge knot topologically slice if and only if it is ribbon, if and
only if it is topologically homotopy-ribbon?
(c) Are the Casson–Gordon ribbon and topological sliceness obstructions [CG86]
complete for two-bridge knots?
(d) Can the difference between the smooth and topological slice genus of a
two-bridge knot be arbitrarily large?
background:
Source: Kirby's Problems in Low-Dimensional Topology notes. Original problem number: KP-1.46.

Literature notes:
(1) Most known methods to bound the topological slice genus from above are
based on Freedman–Quinn’s theorem that knots with Alexander polyno-
mial 1 are topologically slice [FQ90, BKK $^{+}21$]; the exception to this
is [FT05].
(2) The smooth slice genera of torus knots were determined by Kronheimer
and Mrowka using gauge theory: $g_{4}(T(p, q)) = (p - 1)(q - 1)/2$ [KM94].
The first person to show that the topological slice genus of torus knots is
typically less than their 3-genus was Rudolph [Rud84]. The topological
slice genus $g^{\mathrm{top}}_{4}(T(p,q))$ is less than the smooth slice genus $g_{4}(T(p,q))$
unless $T(p,q)$ has maximal signature, and in general
$g^{\mathrm{top}}_{4}(K)<pq/3+p\log_{2}q+q\log_{2}p$ [BFLL18, McC21].
(See [BBL20] for improved bounds in the case of $p = 3$.) All of the known lower bounds on
$g^{\mathrm{top}}_{4}(T(p,q))$
derive from the Seifert form of $T(p,q)$, and the largest of these is half of
the maximal Levine-Tristram signature (see also [Tay79]).
(3) The first part of the question is raised as a conjecture in [FM16, Conjec-
ture 1]. The question whether the Casson-Gordon ribbon obstruction is
complete is raised as a conjecture in [EL09, Conjecture 4.1].

Casson and Gordon introduced obstructions to a knot $K$ being ribbon
and to being topologically slice in [CG86]. They are defined in terms of
signatures associated with $n$-fold cyclic branched covering spaces of $K$ for
a prime power $n$. When $K = K(p, q)$ is a two-bridge knot and $n = 2$,
the ribbon obstruction is conjectured to be complete, but the topological
slice obstruction is known not to be [EL09, Mil18]. The two obstruc-
tions coincide when $p$ is a prime power and $n = 2$. Hence, if the ribbon
obstruction is complete, then the answer to the first part of the question
is affirmative when $p$ is a prime power. The ribbon obstruction actually
obstructs a knot being topologically homotopy-ribbon, meaning that the
map induced by inclusion of the knot complement into the complement
of a disk induces a surjection on fundamental groups. See Section 1.7 for
more discussion of notions of ribbonness.
Casson and Gordon also identified a family $\mathcal{R}$ of ribbon two-bridge
knots. Lisca used an obstruction based on Donaldson’s diagonalization
theorem to prove that $K(p, q)$ is smoothly slice iff $K(p, q) \in \mathcal{R}$ [Lis07]. It
follows that $\mathcal{R}$ accounts for all ribbon two-bridge knots.
The Casson-Gordon ribbon obstruction is expressed in terms of a
count of lattice points in triangular regions in the plane, while Lisca’s
smooth sliceness obstruction is expressed in terms of high-dimensional
lattice embeddings. It is possible that the two obstructions are equivalent
for number theoretic reasons.
If so, it would follow that the Casson-
Gordon ribbon obstruction is complete.
Lastly, it is possible that $K(p, q) \in \mathcal{R}$ if and only if $K(p, q)$ passes
the topological slice obstructions for all prime powers $n$. If so, this would
imply a positive solution to the stated question.
(4) The final question is raised by Feller and McCoy in [FM16, Question 3].
In contrast with the conjectured answer to the second question, they give
examples of 2-bridge knots $K$ for which $g^{\mathrm{top}}_{4}(K)=1$ and $g_{4}(K)=2$.

title: Kirby Problem 1.47
statement:
Given a smooth knot $K \subset S^{3}$, determine its nonorientable 4-
genus $\gamma_{4}$, i.e. the minimal first Betti number for all compact nonorientable smooth
surfaces $F$ properly embedded in $B^{4}$ with boundary $K$. This question may be devel-
oped in several directions:
(1) (Allen’s Geography Question [All23]) For a given knot $K \subset S^{3}$, find
the pairs $(e, b) \in \mathbb{Z}^{2}$ realized by the normal Euler number and first Betti
number of a nonorientable bounding surface $F$.
(2) By analogy with the Milnor Conjecture for the orientable 4-genus of torus
knots, what is the nonorientable 4-genus of a torus knot $T_{p,q}$?
background:
Source: Kirby's Problems in Low-Dimensional Topology notes. Original problem number: KP-1.47.

Literature notes:
The nonorientable 4-genus was first defined by Murakami and Ya-
suhara [MY00] in 2000, though earlier results had been obtained by Viro [Vir75]
and by Yasuhara [Yas96].
These authors, along with Gilmer and Livingston
[GL11], obstructed the existence of Möbius strips and punctured Klein bottles
with boundary $K$ using the classical signature and the Arf invariant of $K$.

The first examples of knots with $\gamma_{4}(K) > 3$ were produced by Batson, who
used an elegant construction and the Heegaard Floer $d$ invariant to prove that
$\gamma_{4}(T_{2k,2k-1}) = k - 1$ [Bat14]. Lobb subsequently showed that Batson’s construc-
tion does not always yield a minimal-genus nonorientable surface for torus knots
[Lob19]. Allen added context by asking how the nonorientable 4-genus interacts
with the normal Euler number of the bounding surfaces for torus (and other) knots
[All23]. See [BKST25, JVC21, OSS17a, Sab23], among others, for further
explorations of the nonorientable 4-genus for torus knots. In [All23], Allen made
three conjectures (Conjectures 1.6, 1.7, and 1.8); Sato [Sat24a] has given coun-
terexamples to Conjectures 1.6 and 1.8.
There are now many knots for which the nonorientable four-genus is known,
including all knots with at most 10 crossings [Gha22]. There are also currently
a variety of lower bounds for $\gamma_{4}$ using modern knot invariants.
Many of these
are what Sato [Sat24b] terms “unoriented slice-torus invariants”, including the $\upsilon$
invariant from Heegaard Floer theory [OSS17a], the $t$ invariant from Khovanov
homology [Bal20], the $h_{\mathbb{Z}}$ invariant from instanton homology [DS24a]. Additional
information about the nonorientable four-genus can be obtained by considering
versions of Seiberg-Witten Floer homology of the double branched cover that take
into account the involution coming from the covering transformation; see [BH24b,
KMT23b].

- [GL11] Patrick M. Gilmer and Charles Livingston. The nonorientable 4-genus of knots. J. Lond. Math. Soc. (2), 84(3):559–577, 2011. doi:10.1112/jlms/jdr024.
- [Bat14] Joshua Batson. Nonorientable slice genus can be arbitrarily large. Math. Res. Lett., 21(3):423–436, 2014. doi:10.4310/MRL.2014.v21.n3.a1.
- [Lob19] Andrew Lobb. A counterexample to Batson’s conjecture. Math. Res. Lett., 26(6):1789, 2019. doi:10.4310/MRL.2019.v26.n6.a8.

title: Kirby Problem 1.48
statement:
(a) Suppose $K$ and $K\#J$ are (smoothly) doubly slice knots.
Must $J$ be a
(smoothly) doubly slice knot?
(b) Does there exist a knot that is smoothly slice, topologically doubly slice, and
not smoothly doubly slice but such that $K\#K$ is smoothly doubly slice?
(c) Let $M$ and $N$ be closed 3-manifolds such that $M$ and $M\#N$ embed (smoothly)
in $S^{4}$. Must $N$ embed (smoothly) in $S^{4}$?
background:
Source: Kirby's Problems in Low-Dimensional Topology notes. Original problem number: KP-1.48.

Literature notes:
(1) A knot $K \subset S^{3}$ is called (smoothly) doubly slice if there is a (smoothly)
unknotted 2-sphere $\mathcal{\operatorname{U}} \subset S^{4}$ such that $K = S^{3} \cap \mathcal{\operatorname{U}}$.
(2) It is natural to try to equip the set of knots with the relation in which
$K_{0} \sim K_{1}$ if $K_{0}\#K_{1}$ is doubly slice. However, to prove this is an equiv-
alence relation, one must provide an affirmative answer to part (a) of
the problem. For more details, see [Mei15] and [Sto78]. This question
is also interesting in the topological category: Replace “smooth” with
“topologically locally flat” above. Question (a) is originally due to Stoltz-
fus [Sto78].
(3) One motivation for Question (a) is that it would allow for the formulation
of the Grothendieck group of knots modulo the relation discussed above.
In the absence of a positive answer to Question (a), there is an alternative
approach. Two knots $K_{0}$ and $K_{1}$ are called (smoothly) doubly concordant
if there exist (smoothly) doubly slice knots $J_{0}$ and $J_{1}$ such that $K_{0}\#J_{0} =$
$K_{1}\#J_{1}$. Let $\mathcal{C}_{\mathcal{D}}$ denote the group (under connected sum) of knots modulo
this equivalence relation, which is called the (smooth) double concordance

group.
An affirmative answer to Question (a) would mean the double
concordance group is the same as the aforementioned Grothendieck group.
A natural problem is to exhibit nontrivial elements in these groups, as we
now outline.
There is a topological version $\mathcal{C}_{\mathcal{D}}^{\mathrm{top}}$
of this group obtained by replacing
“smooth” with “topologically locally flat” above. There are epimorphisms
from $\mathcal{C}_{\mathcal{D}}$ to $\mathcal{C}_{\mathcal{D}}^{\mathrm{top}}$
and to the smooth concordance group $\mathcal{C}$. Let $\mathcal{K}$ denote the
intersection of the kernels of these two homomorphisms. It is known that
$\mathcal{K}$ contains an infinitely generated subgroup $S$ with generators of order at
least 3 [Mei15].
Conjecture. These generators of $S$ have infinite order.
(4) There are many techniques for producing and studying 2-torsion in the
smooth concordance group $\mathcal{C}$; see [HKL16a] for a nice overview. However,
these techniques seem difficult to apply to $\mathcal{C}_{\mathcal{D}}$, which motivates Question
(b).
(5) If $K$ is doubly slice, then any cyclic cover of $S^{3}$ branched along $K$ embeds
(smoothly) in $S^{4}$. This suggests Question (c), which asks about embed-
ding 3-manifolds in $S^{4}$. The connection between doubly slice knots, em-
bedding problems and homology cobordisms was observed by Gilmer and
Livingston [GL83]. See also Problem 4.25.

References cited:
- [Mei15] Jeffrey Meier. Distinguishing topologically and smoothly doubly slice knots. J. Topol., 8(2):315–351, 2015. doi:10.1112/jtopol/jtu027.
- [Sto78] Neal W. Stoltzfus. Algebraic computations of the integral concordance and double null concordance group of knots. In Knot theory (Proc. Sem., Plans-sur-Bex, 1977), volume 685 of Lecture Notes in Math., pages 274–290. Springer, Berlin, 1978.
- [HKL16a] Matthew Hedden, Se-Goo Kim, and Charles Livingston. Topologically slice knots of smooth concordance order two. J. Differential Geom., 102(3):353–393, 2016. http://projecteuclid.org/euclid.jdg/1456754013.
- [GL83] Patrick M. Gilmer and Charles Livingston. On embedding 3-manifolds in 4-space. Topology, 22(3):241–252, 1983. doi:10.1016/0040-9383(83)90011-3.

title: Kirby Problem 1.49
statement:
(a) What is the structure of the equivariant concordance groups?
(b) Is the strongly negative amphichiral concordance group abelian?
(c) For any type of knot involution, is it possible to exhibit $K_{1}$ and $K_{2}$ that
are equivariantly concordant but not standardly equivariantly concordant?
(d) Does there exist a freely periodic slice knot that is not equivariantly slice?
(e) (Boyle-Rouse) Is every periodic or freely periodic $L$-space knot either a
torus knot or an iterated torus knot?
background:
Source: Kirby's Problems in Low-Dimensional Topology notes. Original problem number: KP-1.49.

Literature notes:
(1) Knots may have various sorts of symmetries; an equivariant concordance
is a usual concordance that admits the same sort of symmetry. In the
topological case, we require that the concordance be locally flat, and that
any group action be locally linear. There are several variations discussed
in this problem, each with its own particular set of concerns.
(2) Equivariant concordance groups can be defined for the classes of strongly
invertible and strongly negative amphichiral knots. The strongly invert-
ible concordance group has been studied by several authors: for instance,
there exists a homomorphism to the Laurent polynomial ring $\mathbb{Z}[t, t^{-1}]$
[Sak86]. These groups are not a priori abelian due to (possible) depen-
dence on the choice of the connected sum point, which must be taken to be
one of the two fixed points of the symmetry on the knot. In the strongly
invertible case, it is known that the group is not abelian [DP23b], but in
the amphichiral case this is not known.

Understanding strongly negative amphichiral knots is especially inter-
esting, since the branched covers of such knots may provide examples of
2-torsion in the integer homology cobordism group. Examples of strongly
negative amphichiral knots with determinant one were exhibited by Boyle
and Chen in [BC24b].
(3) In part (c), we say that two knots $K_{1}$ and $K_{2}$ (equipped with the same
type of involution) are standardly equivariantly concordant if they are
connected by a smooth annular cobordism in $S^{3}\times I$ that is invariant under
an involution on $S^{3} \times I$ that restricts to a standard involution on each
$S^{3} \times \{t\}$. One can also consider more general equivariant cobordisms, in
which one requires that the annular cobordism be fixed by some involution
on $S^{3} \times I$ which extends the actions on $S^{3} \times \{0\}$ and $S^{3} \times \{1\}$. It is not
known in any of the possible cases whether these notions coincide. The
question may be asked in either the smooth or the topological category.
In the case of 2-periodic and strongly invertible knots, it is known
that there exists a nonstandard involution on $S^{3} \times I$ that restricts to the
standard involution on $S^{3}\times\{0\}$ and $S^{3}\times\{1\}$. To construct one, start with
an involution on $S^{4}$ with fixed-point set a knotted $S^{2}$ [Sum75]; punctur-
ing such an example gives a nonstandard involution on $S^{3} \times I$ that has
fixed-point set $S^{1}$ on each of the two ends. It is not known whether an
interesting such involution exists in the freely periodic or strongly am-
phichiral cases.
(4) Question (d) appears as Question 1 in [BM23]. Manolescu and Willis
[MW25] gave examples of freely 2-periodic knots that are concordant
but not (standardly) equivariantly concordant.
(5) Evidence for Question (e) comes from classic work of Murasugi [Mur71]
and Hartley [Har81], who established factorization results for the Alexan-
der polynomials of periodic or freely periodic knots. We also have several
well-known restrictions on the Alexander polynomials of L-space knots;
see [OS05b] or [HW18]. As discussed by Boyle and Rouse [BR23b],
the only known examples of Alexander polynomials that simultaneously
satisfy all of these conditions are products of cyclotomic polynomials. On
the other hand, a conjecture of Li and Ni states that the only L-space
knots with Alexander polynomials which are products of cyclotomic poly-
nomials are torus knots or iterated torus knots [LN15]. Based on this,
Boyle and Rouse [BR23b] conjectured a positive answer to Question (e).

References cited:
- [Sak86] Makoto Sakuma. On strongly invertible knots. In Algebraic and topological theories (Kinosaki, 1984), pages 176–196. Kinokuniya, Tokyo, 1986.
- [DP23b] Alessio Di Prisa. The equivariant concordance group is not abelian. Bull. Lond. Math. Soc., 55(1):502–507, 2023. doi:10.1112/blms.12741.
- [BC24b] Keegan Boyle and Wenzhao Chen. Equivariant topological slice disks and negative amphichiral knots. Indiana Univ. Math. J., 73(5):1623–1637, 2024.
- [Sum75] D. W. Sumners. Smooth $\mathbb{Z}_p$-actions on spheres which leave knots pointwise fixed. Trans. Amer. Math. Soc., 205:193–203, 1975. doi:10.2307/1997199.
- [BM23] Keegan Boyle and Jeffrey Musyt. Equivariant cobordisms between freely periodic knots. Canad. Math. Bull., 66(2):450–457, 2023. doi:10.4153/S000843952200042X.
- [MW25] Ciprian Manolescu and Michael Willis. A Rasmussen invariant for links in $\mathbb{RP}^{3}$. Trans. Amer. Math. Soc. Ser. B, 12:789–830, 2025. doi:10.1090/btran/221.
- [Mur71] Kunio Murasugi. On periodic knots. Comment. Math. Helv., 46:162–174, 1971. doi:10.1007/BF02566836.
- [Har81] Richard Hartley. Knots with free period. Canadian J. Math., 33(1):91–102, 1981. doi:10.4153/CJM-1981-009-7.
- [OS05b] Peter Ozsváth and Zoltán Szabó. On knot Floer homology and lens space surgeries. Topology, 44(6):1281–1300, 2005. doi:10.1016/j.top.2005.05.001.
- [HW18] Matthew Hedden and Liam Watson. On the geography and botany of knot Floer homology. Selecta Math. (N.S.), 24(2):997–1037, 2018. doi:10.1007/s00029-017-0351-5.

title: Kirby Problem 1.50
statement:
(a) Is every slice knot a ribbon knot?
(b) Is every slice link ribbon?
(c) Suppose $K$ is a knot with smooth four-genus $g_{4}(K) = g$. Does $K$ bound a
smooth, genus $g$, ribbon surface $F$ in $B^{4}$?
background:
Source: Kirby's Problems in Low-Dimensional Topology notes. Original problem number: KP-1.50.

Literature notes:
(1) The Slice-Ribbon Conjecture (a) was first posed as a question by Fox
in 1961 [Fox62, Problem 25], and was discussed in [Kir97, Problem
4.22].
Very limited progress has been made on this problem, though
the conjecture has been verified for 2-bridge knots by Lisca [Lis07] and
most 3-stranded pretzel knots by Greene and Jabuka [GJ11] and by
Lecuona [Lec15].
(2) There are other notions of “ribbonness” that can be considered: A knot
$K \subset S^{3}$ is called homotopy-ribbon if there is a slice disk $D$ for $K$ with a
surjection $\pi_{1}(S^{3}\setminus K) \twoheadrightarrow\pi_{1}(B^{4}\setminus D)$ and is called handle-ribbon if there is
a slice disk $D$ for $K$ such that $B^{4}\setminus\nu(D)$ admits a handle-decomposition
with only 0-, 1-, and 2-handles; see [Gor81, LM15, MZ23].
(3) The implications
ribbon $\Rightarrow$ handle ribbon $\Rightarrow$ homotopy-ribbon $\Rightarrow$ slice
are immediate, but all three converse implications are open.
(4) For many examples of handle ribbon knots and links that are not known
to be ribbon, as well as connections to the Generalized Property R Con-
jecture, see [GST10, MZ22] and Problem 1.10.
(5) Miyazaki gave many examples of non-simple knots that are not homotopi-
cally ribbon, such as certain linear combinations of algebraic knots and,
famously, the $(2, 1)$-cable of the figure-8 knot [Miy94]. Some of these ex-
amples are now known to be non-slice [HKL12, DKM $^{+}24$, ACM $^{+}26$].
Baker draws connections between the Slice-Ribbon Conjecture for fibered
knots and contact topology in [Bak16]. See Problem 1.54 for more ques-
tions about ribbon concordances.
(6) In part (b), we say that an $n$-component link $L \subset S^{3}$ is called (strongly)
slice if there is a disjoint collection $D \subset B^{4}$ of $n$ disks with $\partial D = L$;
the notions of ribbon, handle-ribbon, and homotopy-ribbon have obvious
analogs for links.
(7) Many examples of handle ribbon links that are not known to be ribbon
are constructed in [GST10] and [MZ22, MZ25].
(8) Eisermann [Eis09] gave an obstruction for a link (with at least two com-
ponents) to be ribbon, in terms of the Jones polynomial. It is not clear
whether his obstruction vanishes when the link is handle ribbon (or homotopy-
ribbon, or slice) so, in principle, it could be used to show that a handle
ribbon link is not ribbon.
(9) The question in part (c) generalizes the Slice-Ribbon Conjecture, and so
it may be easier to find a counterexample. If $g_{4}(K) = g(K)$, then the
push-in of a minimal genus Seifert surface is a ribbon surface realizing

the minimum possible value of $g_{4}(K)$, so the question has an affirmative
answer in this case.
(10) Finally, the question of whether slice implies homotopy-ribbon can be
phrased in the more general setting of knots in homology 3–spheres bound-
ing disks in contractible 4–manifolds. For more details, see [Kir97, Prob-
lem 4.22] and [CG83a].

title: Kirby Problem 1.51
statement: Does every ribbon knot arise as a symmetric union?
background:
Source: Kirby's Problems in Low-Dimensional Topology notes. Original problem number: KP-1.51.

Literature notes:
Symmetric unions were introduced by Kinoshita and Terasaka to
construct knots with Alexander polynomial 1 (by taking a symmetric union of an
unknot diagram) [KT57]. It is straightforward to see that every symmetric union is
a ribbon knot. A census shows that most small ribbon knots do arise as symmetric
unions [Lam21], but there are candidates for ribbon knots that are not symmetric
unions, such as $3_{1}\#8_{10}$ and $3_{1}\#8_{11}$. Other potential counterexamples obtained as
certain satellites of knots of the form $K\# - K$ are given by Aceto [Ace14]. These
knots have ribbon number two, but the symmetric ribbon number is shown to be
arbitrarily large, if not infinite.

References cited:
- [KT57] Shin’ichi Kinoshita and Hidetaka Terasaka. On unions of knots. Osaka Math. J., 9:131–153, 1957.
- [Lam21] Christoph Lamm. The search for nonsymmetric ribbon knots. Exp. Math., 30(3):349–363, 2021. doi:10.1080/10586458.2018.1540313.
- [Ace14] Paolo Aceto. Symmetric ribbon disks. J. Knot Theory Ramifications, 23(9):1450048, 9, 2014. doi:10.1142/S0218216514500485.

title: Kirby Problem 1.52
statement:
Given $K$ in $S^{3}$, is there an algorithm to detect if $K$ is slice?
Ribbon?
background:
Source: Kirby's Problems in Low-Dimensional Topology notes. Original problem number: KP-1.52.

Literature notes:
(1) This is Problem 1.34 from [Kir97], posed by A. Casson.
(2) There is still no algorithm, but there have been some interesting computer-
aided searches: Owens and Swenton search for ribbon bands for alternat-
ing knots [OS23] and Gukov, Halverson, Manolescu, and Ruehle apply
machine learning algorithms to the problem [GHMR23]. Dunfield and
Gong [DG25] have announced the results of a search for ribbon knots,
slice knots, and concordances among the knots with at most 19 crossings.
(3) Casson and Long gave an algorithm to determine if a surface automor-
phism compresses [CL85]. In conjunction with the main results of [CG83a],
this algorithm can be used to determine whether a given fibered knot
bounds a fibered, homotopy-ribbon disk in a homotopy four-ball; see
also [Lon86].

title: Kirby Problem 1.53
statement:
(a) Which knot properties are hereditary under ribbon concordance? Is the
property of being alternating hereditary under ribbon concordance?
(b) Which knot properties imply minimality under ribbon concordance? Are
positive knots minimal under ribbon concordance?
(c) Which knot invariants are monotone under ribbon concordance? Is cross-
ing number, bridge number, or braid index monotone under ribbon con-
cordance?
background:
Source: Kirby's Problems in Low-Dimensional Topology notes. Original problem number: KP-1.53.

Literature notes:
(1) A knot property is a subset $\mathcal{P}$ of the set of knots. It is hereditary under a
directed relation $\mathcal{R}$ on the set of knots if $K_{1} \in \mathcal{P}, K_{0}\mathcal{R}K_{1} \Longrightarrow K_{0} \in \mathcal{P}$.
(2) Using techniques of Silver and the solution of Rapoport’s conjecture given
by Kochloukova, Miyazaki showed that the property of being fibered is
hereditary under ribbon concordance [Koc06, Miy18, Sil92] in the sense
that if $K_{1}$ is ribbon concordant to $K_{0}$ and $K_{1}$ is fibered, then so is $K_{0}$; see
also work of Zemke [Zem19a]. It is conjectured that the property of being
alternating is hereditary under ribbon concordance [GO23, Conjecture 9].
(3) A knot $K_{1}$ is minimal under $\mathcal{R}$ if $K_{0}\mathcal{R}K_{1} \Longrightarrow K_{1} = K_{0}$. It is conjectured
that positive knots are minimal under ribbon concordance [BG24, Con-
jecture 1.6]. Baker and Stoimenow have asked related questions [Bak16,
Sto15]. See also Problem 1.54.
(4) Most knot invariants support natural directed relations $\preceq$ on their codomains:
numerical (real-valued) invariants with respect to the standard ordering
$\leq$; polynomial invariants with respect to divisibility; group-valued invari-
ants with respect to injections; etc. A knot invariant $\iota$ is monotone under
a directed relation $\mathcal{R}$ if $K_{0}\mathcal{R}K_{1} \Longrightarrow \iota(K_{0}) \preceq \iota(K_{1})$.
Several knot invariants are known to be monotone under ribbon con-
cordance. For example, if $K_{1}$ is ribbon concordant to $K_{0}$, the Alexander
polynomial of $K_{0}$ divides that of $K_{1}$ [Gil84, FP20]. Zemke showed that
a ribbon concordance from $K_{1}$ to $K_{0}$ induces a bigraded injection from the
knot Floer homology of $K_{0}$ to $K_{1}$, with the consequence that the Seifert
genus of $K_{0}$ is less than or equal to that of $K_{1}$ [Zem19a]. It is known that
if $K_{1}$ has bridge number 2, then $K_{0}$ has bridge number at most 2 [GO23,
Paragraph after Conjecture 9].
(5) Gordon’s pioneering paper on ribbon concordance contains several fasci-
nating problems related to the ones raised here [Gor81].

- [Miy18] Katura Miyazaki. A note on genera of band sums that are fibered. J. Knot Theory Ramifications, 27(12):1871002, 3, 2018. doi:10.1142/S0218216518710025.

- [Zem19a] Ian Zemke. Knot Floer homology obstructs ribbon concordance. Ann. of Math. (2), 190(3):931–947, 2019. doi:10.4007/annals.2019.190.3.5.
- [GO23] Joshua Evan Greene and Brendan Owens. Alternating links, rational balls, and cube tilings, 2023. J. Eur. Math. Soc., to appear. arXiv:2212.06248.
- [BG24] Joe Boninger and Joshua Evan Greene. Special alternating knots are band prime. Int. Math. Res. Not., 2024(10):8758–8763, 2024. doi:10.1093/imrn/rnae009.

title: Kirby Problem 1.54
statement:
This problem is concerned with the restriction of the partial
ordering $\geq$ coming from ribbon concordance to the concordance class $[K]$ of a knot
$K$.
(a) What can be said about the order type of $[K]$?
(b) Does it depend on $[K]$? Must it contain a (unique) minimal element?
(c) (Gordon) Does there exist a concordance class of knots that contains two
minimal elements with respect to ribbon concordance?
background:
Source: Kirby's Problems in Low-Dimensional Topology notes. Original problem number: KP-1.54.

Literature notes:
(1) The ribbon concordance relation was defined by Gordon in [Gor81], who
proves that some classes $[K]$ contain minimal elements, and asked Ques-
tion (c).
(2) The ribbon concordance relation was conjectured to be a partial ordering
by Gordon. This was proved by Agol [Ago22]. Notice that for any knots
$K$ and $L$, the map from $[K]$ to $[L]$ defined for $J \in [K]$ by

$$
J \mapsto J \# -K \# L
$$

is an order preserving injection.
(3) The Slice-Ribbon Conjecture can be formulated to say the unknot $\operatorname{U}$ is
the unique minimal element of $[\operatorname{U}]$; see Problem 1.50.
See Problem 1.56 for a Heegaard Floer theory perspective.

References cited:
- [Gor81] C. McA. Gordon. Ribbon concordance of knots in the 3-sphere. Math. Ann., 257(2):157–170, 1981. doi:10.1007/BF01458281.
- [Ago22] Ian Agol. Ribbon concordance of knots is a partial ordering. Comm. Amer. Math. Soc., 2:374–379, 2022. doi:10.1090/cams/15.

title: Kirby Problem 1.55
statement:
Suppose that $C$ is a ribbon concordance from a fibered knot $K_{1}$
to a fibered knot $K_{0}$.
(a) Does the capped-off monodromy of $K_{1}$ (i.e. extended over a disk) extend to
a compression body whose lower boundary gives the capped-off monodromy
of $K_{0}$?
(b) Is $C$ fibered by compression bodies?
(c) Suppose a fibered knot in a homology 3-sphere bounds a homotopy-ribbon
disk $D$ in a contractible 4-manifold $V$ . Is $V \setminus\nu(D)$ fibered by handlebodies?
background:
Source: Kirby's Problems in Low-Dimensional Topology notes. Original problem number: KP-1.55.

Literature notes:
(1) Part (a) holds when $K_{0}$ is the unknot by the main theorem of [CG83a].
(2) Miller answers part (b) in the affirmative under the hypothesis that the
ribbon concordance is defined by a collection of ribbon bands that are
transverse to the fibration of the exterior of $K_{1}$ [Mil21, Theorem 1.9].
(3) Part (c) was posed by Casson and Gordon in the Remark before Corol-
lary 5.4 of [CG83a].

References cited:
- [CG83a] A. J. Casson and C. McA. Gordon. A loop theorem for duality spaces and fibred ribbon knots. Invent. Math., 74(1):119–137, 1983. doi:10.1007/BF01388533.
- [Mil21] Maggie Miller. Extending fibrations of knot complements to ribbon disk complements. Geom. Topol., 25(3):1479–1550, 2021. doi:10.2140/gt.2021.25.1479.

title: Kirby Problem 1.56
statement:
(Hom). If $K_{0}$ and $K_{1}$ are ribbon concordant and

$$
\widehat{\mathrm{HFK}}(K_{0}) \cong \widehat{\mathrm{HFK}}(K_{1}),
$$

are $K_{0}$ and $K_{1}$ isotopic?
background:
Source: Kirby's Problems in Low-Dimensional Topology notes. Original problem number: KP-1.56.

Literature notes:
(1) Recall that Zemke [Zem19a] proved that a ribbon concordance induces
a split injection on knot Floer homology.
Gordon asked the following
[Gor81, Question 6.2]: If $K_{1} \geq K_{2} \geq...$ , does there exist some $m$
such that $K_{n} = K_{m}$ for all $n \geq m$? An affirmative answer to Problem
1.56 would answer Gordon’s question in the affirmative. One large class of
concordant knots with the same knot Floer homology is given in [Wan22,

Theorem 1.2] (see also [HW18, Theorem 1]), but none of these are ribbon
concordant to any other, by [Wan22, Theorem 1.8] and [LZ19].
(2) The same question could be asked with Khovanov homology
$\widetilde{\mathrm{Kh}}$ replacing knot Floer homology $\widehat{\mathrm{HFK}}$,
or indeed other homology theories as treated
in [Kan22a].

References cited:
- [Zem19a] Ian Zemke. Knot Floer homology obstructs ribbon concordance. Ann. of Math. (2), 190(3):931–947, 2019. doi:10.4007/annals.2019.190.3.5.

- [Wan22] Joshua Wang. The cosmetic crossing conjecture for split links. Geom. Topol., 26(7):2941–3053, 2022. doi:10.2140/gt.2022.26.2941.
- [HW18] Matthew Hedden and Liam Watson. On the geography and botany of knot Floer homology. Selecta Math. (N.S.), 24(2):997–1037, 2018. doi:10.1007/s00029-017-0351-5.

- [Kan22a] Sungkyung Kang. Link homology theories and ribbon concordances. Quantum Topol., 13(1):183–205, 2022. doi:10.4171/qt/162.

title: Kirby Problem 1.57
statement:
(a) In either the smooth or topological settings, are 0-shake slice knots slice?
(b) Does there exist a knot $K$ whose topological 0-shake slice genus is strictly
less than the topological slice genus?
background:
Source: Kirby's Problems in Low-Dimensional Topology notes. Original problem number: KP-1.57.

Literature notes:
(1) The smooth analogue of the second question was [Kir97, Problem 1.41],
which was answered in the negative by Piccirillo in [Pic19]. Her construc-
tion uses knots with diffeomorphic 0-traces whose smooth slice genera are
distinct. A negative answer to part (a) would imply the existence of a knot
that is slice in an integer homology ball but not in $B^{4}$; see Problem 1.60.
(2) One may also ask analogous questions for $n$-traces of knots, where some
negative answers are known.
For more on this see [Akb77, Lic79,
Akb93, AJOT13].

title: Kirby Problem 1.58
statement:
What concordance information about a knot $K$ is contained in
its 0-trace $X_{0}(K)$ and in its 0-surgery $S^{3}_{0}(K)$?
Specifically,
(a) Suppose $K$ and $K'$ have homeomorphic 0-traces.
(i) Are $K$ and $K'$ topologically concordant?
(ii) What if one just assumes $K$ and $K'$ have homeomorphic 0-surgeries?
(iii) What if one just assumes $K$ and $K'$ have 0-surgeries that are topolog-
ically homology cobordant, preserving the homology class of a merid-
ian.

(b) Suppose $K$ and $K'$ have homeomorphic 0-surgeries, where the image of
the meridian of $K$ is freely homotopic to the meridian of $K'$. Are $K$ and
$K'$ smoothly concordant?
background:
Source: Kirby's Problems in Low-Dimensional Topology notes. Original problem number: KP-1.58.

Literature notes:
(1) This problem originates in a conjecture of Akbulut and Kirby [Kir97,
Problem 1.19] that knots with the same 0-surgery are concordant. It was
motivated, at least in part, by the fact [KM78] that it holds when one
of the knots is unknotted. (The result of [KM78] predates the proof of
Property R, which is of course much stronger.)
Although the original
conjecture is false, there are several variations, as one can ask about the
homeomorphism or diffeomorphism type of $X_{0}(K)$ and about smooth or
topological concordance.
(2) All of the questions in part (a) have negative answers if one is looking for
smooth concordances; see [CFHH13], [Yas17], [MP18]. With reference
to Question (a)(iii) and part (b), note that a concordance would preserve
the free homotopy class (and hence homology class) of a meridian.
(3) Part (b) has a negative answer without the assumption on the meridian,
see [Yas17]. There are no examples in the literature of homeomorphisms,
satisfying the assumption on the meridian, between 0-surgeries on distinct
knots.

References cited:
- [Kir97] R.C. Kirby. Problems in low–dimensional topology. In W. Kazez, editor, Geometric Topology. American Math. Soc./International Press, Providence, 1997.
- [KM78] Robion Kirby and Paul Melvin. Slice knots and property R. Invent. Math., 45(1):57– 59, 1978. doi:10.1007/BF01406223.
- [CFHH13] Tim D. Cochran, Bridget D. Franklin, Matthew Hedden, and Peter D. Horn. Knot concordance and homology cobordism. Proc. Amer. Math. Soc., 141(6):2193–2208, 2013. doi:10.1090/S0002-9939-2013-11471-1.
- [Yas17] Kouichi Yasui. Corks, exotic 4-manifolds and knot concordance, 2017. arXiv:1505.02551.
- [MP18] Allison N. Miller and Lisa Piccirillo. Knot traces and concordance. J. Topol., 11(1):201–220, 2018. doi:10.1112/topo.12054.

title: Kirby Problem 1.59
statement:
Let $K \subset S^{3}$ be a slice knot.
(a) Determine the set $\mathcal{R}(K)$ of ribbon disks bounded by $K$ modulo isotopy.
(b) Determine the set $\mathcal{D}(K)$ of slice disks bounded by $K$ modulo isotopy and
local knotting.
(c) Determine the set $\mathcal{H}\mathcal{R}(K)$ of homotopy-ribbon disks bounded by $K$ modulo
isotopy.
(d) If $K$ is fibered, determine the set $\mathcal{F}\mathcal{H}\mathcal{R}(K)$ of fibered, homotopy-ribbon
disks bounded by $K$ in some homotopy 4-ball, modulo isotopy.
background:
Source: Kirby's Problems in Low-Dimensional Topology notes. Original problem number: KP-1.59.

Literature notes:
(1) There is no knot for which part (a) has been solved. A knot with $|\mathcal{R}(K)| =$
0 would be a counter-example to the Slice-Ribbon Conjecture. It is un-
known whether or not $|\mathcal{R}(\operatorname{U})| = 1$ for the unknot $\operatorname{U}$, though Scharlemann
has shown that any non-standard ribbon disk for the unknot must have at
least three minima [Sch85a]. It is known that $\mathcal{R}(Q_{p,2})$ is infinite [MZ25],
where $Q_{p,q} = T_{p,q}\#\overline{T}_{p,q}$ is the connected sum of a torus knot with its mir-
ror.
(2) There are many knots that bound isotopic ribbon disks that are dis-
tinct when considered up to isotopy rel. boundary: Any knot of the form
$J\# - J$ bounds infinitely many isotopic ribbon disks that are pairwise
non-isotopic rel. boundary, as follows from Zeeman’s twist-spinning con-
struction [Zee65]; see, for example, [MZ25, Proposition 2.2]. Addition-
ally, many simple knots such as the stevedore knot $6_{1}$ and pretzel knots

$P(p, -p, p)$ bound pairs of such disks. The problems of studying disks
modulo isotopy and modulo isotopy rel. boundary are closely related via
an understanding of the symmetries of the boundary knot; see the proofs
of [JZ20b, Lemma 2.2], [MZ25, Theorem 1.5], and [MM25b, Theo-
rem 4.2].
(3) The set $\mathcal{D}(K)$ has recently been studied using modern invariants [JZ20b],
classical invariants [MP19], and geometric techniques [MM25b]. It is
immediate that $|\mathcal{D}(\operatorname{U})| = 1$ for $\operatorname{U}$ the unknot, but $\mathcal{D}(K)$ is not known for
any nontrivial knot $K$.
(4) Consider the map $\iota_{K}: \mathcal{H}\mathcal{R}(K) \to \mathcal{D}(K)$. Is there a knot $K$ such that
this map is injective, surjective, or has finite image? See [MM25b, Sec-
tion 1.1]. There is no knot for which part (c) has been solved.
(5) Given the apparent difficulty in solving the above problems, it is rea-
sonable to look for more tractable alternatives in which there is more
structure, such as part (d).
Casson and Gordon found a beautiful connection between fibered,
homotopy-ribbon disks bounded by a fibered knot $K$ and handlebody
extensions of the closed monodromy of $K$ [CG83a].
Here, the extra
structure yields more positive results. First, $|\mathcal{F}\mathcal{H}\mathcal{R}(\operatorname{U})| = 1$. Second, for
all coprime $p > q > 1$, the set $\mathcal{F}\mathcal{H}\mathcal{R}(Q_{p,q})$ has been explicitly determined;
the set $\mathcal{F}\mathcal{H}\mathcal{R}_{\partial}(Q_{p,q})$ of fibered, homotopy-ribbon disks modulo isotopy
rel. boundary is in explicit bijection with $\{c/d \in \mathbb{Q}: c$ even $\}$ [MZ25].

References cited:
- [Sch85a] Martin Scharlemann. Smooth spheres in $\mathbb{R}^{4}$ with four critical points are standard. Invent. Math., 79(1):125–141, 1985. doi:10.1007/BF01388659.
- [MZ25] Jeffrey Meier and Alexander Zupan. Knots bounding nonisotopic ribbon disks. J. Topol., 18(4):Paper No. e70047, 18, 2025. doi:10.1112/topo.70047.
- [Zee65] E. C. Zeeman. Twisting spun knots. Trans. Amer. Math. Soc., 115:471–495, 1965. doi:10.2307/1994281.
- [JZ20b] András Juhász and Ian Zemke. Distinguishing slice disks using knot Floer homology. Selecta Math. (N.S.), 26(1):Paper No. 5, 18, 2020. doi:10.1007/s00029-019-0531-6.
- [MM25b] Jeffrey Meier and Allison N. Miller. Slice disks modulo local knotting, 2025. arXiv: 2503.09870.
- [MP19] Allison N. Miller and Mark Powell. Stabilization distance between surfaces. Enseign. Math., 65(3-4):397–440, 2019. doi:10.4171/lem/65-3/4-4.
- [CG83a] A. J. Casson and C. McA. Gordon. A loop theorem for duality spaces and fibred ribbon knots. Invent. Math., 74(1):119–137, 1983. doi:10.1007/BF01388533.

title: Kirby Problem 1.60
statement:
Is there a knot in $S^{3}$ that is not smoothly slice in $B^{4}$ but is
smoothly slice in an integer homology ball? What about a $\mathbb{Z}$/2-homology ball?
background:
Source: Kirby's Problems in Low-Dimensional Topology notes. Original problem number: KP-1.60.

Literature notes:
(1) As discussed in [FGMW10], one strategy to disprove the smooth Poincaré
conjecture is to find a homotopy four-sphere $X$ and a knot $K$ in $S^{3}$ that is
smoothly slice in $X - B^{4}$ but not in $B^{4}$; see also Problem 4.1. It is worth
remarking that just about all known slice obstructions necessarily vanish
for a knot that is slice in an integer homology ball. One invariant that
can potentially make this distinction is the $s$-invariant from Khovanov
homology [Ras10]. As a warm-up, it would be interesting to find a knot
$K$ with $s(K) \neq 0$ that is smoothly slice in a rational homology ball.
(2) Fintushel-Stern showed the figure-eight knot is smoothly slice in a rational
homology ball with $\pi_{1} = \mathbb{Z}/2$ [FS84], but is not even topologically slice
in $B^{4}$ by the Fox-Milnor condition. For all known examples of knots that
are slice in a rational ball but not $B^{4}$, the rational ball has 2-torsion
in $H_{1}$. Kawauchi shows that all strongly negative-amphichiral knots are
rationally slice [Kaw09] and Levine showed they are slice in the same
rational homology ball $Z_{0}$ [Lev23]; in fact, he asks if it is possible that
all rationally slice knots are slice in boundary sums of $Z_{0}$.

References cited:
- [FGMW10] Michael Freedman, Robert Gompf, Scott Morrison, and Kevin Walker. Man and machine thinking about the smooth 4-dimensional Poincaré conjecture. Quantum Topol., 1(2):171–208, 2010. doi:10.4171/QT/5.
- [Ras10] Jacob Rasmussen. Khovanov homology and the slice genus. Invent. Math., 182(2):419–447, 2010. doi:10.1007/s00222-010-0275-6.
- [FS84] Ronald Fintushel and Ronald J. Stern. A µ-invariant one homology 3-sphere that bounds an orientable rational ball. In Four-manifold theory (Durham, N.H., 1982), volume 35 of Contemp. Math., pages 265–268. Amer. Math. Soc., Providence, RI, 1984. doi:10.1090/conm/035/780582.
- [Kaw09] Akio Kawauchi. Rational-slice knots via strongly negative-amphicheiral knots. Commun. Math. Res., 25(2):177–192, 2009.
- [Lev23] Adam Simon Levine. A note on rationally slice knots. New York J. Math., 29:1363– 1372, 2023. https://nyjm.albany.edu/j/2023/29-52p.pdf.
