title: Kirby Problem 1.61
statement:
A knot in $S^{3}$ bounds a topological disk in $B^{4}$ by coning (not
necessarily locally flat); this problem asks about topological disks that a knot in a
homology sphere $Y$ might bound in a homology or homotopy ball bounded by $Y$ .
(a) Given a locally flat knot in an integer homology 3-sphere, is it concordant
to a knot in $S^{3}$, via a locally flat annulus in a topological integer homology
cobordism? Variation: Can the homology cobordism be taken to be simply
connected?
(b) Given an arbitrary knot in an integer homology 3-sphere $Y$ , does it bound
an embedded disc (not necessarily locally flat) in $\Delta$, the Freedman filling
of $Y$ ? Variation: Is there such a disk in a homology ball bounded by $Y$ ?
(c) Is there a link in an integer homology 3-sphere, each of whose components
is independently concordant to a knot in $S^{3}$, that is not itself concordant
to a link in $S^{3}$.
(d) Suppose that $\mathbb{Z}_{n}$ acts semi-freely on the homology sphere $Y$ , with fixed
point set a knot $K$. Does the action of $\mathbb{Z}_{n}$ extend semi-freely over $\Delta$?
background:
Source: Kirby's Problems in Low-Dimensional Topology notes. Original problem number: KP-1.61.

Literature notes:
(1) By the proof of [Fre82, Theorem 1.4'] every integer homology 3-sphere
bounds a compact, contractible 4-manifold $\Delta$, which we call the Freed-
man filling of $Y$ . It is known to be unique up to homeomorphism, by
Freedman’s $h$-cobordism theorem [Fre82, Theorems 1.3 and 1.6].
(2) The smooth analogue of (a) was disproved by A. Levine [Lev16], answer-
ing Problem 1.31 in [Kir97]; see also [HLL22b, Zho21]. An affirmative
answer to (a) gives an affirmative answer to (b) for locally flat knots,
via an embedding with an isolated, piecewise linear singularity obtained
by coning off the knot in $S^{3}$.
Note that topological embeddings need
not be approximable by piecewise linear or locally flat embeddings. Such
a wild topological embedding of a disk was constructed by Giffen using
a shift-spinning construction in unpublished work, explained in [DV09,
Section 6.6]. Recent work of Davis [Dav20, Dav25] gives evidence in
support of an affirmative answer to (a), in terms of the solvable filtration
of the knot concordance group [COT03].
(3) Part (d) is related to questions about extending topological group actions,
without any requirement of local linearity.
Recall [FQ90] that a free
action of a cyclic group on a homology sphere $Y$ extends to an action
on the Freedman filling $\Delta$ of $Y$ with one fixed point; the action is not
necessarily locally linear at that point.
Suppose instead that $\mathbb{Z}_{n}$ acts
semi-freely on $Y$ , with fixed point set a knot $K$. If $n$ is a prime, say $p$,
then the fixed point set of the extension would be a $\mathbb{Z}_{p}$-homology disk
with boundary equal to $K$. So in some weak sense, $K$ would be slice in
$\Delta$. This problem is rather different in character from the smooth version,
discussed in problem 3.75.

References cited:

- [Lev16] Adam Simon Levine. Nonsurjective satellite operators and piecewise-linear concordance. Forum Math. Sigma, 4:Paper No. e34, 47, 2016. doi:10.1017/fms.2016.31.
- [Kir97] R.C. Kirby. Problems in low–dimensional topology. In W. Kazez, editor, Geometric Topology. American Math. Soc./International Press, Providence, 1997.
- [HLL22b] Jennifer Hom, Adam Simon Levine, and Tye Lidman. Knot concordance in homology cobordisms. Duke Math. J., 171(15):3089–3131, 2022. doi:10.1215/00127094-2021-0110.
- [Zho21] Hugo Zhou. Homology concordance and an infinite rank free subgroup. J. Topol., 14(4):1369–1395, 2021. doi:10.1112/topo.12211.
- [DV09] Robert J. Daverman and Gerard A. Venema. Embeddings in manifolds, volume 106 of Graduate Studies in Mathematics. American Mathematical Society, Providence, RI, 2009. doi:10.1090/gsm/106.
- [Dav20] Christopher W. Davis. Topological concordance of knots in homology spheres and the solvable filtration. J. Topol., 13(1):343–355, 2020. doi:10.1112/topo.12126.
- [Dav25] Christopher W. Davis. Whitney tower concordance and knots in homology spheres. Algebr. Geom. Topol., 25(6):3503–3521, 2025. doi:10.2140/agt.2025.25.3503.

title: Kirby Problem 1.62
statement:
(a) Are all good boundary links topologically slice? Freely topologically slice?
(b) A special case of interest: Is the Whitehead double of the Borromean rings
(with any choice of clasps) topologically slice?
background:
Source: Kirby's Problems in Low-Dimensional Topology notes. Original problem number: KP-1.62.

Literature notes:
(1) A boundary link $(L, \varphi)$ is an $n$-component link $L \subseteq S^{3}$ together with a
surjection $\varphi: \pi_{1}(S^{3}\setminus L) \twoheadrightarrow F_{n}$, sending a set of meridians of $L$ to a free
generating set of the free group on $n$ generators. A link $L$ admits such
a homomorphism $\varphi$ if and only if the components of $L$ bound pairwise
disjoint Seifert surfaces in $S^{3}$ [Smy66] (see also [CS80, Proposition 1.1]).
Following [FQ90, Section 11.7C], a boundary link $(L, \varphi)$ is said to be a
good boundary link if the kernel of $\varphi$ is a perfect group. Note that a 1-
component good boundary link is a knot with Alexander polynomial one.
Whitehead doubles of links with vanishing pairwise linking numbers are
good boundary links.
(2) Part (a) is posed in [Kir97, Problem 1.36], with a slightly different def-
inition of good boundary links than appears here. The first half of that
problem asked whether Alexander polynomial one knots are topologically
slice. The answer to that question is now known to be yes [GT04], [FQ90,
Theorem 11.7B], [Fre84, Theorem 7] (see also [BPR21, Theorem 1.14]
and [PR21, Section 21.6.3]).
(3) If the surgery sequence is exact (see Problem 4.46), then a link in $S^{3}$
is freely slice if and only if it is a good boundary link [FQ90, Corol-
lary 11.7C]. More surprisingly, the topological surgery sequence in dimen-
sion four is defined and exact if and only if all good boundary links are
freely slice [FQ90, Corollary 12.3C] (see also [KOPR21a, Section 23.2.1]).
(4) [CKP20, Corollary 2.2] gives a characterization of good boundary links
in terms of Seifert matrices. This is very useful in confirming whether
a given boundary link is good. For example, this gives an easy method
to verify that Whitehead doubles of links with vanishing pairwise linking
numbers are good boundary links.
(5) Several families of good boundary links have been shown to be freely
topologically slice. The most general result is due to Cha, Kim, and Pow-
ell [CKP20, Theorem A], generalizing previous work focusing on White-
head doubles, e.g. in [FT95b].
(6) Not all good boundary links are smoothly slice, even with more than one
component.
For example, Levine [Lev12] showed that the Whitehead
double of the Borromean rings, with all positive clasps, is not smoothly
slice. The question of whether the Whitehead double of the Borromean
rings is topologically slice appeared as Problem 4.46 in [Kir97], and we
restate it here in part (b) as a special case of the problem.

Question. Is the Whitehead double of the Borromean rings (with any
choice of clasps) topologically slice?

title: Kirby Problem 1.63
statement:
Is there a knot type with Legendrian representatives that do
not destabilize but have arbitrarily negative Thurston–Bennequin number?
background:
Source: Kirby's Problems in Low-Dimensional Topology notes. Original problem number: KP-1.63.

Literature notes:
(1) This is Etnyre-Ng [EN03, Question 44]; see also [CGH09, Question 61].

(2) It is known by work of Etnyre and Honda that for any $N$ there is a
knot type having peaks of height $N$ in its Legendrian mountain range
[EH03]. For any choice of knot type and Thurston-Bennequin number,
there are finitely many distinct Legendrian representatives, so this ques-
tion is equivalent to asking if there is a knot type with infinitely many
non-destabilizable representatives. This has been proved for many knot
types, including the unknot [EF09], torus knots [EH01a], cables of torus
knots [ELT12, LaF10], and twist knots [ENV13].
(3) The finiteness of non-destabilizable Legendrian representatives problem
is equivalent to whether there are finitely many non-destabilizable grid
diagrams for a given knot [DP13].
It is proved in [Dyn06] that any
non-minimal rectangular diagram of the unknot can be destabilized. This
gives an algorithm to detect the unknot using monotonic simplification.
A first step towards generalizing this result to arbitrary topological knots
is to answer the question above.

- [EH01a] John B. Etnyre and Ko Honda. Knots and contact geometry. I. Torus knots and the figure eight knot. J. Symplectic Geom., 1(1):63–120, 2001. http://projecteuclid.org/euclid.jsg/1092316299.

title: Kirby Problem 1.64
statement:
(a) Let $L \subset (S^{3}, \xi_{std})$ be a transverse link such that the branched double cover
$(\Sigma_{2}(L), \xi_{L})$ is Stein fillable. Is $L$ transversely isotopic to the closure of a
quasipositive braid?
(b) Is the same true if $(\Sigma_{n}(L), \xi_{L})$ is Stein fillable for some $n > 2$?
(c) Does Stein fillability of the branched cover imply that the slice-Bennequin
inequality must be sharp for the given link?
background:
Source: Kirby's Problems in Low-Dimensional Topology notes. Original problem number: KP-1.64.

Literature notes:
(1) Here, $(S^{3}, \xi_{std})$ denotes the standard contact structure on $S^{3}$.
If $L \subset$
$(S^{3}, \xi_{std})$ is a transverse link, then the cyclic $n$-fold branched cover $\Sigma_{n}(L)$
has an induced contact structure $\xi_{L}, n \geq 2$.
(2) See Problems 1.69 and 1.70 for definitions, background on quasipositive
braids, and related questions.
(3) A closed braid is quasipositive if and only if it can be represented as
a transverse intersection $S^{3} \cap \mathcal{V}$ for some smooth, complex curve $\mathcal{V} \subset$
$\mathbb{C}^{2}$ [Rud83, BO01].Thus if $L$ is isotopic to the closure of a quasiposi-
tive braid, then $(\Sigma_{n}(L), \xi_{L})$ is Stein fillable, because it bounds the Stein
manifold obtained as the cover of $B^{4}$ branched over the complex curve
$\mathcal{V} \cap B^{4}$. The question asks whether fillability of branched covers charac-
terizes quasipositive braids. For more results on the branched covers of
transverse links, see [Pla06]. More discussion of relations between dif-
ferent monoids related to quasipositivity and contact geometry is given
in [EVHM15].

References cited:
- [Rud83] Lee Rudolph. Algebraic functions and closed braids. Topology, 22(2):191–202, 1983. doi:10.1016/0040-9383(83)90031-9.
- [BO01] Michel Boileau and Stepan Orevkov. Quasi-positivité d’une courbe analytique dans une boule pseudo-convexe. C. R. Acad. Sci. Paris Sér. I Math., 332(9):825–830, 2001. doi:10.1016/S0764-4442(01)01945-0.
- [Pla06] Olga Plamenevskaya. Transverse knots, branched double covers and Heegaard Floer contact invariants. J. Symplectic Geom., 4(2):149–170, 2006. doi:10.4310/jsg.2006.v4.n2.a2.
- [EVHM15] John B. Etnyre and Jeremy Van Horn-Morris. Monoids in the mapping class group. In Interactions between low-dimensional topology and mapping class groups, volume 19 of Geom. Topol. Monogr., pages 319–365. Geom. Topol. Publ., Coventry, 2015. doi:10.2140/gtm.2015.19.319.

title: Kirby Problem 1.65
statement:
Decomposable Lagrangian cobordisms between Legendrian knots
or links in $\mathbb{R}^{3}$ are compositions of certain simple pieces admitting diagrammatic de-
scriptions [EHK16]. Such cobordisms necessarily have no index 2 critical points.
Is every exact Lagrangian cobordism without index 2 critical points Lagrangian iso-
topic to a decomposable Lagrangian cobordism?
background:
Source: Kirby's Problems in Low-Dimensional Topology notes. Original problem number: KP-1.65.

Literature notes:
(1) At the time of writing, a candidate for a non-decomposable cobordism is
given in [CNS16, Conjecture 3.3]. This can be built using another ele-
mentary construction, Guadagni’s tangle move, see [BLL $^{+}21$, GSY22],
which could in principle produce additional non-decomposable cobordisms.
(2) The hypotheses on index 2 critical points is necessary for a variety of
reasons. For example, Lagrangian caps (see, e.g., [Lin16]) are, by defini-
tion, not decomposable; for decomposability, the positive boundary of the
cobordism must be nonempty or else index 2 critical points are necessary.
In the recent preprint [DRG24], an example of a non-decomposable La-
grangian concordance between knots is given. However, the authors there
show that the concordance must contain index 2 critical points.
(3) Conway, Etnyre, and Tosun prove that decomposable Lagrangians are reg-
ular [CET21], which means there is a Weinstein structure on the cobor-
dism where the Liouville vector field is tangent to the cobordism. Using
this, [EGL20] implies the exterior of a decomposable Lagrangian disk
necessarily has a Stein structure, and hence the exterior can be built out
of particularly constrained elementary pieces, akin to the decomposable
Lagrangian itself. (It is worth pointing out that the non-decomposable
examples of [DRG24] above are not regular either.)
(4) Here is a variant of the problem: Is every filling (exact Lagrangian cobor-
dism with empty negative boundary) Lagrangian isotopic to a decom-
posable Lagrangian cobordism? This question is sometimes stated more
generally for exact Lagrangian cobordisms with negative boundary given
by any (possibly empty) non-destabilizable Lagrangian link; the non-
destabilizability condition rules out the presence of a Lagrangian cap as
in [Lin16].
The possibly non-decomposable candidate from [CNS16],
which is a concordance with a Legendrian trefoil as its negative boundary,
can be glued to a filling of the trefoil to produce a potential counterexam-
ple to this version of the problem.

title: Kirby Problem 1.66
statement:
For Legendrian links $\Lambda_{1}, \Lambda_{2} \subset (\mathbb{R}^{3}, \xi_{std})$, write $\Lambda_{1} \preceq \Lambda_{2}$ if
there is an exact Lagrangian cobordism in the symplectization $\mathbb{R} \times \mathbb{R}^{3}$ from $\Lambda_{1}$ to
$\Lambda_{2}$. Is $\preceq$ a partial order?
background:
Source: Kirby's Problems in Low-Dimensional Topology notes. Original problem number: KP-1.66.

Literature notes:
(1) One can ask an analogous question in any contact 3-manifold, as well as
in higher dimensions.
(2) The fact that $\preceq$ is not symmetric was first shown by Chantraine [Cha15].

(3) As for ribbon concordance in the smooth setting, many invariants of Leg-
endrian knots are monotone under $\preceq$. For example, the behavior of rul-
ings [CNS16], contact homology [Pan17a] and the contact invariant in
monopole Floer homology [BS18a] support this conjecture.
(4) One can ask an analogous question about symplectic concordances be-
tween transverse knots.

References cited:
- [Cha15] Baptiste Chantraine. Lagrangian concordance is not a symmetric relation. Quantum Topol., 6(3):451–474, 2015. doi:10.4171/QT/68.
- [CNS16] Christopher Cornwell, Lenhard Ng, and Steven Sivek. Obstructions to Lagrangian concordance. Algebr. Geom. Topol., 16(2):797–824, 2016. doi:10.2140/agt.2016.16.797.

title: Kirby Problem 1.67
statement:
Given a Legendrian link in the standard contact $\mathbb{R}^{3}$ besides the
standard unknot or Hopf link, classify its exact Lagrangian fillings up to compactly
supported Hamiltonian isotopy.
background:
Source: Kirby's Problems in Low-Dimensional Topology notes. Original problem number: KP-1.67.

Literature notes:
Eliashberg-Polterovich [EP96] showed that the unknot has a single
filling. A recent preprint of Thomson claims that the Hopf link has exactly 2 fillings
[Tho25]. These are the only links with known classification. The right-handed tre-
foil famously has 5 fillings [EHK16], distinguished through augmentations of the
Legendrian contact homology. Casals and Gao showed there are examples of links
with infinitely many non-isotopic fillings [CG22]. Casals has a more general con-
jectured classification for some large families of links in [Cas22, Conjecture 5.1]. A
special case would be that the $T(2, n)$ torus link has exactly $C_{n}$ fillings up to isotopy
through exact Lagrangians, where $C_{n}$ is the $n^{th}$ Catalan number, generalizing the
count for the unknot and Hopf link. (See the work of Ekholm-Honda-Kalman for
earlier questions on classifying Lagrangian fillings by augmentations of Legendrian
contact homology [EHK16], including for the $T(2, n)$ torus links.) A lower bound
of $C_{n}$ in this case is due to Pan [Pan17b] and independently Shende-Treumann-
Williams-Zaslow [STWZ19].

title: Kirby Problem 1.68
statement:
Determine the smooth knot types that have Legendrian repre-
sentatives with orientable exact Lagrangian fillings.
background:
Source: Kirby's Problems in Low-Dimensional Topology notes. Original problem number: KP-1.68.

Literature notes:
(1) This problem appears in [HS15] together with a conjecture that such fill-
ings exist if and only if the knot type $K$ is quasi-positive and tb $(K) =$
$-$ deg $_{a}P_{K} - 1$, where tb $(K)$ denotes the maximal Thurston-Bennequin
number of a Legendrian representative of $K$ and $P_{K}(a, z)$ the HOM-
FLYPT polynomial.
These conditions are necessary for existence of a
filling (see [HS15] and references therein) as is the sharpness of the slice-
Bennequin inequality, tb $(K) = 2g_{4}(K)-1$, as shown in [Cha10, Theorem
1.4].
(2) For alternating knots [CNS16], an answer is that a filling exists if and
only if the knot type is positive. In general, constructions of fillings exist
for all positive knots [HS15] and all almost positive knots with diagrams
of Type II [Tag19]. A variant of the question allows for nonorientable
Lagrangian fillings; see [CCPR $^{+}24$].

(3) For comparison, the analogous question involving transverse knots has a
succinct answer: Transverse knots with symplectic fillings exist within
a smooth knot type if and only if the knot type is quasi-positive; see
[Rud83, BO01].

title: Kirby Problem 1.69
statement:
Let $L \subset (S^{3}, \xi_{std})$ be a transverse link with

$$
sl_{\Sigma}(L) = -\chi(\Sigma),
$$

for some Seifert surface $\Sigma$. Must $L$ be strongly quasipositive?
background:
Source: Kirby's Problems in Low-Dimensional Topology notes. Original problem number: KP-1.69.

Literature notes:
(1) The self-linking number of an oriented link transverse to the standard
contact structure $\xi_{std}$ on $S^{3}$ satisfies the well-known Bennequin bound
[Ben83, Etn05]:

$$
sl_{\Sigma}(L) \leq -\chi(\Sigma),
$$

where $\Sigma$ is any Seifert surface for $L$. This problem therefore attempts to
characterize when this bound is sharp.
(2) Strongly quasipositive links are those which possess a quasipositive Seifert
surface, constructed from parallel disks by attaching bands with positive
half-twists [Rud92]. Such a surface is properly isotopic to the intersection
of the 4-ball with a non-singular complex curve [Rud83]. It is known
that if a link is strongly quasipositive, or bounds a complex curve of
Euler characteristic equal to that of some Seifert surface for the link, then
the Bennequin bound is sharp (see [Shu07, Proposition 1.G] or [Hed10,
Proof of Theorem 1.5] for a proof).
(3) In light of the above remark, one can ask if sharpness of the Bennequin
bound implies $\Sigma$ is quasipositive.
If so, then it follows that that any
minimal genus Seifert surface for $L$ is quasipositive. This is because the
self-linking number depends only on the relative homology class of $\Sigma$,
hence the Bennequin bound will be sharp for any other minimal genus
Seifert surface $\Sigma'$.
(4) The question in this problem has an affirmative answer for fibered links
[Hed10], links represented by minimal-index braids with fractional Dehn
twist coefficient $> 1$ [IK19], 3-braids [IK19], positive knots [Rud99],
almost positive knots [FLL23], and knots whose canonical and Seifert
genus agree [FLL23]. Hedden and Tovstopyat-Nelip have announced an
affirmative answer for links with two dimensional top group of Heegaard
knot Floer homology.
(5) These notions generalize to arbitrary contact 3-manifolds, with the Ben-
nequin bound generalized by Eliashberg to tight contact 3-manifolds [Eli92]
and strong quasipositivity generalized via braids in open books [BEH $^{+}15$,
IK19, Hay21b]. Geometrically, the class of quasipositive Seifert surfaces
is the same as the class of ribbons of Legendrian graphs [BI09, Hay22].
One can therefore ask the following more general question: Suppose there
exists a transverse link $L \subset (Y, \xi)$ for which

$$
sl_{\xi,\Sigma}(Y, L) = -\chi(\Sigma),
$$

for some Seifert surface $\Sigma$. Is $\Sigma$ isotopic to the Legendrian ribbon of a
Legendrian graph $\Gamma \subset (Y, \xi)$? This generalized question has an affirmative
answer for overtwisted contact structures [BCV09].

- [Etn05] John B. Etnyre. Legendrian and transversal knots. In Handbook of knot theory, pages 105–185. Elsevier B. V., Amsterdam, 2005. doi:10.1016/B978-044451452-3/50004-6.
- [Rud92] Lee Rudolph. Constructions of quasipositive knots and links. III. A characterization of quasipositive Seifert surfaces. Topology, 31(2):231–237, 1992. doi:10.1016/0040-9383(92)90017-C.
- [Rud83] Lee Rudolph. Algebraic functions and closed braids. Topology, 22(2):191–202, 1983. doi:10.1016/0040-9383(83)90031-9.
- [Shu07] Alexander N. Shumakovitch. Rasmussen invariant, slice-Bennequin inequality, and sliceness of knots. J. Knot Theory Ramifications, 16(10):1403–1412, 2007. doi: 10.1142/S0218216507005889.
- [Hed10] Matthew Hedden. Notions of positivity and the Ozsváth-Szabó concordance invariant. J. Knot Theory Ramifications, 19(5):617–629, 2010. doi:10.1142/S0218216510008017.
- [IK19] Tetsuya Ito and Keiko Kawamuro. The defect of the Bennequin-Eliashberg inequality and Bennequin surfaces. Indiana Univ. Math. J., 68(3):799–833, 2019. doi:10.1512/iumj.2019.68.7662.

title: Kirby Problem 1.70
statement:
(a) Let $L \subset (S^{3}, \xi_{std})$ be a transverse link with

$$
sl_{\Sigma}(L) = -\chi(\Sigma),
$$

for some smooth surface $\Sigma \subset B^{4}$ bounded by $L$. Is $L$ quasipositive?
(b) Is the class of strongly quasipositive links equal to the class of quasipositive
links whose Seifert and smooth slice genera are equal?
background:
Source: Kirby's Problems in Low-Dimensional Topology notes. Original problem number: KP-1.70.

Literature notes:
(1) Quasipositivity implies that $L$ is isotopic to the transverse intersection
of a complex curve in $\mathbb{C}^{2}$ with the unit 3-sphere [Rud83], and any link
arising from such an intersection is quasipositive [BO01]. It is not true,
however, that any surface in $B^{4}$ bounding $L$ realizing equality in the slice-
Bennequin bound is isotopic to a subsurface of a complex curve. Indeed,
a complex curve is ribbon (in the sense that the radius function on the 4-
ball, restricted to the curve, can be assumed to be Morse without critical
points of index 2).
On the other hand, tubing a complex curve to a
smoothly knotted 2-sphere in its complement will produce a surface that
is not ribbon, yet will still realize equality in the slice-Bennequin bound.
One can ask, however, whether a ribbon surface realizing equality in the
slice-Bennequin bound is properly isotopic to a piece of complex curve.
(2) Since quasipositive links have transverse representatives for which the
slice-Bennequin bound is sharp (again, see [Shu07, Proposition 1.G] or
[Hed10, Proof of Theorem 1.5]) we observe that Problem 1.69 implies an
affirmative answer to part (b).
(3) Part (b) is asking whether there exists a link $L$ bounding a complex curve
whose Euler characteristic is the same as that of some Seifert surface
for $L$, but for which no complex curve bounded by $L$ is isotopic to a
Seifert surface. The existence of such a link would answer part (b) in
the negative, from which it would follow that Problem 1.69 is false. Note
that part (b) has an affirmative answer for fibered links, by [Hed10].
Since complex curves are ribbon and Seifert surfaces are ribbon-immersed
without singularities, this problem can be thought of as asking about the
minimum number of ribbon singularities required across complex curves
bounded by $L$.

References cited:
- [Rud83] Lee Rudolph. Algebraic functions and closed braids. Topology, 22(2):191–202, 1983. doi:10.1016/0040-9383(83)90031-9.
- [BO01] Michel Boileau and Stepan Orevkov. Quasi-positivité d’une courbe analytique dans une boule pseudo-convexe. C. R. Acad. Sci. Paris Sér. I Math., 332(9):825–830, 2001. doi:10.1016/S0764-4442(01)01945-0.

- [Hed10] Matthew Hedden. Notions of positivity and the Ozsváth-Szabó concordance invariant. J. Knot Theory Ramifications, 19(5):617–629, 2010. doi:10.1142/S0218216510008017.

title: Kirby Problem 1.71
statement: Does a Gordian unknot exist?
background:
Source: Kirby's Problems in Low-Dimensional Topology notes. Original problem number: KP-1.71.

Literature notes:
A physical link is a collection of disjoint embedded loops of given
finite lengths in a configuration with thickness at least 1.
Thickness has many
equivalent definitions [GM99, CKS02], but an appealing one is the same as Fed-
erer’s definition [Fed59] of reach: the infimal $r$ so that every point in $\mathbb{R}^{3}$ within $r$
of the curve has a unique nearest neighbor on the curve. Alternatively, for smooth
knots, thickness 1 means that a radius-1 tubular neighborhood is also embedded
[Sim02]. A physical isotopy preserves the length of each loop while respecting this
thickness constraint. The thickness lower bound yields an upper bound 1 for the
curvature of a physical link, implying a least-length configuration exists in each
physical isotopy class [CKS02]. By a Gordian pair we mean physical link config-
urations that are isotopic but not physically isotopic; see [Nab95, LN21] which
provide Gordian pairs of higher dimensional knots, the latter giving an explicit con-
struction of a Gordian unknot in $S^{4}$. Gordian pairs with two or more components
[CH15, KK23] are known — even for unlinks [AH25, KK25] — but it remains
unknown for knots, and especially for the unknot.

- [Nab95] Alexander Nabutovsky. Non-recursive functions, knots “with thick ropes”, and self-clenching “thick” hyperspheres. Comm. Pure Appl. Math., 48(4):381–428, 1995. doi:10.1002/cpa.3160480402.

title: Kirby Problem 1.72
statement:
(The equilateral stuck unknots conjecture.). Are there equilat-
eral embedded polygons that are unknotted yet cannot be unknotted through polygons
preserving edge lengths? Such an unknot is said to be stuck.
background:
Source: Kirby's Problems in Low-Dimensional Topology notes. Original problem number: KP-1.72.

Literature notes:
(1) The celebrated Carpenter’s Rule problem asks whether an embedded poly-
gon in the plane may be deformed to a convex configuration through em-
bedded polygons with the same edge lengths. Solutions in the affirmative
were given more or less simultaneously by Streinu [Str00] and Connelly,
Demaine, and Rote [CDR03].
(2) The natural extension of this theorem to PL knots in codimension two
asks whether polygons of knot type $K$ may be deformed into one another
through embedded polygons of the same edge lengths. For arbitrary edge
lengths, the answer is known to be ‘no’: there are stuck unknots with as
few as six edges [CKS98, Tou01, AET04] (see Figure 2) which cannot be
convexified through embedded configurations with the same edge lengths.
(3) Interestingly, all of the known examples of stuck unknots have very dif-
ferent edge lengths, which they seem to require in an essential way. This
leads to the question: are there equilateral stuck unknots?

Figure 2. Stuck unknots

There is some reason to believe that there are not. Khoi [Kho05]
proved that the symplectic volume of the space of equilateral $n$-gons in
$\mathbb{R}^{3}$ is the largest symplectic volume of any space of $n$-gons with the same
total length.
That is, in this sense, equilateral polygons are the most
flexible polygons. On the other hand, it is quite difficult to imagine an
algorithm for unfolding an equilateral unknot of $n$ edges.

title: Kirby Problem 1.73
statement:
(The 15 pearls conjecture). Is the pearl number of the trefoil
equal to 15?
background:
Source: Kirby's Problems in Low-Dimensional Topology notes. Original problem number: KP-1.73.

Literature notes:
(1) A pearl necklace with $n$ pearls is an embedding of an equilateral $n$-gon
in $\mathbb{R}^{3}$ so that each vertex is surrounded by a sphere with diameter equal
to the edgelength and the interiors of all the spheres are disjoint. This
is a common off-lattice model of a self-avoiding polygon, usually called
the hard sphere polymer (see [SJ23]). The pearl number of a knot $K$ is
the minimum number of pearls in any necklace whose polygon has knot
type $K$.
(2) A self-avoiding polygon on a cubic lattice is a common model for random
knots with self-interactions. The “minimum step numbers” are known for
self-avoiding polygons on the cubic lattice for a number of knot types by a
combination of geometric arguments and computer enumeration [SIA $^{+}09$].
For instance, the minimal step number of the trefoil on the simple cubic
lattice is 24 [Dia93].
(3) Very little is known about the pearl number. Oshiro and Maehara [MO99]
give a construction for a 15-pearl trefoil and conjecture that this configu-
ration is minimal (so the pearl number of the trefoil is 15). Interestingly,
their configuration is similar to the 15 step embedding of the trefoil on
the face-centered cubic lattice (shown in Figure 3) found by Rechnitzer
and Janse van Rensburg [RR11], which those authors conjecture to be
minimal. By putting balls of radius $1/2$ on the vertices of a realization
on the cubic lattice one obtains a hard sphere polymer. Thus the pearl
number is bounded above by the length of any lattice representation.
Conversely, the pearl number is an upper bound on the equilateral stick
number of any knot. The difference between the three integer invariants

Figure 3. Face-centered cubic lattice embedding of trefoil

should be quite large for most knot types as can be seen for the trefoil
with an equilateral stick number of six [Jin97].
(4) In [Mae07], Maehara proves that the pearl number of the trefoil is at
least 11.

References cited:
- [SJ23] Stefan Schnabel and Wolfhard Janke. Monte Carlo simulation of long hard-sphere polymer chains in two to five dimensions. Macromolecular Theory and Simulations, 32:2200080, 2023. doi:10.1002/mats.202200080.
- [SIA+09] Rob Scharein, Kai Ishihara, Javier Arsuaga, Yuanan Diao, Koya Shimokawa, and Mariel Vazquez. Bounds for the minimum step number of knots in the simple cubic lattice. Journal of Physics A: Mathematical and Theoretical, 42, 2009. doi:10.1088/1751-8113/42/47/475006.
- [Dia93] Yuanan Diao. Minimal knotted polygons on the cubic lattice. Journal of Knot Theory and Its Ramifications, 02:413–425, 1993. doi:10.1142/S0218216593000234.
- [MO99] Hiroshi Maehara and Ai Oshiro. On knotted necklaces of pearls. European Journal of Combinatorics, 20:411–420, 1999. doi:10.1006/eujc.1998.0279.
- [RR11] E. J. Janse Van Rensburg and Andrew Rechnitzer. Generalized atmospheric sampling of knotted polygons. Journal of Knot Theory and its Ramifications, 20:1145– 1171, 2011. doi:10.1142/S0218216511009170.

- [Mae07] Hiroshi Maehara. On configurations of solid balls in 3-space: Chromatic numbers and knotted cycles. Graphs and Combinatorics, 23:307–320, 2007. doi:10.1007/s00373-007-0702-7.

title: Kirby Problem 1.74
statement:
How does ropelength behave under connected sum of knots?
Here are two conjectures, the second a weakening of the first.
(a) For any knot or link types $K_{1}$ and $K_{2}$,
Rop $(K_{1}\#K_{2}) \leq$ Rop $(K_{1}) +$ Rop $(K_{2}) - (4\pi - 4).$
(b) For any knot or link types $K_{1}$ and $K_{2}$,

$$
Rop(K_{1}\#K_{2}) \leq Rop(K_{1}) + Rop(K_{2}) - c,
$$

where $c > 0$ is some constant independent of knot type.
background:
Source: Kirby's Problems in Low-Dimensional Topology notes. Original problem number: KP-1.74.

Literature notes:
(1) The (minimum) ropelength Rop $(K)$ of a knot is defined to be the small-
est quotient of length and thickness (defined in Problem 1.71) among
all rectifiable curves in $\mathbb{R}^{3}$ realizing the knot type. It is known that ro-
pelength minimizers exist in every knot and link type [GMSvdM02,
GL03, CKS02], but their shapes (and rope-lengths) are known only in
a few special cases of links with planar components. In all other case we
only have numerical results approximating the rope-length.
(2) The ropelength minimizing Hopf link $2^{2}_{1}$ is a pair of circles of equal radius
in orthogonal planes, passing through each other’s centers. Ropelength
is scale-invariant, so we can assume that the circles have radius 2. Their
thickness is then 1 and $\operatorname{Rop}(2^{2}_{1})=8\pi$. The ropelength-minimizing com-
posite link $2^{2}_{1}\#2^{2}_{1}$ (a chain of three linked circles) is composed of two round

circles in the same plane, each passing through a center of the semicircular
arc of a stadium curve in the orthogonal plane. This has ropelength $8\pi$
(for the circles) plus $4\pi + 4$ (for the stadium curve), so

$$
\operatorname{Rop}(2^{2}_{1}\#2^{2}_{1}) = 12\pi+4
= \operatorname{Rop}(2^{2}_{1})+\operatorname{Rop}(2^{2}_{1})-(4\pi-4),
$$

and we have saved some rope by splicing these links together. Katritch
et al. [KOP $^{+}97$] conjectured in 1997 that we can save at least as much
rope on any connect sum; leading to Conjecture (a).
(3) The work of Diao [Dia24] on alternating knots uses the braid index as
a lower bound on ropelength.
The braid index of a connected sum is
$b(K_{1}\#K_{2}) = b(K_{1}) + b(K_{2}) - 1$ for two alternating knots $K_{1}$ and $K_{2}$.
Thus the lower bound on ropelength of a connected sum of the two knots
$b(K_{1}\#K_{2})$ will be slightly less than the sum of the lower bounds of the
two knots $K_{1}$ and $K_{2}$.
Hence it is worth considering the weaker version, Conjecture (b), with
an undetermined constant.
(4) In general, it would be important to have any theoretical lower bound on
ropelength for knot types that approximates the numerical results. This
has been done for the trefoil, but the techniques used do not generalize
to other knot types, for which there remains a wide gap between the
numerical results and the theoretical lower bounds.

References cited:
- [GMSvdM02] O. Gonzalez, J. H. Maddocks, F. Schuricht, and H. von der Mosel. Global curvature and self-contact of nonlinearly elastic curves and rods. Calc. Var. Partial Differential Equations, 14(1):29–68, 2002. doi:10.1007/s005260100089.
- [GL03] Oscar Gonzalez and R. De La Llave. Existence of ideal knots. Journal of Knot Theory and its Ramifications, 12:123–133, 2003. doi:10.1142/S0218216503002354.
- [CKS02] Jason Cantarella, Robert B. Kusner, and John M. Sullivan. On the minimum ropelength of knots and links. Inventiones Mathematicae, 150:257–286, 2002. URL: http://www.springerlink.com/index/10.1007/s00222-002-0234-y, doi: 10.1007/s00222-002-0234-y.
- [KOP+97] Vsevolod Katritch, Wilma K. Olson, Piotr Pieranski, Jacques Dubochet, and Andrzej Stasiak. Properties of ideal composite knots. Nature, 388:148–151, 1997. doi:10.1038/40582.
- [Dia24] Yuanan Diao. The ropelength conjecture of alternating knots. Math. Proc. Cambridge Philos. Soc., 177(2):367–369, 2024. doi:10.1017/S0305004124000288.

title: Kirby Problem 1.75
statement:
(a) Find some knot energy on the space of smoothly embedded unknotted circles
in $\mathbb{S}^{3}$ for which all unknotted critical points are great circles.
(b) Define a gradient flow for this knot energy which yields a deformation
retract of the space of unknots to the subspace of great circles.
background:
Source: Kirby's Problems in Low-Dimensional Topology notes. Original problem number: KP-1.75.

Literature notes:
(1) These questions were posed by Freedman, He, and Wang [FHW94]. The
motivation is one of the many equivalent formulations of the Smale conjec-
ture mentioned in the Appendix to Hatcher’s 1983 paper (which actually
proves this conjecture). Variation (7) states [Hat83, p. 606] that “the
space of smoothly embedded unknotted circles in $\mathbb{S}^{3}$ deformation retracts
onto the space of great circles in $\mathbb{S}^{3}$, (i.e., O $(4)/$ O $(2) \times$ O $(2))$.”Of course,
it would be of some interest to construct a more or less explicit example
of such a retract.
(2) Beginning in the 1980s, several repulsive functionals, so-called knot ener-
gies, have been defined in the pursuit of disentangling complicated knot-
ted curves and deforming them into ‘simpler’ curves within the same knot
class; see, e.g., the survey by Strzelecki et al. [SSvdM13] and references
therein. The most prominent example is the Möbius energy introduced
by O’Hara [O’H91] in 1991.
(3) As pointed out by Freedman, He, and Wang [FHW94], it is tempting to
conjecture that a suitable gradient flow for a knot energy actually defines

a retraction as stated by Hatcher, i.e., it will deform any curve from the
unknot class to a round circle. Of course, this can only work if, except
for the circles, there are no critical points within the unknot class; cf.
Budney’s post [Bud16]. Currently, we do not know whether any of the
many smooth knot energies that have been proposed so far enjoys this
property.

References cited:
- [FHW94] Michael H. Freedman, Zheng-Xu He, and Zhenghan Wang. Möbius energy of knots and unknots. Ann. of Math. (2), 139(1):1–50, 1994. doi:10.2307/2946626.
- [Hat83] Allen E. Hatcher. A proof of the Smale conjecture, Diffp$S^{3}$q » $O(4)$. Ann. of Math. (2), 117(3):553–607, 1983. doi:10.2307/2007035.
- [SSvdM13] Pawel Strzelecki, Marta Szumańska, and Heiko von der Mosel. On some knot energies involving Menger curvature. Topology Appl., 160(13):1507–1529, 2013. doi:10.1016/j.topol.2013.05.022.
- [O’H91] Jun O’Hara. Energy of a knot. Topology, 30(2):241–247, 1991. doi:10.1016/0040-9383(91)90010-2.
- [Bud16] Ryan Budney. A gorgeous but incomplete proof of “The Smale Conjecture”, 2016. https://ldtopology.wordpress.com/2016/10/02/a-gorgeous-but-incomplete-proof-of-the-smale-conjecture/. Accessed: 2024-01-25.

title: Kirby Problem 1.76
statement:
(a) Is there an algorithm to detect the unknot that runs in polynomial time
(as a function of the number of crossings in an input diagram)?
(b) What is the structure of the unknot Reidemeister graph?
background:
Source: Kirby's Problems in Low-Dimensional Topology notes. Original problem number: KP-1.76.

Literature notes:
(1) There are now many algorithms to detect the unknot. The first was due to
Haken [Hak61] and used normal surfaces. Hass, Lagarias and Pippenger
[HLP99] refined his methods to prove that unknot recognition lies in NP.
Dynnikov [Dyn06] used grid diagrams to find a very different algorithm.
He showed that any grid diagram for the unknot can be reduced to the
trivial diagram through a sequence of moves, none of which increases the
grid number.
(2) There are now many invariants that detect the unknot, including Kho-
vanov homology [KM11] and Heegaard Floer homology [OS04b]. How-
ever, none of these invariants seem to be computable in polynomial time.
A further significant result was proved by Kuperberg [Kup14] who showed
that unknot recognition lies in co-NP, assuming the Generalized Riemann

Hypothesis. In other words, if a knot is nontrivial, then there is an efficient
way of certifying this. This result was proved unconditionally, removing
the GRH assumption, by Lackenby [Lac21a] using sutured manifold hi-
erarchies.
(3) The unknot Reidemeister graph in part (b) is formed by assigning a vertex
to each diagram of the unknot and connecting two vertices by an edge if
there is a Reidemeister move connecting them; it is locally finite. There
are pairs of vertices representing two diagrams with $n$ crossings such that
the shortest path connecting them has length at least $n^{2}/25$ [HN10]. No
two vertices representing diagrams with $n$ crossings have distance greater
than $2(236n)^{11}$ [Lac15].
This problem is complicated by the existence of “hard” unknot dia-
grams [BCL $^{+}24$, PZ16], which have the property that any sequence of
Reidemeister moves taking them to the trivial diagram must go via dia-
grams with higher crossing number. The question may be more tractable
if different sets of basic moves are allowed in addition to or in place of
the standard Reidemeister moves; in the related setting of grid diagrams,
monotonic simplification has been established [Dyn06].

References cited:
- [Hak61] Wolfgang Haken. Theorie der Normalflächen. Acta Math., 105:245–375, 1961. doi: 10.1007/BF02559591.
- [HLP99] Joel Hass, Jeffrey C. Lagarias, and Nicholas Pippenger. The computational complexity of knot and link problems. J. ACM, 46(2):185–211, 1999. doi:10.1145/301970.301971.
- [Dyn06] I. A. Dynnikov. Arc-presentations of links: monotonic simplification. Fund. Math., 190:29–76, 2006. doi:10.4064/fm190-0-3.
- [KM11] P. B. Kronheimer and T. S. Mrowka. Khovanov homology is an unknotdetector. Publ. Math. Inst. Hautes Études Sci., 113:97–208, 2011. doi:10.1007/s10240-010-0030-y.
- [OS04b] Peter Ozsváth and Zoltán Szabó. Holomorphic disks and genus bounds. Geom. Topol., 8:311–334, 2004. doi:10.2140/gt.2004.8.311.
- [Kup14] Greg Kuperberg. Knottedness is in NP, modulo GRH. Adv. Math., 256:493–506, 2014. doi:10.1016/j.aim.2014.01.007.
- [Lac21a] Marc Lackenby. The efficient certification of knottedness and Thurston norm. Adv. Math., 387:Paper No. 107796, 142, 2021. doi:10.1016/j.aim.2021.107796.
- [HN10] Joel Hass and Tahl Nowik. Unknot diagrams requiring a quadratic number of Reidemeister moves to untangle. Discrete Comput. Geom., 44(1):91–95, 2010. doi:10.1007/s00454-009-9156-4.
- [Lac15] Marc Lackenby. A polynomial upper bound on Reidemeister moves. Ann. of Math. (2), 182(2):491–564, 2015. doi:10.4007/annals.2015.182.2.3.
- [BCL+24] Benjamin A. Burton, Hsien-Chih Chang, Maarten Löffler, Clément Maria, Arnaud de Mesmay, Saul Schleimer, Eric Sedgwick, and Jonathan Spreer. Hard diagrams of the unknot. Exp. Math., 33(3):482–500, 2024. doi:10.1080/10586458.2022.2161676.

title: Kirby Problem 1.77
statement:
How many Reidemeister moves are required to relate two dia-
grams of a knot (as a function of their numbers of crossings)?
background:
Source: Kirby's Problems in Low-Dimensional Topology notes. Original problem number: KP-1.77.

Literature notes:
(1) One reason why this question is interesting is that a computable upper
bound leads to an algorithm to decide whether two knots are equivalent.
(2) Lackenby [Lac15] proved that, for a diagram of the unknot with $c$ cross-
ings, there is a sequence of Reidemeister moves taking it to the trivial
diagram with length at most $(236c)^{11}$. It is not inconceivable that there is
a polynomial upper bound that applies to every knot type. However, the
best known upper bound on the number of Reidemeister moves required
to relate two diagrams of a knot with $c_{1}$ and $c_{2}$ crossings is due to Coward
and Lackenby [CL14]:

$$
2^{2^{\cdot^{\cdot^{\cdot^{2}}}}},
$$

where the height of the tower is $k^{c_1+c_2}$ and where $k = 10^{1000000}$.
(3) A nontrivial lower bound was established by Hass and Nowik [HN10],
who proved that for each natural number $n$ there exists a diagram of the
unknot with $7n-1$ crossings and where the number of Reidemeister moves
required to take it to the trivial diagram is at least $2n^{2} + 3n - 2$.

References cited:
- [Lac15] Marc Lackenby. A polynomial upper bound on Reidemeister moves. Ann. of Math. (2), 182(2):491–564, 2015. doi:10.4007/annals.2015.182.2.3.

- [HN10] Joel Hass and Tahl Nowik. Unknot diagrams requiring a quadratic number of Reidemeister moves to untangle. Discrete Comput. Geom., 44(1):91–95, 2010. doi:10.1007/s00454-009-9156-4.

title: Kirby Problem 1.78
statement:
Let $D$ be any diagram of the unknot with $n$ crossings. Let $h(D)$
be the smallest number such that some series of Reidemeister moves that transforms

$D$ to a 0-crossing diagram has the property that all intermediate diagrams have at
most $h(D)$ crossings. Define $h(n)$ to be the maximum of $h(D)$ over all $n$-crossing
diagrams of the unknot. A diagram represents a hard unknot if $h(D) > n$. What
is $h(n)$?
background:
Source: Kirby's Problems in Low-Dimensional Topology notes. Original problem number: KP-1.78.

Literature notes:
It is known [BCL $^{+}24$] that $h(n) \geq n + 3$ for certain values of $n$.

References cited:

title: Kirby Problem 1.79
statement:
Are there additional moves that, when added to the three Rei-
demeister moves, allow for strict monotonic descent in the crossing number of an
unknot diagram?
background:
Source: Kirby's Problems in Low-Dimensional Topology notes. Original problem number: KP-1.79.

Literature notes:
(1) Additional moves allow increased efficiency in diagram simplification. Sev-
eral attempts at finding such moves have been given, but none are known
to suffice [PZ16]. Work of Dynnikov gives a monotonic, but not strictly
monotonic, process [Dyn03].
(2) A strictly monotonic process would lead to a polynomial time algorithm
for unknot detection; see Problem 1.76.
(3) The collection of additional moves can grow with the number of crossings,
e.g. moving an arc across a twist region of a diagram. However the set of
additional moves cannot be arbitrary; moves consisting of any sequence
of Reidemeister moves would allow any knot equivalence to be carried out
in one step. A reasonable restriction is to allow moves that reduce the
crossing number and can be found in polynomial time (polynomial in the
crossing number).

References cited:
- [PZ16] Carlo Petronio and Adolfo Zanellati. Algorithmic simplification of knot diagrams: new moves and experiments. J. Knot Theory Ramifications, 25(10):1650059, 2016. doi:10.1142/S0218216516500590.
- [Dyn03] I. A. Dynnikov. Recognition algorithms in knot theory. Uspekhi Mat. Nauk, 58(6(354)):45–92, 2003. doi:10.1070/RM2003v058n06ABEH000675.

title: Kirby Problem 1.80
statement:
Is unknotting number computable? Is there even an algorithm
to decide whether a knot has unknotting number one?
background:
Source: Kirby's Problems in Low-Dimensional Topology notes. Original problem number: KP-1.80.

Literature notes:
(1) Many elementary knot invariants, such as the crossing number, are known
to be computable. However, it seems extremely challenging to determine
whether the unknotting number is computable.
(2) Recall that the unknotting number of a knot is the minimum number of
crossing changes required to unknot the knot, where the minimum is taken
over all diagrams of the knot. One can also consider the unlinking number
of a link, which is the minimal number of crossing changes required to
turn it into an unlink. Closely related is the splitting number, which is the
minimal number of crossing changes required to turn into a split link.
(3) Some lower bounds on the computational complexity of determining un-
linking number are known: it was shown by de Mesmay, Rieck, Sedgwick
and Tancer [dMRST21] and Koenig and Tsvietkova [KT21] that deter-
mining the unlinking number of a link is NP-hard.

(4) The second question in the problem seems more tractable, since many
structural results are known about knots with unknotting number one
[ST89], [Sch85b]. The analogous problem of determining whether a link
has unlinking number one was solved for a large class of links by Lackenby
[Lac21b].
(5) This problem was also stated in [Lac17a].

References cited:
- [dMRST21] Arnaud de Mesmay, Yo’av Rieck, Eric Sedgwick, and Martin Tancer. The unbearable hardness of unknotting. Adv. Math., 381:Paper No. 107648, 36, 2021. doi:10.1016/j.aim.2021.107648.
- [KT21] Dale Koenig and Anastasiia Tsvietkova. NP-hard problems naturally arising in knot theory. Trans. Amer. Math. Soc. Ser. B, 8:420–441, 2021. doi:10.1090/btran/71.
- [ST89] Martin Scharlemann and Abigail Thompson. Link genus and the Conway moves. Comment. Math. Helv., 64(4):527–535, 1989. doi:10.1007/BF02564693.
- [Sch85b] Martin G. Scharlemann. Unknotting number one knots are prime. Invent. Math., 82(1):37–55, 1985. doi:10.1007/BF01394778.
- [Lac21b] Marc Lackenby. Links with splitting number one. Geom. Dedicata, 214:319–351, 2021. doi:10.1007/s10711-021-00618-x.
- [Lac17a] Marc Lackenby. Elementary knot theory. In Lectures on geometry, Clay Lect. Notes, pages 29–64. Oxford Univ. Press, Oxford, 2017.

title: Kirby Problem 1.81
statement:
(a) Are all knots trivial?
(b) Conjecture: The Bing sling is knotted.
background:
Source: Kirby's Problems in Low-Dimensional Topology notes. Original problem number: KP-1.81.

Literature notes:
(1) For this problem, a knot is a topological embedding (a homeomorphism
onto its image) of a circle in $S^{3}$. A knot is trivial if it is isotopic, i.e. con-
nected by an arc of embeddings, to the unknot. A smooth knot in a string
is trivial in this sense by simply pulling the string tight so that the knot
becomes a point. A similar argument works for locally flat embeddings:
the problem is only interesting for wild embeddings.
(2) The Bing Sling [Bin56, DV09] (see also [Nan18, amd22] and [Shi73])
is drawn in Figure 1.12.
(3) Brin [Bri83] shows that there are knots that at each point are locally
equivalent to the Bing sling but are non-ambiently isotopic to the unknot.

Figure 4. The Bing Sling

title: Kirby Problem 1.82
statement:
(a) What is a positive knot?
(b) Describe a simple set of moves to convert between two positive diagrams
of the same knot or link.
background:
Source: Kirby's Problems in Low-Dimensional Topology notes. Original problem number: KP-1.82.

Literature notes:
(1) Positive knots and alternating knots are both defined in diagrammatic
terms, but somewhat orthogonally to one another.
The corresponding
problems for alternating knots have been settled.
(2) The first problem is meant to evoke Ralph Fox’s question, ‘What is an
alternating knot?’ [Lic97, p.32]. It seeks a characterization of the class
of positive knots in terms intrinsic to the knot exterior, e.g.
a condi-
tion on the knot group or the existence of a special kind of geometric
structure or spanning surface. It echoes a related question of Rudolph,
who proved that positive links are strongly quasipositive. He asked, as
a kind of converse to his result: “Can positive links be characterized as
strongly quasipositive links that satisfy some extra geometric conditions?”
[Rud99, Question, p.556]. Baader made progress on Rudolph’s question
by showing that a knot is positive if and only if it is strongly quasiposi-
tive and homogeneous [Baa05]. In light of this, an answer to Problem 1
could be obtained by giving a geometric characterization of homogeneity.
Note that Fox’s question was addressed in related papers by Greene and
by Howie [Gre17, How17], which led to new applications for alternating
knots.
(3) The second problem is meant to evoke the Tait flyping conjecture for alter-
nating links, which was proven by Menasco and Thistlethwaite [MT93].
The quest for a set of moves satisfying Problem (b) is complicated by the
fact that a knot can have reduced positive diagrams with different crossing
numbers.

References cited:
- [Lic97] W. B. Raymond Lickorish. An introduction to knot theory, volume 175 of Graduate Texts in Mathematics. Springer-Verlag, New York, 1997. doi:10.1007/978-1-4612-0691-0.
- [Rud99] Lee Rudolph. Positive links are strongly quasipositive. In Proceedings of the Kirbyfest (Berkeley, CA, 1998), volume 2 of Geom. Topol. Monogr., pages 555–562. Geom. Topol. Publ., Coventry, 1999. doi:10.2140/gtm.1999.2.555.
- [Baa05] S. Baader. Quasipositivity and homogeneity. Math. Proc. Cambridge Philos. Soc., 139(2):287–290, 2005. doi:10.1017/S0305004105008698.
- [Gre17] Joshua Evan Greene. Alternating links and definite surfaces. Duke Math. J., 166(11):2133–2151, 2017. With an appendix by András Juhász and Marc Lackenby. doi:10.1215/00127094-2017-0004.
- [How17] Joshua A. Howie. A characterisation of alternating knot exteriors. Geom. Topol., 21(4):2353–2371, 2017. doi:10.2140/gt.2017.21.2353.
- [MT93] William Menasco and Morwen Thistlethwaite. The classification of alternating links. Ann. of Math. (2), 138(1):113–171, 1993. doi:10.2307/2946636.

title: Kirby Problem 1.83
statement:
Determine the algebraic structure of the concordance group $\mathcal{O}$
of open strings.
(a) Is it abelian?
(b) Does it contain torsion?
background:
Source: Kirby's Problems in Low-Dimensional Topology notes. Original problem number: KP-1.83.

Literature notes:
(1) Virtual strings, also known as flat virtual knots [Kau99], were introduced
by Turaev [Tur04] as homotopy classes of immersions of $S^{1}$ in compact
oriented surfaces, up to stabilization of the surface.
(2) Two virtual strings in $\Sigma_{1}$ and $\Sigma_{2}$ are said to be concordant if they cobound
an immersed annulus in an oriented 3-manifold $M$ with boundary $\partial M =$
$\Sigma_{1} \cup -\Sigma_{2}$. A virtual string $\alpha$ in $\Sigma$ is said to be slice if there exists an
oriented 3-manifold $M$ and immersed disk $D$ in $M$ such that $\partial M = \Sigma$ and

$\partial D = \alpha$. The first example of an immersed curve in a surface that does
not bound an immersed disk in any 3-manifold is due to Carter [Car91].
(3) Concordance classes of open strings form a group $\mathcal{O}$, which is known to be
infinitely generated [Tur04]. Turaev also introduced the related notion of
algebraic concordance for virtual strings, and Jie Chen [Che23, Example
3.19] has found examples of flat knots that are algebraically slice but not
slice. There is a surjection to $\mathcal{O}$ from the concordance group of virtual
knots (see the following Problem 1.84), which was shown to be non-abelian
by Chrisman [Chr22].

References cited:
- [Kau99] Louis H. Kauffman. Virtual knot theory. European J. Combin., 20(7):663–690, 1999. doi:10.1006/eujc.1999.0314.
- [Tur04] Vladimir Turaev. Virtual strings. Ann. Inst. Fourier (Grenoble), 54(7):2455–2525, 2004. URL: http://aif.cedram.org/item?id=AIF 2004 54 7 2455 0.
- [Car91] J. Scott Carter. Extending immersions of curves to properly immersed surfaces. Topology Appl., 40(3):287–306, 1991. doi:10.1016/0166-8641(91)90111-X.
- [Che23] Jie Chen. Flat knots and invariants. PhD thesis, McMaster University, 2023. URL: https://www.math.mcmaster.ca/\%7Eboden/students/Chen-PhD.pdf.
- [Chr22] Micah Chrisman. Milnor’s concordance invariants for knots on surfaces. Algebr. Geom. Topol., 22(5):2293–2353, 2022. doi:10.2140/agt.2022.22.2293.

title: Kirby Problem 1.84
statement:
For a classical knot, does its slice genus as a virtual knot agree
with its slice genus as a classical knot?
background:
Source: Kirby's Problems in Low-Dimensional Topology notes. Original problem number: KP-1.84.

Literature notes:
(1) Virtual knots were originally defined combinatorially by Kauffman [Kau99].
For the purposes of this problem a virtual knot $K$ may be regarded as an
embedding of $S^{1}$ into $\Sigma \times [0, 1],$ where $\Sigma$ is a compact oriented surface.
The virtual slice genus of $K$ is the minimal genus, taken over all sur-
faces $F$ and all 3-manifolds $M$, such that $F$ embeds into $M \times [0, 1]$ with
$\partial F = K$. Here $M$ is a compact oriented 3-manifold with $\partial M = \Sigma$. A
virtual knot is said to be virtually slice if it bounds a disk in $M \times [0, 1]$
for some 3-manifold $M$.
(2) This question is due to Dye-Kaestner-Kauffman [DKK17, §6], who gave
an affirmative answer any knot for which the slice genus is determined by
the Rasmussen invariant, including torus knots. Their results support the
conjecture that for classical knots, their slice genus as virtual knots agrees
with their slice genus as classical knots. It is known that a classical knot
is virtually slice if and only if it is slice [BN17], thus the conjecture is
true for knots with slice genus one.
(3) This problem has two versions, one for the smooth slice genus and the
other for the topological (locally flat) slice genus.

References cited:
- [Kau99] Louis H. Kauffman. Virtual knot theory. European J. Combin., 20(7):663–690, 1999. doi:10.1006/eujc.1999.0314.
- [DKK17] Heather A. Dye, Aaron Kaestner, and Louis H. Kauffman. Khovanov homology, Lee homology and a Rasmussen invariant for virtual knots. J. Knot Theory Ramifications, 26(3):1741001, 57, 2017. doi:10.1142/S0218216517410012.
- [BN17] Hans U. Boden and Matthias Nagel. Concordance group of virtual knots. Proc. Amer. Math. Soc., 145(12):5451–5461, 2017. doi:10.1090/proc/13667.

title: Kirby Problem 1.85
statement:
Let $K$ be a hyperbolic knot in $S^{3}$ and $\chi(K)$ the space of con-
jugacy classes of $\operatorname{PSL}_{2}(\mathbb{C})$ representations of $\pi_{1}(S^{3} - K)$. There is a distinguished
component of $\chi(K)$ that contains the discrete faithful representation coming from
the finite volume hyperbolic structure on the complement of $K$. Does this component
always contain an arc of representations to $\operatorname{SO}(3)$?
background:
Source: Kirby's Problems in Low-Dimensional Topology notes. Original problem number: KP-1.85.

Literature notes:
(1) Chinburg-Reid-Stover conjectured [CRS22, Conjecture 1.9] that there
always is such an arc of representations. A positive answer would in fact
prove that the knot groups of hyperbolic knots always have faithful $\operatorname{SO}(3)$
representations.
(2) It is explained in [Ago22] that an affirmative answer to this question
would prove there are no infinite descending chains of hyperbolic knots in
the ribbon concordance partial order [Gor81, Question 6.2]. See Prob-
lem 1.56 for a knot Floer homology perspective on Gordon’s question.

References cited:
- [CRS22] Ted Chinburg, Alan W. Reid, and Matthew Stover. Azumaya algebras and canonical components. Int. Math. Res. Not. IMRN, 2022(7):4969–5036, 2022. doi:10.1093/imrn/rnaa209.
- [Ago22] Ian Agol. Ribbon concordance of knots is a partial ordering. Comm. Amer. Math. Soc., 2:374–379, 2022. doi:10.1090/cams/15.
- [Gor81] C. McA. Gordon. Ribbon concordance of knots in the 3-sphere. Math. Ann., 257(2):157–170, 1981. doi:10.1007/BF01458281.

title: Kirby Problem 1.86
statement:
(a) Every connected cubic $($ i.e. trivalent $)$ graph has freeness index at least 2.
(b) Every graph has freeness index at least two.
(c) There is a graph with freeness index two.
background:
Source: Kirby's Problems in Low-Dimensional Topology notes. Original problem number: KP-1.86.

Literature notes:
(1) A knot in the 3-sphere is the trivial knot if and only if its complement is
a solid torus. One can extend the notion of triviality from knots to em-
bedded (finite) graphs by considering a graph embedded in the 3-sphere
to be “unknotted” if its complement is a connected sum of handlebod-
ies. Every connected graph has an embedding into $S^{3}$ with handlebody
complement; in fact, using induction and 2-handle addition, one can show
that every graph has an unknotted embedding with the additional feature
that every subgraph obtained by erasing the interior of a single edge is
also unknotted [Tho22].
(2) Conway and Gordon showed that some graphs (for example, the complete
graph with 7 vertices, $K_{7}$) have some knotted subgraphs no matter how
they are embedded into $S^{3}$ [CG83b]. Planar graphs, by contrast, can
be embedded in $S^{3}$ such that every subgraph is unknotted; so can some
non-planar graphs, such as $K_{5}$.
(3) One can define an integer invariant of a finite (connected) graph $\Gamma$, the
freeness index, which measures the extent to which $\Gamma$ can be embedded in
the 3-sphere such that it and its subgraphs are unknotted.
Definition. An embedding $f$ of $\Gamma$ into $S^{3}$ such that the complement
of $\Gamma'$ is unknotted for every subgraph of $\Gamma'$ of $\Gamma$ obtained by deleting up to
$k$ edges from $\Gamma$ is called $k$-free. The freeness index of $\Gamma$ is the maximum
of this integer over all embeddings $f$.

(4) In [Tho22] it is shown that every graph has freeness index at least one,
while the graph $K_{6}$ has freeness index 8 and the Petersen graph has free-
ness index 4. [Tho22].
(5) We can relate the freeness index to the long-standing orientable cycle
double cover conjecture (OCDCC) from combinatorics ([Sze73, Sey80]).
The OCDCC for (bridgeless) cubic graphs implies the OCDCC for all
graphs. For bridgeless cubic graphs $\Gamma$, the OCDCC is equivalent to the

statement that $\Gamma$ has an embedding into a closed orientable surface $F$ such
that every complementary region is a disk and the closure of every com-
plementary region is also a disk (this is a strong embedding of $\Gamma$ into $F$).
In order to make a connection with the freeness index, one can exploit the
fact that once a graph is embedded into a closed orientable surface $F, F$
can then be embedded into $S^{3}$ as a Heegaard surface. If both the embed-
ding of the graph into the surface, and of the surface into the 3-sphere, are
sufficiently “nice”, one can conclude that the induced embedding of the
graph into the 3-sphere satisfies some strong freeness conditions. This can
be used to show that a cubic graph satisfying the OCDCC has freeness
index at least 2 [Tho22].
(6) Note that a connected bridgeless cubic graph with freeness index 1 would
provide a counter-example to the OCDCC.

References cited:
- [Tho22] Abigail Thompson. The freeness index of a graph, 2022. arXiv:2206.12939.
- [CG83b] J. H. Conway and C. McA. Gordon. Knots and links in spatial graphs. J. Graph Theory, 7(4):445–453, 1983. doi:10.1002/jgt.3190070410.
- [Sze73] G. Szekeres. Polyhedral decompositions of cubic graphs. Bulletin of the Australian Mathematical Society, 8(3):367–387, 1973. doi:10.1017/S0004972700042660.
- [Sey80] P. D. Seymour. Disjoint paths in graphs. Discrete Math., 29(3):293–309, 1980. doi: 10.1016/0012-365X(80)90158-2.

title: Kirby Problem 1.87
statement:
Is every fibered link in $S^{3}$ realized as the link of an isolated
singular point of a polynomial map $\mathbb{R}^{4} \to \mathbb{R}^{2}$?
background:
Source: Kirby's Problems in Low-Dimensional Topology notes. Original problem number: KP-1.87.

Literature notes:
(1) This problem is due to Benedetti–Shiota [BS98], and originates in the
celebrated Milnor book [Mil68b].
(2) Let $f: \mathbb{R}^{4} \to \mathbb{R}^{2}$ be a polynomial map with $f(0) = 0$ and set $V = f^{-1}(0)$.
Assume that $0 \in \mathbb{R}^{4}$ is an isolated point of the intersection of $V$ and the
set of singular points of $f$. Such a point is often called a weakly isolated
singularity.
As instances of Milnor’s cone structure and fibration theorems [Mil68b],
we have:
(i) There exists a small positive real number $\epsilon_{0}$ such that for every $0 <$
$\epsilon < \epsilon_{0}$, the sphere $S^{3}_{\epsilon}$ in $\mathbb{R}^{4}$ with radius $\epsilon$ centered at 0 is transverse
to the surface $V$, and the link type $L$ of
$L_{\epsilon}=(1/\epsilon)(S^{3}_{\epsilon}\cap V)\subset S^{3}$
does not depend on the choice of $\epsilon$.
(ii) Under the stronger assumption that $0 \in \mathbb{R}^{4}$ is an isolated singular
point of the map $f$, the link $L \subset S^{3}$ is fibered.
(3) In [Mil68b], one is mainly concerned with the links of (the realifications
of) complex polynomial maps $\mathbb{C}^{2} \to \mathbb{C}$ at an isolated singular point; in
such a case, a weakly isolated singularity in (1) above is equivalent to
a usual isolated singularity as in (2), and we obtain a distinguished and
well understood family of fibered links (see [Neu03, Web08]). In the
general case, there are no evident obstructions against a positive answer
to the problem. As remarked in [Mil68b, Page 84], the first example of
a fibered knot to be considered not belonging to that family for complex
polynomials, was the figure-eight knot. Later, an explicit realization of the
figure-eight knot as the link of a real isolated singularity was obtained in
[Per82]. Further partial positive results have been worked out in [Loo71,
Rud87, Pic05, Bod19, Bod20, Bod23, AdSSQ24].

(4) It is known [AK81] that every link $L$ in $S^{3}$ can be realized as the link
of a polynomial map as in (i) above, only requiring that 0 is an isolated
point of the intersection of $V$ and the set of singular points of $f$.

References cited:
- [BS98] R. Benedetti and M. Shiota. On real algebraic links in $S^{3}$. Boll. Unione Mat. Ital. Sez. B Artic. Ric. Mat. (8), 1(3):585–609, 1998.
- [Mil68b] John Milnor. Singular points of complex hypersurfaces, volume No. 61 of Annals of Mathematics Studies. Princeton University Press, Princeton, NJ; University of Tokyo Press, Tokyo, 1968. https://www.jstor.org/stable/j.ctt1bd6kvv.
- [Neu03] W. Neumann. Topology of hypersurface singularities. In Erich Kähler Mathematische Werken, pages 727–736. de Gruyter, 2003. See also https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.04386.
- [Web08] Claude Weber. On the topology of singularities. In Singularities II, volume 475 of Contemp. Math., pages 217–251. Amer. Math. Soc., Providence, RI, 2008. doi: 10.1090/conm/475/09285.
- [Per82] B. Perron. Le nœud “huit” est algébrique réel. Invent. Math., 65(3):441–451, 1981/82. doi:10.1007/BF01396628.
- [Loo71] Eduard Looijenga. A note on polynomial isolated singularities. Indag. Math., 33:418–421, 1971. Nederl. Akad. Wetensch. Proc. Ser. A 74.
- [Rud87] Lee Rudolph. Isolated critical points of mappings from $\mathbb{R}^{4}$ to $\mathbb{R}^{2}$ and a natural splitting of the Milnor number of a classical fibered link. I. Basic theory; examples. Comment. Math. Helv., 62(4):630–645, 1987. doi:10.1007/BF02564467.
- [Pic05] Anne Pichon. Real analytic germs fg and open-book decompositions of the 3-sphere. Internat. J. Math., 16(1):1–12, 2005. doi:10.1142/S0129167X05002710.

title: Kirby Problem 1.88
statement:
Are there infinitely many congruence arithmetic links in the
3-sphere?
background:
Source: Kirby's Problems in Low-Dimensional Topology notes. Original problem number: KP-1.88.

Literature notes:
(1) This problem relates to the more general question posed by Thurston
to find the topological and geometric properties of quotients of $\mathbb{H}^{3}$ by
arithmetic subgroups of $\operatorname{PSL}(2, \mathbb{C})$ [Thu82].
(2) A link complement is arithmetic if it is of the form $\mathbb{H}^{3}/\Gamma$ for some discrete
subgroup $\Gamma \leq \operatorname{PSL}(2, \mathbb{C})$ with the property that $\Gamma$ is commensurable with
$\operatorname{PSL}(2, O_{d})$, where $O_{d}$ the ring of integers in $\mathbb{Q}($
$?$
$-d)$. Famously, Reid
[Rei91] proved that the figure-eight knot is the only arithmetic knot in
the 3-sphere. However, there are infinitely many arithmetic links (see for
example the discussion in [BR23a]).
(3) The question is concerned with a particular type of arithmetic link called
congruence links, which are defined as follows. A principal congruence
subgroup $\Gamma$ is equal to the kernel of

$$
\operatorname{PSL}(2, O_{d}) \to \operatorname{PSL}(2, O_{d}/I)
$$

for some ideal $I$ in $O_{d}$. More generally, $\Gamma$ is called congruence if it contains
a principal congruence subgroup. When $\mathbb{H}^{3}/\Gamma$ is a link complement, the
link is said to be principal congruence and congruence respectively.
(4) In [BGR19], Baker, Goerner and Reid gave a complete classification of
principal congruence arithmetic links in the 3-sphere. In particular, there
are finitely many such links. (See [BGR22] for all known link diagrams
of principal congruence links.) The question asks whether this remains
true for congruence arithmetic links.
(5) Much information is known about arithmetic links in the 3-sphere and in
particular about congruence links. For example, any arithmetic link in
the 3-sphere commensurable with $\operatorname{PSL}(2, O_{d})$ must have

$$
d \in \{1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 7, 11, 15, 19, 23, 31, 39, 47, 71\}.
$$

References cited:
- [Thu82] William P. Thurston. Three-dimensional manifolds, Kleinian groups and hyperbolic geometry. Bull. Amer. Math. Soc. (N.S.), 6(3):357–381, 1982. doi:10.1090/S0273-0979-1982-15003-0.
- [Rei91] Alan W. Reid. Arithmeticity of knot complements. J. London Math. Soc. (2), 43(1):171–184, 1991. doi:10.1112/jlms/s2-43.1.171.
- [BR23a] Mark D. Baker and Alan W. Reid. Infinitely many arithmetic alternating links. Algebr. Geom. Topol., 23(6):2857–2866, 2023. doi:10.2140/agt.2023.23.2857.
- [BGR19] M. D. Baker, M. Goerner, and A. W. Reid. All principal congruence link groups. J. Algebra, 528:497–504, 2019. doi:10.1016/j.jalgebra.2019.02.023.
- [BGR22] Mark D. Baker, Matthias Goerner, and Alan W. Reid. All known principal congruence links, 2022. arXiv:1902.04426.

title: Kirby Problem 1.89
statement:
(a) Fix a long link L. What is the homotopy type of the embedding space of
links isotopic to L?
(b) Fix a link L in a 3-manifold M. What is the homotopy type of the embed-
ding space of links in M isotopic to L?

(c) Given a link $L$ obtained by infecting a link $L_{1}$ by another link $L_{2}$, describe
the homotopy type of component of $L$ in the space of links in terms of the
components of $L_{1}$ and $L_{2}$.
background:
Source: Kirby's Problems in Low-Dimensional Topology notes. Original problem number: KP-1.89.

Literature notes:
(1) A long link is an embedding of a disjoint union of lines that agree with
a fixed collection of affine lines outside of a box. The answer to the first
question, due to Hatcher and Budney, is known for long knots in the sense
that the knot spaces are shown to be homotopy equivalent to standard
combinations of standard spaces; see Remark (3) below.
(2) Spaces of long links have applications in 4-manifold theory as well as high-
dimensional manifold theory. For example, the recent work of Budney and
Gabai [BG19] on the homotopy-type of $\operatorname{Diff}(S^{1} \times D^{n-1})$ for $n \geq 4$ uses
the low-dimensional homotopy groups of the space of long embeddings
$\operatorname{Emb}(I, S^{1} \times D^{n-1})$. This space can be thought of as the homotopy fiber
of the forgetful map $\operatorname{Emb}(I \sqcup D^{n-2}, D^{n}) \to \operatorname{Emb}(D^{n-2}, D^{n})$, i.e. it is the
space of 2-component ‘long links’ where one component is trivial.
(3) A major step in the description of long knot spaces was Hatcher’s proof
of the Smale conjecture, which is equivalent [Hat83, Appendix] to the
statement that $\operatorname{Diff}(D^{3}; \partial D^{3})$ is contractible, which in turn implies that
the component of the long unknot is contractible. Combined with work of
Hatcher [Hat76] and Ivanov [Iva76] on diffeomorphisms of 3-manifolds,
it also implies that each component in the space of long knots is a $K(\pi, 1)$
space [Bud07].
Hatcher [Hat02] determined the homotopy type of a
long torus knot and, building on his work with McCullough [HM97a], of
a long hyperbolic knot.
Budney [Bud10] determined the homotopy type of the component of
any long knot $K$ in $\operatorname{Emb}(\mathbb{R}, \mathbb{R}^{3})$ in terms of the satellite decomposition
of $K$, i.e. in terms of splicing operations, thus answering part (a) above
when $L$ has one component.
The homotopy type is roughly a twisted
product of factors of $S^{1}, S^{1} \times S^{1}$, and configuration spaces of points in
the plane, with one factor for each knot or link appearing in the satellite
decomposition.
(4) Havens and Koytcheff [HK21] generalized Hatcher and Budney’s results
to the space of closed links in $S^{3}$ modulo rotations, whose components are
$K(\pi, 1)$ spaces for irreducible links. They did not completely determine
the homotopy types of spaces of split links because $\operatorname{Diff}(M)$ for a reducible
3-manifold $M$ is not completely understood. However, Boyd and Bregman
[BB25] obtained more detailed information on spaces of split links, espe-
cially their fundamental groups, using semi-simplicial spaces that model
them. Kosanović [Kos24] related Vassiliev invariants to the Goodwillie–
Weiss embedding calculus in the setting of a long knot $K$ in any compact
oriented 3-manifold $M$ with boundary.
(5) In part (c), infection generalizes splicing from long knots to string (a.k.a. long)
links. Budney [Bud07, Bud12] developed the operations of connect-sum
and splicing at the space level, parameterizing them by operads.
For
both operations, he obtained space-level decomposition results, which for
connect-sum he further developed at the homological level with F. Cohen
[BC09].

Burke and Koytcheff [BK15b] generalized Budney’s splicing operad
to a (colored) operad for string link infection. They obtained a partial
decomposition result for 2-component string links, building upon a re-
sult on isotopy classes in their joint work with Blair [BBK15]. This de-
composition was completed for 2-component string links by Batelier and
Ducoulombier [BD23]. It is essentially in terms of the stacking of string
links rather than the more general infection operation. An answer to part
(c) would be related to a decomposition of a 3-manifold analogous to the
JSJ decomposition but with tori replaced by surfaces of higher genus.

title: Kirby Problem 2.1
statement:
(Ivanov conjecture). Let $S$ be an orientable surface of finite type
with genus at least three. If $G \leq \operatorname{Mod}(S)$ is a subgroup of finite index, does $G$ have
finite abelianization?
background:
Source: Kirby's Problems in Low-Dimensional Topology notes. Original problem number: KP-2.1.

Literature notes:
(1) The Ivanov conjecture is a weaker version of the question of whether or
not the mapping class group has property (T). (The unpublished preprint
[And07] announced a negative answer to the latter, which does not resolve
the Ivanov conjecture in any case). It was recently shown that automor-
phism groups of most free groups do have property (T) and hence every
finite index subgroup has finite abelianization: this was resolved for rank
5 by Kaluba–Nowak–Ozawa [KNO19] and for $\operatorname{rank} \geq 6$ by [KKN21a].
A resolution for rank 4 was announced by Nitsche [Nit22].
(2) The Ivanov conjecture has an equivalent reformulation in terms of map-
ping class group actions on the homology of finite covers of surfaces [PW13].
The corresponding statement about these actions has become known as
the Putman–Wieland conjecture. Some progress on the Putman–Wieland
conjecture has been made [LL23b, LL23a, MT24].
(3) For braid groups and mapping class groups of surfaces of genus two or
lower, virtual surjections to the integers exist by virtue of the existence of
such maps for braid groups.

References cited:

- [KKN21a] Marek Kaluba, Dawid Kielak, and Piotr W. Nowak. On property (T) for $\mathrm{Aut}(F_n)$ and $\mathrm{SL}_n(\mathbb{Z})$. Ann. of Math. (2), 193(2):539–562, 2021. doi:10.4007/annals.2021.193.2.3.
- [Nit22] Martin Nitsche. Computer proofs for Property (T), and SDP duality, 2022. arXiv: 2009.05134.
- [PW13] Andrew Putman and Ben Wieland. Abelian quotients of subgroups of the mappings class group and higher Prym representations. J. Lond. Math. Soc. (2), 88(1):79–96, 2013. doi:10.1112/jlms/jdt001.
- [LL23b] Aaron Landesman and Daniel Litt. An introduction to the algebraic geometry of the Putman-Wieland conjecture. Eur. J. Math., 9(2):Paper No. 40, 25, 2023. doi: 10.1007/s40879-023-00637-w.

title: Kirby Problem 2.2
statement:
(Congruence subgroup problem). Does every finite-index sub-
group of the mapping class group of $S$ contain a congruence subgroup?
background:
Source: Kirby's Problems in Low-Dimensional Topology notes. Original problem number: KP-2.2.

Literature notes:
(1) Let $S$ be a finite-type surface, and let $K \leq \pi_{1}(S)$ be a finite-index charac-
teristic (i.e., $\operatorname{Aut}(\pi_{1}(S))$-invariant) subgroup. A congruence subgroup of
the mapping class group of $S$ is the kernel of the natural map from the
mapping class group of $S$ to $\operatorname{Out}(\pi_{1}(S)/K)$. This definition is analogous
to congruence subgroups of integral special linear groups.
(2) The congruence subgroup problem is known to have a positive answer
in certain low-genus cases. For punctured spheres, this was established
by Diaz–Donagi–Harbater [DDH89], with subsequent alternative proofs
given by Asada [Asa01], Thurston, and McReynolds [McR12]. The case
of genus one was originally addressed by Asada [Asa01], with further
work done by Kent [Ken16] and Bux–Ershov–Rapinchuk [BER11].
(3) A positive resolution to the congruence subgroup problem has applications
in anabelian geometry [Mar19].

References cited:
- [DDH89] Steven Diaz, Ron Donagi, and David Harbater. Every curve is a Hurwitz space. Duke Math. J., 59(3):737–746, 1989. doi:10.1215/S0012-7094-89-05933-4.
- [Asa01] Mamoru Asada. The faithfulness of the monodromy representations associated with certain families of algebraic curves. J. Pure Appl. Algebra, 159(2-3):123–147, 2001. doi:10.1016/S0022-4049(00)00056-6.
- [McR12] D. B. McReynolds. The congruence subgroup problem for pure braid groups: Thurston’s proof. New York J. Math., 18:925–942, 2012. http://nyjm.albany.edu: 8000/j/2012/18 925.html.
