title: Kirby Problem 2.3
statement: Is the mapping class group of a surface of finite type linear?
background:
Source: Kirby's Problems in Low-Dimensional Topology notes. Original problem number: KP-2.3.

Literature notes:
(1) Recall that a group is linear if it can be embedded as a subgroup of $\operatorname{GL}_{n}(\mathbb{C})$
for some $n$.
(2) Following the linearity of the braid group (see Remark (4) below), there
are some low-complexity cases for which linearity is known to hold. This
is true, in particular, for mapping class groups of punctured spheres and
hyperelliptic mapping class groups, including the full mapping class group
in genus 2 [Kor00, BB01]. In addition, if one can prove that a non-
closed mapping class group is nonlinear (say of genus $g$ with one puncture
or boundary component) then all mapping class groups of genus $h > g$
have nonlinear mapping class groups. Unsurprisingly, there are examples
of infinite-type surfaces with nonlinear mapping class groups [APV21].
(3) The analogous question of linearity for $\operatorname{Aut}(F_{n})$, the automorphism group
of a free group $F_{n}$ of $\operatorname{rank} n$, has been resolved in the negative by Formanek–
Procesi [FP92]. They construct certain “poison subgroups” of $\operatorname{Aut}(F_{n})$
that are known to be nonlinear. Subsequently, such poison subgroups were
shown not to exist in mapping class groups by Brendle–Hamidi-Tehrani
[BHT01].
(4) On the other hand, braid groups are known to be linear, due to the work
of Bigelow and Krammer [Big01, Kra02].
The Lawrence–Krammer–
Bigelow representations used to certify this are constructed as the action
on the homology of a certain 4-manifold given as an infinite abelian cover
of the configuration space of two points in the $n$-punctured disk. It is
tempting to speculate about carrying out an analogous construction in
higher genus, but various complications arise; ultimately, the natural ho-
mology representations of braid groups are simply symmetric groups, and
the Lawrence–Krammer–Bigelow representation arises as a deformation of
a symmetric group representation [Jon87]. The corresponding homology

actions of mapping class groups of surfaces in positive genus have infinite
image.
(5) One possible approach to establishing nonlinearity would be to make effec-
tive the residual finiteness of mapping class groups. In particular, super-
polynomial residual finiteness growth would imply nonlinearity by work
of Bou-Rabee–McReynolds [BRM15].
(6) There is a categorified faithful, finite-dimensional, linear representation
with mapping classes acting by functors; see [LOT13].
(7) Certain constraints on the properties of a faithful representation have
been established. In [Kor23], Korkmaz shows that for $g \geq 3$, any faith-
ful representation must have dimension $n > 3g - 3$.
For any finite-
dimensional linear representation of a mapping class group in genus $g \geq 3$,
Bridson [Bri10] proved that Dehn twists are necessarily sent to quasi-
unipotent matrices (i.e., ones whose eigenvalues are roots of unity). From
this one can easily show that mapping class groups have no faithful linear
representations in positive characteristic. For more recent further devel-
opments in this direction, see [AS16, But19, KLS19].
(8) For a much more extensive discussion and bibliography, see the article of
Margalit [Mar19].

- [APV21] Tarik Aougab, Priyam Patel, and Nicholas G. Vlamis. Isometry groups of infinite genus hyperbolic surfaces. Math. Ann., 381:459–498, 2021.
- [FP92] Edward Formanek and Claudio Procesi. The automorphism group of a free group is not linear. J. Algebra, 149(2):494–499, 1992. doi:10.1016/0021-8693(92)90029-L.
- [BHT01] Tara E. Brendle and Hessam Hamidi-Tehrani. On the linearity problem for mapping class groups. Algebr. Geom. Topol., 1:445–468, 2001. doi:10.2140/agt.2001.1.445.

title: Kirby Problem 2.4
statement:
Let $S_{1}$ and $S_{2}$ be orientable surfaces of finite type. Under what
conditions do injective maps from (finite-index subgroups of) the mapping class
group of $S_{1}$ to the mapping class group of $S_{2}$ necessarily arise from “manipulations”
(e.g., inclusions, (branched) coverings, etc.) taking $S_{1}$ to $S_{2}$?
background:
Source: Kirby's Problems in Low-Dimensional Topology notes. Original problem number: KP-2.4.

Literature notes:
(1) It is known that all such injections arise from inclusions of surfaces pro-
vided that the genus of $S_{2}$ is not much larger than the genus of $S_{1}$ [AS12].
For braid groups, a detailed study of injective maps in a certain range
was announced by Chen–Kordek–Margalit [CKM19]; see also Problem
\section*{2.7. Both of these results pertain only to injections at the level of the full}
mapping class group; the case of arbitrary finite-index subgroups seems
much harder.
(2) There are many natural variations on this problem, replacing mapping
class groups by curve graphs and related graphs associated to surfaces.
The literature on this subject is vast, with two central results being [Iva97]
and [BM19]. It has been announced that a (model-theoretic) interpreta-
tion between curve graphs of surfaces induces a virtual injection between
mapping class group [DKdlNG20].

- [CKM19] Lei Chen, Kevin Kordek, and Dan Margalit. Homomorphisms between braid groups, 2019. arXiv:1910.00712.
- [Iva97] Nikolai V. Ivanov. Automorphism of complexes of curves and of Teichmüller spaces. Internat. Math. Res. Notices, 1997(14):651–666, 1997. doi:10.1155/$S^{1}$073792897000433.

title: Kirby Problem 2.5
statement:
For $g \geq 3$, determine a finite presentation for the Torelli
group $\mathcal{I}_{g}$, or show that no finite presentation exists.
background:
Source: Kirby's Problems in Low-Dimensional Topology notes. Original problem number: KP-2.5.

Literature notes:
(1) The Torelli group $\mathcal{I}_{g} \leq \operatorname{Mod}(S_{g})$ is the subgroup of $\operatorname{Mod}(S_{g})$ consisting of
mapping classes acting trivially on $H_{1}(S_{g}; \mathbb{Z})$. Work of Johnson [Joh83]
shows that $\mathcal{I}_{g}$ is finitely generated for $g \geq 3$.
(2) This is [Kir78, Problem 2.9]. The question was raised by Magnus, and
described by Birman in [Bir71].
(3) For $g = 1$, the Torelli group is trivial, and for $g = 2$, Mess showed it is a
free group of infinite rank [Mes92].
(4) For any finitely presented group $G$, the second homology $H_{2}(G; \mathbb{Q})$ is finite
dimensional, though the converse does not hold. Recent work of Minahan–
Putman [MP25] announced that $H_{2}(\mathcal{I}_{g}; \mathbb{Q})$ is finite dimensional for $g \geq 6$.
It is still open whether or not $H_{2}(\mathcal{I}_{g}; \mathbb{Z})$ is finitely generated for large $g$.

title: Kirby Problem 2.6
statement:
Give a classification or enumeration of the finite-index sub-
groups of $\operatorname{Mod}(S_{g})$ that are generated by Dehn twists, Dehn multitwists, or powers
thereof. Which of these subgroups are “geometrically meaningful”, in the sense that
they are given as the stabilizers of some kind of geometric or topological struc-
ture on the surface? Conversely, when is a geometrically meaningful subgroup (not
necessarily of finite index) generated by powers of Dehn multitwists?
background:
Source: Kirby's Problems in Low-Dimensional Topology notes. Original problem number: KP-2.6.

Literature notes:
(1) The classical Dehn–Lickorish theorem asserts that the mapping class group
of a closed orientable surface is generated by a finite collection of Dehn
twists.
Any finite-index subgroup contains some power of every Dehn
twist, but a general finite-index subgroup need not contain any single twist
$T_{c}$ at all, nor is a general finite-index subgroup generated by the powers
of Dehn twists that it does contain. Indeed, work of Funar [Fun99] and
Masbaum [Mas99] shows that for general values of $r$, the subgroup of
$\operatorname{Mod}(\Sigma_{g})$ generated by $r^{th}$ powers of Dehn twists is of infinite index.
(2) Salter and Calderon–Salter [Sal19, CS21] show that one such example
is the class of $r$-spin mapping class groups, i.e., the stabilizers of a chosen
$r$-spin structure on $S_{g}$, for $g \geq 5$. In [CS23], they proved that the framed
mapping class group for a framing (i.e., the stabilizer of the isotopy class
of that framing) is likewise generated by Dehn twists; these subgroups are
of infinite index. Salter–Sane [SS23] announced a generating set for the
stabilizer of a mod-2 homology class $[x]$ consisting of Dehn twists together
with a single square-twist $T_{c}^{2}$.
(3) The terms “geometrically meaningful” and “geometric or topological struc-
ture” in the problem statement are intentionally vague, but the examples
discussed in the remarks above are meant to be representative. To dis-
ambiguate, we do not (necessarily) mean “geometric structure” in the
Thurstonian sense of a $(G, X)$-structure.

(4) One motivation for this question comes from the theory of (achiral) Lef-
schetz pencils, which are encoded in the mapping class group as sequences
of Dehn twists whose product is the boundary multi-twist. When these
Dehn twists lie in some “geometrically meaningful” subgroup, one can
ask if this endows the ambient 4–manifold with an additional structure.
One instance of this is the case of $r = 2$ (i.e., classical) spin mapping class
groups, where the question of whether a symplectic 4-manifold is also spin
is related to whether it admits a symplectic Lefschetz pencil whose twists
lie in a spin mapping class group [Sti01, BHM23, BH24c, AB23].

References cited:

title: Kirby Problem 2.7
statement:
Classify the homomorphisms from the braid group $B_{n}$ on $n$
strands to the braid group $B_{m}$ on $m$ strands, where $n, m \in \mathbb{N}$ are arbitrary.
background:
Source: Kirby's Problems in Low-Dimensional Topology notes. Original problem number: KP-2.7.

Literature notes:
(1) There are several works in this direction including those of Artin [Art47],
Lin [Lin04], Dyer–Grossman [DG81], Bell–Margalit [BM06], Castel [Cas16]
and, finally, Chen–Kordek–Margalit [CKM19], where the most general
result known to date was announced (the complete classification for $m \leq$
$2n$ and $n \geq 5$).
(2) There is a more precise formulation of this question. We view the group
$B_{m}$ as the mapping class group $\operatorname{Mod}(S_{0,m}^{1})$ of the $m$-punctured disk and
denote by $\mathcal{C}(S_{0,m}^{1})$ the curve complex of $S_{0,m}^{1}$. We say that a homomor-
phism $\phi: B_{n} \to B_{m} = \operatorname{Mod}(S_{0,m}^{1})$ is reducible if there exists a nonempty
simplex $\mathcal{A}$ of $\mathcal{C}(S_{0,m}^{1})$ such that $\phi(\beta)(\mathcal{A}) = \mathcal{A}$ for all $\beta \in B_{n}$. That is,
every element of $\phi(B_{n})$ is reducible, and moreover preserves the same set
of curves. Then we have the following conjecture, which can be compared
with the Nielsen–Thurston classification.
Conjecture. Let $n, m \in \mathbb{N}$ with $5 \leq n \leq m$, and let $\phi: B_{n} \to B_{m}$ be
a homomorphism. Then we have one of the following three possibilities.
(a) The image of $\phi$ is a cyclic group.
(b) $n = m$, and $\phi$ is an injective homomorphism as described in [BM06].
(c) $\phi$ is reducible.

(3) In light of the identification of $B_{m}$ with the mapping class group $\operatorname{Mod}(S_{0,m}^{1})$,
this question admits a natural generalization to the problem of classifying
all homomorphisms between mapping class groups of surfaces; see Prob-
lem 2.4. For further discussion, see the survey article [AS16].

References cited:
- [Art47] E. Artin. Braids and permutations. Ann. of Math. (2), 48:643–649, 1947. doi: 10.2307/1969131.
- [Lin04] Vladimir Lin. Braids and permutations, 2004. arXiv:math/0404528.
- [DG81] Joan L. Dyer and Edna K. Grossman. The automorphism groups of the braid groups. Amer. J. Math., 103(6):1151–1169, 1981. doi:10.2307/2374228.
- [BM06] Robert W. Bell and Dan Margalit. Braid groups and the co-Hopfian property. J. Algebra, 303(1):275–294, 2006. doi:10.1016/j.jalgebra.2005.10.038.
- [Cas16] Fabrice Castel. Geometric representations of the braid groups. Astérisque, 378:vi+175, 2016.
- [CKM19] Lei Chen, Kevin Kordek, and Dan Margalit. Homomorphisms between braid groups, 2019. arXiv:1910.00712.
- [AS16] Javier Aramayona and Juan Souto. Rigidity phenomena in the mapping class group. In Handbook of Teichmüller theory. Vol. VI, volume 27 of IRMA Lect. Math. Theor. Phys., pages 131–165. Eur. Math. Soc., Zürich, 2016.

title: Kirby Problem 2.8
statement:
Fix distinct trivial tangles $\tau_{1}, \tau_{2}$ for which $\tau_{1} \cup\tau_{2}$ is the unknot.
Describe the intersection of the associated wicket groups $W_{n}(\tau_{1}) \cap W_{n}(\tau_{2}) \leq B_{2n}$.
Is this group finitely generated? Finitely presented?
background:
Source: Kirby's Problems in Low-Dimensional Topology notes. Original problem number: KP-2.8.

Literature notes:
(1) A tangle on $n$ strands is a proper embedding of $n$ disjoint arcs into the
upper half-space in $\mathbb{R}^{3}$, considered up to isotopy rel boundary. Tangles
$\tau_{1}, \tau_{2}$ based at the same set of $2n$ points in $\mathbb{R}^{2} \subset \mathbb{R}^{3}$ can be combined
into the link $\tau_{1} \cup \tau_{2}$, where $\overline{\tau}_{2}$ denotes the reflection of $\tau_{2}$ through the
$xy$-plane. A trivial tangle is any tangle that can be isotoped so that each
strand has a single local maximum with respect to the standard height
function on $\mathbb{R}^{3}$. There is a natural transitive action of the braid group
$B_{2n}$ on the set of trivial tangles based at a fixed set of $2n$ points, and the
stabilizer of a fixed trivial tangle $\tau$ is known as a wicket group, written
$W_{n}$ or $W_{n}(\tau)$ when we wish to emphasize the particular trivial tangle.
(2) The questions in the problem originate from the works of S. Hirose,
D. Iguchi, E. Kin, and Y. Koda that are discussed below.
(3) Note that $W_{n}(\tau_{1})$ and $W_{n}(\tau_{2})$ are conjugate in $B_{2n}$.
Brendle–Hatcher
[BH13] determined a finite presentation for $W_{n}$. This problem has a nat-
ural generalization in which one allows $\tau_{1} \cup \overline{\tau}_{2}$ to be an unlink of $c$ com-
ponents for $c \geq 1$ [HIKK22, Question 2.10]. The group $W_{n}(\tau_{1})\cap W_{n}(\tau_{2})$
could be called the Goeritz group of the bridge splitting $\tau_{1} \cup \overline{\tau}_{2}$ of the un-
link. Hirose–Iguchi–Kin–Koda defined and studied this group as the hy-
perelliptic Goeritz group, proving that this group is finitely presented when
the Heegaard splitting is a 3-bridge splitting of a 2-bridge link [HIKK22].
If the distance of an $n$-bridge decomposition of a link in $S^{3}$ with $n \geq 3$
is at least 5, then its Goeritz group is a finite group [IK20, Theorem 0.1].
(4) There is a connection with the study of knotted surfaces through the the-
ory of bridge trisections [MZ17a]: Any smooth surface-link in $\mathbb{R}^{4}$ can be
represented by a tri-plane diagram in which the first two tangle diagrams
are arranged to have no crossings. Given this, the Goeritz group of the
bridge splitting of the unlink given by the first two tangles is precisely the
set of braids that act on the tri-plane diagram without changing the first
two tangles. Thus, an understanding of this group could be applied to the
problem of finding equivalences between bridge trisected surface-links.

References cited:
- [BH13] Tara E. Brendle and Allen Hatcher. Configuration spaces of rings and wickets. Comment. Math. Helv., 88(1):131–162, 2013. doi:10.4171/CMH/280.
- [HIKK22] Susumu Hirose, Daiki Iguchi, Eiko Kin, and Yuya Koda. Goeritz groups of bridge decompositions. Int. Math. Res. Not. IMRN, 2022(12):9308–9356, 2022. doi:10.1093/imrn/rnab001.
- [IK20] Daiki Iguchi and Yuya Koda. Twisted book decompositions and the Goeritz groups. Topology Appl., 272:107064, 15, 2020. doi:10.1016/j.topol.2020.107064.
- [MZ17a] Jeffrey Meier and Alexander Zupan. Bridge trisections of knotted surfaces in $S^{4}$. Trans. Amer. Math. Soc., 369(10):7343–7386, 2017. doi:10.1090/tran/6934.

title: Kirby Problem 2.9
statement:
Is there a nice presentation of the $n$-stranded braid group whose
generating set is the set of all positive elementary braid half-twists?
background:
Source: Kirby's Problems in Low-Dimensional Topology notes. Original problem number: KP-2.9.

Literature notes:
(1) The adjective “nice” here should at least mean that all relations consist
of equating two words in the positive generators of the same length, and
perhaps also that there be a finite number of local pictures describing the
required relations.
(2) The positive monoid in the standard Artin presentation consists of all
positive braids. In the Birman–Ko–Lee presentation [BKL98], the pos-
itive monoid is the strongly quasipositive braids. The positive monoid
for the desired presentation would correspond to the quasipositive braids
and would hopefully provide interesting algorithmic tools similar to Gar-
side [Gar69] for solving questions regarding quasipositivity. Similar infi-
nite presentations hold for the mapping class groups of surfaces (Gervais
[Ger96]) as well as the Torelli group (Putman [Put07]).

References cited:
- [BKL98] Joan Birman, Ki Hyoung Ko, and Sang Jin Lee. A new approach to the word and conjugacy problems in the braid groups. Adv. Math., 139(2):322–353, 1998. doi:10.1006/aima.1998.1761.
- [Gar69] F. A. Garside. The braid group and other groups. Quart. J. Math. Oxford Ser. (2), 20:235–254, 1969. doi:10.1093/qmath/20.1.235.

title: Kirby Problem 2.10
statement:
(a) Is there an efficient algorithm to compute distances in the curve complex
of a surface? The input to the algorithm should be the surface and the
curves. One may ask similar questions for related complexes, such as the
arc complex of a surface with boundary.
(b) Is there an algorithm (efficient or otherwise) to compute the distance be-
tween quasi-convex subsets of the curve complex? This question is partic-
ularly interesting in the case where the quasi-convex subsets are the disk
sets of handlebodies.
background:
Source: Kirby's Problems in Low-Dimensional Topology notes. Original problem number: KP-2.10.

Literature notes:
(1) The curve complex has proved to be particularly important in Kleinian
group theory and in the study of the mapping class groups of surfaces
[Min06].
One notable feature of $\mathcal{C}(S)$, proved by Masur and Minsky
[MM99], is that it is Gromov hyperbolic.
(2) The complex is not locally finite, and so there is no naive way of comput-
ing distances. However, distances in $\mathcal{C}(S)$ are known to be computable,
by work of Leasure [Lea02], Shackleton [Sha12], Webb [Web15], Bir-
man, Margalit, and Menasco [BMM16] and Watanabe [Wat16]. Bell
and Webb [BW16a] announced an algorithm with running time that is
bounded above by a polynomial function of the logarithm of the weight of

the two curves, given as normal curves in some triangulation of $S$. How-
ever, the running time of their algorithm grows very rapidly as the surface
$S$ is allowed to vary. The aim of Problem (a) is to find such an algorithm
that runs in polynomial time even as the surface varies.
Baroni [Bar24] has announced an efficient algorithm to compute dis-
tances up to a bounded multiplicative error, the bound depending only
on $S$. He used this to find an efficient algorithm to determine whether a
given surface automorphism is pseudo-Anosov, reducible, or periodic.
(3) A related problem is as follows. Given a reducible element of the mapping
class group, can an invariant multi-curve be found efficiently (in polyno-
mial time as function of the ‘size’ of the mapping class and also in the
Euler characteristic of $S$)?
(4) When $S$ is the boundary of a handlebody $H$, the associated disk set con-
sists of the subcomplex of $\mathcal{C}(S)$ induced by the curves bounding disks
in $H$. This was proved to be quasi-convex in $\mathcal{C}(S)$ by Masur and Min-
sky [MM04]. When $S$ is a Heegaard surface for a closed 3-manifold, it
bounds a handlebody on each side and so there are two associated disk
sets. The distance between them in $\mathcal{C}(S)$ is the Hempel distance of the
splitting [Hem01]. This is not known to be computable. However, it
was proved by Masur and Schleimer [MS13] that it is computable up to
a bounded additive error. The Hempel distance of a Heegaard splitting
encodes important information. For example, the Hempel distance is zero
if and only if the splitting is reducible, and the Hempel distance is one if
and only if the splitting is weakly reducible but irreducible.

References cited:

- [MM99] Howard A. Masur and Yair N. Minsky. Geometry of the complex of curves. I. Hyperbolicity. Invent. Math., 138(1):103–149, 1999. doi:10.1007/s002220050343.
- [Lea02] Jason Paige Leasure. Geodesics in the complex of curves of a surface. ProQuest LLC, Ann Arbor, MI, 2002. Thesis (Ph.D.)–The University of Texas at Austin. URL: http://gateway.proquest.com/openurl?url ver=Z39.88-2004\&rft val fmt= info:ofi/fmt:kev:mtx:dissertation\&res dat=xri:pqdiss\&rft dat=xri:pqdiss:3114766.

- [Web15] Richard C. H. Webb. Combinatorics of tight geodesics and stable lengths. Trans. Amer. Math. Soc., 367(10):7323–7342, 2015. doi:10.1090/tran/6301.

title: Kirby Problem 2.11
statement:
Find precise estimates for both the extremal and average behav-
ior of the simple lifting degree of curves, in terms of combinatorial (e.g., intersection
number) and/or geometric (e.g., geodesic length, word length) data.
background:
Source: Kirby's Problems in Low-Dimensional Topology notes. Original problem number: KP-2.11.

Literature notes:
(1) A result of Peter Scott [Sco78] tells us that for any closed geodesic $\gamma$ on
a hyperbolic surface $S$, there exists a finite degree cover $S' \to S$ such that
$\gamma$ lifts to $S'$ (i.e., choosing basepoints, $\gamma \in \pi_{1}(S') \leq \pi_{1}(S)$) and is a simple
closed curve in $S'$. The simple lifting degree of $\gamma$, which we will write as
$\deg(\gamma)$, is defined to be the minimal degree of such a covering $S'$ to which
$\gamma$ lifts simply.
(2) To precisely formulate the relationship between simple lifting degree and
combinatorial/geometric complexity, define the functions

$$
f_{S}(n)=\max\{\deg(\gamma): i(\gamma,\gamma)\leq n\}.
$$

and, for a choice of hyperbolic metric $\rho$ on $S$,

$$
f_{\rho}(L)=\max\{\deg(\gamma): \ell_{\rho}(\gamma)\leq L\}.
$$

The extremal behavior (i.e., upper bounds) of these functions has been
studied in work of Patel [Pat14], Gaster [Gas16], and Aougab–Gaster–
Patel–Sapir [AGPS17]. A lower bound for average behavior of $\deg(\gamma)$ was

obtained by Aougab–Gaster [AG22], but work of Sisto–Taylor [ST19]
implies that some mechanism other than what Gaster finds in the extremal
case is responsible for the average behavior. What is this mechanism?
Progress in the study of $f_{S}(n)$ has been obtained by Arenas and
Neumann-Coto [ANC20]. They establish the inequality $f_{S}(n) \leq 5(n+1)$;
note that this is independent of the surface $S$. They conjecture that the
tighter bound $f_{S}(n) \leq 2(n + 1)$ should hold. At the time of this writing,
no examples exist with $f_{S}(n) - n$ more than 2.
(3) Variations of these questions can be posed by, e.g., restricting to the class
of regular covers or to families of curves intersecting on a surface $S$. These
have been largely unexplored.

References cited:
- [Sco78] Peter Scott. Subgroups of surface groups are almost geometric. J. London Math. Soc. (2), 17(3):555–565, 1978. doi:10.1112/jlms/s2-17.3.555.
- [Pat14] Priyam Patel. On a theorem of Peter Scott. Proc. Amer. Math. Soc., 142(8):2891– 2906, 2014. doi:10.1090/S0002-9939-2014-12031-4.
- [Gas16] Jonah Gaster. Lifting curves simply. Int. Math. Res. Not. IMRN, 2016(18):5559– 5568, 2016. doi:10.1093/imrn/rnv316.
- [AGPS17] Tarik Aougab, Jonah Gaster, Priyam Patel, and Jenya Sapir. Building hyperbolic metrics suited to closed curves and applications to lifting simply. Math. Res. Lett., 24(3):593–617, 2017. doi:10.4310/MRL.2017.v24.n3.a1.
- [AG22] Tarik Aougab and Jonah Gaster. Combinatorially random curves on surfaces, 2022. arXiv:2209.11309.
- [ST19] Alessandro Sisto and Samuel J. Taylor. Largest projections for random walks and shortest curves in random mapping tori. Math. Res. Lett., 26(1):293–321, 2019. doi:10.4310/MRL.2019.v26.n1.a14.

title: Kirby Problem 2.12
statement:
(a) What is the maximum number of systoles on a closed, hyperbolic surface
of genus $g$?
(b) What is the maximum cardinality of a set of pairwise non-isotopic, essen-
tial, simple closed curves on a closed surface of genus $g$ with the property
that no two curves in the set intersect in more than one point?
background:
Source: Kirby's Problems in Low-Dimensional Topology notes. Original problem number: KP-2.12.

Literature notes:
(1) A systole on a closed hyperbolic surface is a closed geodesic of shortest
length. A systole is necessarily an essential, simple closed curve. On a
closed surface, any two systoles intersect in at most one point (in the
presence of punctures, systoles may intersect twice; see [FP15]). Hence
the first problem arises as a special case of the second. This quantity is
sometimes called the “kissing number”; kissing numbers of lattices have
been studied in a variety of contexts.
(2) The first problem was first seriously studied by Schmutz Schaller [Sch96].
The answer is known to lie between $C_{1}(\epsilon)\cdot g^{4/3-\epsilon}$ and $C_{2} \cdot g^{2}/ \log(g)$. Here
$C_{1}(\epsilon)$ is a function of an arbitrary value $\epsilon > 0$ and $C_{2}$ is an absolute
constant. The lower bound is a construction of Schmutz Schaller using
arithmetic surfaces [SS97]. The upper bound is due to Parlier using com-
binatorial and hyperbolic techniques [Par13b]. Schmutz Schaller conjec-
tured that the lower bound is optimal, in that the maximum cardinality
cannot exceed $C_{3} \cdot g^{4/3}$ for some absolute constant $C_{3}$ [SS97, Conjecture].
(3) The second problem was raised independently by Juvan, Malnic, and Mo-
har [JMM96] and by Farb and Leininger, as recorded in [MRT14, Ques-
tion 1].
The answer is known to lie between $C_{1} \cdot g^{2}$ and $C_{2} \cdot g^{2} \log g$.
The lower bound is a construction due to Malestein, Rivin, and Theran
[MRT14]. The upper bound is due to Greene, using probabilistic com-
binatorics and geometric techniques [Gre19]. The lower bound is conjec-
tured to be optimal, i.e., there exists an upper bound of the form $C_{3} \cdot g^{2}$
to match it.

Przytycki solved the corresponding problem for arcs: if $S$ is a con-
nected, orientable, punctured surface of finite type, then the maximum
number of pairwise non-isotopic, essential, simple arcs that limit to the
punctures is $(|\chi(S)| + 1)(|\chi(S)| + 2)$ [Prz15]. His methods involve hyper-
bolic geometry.
Replacing “one” by $k$ in the problem, the answer is known to lie
between $C_{1}(k) \cdot g^{k+1}$ and $C_{2}(k) \cdot g^{k+1} \log g$, for some functions $C_{1}(k)$ and
$C_{2}(k)$ independent of $g$. Once more, the lower bound is conjectured to
be optimal, i.e., there exists an upper bound of the form $C_{3}(k) \cdot g^{k+1}$ to
match it [Gre19, Conjecture 1].

References cited:
- [FP15] Federica Fanoni and Hugo Parlier. Systoles and kissing numbers of finite area hyperbolic surfaces. Algebr. Geom. Topol., 15(6):3409–3433, 2015. doi:10.2140/agt.2015.15.3409.
- [Sch96] Paul Schmutz. Compact Riemann surfaces with many systoles. Duke Math. J., 84(1):191–198, 1996. doi:10.1215/S0012-7094-96-08406-9.
- [SS97] Paul Schmutz Schaller. Extremal Riemann surfaces with a large number of systoles. In Extremal Riemann surfaces (San Francisco, CA, 1995), volume 201 of Contemp. Math., pages 9–19. Amer. Math. Soc., Providence, RI, 1997. doi:10.1090/conm/201/02617.
- [Par13b] Hugo Parlier. Kissing numbers for surfaces. J. Topol., 6(3):777–791, 2013. doi: 10.1112/jtopol/jtt012.
- [JMM96] M. Juvan, A. Malnič, and B. Mohar. Systems of curves on surfaces. J. Combin. Theory Ser. B, 68(1):7–22, 1996.
- [MRT14] Justin Malestein, Igor Rivin, and Louis Theran. Topological designs. Geom. Dedicata, 168:221–233, 2014. doi:10.1007/s10711-012-9827-9.
- [Gre19] Joshua Evan Greene. On loops intersecting at most once. Geom. Funct. Anal., 29(6):1828–1843, 2019. doi:10.1007/s00039-019-00517-0.
- [Prz15] Piotr Przytycki. Arcs intersecting at most once. Geom. Funct. Anal., 25(2):658–670, 2015. doi:10.1007/s00039-015-0320-0.

title: Kirby Problem 2.13
statement:
Let $S$ be a surface, and let $\Gamma_{1}, \Gamma_{2}$ be isotopy classes of embedded
graphs in $S$. Determine when $\Gamma_{1}$ and $\Gamma_{2}$ are related by a sequence of surgeries.
background:
Source: Kirby's Problems in Low-Dimensional Topology notes. Original problem number: KP-2.13.

Literature notes:
(1) A surgery of an embedded graph $\Gamma \subset S$ is defined as follows. Suppose
some component of $S\setminus\Gamma$ is a disk $D$. Let $x$ and $y$ be oriented edges in $\Gamma$
bounding $D$. There is a unique isotopy class $\lambda_{x,y}$ of arc connecting $x$ to
$y$ inside $D$. A regular neighborhood $N_{x,y}$ of $\lambda_{x,y}$ is a rectangle with two
opposite sides comprising subarcs of $x$ and $y$, and remaining sides running
parallel to $\lambda_{x,y}$. The surgery of $\Gamma$ along $\lambda_{x,y}$ is the graph $\Gamma'$ obtained from
$\Gamma$ by deleting the edges of $N_{x,y}$ lying on $x, y$ and replacing them with the
two edges parallel to $\lambda_{x,y}$. Note that surgery can change the topology of
the complement; there is a simple combinatorial criterion to determine
when this does or does not happen [San21].
(2) The number of vertices and edges are manifestly preserved under surgery,
but the isomorphism type of the graph can change. Sane has investigated
the “surgery graph” that tracks when two embedded graphs are related
by a surgery and has studied connectivity properties of this graph in a
number of cases, discussed below.
When every vertex of $\Gamma$ has even valence, $\Gamma$ determines a class in
$H_{1}(S; \mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z})$. This homology class is readily seen to be invariant under
surgery. The case where every vertex has valence 4 and the complement
is a single disk was studied by Salter–Sane [SS23], who announced that
in this case, graphs $\Gamma$ and $\Gamma'$ are related via a sequence of surgeries if and
only if their mod-2 homology classes are equal. In the case where every
vertex has valence 3 and the complement is a single disk, Sane announced
in [San20] that any two such graphs on the same surface can be connected
via a sequence of surgeries.
(3) This problem is more topological (and less purely combinatorial) than it
might appear to be at first glance. It is closely connected to the action of
the mapping class group on embedded graphs, and to the general prob-
lem of understanding subgroups of the mapping class group. A surgery
equivalence class determines a “stabilizer subgroup” of the mapping class
group of $S$, consisting of all mapping classes $f$ for which $f(\Gamma)$ can be

taken to $\Gamma$ via surgery. The result of Salter–Sane mentioned above can
be rephrased as the assertion that the stabilizer subgroup for the class of
graphs they consider is the stabilizer of a mod-2 homology class. Other
classes of graphs appear to have smaller stabilizer subgroups that are not
so easily characterized. Given the enduring mystery of classifying sub-
groups of the mapping class group (especially those of finite index), a
primary motivation for understanding graph surgery is that it may lead
to novel examples and phenomena in this arena.
(4) The literature mentioned above restricts attention to the unicellular case,
when $S\setminus\Gamma$ is a single disk (note that these authors further restrict to surg-
eries that preserve this property). One reason to be particularly interested
in this setting is that the enumeration of such “unicellular graphs” is a key
ingredient in Harer and Zagier’s computation of the Euler characteristic
of the moduli space of Riemann surfaces [HZ86].

References cited:
- [San21] Abdoul Karim Sane. Curves on surfaces and surgeries. European J. Combin., 93:Paper No. 103281, 20, 2021. doi:10.1016/j.ejc.2020.103281.
- [SS23] Nick Salter and Abdoul Karim Sane. Connected components of the topological surgery graph of a unicellular collection, 2023. arXiv:2308.09165.
- [San20] Abdoul Karim Sane. Unicellular maps and filtrations of the mapping class group, 2020. arXiv:2006.15880.
- [HZ86] J. Harer and D. Zagier. The Euler characteristic of the moduli space of curves. Invent. Math., 85(3):457–485, 1986. doi:10.1007/BF01390325.

title: Kirby Problem 2.14
statement:
(a) Does every Jordan curve in the Euclidean plane contain the vertices of a
square?
(b) Does every Jordan curve in the Euclidean plane contain the vertices of the
affine image of a regular hexagon?
(c) Let $\gamma \subset \mathbb{C}$ be a smooth Jordan curve, and let $S \subset \mathbb{C}$ consist of $2n \geq 4$
concyclic points. Does there exist a non-constant polynomial $p(z) \in \mathbb{C}[z]$
of degree $< n$ such that $p(S) \subset \gamma$?
(d) Suppose that $h$ is a continuous, real-valued function defined on the unit
sphere $S^{2} \subset \mathbb{R}^{3}$ and that points $x_{1},..., x_{4} \in S^{2}$ form the vertices of
a square.
Is there an isometry $\rho \in \operatorname{SO}(3)$ such that $h$ is constant on
$\rho(x_{1}),..., \rho(x_{4})$?
background:
Source: Kirby's Problems in Low-Dimensional Topology notes. Original problem number: KP-2.14.

Literature notes:
(1) The first problem is known as the Square Peg Problem. It was posed by
Otto Toeplitz in 1911 [Toe11]. It is solved affirmatively for several classes
of curves, including $C^{1}$ curves (see [Mat14]).
More generally, a curve inscribes an $n$-gon (and the $n$-gon inscribes
in the curve) if there exists an orientation-preserving similar copy of the
$n$-gon whose vertices lie on the curve. Every Jordan curve inscribes ev-
ery triangle (a noncolinear 3-gon) [Nie92], but no two dissimilar ellipses
inscribe the same pentagon. Vaughn proved that every Jordan curve in-
scribes a rectangle (of some uncontrolled aspect ratio) [Mey81]. Greene
and Lobb proved the optimal result for smooth curves: every smooth Jor-
dan curve inscribes every cyclic quadrilateral (i.e., a quadrilateral whose
vertices lie on a circle) [GL23]. By contrast, Pak observed that the quadri-
laterals that inscribe in all triangles are the isosceles trapezoids [Pak08].
It is possible that the widest class of quadrilaterals that inscribe in all
Jordan curves are the isosceles trapezoids.

(2) The second problem was raised as a conjecture by Grünbaum [Gru72,
Conjecture 4.3]. It is known to hold if the curve is convex [Gru72, p.84].
It is known that every $C^{1}$ Jordan curve either contains the vertices of the
affine image of a regular hexagon or six colinear points that are the limit
of the vertices of a sequence of affine images of regular hexagons [Vv11,
Theorem 7]. However, the problem is open in general, even for smooth
curves.
(3) The third problem was raised as a conjecture by Greene and Lobb [GL24,
Conjecture 1.1]. The case $n = 2$ is true and is equivalent to the result
about cyclic quadrilaterals noted above in the discussion of the first prob-
lem.
The case $n = 3$, and some special instances when $n \geq 4$, was
announced in [GL24]. These results all involve symplectic geometry.
(4) The fourth problem is known as the Table Problem, and it is related to the
Knaster problem (which has been solved in the negative). It is posed as
a conjecture in [Mat14, Conjecture 13]. The case in which $x_{1},..., x_{4}$ are
equally spaced around a great circle was solved affirmatively by Dyson
[Dys51].
The case in which $h$ is an even function was announced by
Naseri Sadr, who also announced a proof of a variation for Riemannian
surfaces [NS24]. Call a set of four points $x_{1},..., x_{4} \in S^{2}$ balancing if for
every $h$ there exists a $\rho$ as in the problem statement. The Table Problem
therefore asserts that the vertices of a square are a balancing set. The
case of the standard height function shows that a balancing set of points
must be concyclic. On the other hand, there exist concyclic $x_{1},..., x_{4}$
that are not a balancing set [Kar13]. Livesay proved that the vertices
of a rectangle contained in a great circle form a balancing set [Liv54].
It is possible that the vertices of any rectangle on $S^{2}$ form a balancing
set. A proof was claimed in [Gri91], but that paper was later invalidated
[Mat14].
Remarks on these and related problems appear in Klee and Wagon’s book [KW91]
and Matschke’s survey article [Mat14].

References cited:

- [Mat14] Benjamin Matschke. A survey on the square peg problem. Notices Amer. Math. Soc., 61(4):346–352, 2014. doi:10.1090/noti1100.

title: Kirby Problem 2.15
statement:
Is the genus $g$ Goeritz group $\mathcal{G}_{g}$ finitely generated when $g \geq 4$?
If so, find a set of generators.
background:
Source: Kirby's Problems in Low-Dimensional Topology notes. Original problem number: KP-2.15.

Literature notes:
(1) The Goeritz group $\mathcal{G}_{g}$ is the group of isotopy classes of orientation-preserving
homeomorphisms of $S^{3}$ that preserve an unknotted genus $g$ handlebody,
that is, one side of a genus $g$ Heegaard splitting. It is a rough analogue
for $S^{3}$ of the braid group for $S^{2}$. The notion can be extended to Heegaard
splittings of other 3-manifolds, as well [JM13].
(2) Goeritz [Goe33] exhibited a complete set of three generators for $\mathcal{G}_{2}$ and
Akbas [Akb08] found associated relators, providing a complete presen-
tation of $\mathcal{G}_{2}$. Powell [Pow80] believed he had found a complete set of
5 generators for $\mathcal{G}_{g}$, for any $g$, but there was a serious gap in the proof
(see footnote of [Sch04]). This is now known as the Powell Conjecture.
In [Sch20] it is shown that one of Powell’s proposed five generators is
redundant.
Freedman and Scharlemann [FS18] announced a proof of the Powell
Conjecture for $g = 3$. Their methods break down for higher genus, and
it is suspected that for $g \geq 4$ the group $\mathcal{G}_{g}$ is not even finitely generated.
Freedman [Fre22] suggests a method by which this might be proven.
(3) In [Sch24], Scharlemann generalizes Powell’s proposed generators and
shows that this generalized set suffices.
The set itself is infinite, but
Scharlemann announced that it can be used to demonstrate that the Pow-
ell Conjecture is stably true [Sch25]. That is, any element of $\mathcal{G}_{g}$, when
viewed as acting on the genus $g + 1$ unknotted handlebody obtained by
adding a single genus 1 summand to the original genus $g$ handlebody, is
a consequence of the 5 Powell elements of $\mathcal{G}_{g+1}$.
(4) In another approach, Zupan [Zup20] identifies a certain graph $\mathcal{R}_{g}$ in the
curve complex of a genus $g$ Heegaard surface and shows that, in general,
the genus $k$ Powell conjecture is true for all $k \leq g$ if and only if $\mathcal{R}_{k}$ is
connected for all $k \leq g$.

References cited:

title: Kirby Problem 2.16
statement:
If two hyperbolic surfaces have the same unmarked simple
length spectra (i.e., the same multiset of lengths that correspond to simple closed
curves), are they isometric?
background:
Source: Kirby's Problems in Low-Dimensional Topology notes. Original problem number: KP-2.16.

Literature notes:
(1) Let $M$ be a closed Riemannian manifold with negative sectional curva-
ture, and let $\mathcal{C}$ denote the set of free homotopy classes of closed curves in
$M$. In each homotopy class, there is a unique closed geodesic. This de-
fines a marked length spectrum function $\ell: \mathcal{C} \to \mathbb{R}_{>0}$ that assigns to each

class $g$ the length $\ell(g)$ of this closed geodesic. Burns and Katok asked
whether the function $\ell$ determines $M$ up to isometry [BK85]. While this
question is open in general, the answer is yes in the case of surfaces; this
is called marked length spectrum rigidity. Fricke and Klein showed this
holds for closed hyperbolic surfaces, in which case there are $6g - 5$ geo-
desic curves whose lengths determine the surface us to isometry [FK65].
Otal and, independently, Croke showed that surfaces with variable neg-
ative curvature are also marked length spectrum rigid [Ota90, Cro90];
see [CFF92, HP97] for other classes of metrics with respect to which
surfaces are marked length spectrum rigid.
In this problem, the length spectrum is unmarked, in the sense that
we no longer consider the function $\ell$ but only the image of $\ell$ as a multiset
in $\mathbb{R}_{>0}$; that is, we simply have a list of the lengths of closed geodesics on
the surface, counted with multiplicity. Moreover, we consider only lengths
corresponding to simple closed curves.
If we drop the assumption that curves we consider are simple, then the
answer is no; that is, hyperbolic surfaces do not enjoy unmarked length
spectrum rigidity. Vignéras constructed the first examples of isospectral
but non-isometric closed surfaces [Vig80], and Sunada gave a general
construction of such surfaces [Sun85].
However, the length spectrum
does determine the isometry class of the surface in some low-complexity
cases, such as a one-holed torus with one boundary component [Haa85,
BS88b].
On the other hand, the question of simple length spectrum rigidity is
still open. It is known that the examples of isospectral but non-isometric
surfaces constructed by Sunada can be distinguished by their simple length
spectra [Mau13].
(2) One can ask a family of analogous questions for each natural number:
suppose two hyperbolic surfaces have the same unmarked “$n$-spectra”,
which is the super-set of lengths corresponding to all curves with at most
$n$ self-intersections.
Are they isometric?
Above, “superset of lengths”
means the sets of lengths counting multiplicity.
(3) Baik–Choi–Kim [BCK21] recently announced that there is an open dense
set in Teichmüller space where the unmarked simple length spectrum is in-
deed rigid. The introduction to this paper contains a thorough discussion
of the history and context of this problem.
(4) See also Problem 3.17 for a discussion of length spectrum regidity for
higher-dimensional hyperbolic manifolds.

Teubner Verlagsgesellschaft, Stuttgart, 1965.

- [CFF92] C. Croke, A. Fathi, and J. Feldman. The marked length-spectrum of a surface of nonpositive curvature. Topology, 31(4):847–855, 1992. doi:10.1016/0040-9383(92) 90013-8.

title: Kirby Problem 2.17
statement:
Suppose that $c$ is a geodesic current on a hyperbolic surface,
and suppose that, on the space of hyperbolic metrics on the surface, $c$ has the same
length function as a closed geodesic.
Must $c$ be a convex combination of closed
curves?
background:
Source: Kirby's Problems in Low-Dimensional Topology notes. Original problem number: KP-2.17.

Literature notes:
(1) For an introduction to the theory of geodesic currents in general, see the
foundational work of Bonahon [Bon86, Bon88], as well as the contem-
porary book of Erlandsson–Souto [ES22].
(2) As an example, suppose that $c_{1}$ and $c_{2}$ are so-called “length-twins,” i.e.,
non-homotopic closed curves that have the same length in any hyperbolic
metric. Then the geodesic current $\frac{1}{2}c_{1}+\frac{1}{2}c_{2}$ is not a closed curve, but it
will also have the same length as $c_{1}$ and $c_{2}$. It is a convex combination of
$c_{1}$ and $c_{2}$; thus, the question asks whether there exists some more exotic
type of current (for example one whose support in $\mathbb{H}^{2}$ is not a discrete set
of geodesics) that can also have the same length as either $c_{1}$ or $c_{2}$.

References cited:
- [Bon86] Francis Bonahon. Bouts des variétés hyperboliques de dimension 3. Annals of Mathematics, 124(1):71–158, 1986. URL: http://www.jstor.org/stable/1971388.
- [Bon88] Francis Bonahon. The geometry of Teichmüller space via geodesic currents. Inventiones mathematicae, 92(1):139–162, 1988. doi:10.1007/BF01393996.
- [ES22] Viveka Erlandsson and Juan Souto. Mirzakhani’s curve counting and geodesic currents, volume 345 of Progress in Mathematics. Birkhäuser/Springer, Cham, [2022] ©2022. doi:10.1007/978-3-031-08705-9.

title: Kirby Problem 2.18
statement:
What is the best lower bound on the volume of a fibered hyper-
bolic 3-manifold one can give in terms of the translation length of the monodromy
with respect to various metric spaces, such as Teichmüller space with the Weil–
Peterson metric or the pants complex?
background:
Source: Kirby's Problems in Low-Dimensional Topology notes. Original problem number: KP-2.18.

Literature notes:
(1) The monodromy of a hyperbolic 3–manifold that fibers over the circle is
a pseudo-Anosov homeomorphism, which acts with positive translation
length on several well-studied spaces, including Teichmüller space with
either the Teichmüller or Weil-Peterson metric and the pants complex.
Brock [Bro03] shows that for a finite-type surface $S$ and a pseudo-
Anosov homeomorphism $f$ of $S$, the hyperbolic volume of the mapping
torus $M_{f}$ is comparable to the translation length $\tau_{WP}(f)$ of $f$ acting on
the Teichmüller space of $S$ with the Weil-Peterson metric. In particular,
he shows that there exist constants $\kappa_{1}$ and $\kappa_{2}$, depending on the topology
of $S$, such that

$$
\kappa_{2}\tau_{WP}(f) \leq \operatorname{Vol}(M_{f}) \leq \kappa_{1}\tau_{WP}(f).
$$

(3)
He also proves the analogous inequality with the translation length of $f$
acting on the pants complex.
The heart of the question, therefore, lies in making the constant $\kappa_{2}$
(or the analogous constant for other metric spaces) effective by describing
precisely how it depends on the genus $g$ of $S$.
(2) Kojima–McShane [KM18] and Brock–Bromberg [BB16] give effective
upper bounds on the volume in terms of the translation length of the
monodromy with respect to the Teichmüller and Weil-Peterson metrics on
Teichmüller space, respectively. A related question is to find an effective
upper bound on $\operatorname{Vol}(M_{f})$ in terms of the translation length with respect
to the pants complex.
A lower bound was obtained by Bridgeman–Brock–Bromberg for the
Weil-Peterson translation length in the case the 3–manifold is relatively
acylindrical [BBB23], but the bound is not effective. In the unpublished

work of Aougab–Taylor–Webb, they show that when considering the trans-
lation length of $f$ on the pants complex, the constant $\kappa_{2}$ decays like
$1/g!$.
No effective lower bounds are known.
(3) There is no such lower bound in terms of the translation length of the mon-
odromy with respect to the Teichmüller metric on Teichmüller space. Mc-
Mullen gives an explicit counterexample in which the Teichmüller transla-
tion lengths of the monodromies $f_{n}$ tend to infinity but the mapping tori
$M_{fn}$ have bounded volume [McM14].
(4) The analogue of the upper bound of the inequality (3) was proved for irre-
ducible end-periodic homeomorphisms of infinite-type surfaces by Field–
Kim–Leininger–Loving [FKLL23], and the analogue of the lower bound
was recently announced by Field–Kent–Leininger–Loving [FKLL25]. They
give a universal constant for $\kappa_{1}$ and show that the constant $\kappa_{2}$ depends
on the topology of the finite-type subsurface on which the irreducible
end-periodic is acting “interestingly” (not just by translation). It would
interesting to make their lower bound effective and compare it to the
description of $\kappa_{2}$ one might achieve in the finite-type case.
(5) This problem falls into the larger category of questions asking what hyperbolic-
geometric data about a fibered 3-manifold one can obtain from the surface
and homeomorphism data used to construct it. For instance, in any of
the cases mentioned above, is it possible to gather data about the short
geodesics in the 3-manifold $M_{f}$ from information about $S$ and $f$?

title: Kirby Problem 2.19
statement:
Which mapping classes give rise to arithmetic hyperbolic 3-
manifolds as their mapping tori?
background:
Source: Kirby's Problems in Low-Dimensional Topology notes. Original problem number: KP-2.19.

Literature notes:
(1) Roughly speaking, arithmetic hyperbolic manifolds are a special class of
hyperbolic manifolds constructed by “number-theoretic” methods. They
enjoy many special properties, e.g., possessing a very rich group of com-
mensurations (isometries of finite covers). For a general introduction, see
[MR03]; also see Problem 3.10.
(2) This is likely to be a deep and difficult question, since Thurston’s proof
of the existence of the hyperbolic structure on $M_{f}$ is non-constructive.
It would be useful to amass some systematic data on the monodromies
of known fibered arithmetic 3-manifolds. Are the elements that appear
distinctive or exceptional from the point of view of the mapping class
group?
As alluded to above, arithmetic hyperbolic manifolds are distinguished
in the class of all hyperbolic manifolds by the property that their funda-
mental groups have infinite index in their commensurators (indeed, the
commensurator is dense in $\operatorname{PSL}_{2}(\mathbb{C})$). One place to start would be to bet-
ter understand how the commensurator of the mapping torus is encoded
in the mapping class itself.

(3) In the world of knots, there is an analogous question which, remarkably,
has been resolved.
Alan Reid [Rei91] has shown that the only knot
$K \subset S^{3}$ for which the complement $S^{3}\setminus K$ is arithmetic hyperbolic is the
figure-8 knot. The figure-8 knot is fibered with fiber a once-punctured
torus. More generally, work of Bowditch-Maclachlan-Reid [BMR95] clas-
sifies the monodromies of all arithmetic hyperbolic once-punctured torus
bundles over $S^{1}$. In spite of this, it is not clear what special properties
these elements possess that single them out from other elements of $\operatorname{SL}_{2}(\mathbb{Z})$.
(4) The paper [BMR95] also proves some other results of relevance.
For
example, it shows that there are at most finitely many cyclic commen-
surability classes of arithmetic hyperbolic surface bundles with surface of
fixed non-compact topological type.
(5) Associated to any hyperbolic manifold is an invariant called the invari-
ant trace field, the field generated by the traces of squares of elements of
the fundamental group, viewed via the hyperbolic structure as isometries
in $\operatorname{PSL}_{2}(\mathbb{C})$. Arithmetic hyperbolic 3-manifolds are known to be char-
acterizable in terms of properties of their traces (see [MR03]). A more
general problem is to determine the invariant trace field associated to any
pseudo-Anosov element.

References cited:
- [MR03] Colin Maclachlan and Alan W. Reid. The arithmetic of hyperbolic 3-manifolds, volume 219 of Graduate Texts in Mathematics. Springer-Verlag, New York, 2003. doi:10.1007/978-1-4757-6720-9.
- [Rei91] Alan W. Reid. Arithmeticity of knot complements. J. London Math. Soc. (2), 43(1):171–184, 1991. doi:10.1112/jlms/s2-43.1.171.
- [BMR95] B. H. Bowditch, C. Maclachlan, and A. W. Reid. Arithmetic hyperbolic surface bundles. Math. Ann., 302(1):31–60, 1995. doi:10.1007/BF01444486.

title: Kirby Problem 2.20
statement:
Can one detect holomorphicity from a monodromy factoriza-
tion of a Lefschetz pencil, fibration, or a surface bundle over a surface? What are
the special properties of monodromy factorizations of holomorphic fibrations?
background:
Source: Kirby's Problems in Low-Dimensional Topology notes. Original problem number: KP-2.20.

Literature notes:
(1) Unless $\ell= g -1 = 0$, any fibration corresponding to a monodromy factor-
ization as above can be made symplectic and $J$-holomorphic for an almost
complex structure $J$ compatible with the symplectic form. However, $J$ is
not necessarily integrable.
(2) Let $f: X \to S_{h}$ be a relatively minimal genus–$g$ Lefschetz fibration.
Clearly, for it to be holomorphic, the total space $X$ should have the ho-
motopy type of a compact complex surface, e.g., the fundamental group
one reads from the monodromy factorization should be a Kähler group,
the odd Betti numbers should be even, and such.
Set $\chi_{f}:=\frac{1}{4}(\chi(X)+\sigma(X))-(g-1)(h-1)$ and
$K_{f}^{2}:=c_{1}^{2}(X)-8(g-1)(h-1)$. A few other known constraints are:
$\bullet$ Beauville’s inequality [Bea79]: $\chi_{f} \geq 0$;
$\bullet$ Arakelov’s inequality [Ara71]: $K_{f}^{2} \geq 0$; and
$\bullet$ Xiao’s slope inequality [Xia87]: $(4 - 4/g)\chi_{f} \leq K_{f}^{2} \leq 12\chi_{f}$.
Further constraints on $\chi_{f}$ and $K_{f}^{2}$ are available for holomorphic fibrations
of special types (hyperelliptic, non-hyperelliptic, trigonal, non-trigonal,
bielliptic, etc.); see e.g., [AK02].
(3) There is an additional constraint formulated in terms of the Nielsen-
Thurston classification. A subgroup $\Gamma < \operatorname{Mod}(S_{g})$ is reducible if there
is a multi-curve $C \subset S_{g}$ with only essential components fixed up to ho-
motopy by each element of $\Gamma$. The monodromy group $\Gamma$ of a nontrivial
holomorphic surface bundle over $B\setminus f(\operatorname{Crit}(f))$ must be infinite and irre-
ducible [Shi97].

- [Ara71] S. Ju. Arakelov. Families of algebraic curves with fixed degeneracies. Izv. Akad. Nauk SSSR Ser. Mat., 35:1269–1293, 1971.
- [Xia87] Gang Xiao. Fibered algebraic surfaces with low slope. Math. Ann., 276(3):449–466, 1987. doi:10.1007/BF01450841.
- [AK02] Tadashi Ashikaga and Kazuhiro Konno. Global and local properties of pencils of algebraic curves. In Algebraic geometry 2000, Azumino (Hotaka), volume 36 of Adv. Stud. Pure Math., pages 1–49. Math. Soc. Japan, Tokyo, 2002. doi:10.2969/aspm/03610001.
- [Shi97] Hiroshige Shiga. On monodromies of holomorphic families of Riemann surfaces and modular transformations. Math. Proc. Cambridge Philos. Soc., 122(3):541– 549, 1997. doi:10.1017/S0305004197001825.

title: Kirby Problem 2.21
statement:
What is the minimum number, $m_{g,b}$, of right-handed Dehn
twists along essential curves into which the boundary multi-twist, $\Delta:= T_{\delta_{1}} \cdots T_{\delta_{b}}$,
can be factorized in $\operatorname{Mod}(S_{g}^{b})$? Find factorizations realizing the minimum.
background:
Source: Kirby's Problems in Low-Dimensional Topology notes. Original problem number: KP-2.21.

Literature notes:
(1) A factorization $T_{c_1} \cdots T_{c_\ell}= \Delta$, where no $c_{i}$ is homotopic to a boundary
component or point, is often called a positive factorization of $\Delta$. A positive
factorization of the boundary multi-twist $\Delta= T_{\delta_{1}} \cdots T_{\delta_{b}}$ in $\operatorname{Mod}(S_{g}^{b})$,
where each $\delta_{j}$ is parallel to a distinct boundary component of $S_g^b$ and
$b > 0$, corresponds to a genus-$g$ Lefschetz pencil with $b$ base points and $\ell$
nodes.
With these in mind, the problem amounts to determining the small-
est second Betti number $b_{2}$ of genus-$g$ Lefschetz pencils/fibrations with
$b$ base points.
It is motivated by a central problem regarding the ex-
istence of small symplectic and exotic 4-manifolds.
See, e.g., [BK17,

Bay22, BH24c] for some successful implementations of this approach to
4-dimensional exotica.
(2) The pairs $g, b \in \mathbb{N}$ for which there is no positive factorization of the bound-
ary multi-twist are determined in [BMVHM17]; namely, when $g = 1$ and
$b > 9$, or $g \geq 2$ and $b > 4g + 4$. In all other cases, the minimum is known
to exist. The only cases when the problem has been completely settled
are $g = 1$ [Kas77, Moi77b] and $g = 2$ [BK17], for any $b \geq 0$.
For $g \geq 3$, there are reasonable upper bounds for every genus; the
positive factorizations discovered in [Mat96, Cad98, Kor01, Ham17]
imply that $m_{g,b} \leq 2g+4$ when $g$ is even and $b \leq 4$, and $m_{g,b} \leq 2g+10$ when
$g$ is odd and $b \leq 8$. These bounds are known to not be sharp, at least in
low genera. For example, $m_{g,b} = 7$ when $g = 2$ and $b \leq 3$ [BK17, Bay22],
whereas $m_{g,b} \leq 12$ when $g = 3$ and $b \leq 4$ [Smi01b, Bay22, HH18a].
For large $b \leq 4g + 4$, another upper bound is $m_{g,b} \leq 8g + 4$, which is
realized by genus–$g$ pencils on $S^{2} \times S^{2}$ [SS94, Tan12].
There are also lower bounds available in every genus, derived from
Seiberg-Witten theory of symplectic 4-manifolds, roughly implying that
$m_{g,b} \geq g$ [Li00, Sti99, BK03]—which is unlikely to be sharp in any
genus.
(3) There are several variations of this problem studied in the literature.
The minimum number of Dehn twists in positive factorizations of any
$h \geq 1$ commutators in $\operatorname{Mod}(S_{g})$ (which correspond to genus-$g$ Lefschetz
fibrations over $S_{h}$) is almost completely determined in [KO01, Mon12,
Ham14, SY17, BH23]; the only open cases are when $g \geq 3$ and $h = 1$.
When $b > 0$, one can also inquire about the maximum number of
Dehn twists, related to the uniform topology of Stein fillings of con-
tact 3-manifolds. This problem was completely answered in [BVHM15,
BVHM16, BMVHM17], establishing in particular that in many cases
one may have arbitrarily long positive factorizations of $\Delta$ in $\operatorname{Mod}(S_{g}^{b})$.
In some cases, one can obtain more leverage on the stated problem by
imposing additional conditions, say by assuming that the factorization lies
in a smaller mapping class group (e.g., [Alt20]) or by fixing some topo-
logical invariants of the corresponding Lefschetz pencils (e.g., [Sti02]).

- [Bay22] R. İnanç Baykur. Small exotic 4-manifolds and symplectic Calabi-Yau surfaces via genus-3 pencils. In Gauge theory and low-dimensional topology—progress and interaction, volume 5 of Open Book Ser., pages 185–221. Math. Sci. Publ., Berkeley, CA, 2022. https://msp.org/obs/2022/5-1/p09.xhtml.

title: Kirby Problem 2.22
statement:
Does every Lefschetz fibration over the 2–sphere admit a sec-
tion?
background:
Source: Kirby's Problems in Low-Dimensional Topology notes. Original problem number: KP-2.22.

Literature notes:
(1) Here we assume the fibration has critical points; otherwise, there exist
$T^{2}$–bundles over $S^{2}$ without sections.
Lefschetz fibrations that arise from blowing up the base locus of Lef-
schetz pencils naturally admit sections—namely, the exceptional divisors.
However, if say the fibration is constructed through branched covers, or ab-
stractly via a group-theoretic factorization, it is not a priori clear whether
a section exists.

Equivalently, one can ask if every positive Dehn twist factorization of
the identity in $\operatorname{Mod}(S_{g})$ lifts to $\operatorname{Mod}(S_{g}, p)$, the mapping class group of
the (fiber) surface fixing a point $p \in \Sigma_{g}$.
(2) This question has been raised repeatedly in the literature; e.g. [Smi01a,
Aur05, Ona10, Gom25], and Problems 2.8, 4.1, 7.1 and 8.1 in [Kor06],
[Sti15], [KS09], and [End21] respectively.
(3) More generally we can ask about the existence of multisections (in the
sense of [DS03, BH16b]):
Question. Does every Lefschetz fibration over the 2–sphere admit a
multisection? How about a 2-section?
Similarly, one can reformulate the existence of an $n$–section in terms of
the existence of a lift of a positive Dehn twist factorization of the identity
in $\operatorname{Mod}(S_{g})$ to a positive factorization also involving positive arc twists in
$\operatorname{Mod}(S_{g}, \{p_{1},..., p_{n}\})$, the mapping class group of $S_{g}$ fixing the set of $n$
distinct points $p_{1},..., p_{n} \in S_{g}$ [BH16b, BH16a].
(4) It is worth noting that for achiral Lefschetz fibrations, where the Dehn
twists in the factorization can be a mix of right-handed and left-handed
twists, there are counterexamples to the question. For instance, there is a
genus–1 achiral Lefschetz fibration on $S^{4}$ [Mat82], which, for homological
reasons, cannot admit a section. (In contrast, every genus–1 Lefschetz
fibration admits a section.) More examples are given in a recent preprint
of Gompf [Gom25].
(5) An ad hoc method for finding sections of a Lefschetz fibration with an
explicit monodromy factorization is to reverse-engineer the monodromy
factorization using elementary relations (among Dehn twists) in the map-
ping class group (e.g., [KO08, Ham17, Tan12]).
A potential counterexample to the existence of a section, where this ad
hoc method essentially fails, is the (spin, signature-zero) genus–9 Lefschetz
fibration of Baykur–Hamada in [BH24c].

title: Kirby Problem 2.23
statement:
Does there exist a surface bundle over a surface that admits
a complete hyperbolic metric, or, more generally, a complete metric of variable
negative curvature?
background:
Source: Kirby's Problems in Low-Dimensional Topology notes. Original problem number: KP-2.23.

Literature notes:
(1) Thurston’s hyperbolization theorem provides for an enormous wealth of 3-
manifolds that are surface bundles over $S^{1}$, and that moreover admit com-
plete hyperbolic metrics. Moving up a dimension, the same phenomenon
becomes quite mysterious. As in the 3-manifold case, it is necessary that
the monodromy of every nontrivial loop in the base be pseudo-Anosov. A
construction of such purely pseudo-Anosov surface subgroups of mapping
class groups has been announced in very recent work of Kent–Leininger
[KL24], resolving a major open question in its own right. It is not yet clear
whether every purely pseudo-Anosov subgroup induces a word-hyperbolic

surface-by-surface group extension, which is a necessary condition for the
total space to admit a metric of negative curvature, and indeed, it is
presently not known if the Kent-Leininger examples are word-hyperbolic.
A weak version of Problem 2.23 is then simply to furnish examples of
surface bundles over surfaces with word-hyperbolic fundamental group.
(2) Bowditch [Bow09] shows that for fixed base and fiber genus, there are
only finitely many possible examples of hyperbolic surface bundles over a
surface.
(3) As detailed in [Rei06], the existence of a hyperbolic surface bundle over a
surface would contradict the long-standing conjecture of LeBrun [LeB02]
that the Seiberg-Witten invariants of a closed hyperbolic 4-manifold must
vanish (see Problem 4.95).
(4) Work of Kapovich [Kap98] shows that surface bundles over surfaces can
never admit complex hyperbolic metrics.
(5) For an extensive account of the questions raised here, see [KL24, Section
1].

title: Kirby Problem 2.24
statement:
Does there exist a complex surface $X$ that admits three or more
non-isomorphic structures as a surface bundle over a surface?
background:
Source: Kirby's Problems in Low-Dimensional Topology notes. Original problem number: KP-2.24.

Literature notes:
(1) The analogous situation in the case of surface bundles over the circle is
organized by the Thurston norm [Thu86]: if a surface bundle over the
circle admits two different fibrations, then it admits infinitely many. By
contrast, work of F.E.A. Johnson [Joh99] shows that a given 4-manifold
admits only finitely many structures as a surface bundle over a surface
with base and fiber both of genus $\geq 2$.
(2) Atiyah [Ati69] and Kodaira [Kod67] constructed complex surfaces $X$
that are surface bundles over surfaces in two distinct ways. These are
constructed as branched covers of products of algebraic curves; the two
bundle structures arise from the projections onto either factor. Certain
families of these examples admit exactly two fiberings by work of Chen
[Che18], Salter–Tshishiku [ST20], and Landesman–Litt–Sawin [LLS25].
The problem formulated here was also raised by Catanese [Cat17].
(3) In the smooth category, Salter [Sal15] gave a method of constructing
surface bundles over surfaces (with base and fiber each of genus at least
2) with an arbitrary finite number of fiberings. However, these are known
not to admit complex structures.

- [Thu86] William P. Thurston. A norm for the homology of 3-manifolds. Mem. Amer. Math. Soc., 59(339):i–vi and 99–130, 1986.

- [ST20] Nick Salter and Bena Tshishiku. Arithmeticity of the monodromy of some Kodaira fibrations. Compos. Math., 156(1):114–157, 2020. doi:10.1112/s0010437x19007668.
- [LLS25] Aaron Landesman, Daniel Litt, and Will Sawin. Big monodromy for higher Prym representations. Geom. Topol., 29(5):2733–2782, 2025. doi:10.2140/gt.2025.29.2733.

title: Kirby Problem 2.25
statement:
Consider surface bundles over surfaces where both fiber $F$ and
base $B$ have genus $\geq 2$ and where $\pi_{1}(B)$ injects in the mapping class group of the

fiber. Does such a bundle have a $k$–multisection for some $k > 0$ (i.e., a continuous
choice of $k$ everywhere distinct points)?
background:
Source: Kirby's Problems in Low-Dimensional Topology notes. Original problem number: KP-2.25.

Literature notes:
(1) This is Problem 2.17 in [Kir97] by G. Mess. In [Mor89], Morita gives
a cohomological obstruction for a surface bundle to admit a section (i.e.
the case $k = 1$). Using this obstruction, Hillman gave examples of surface
bundles over surfaces (with both base and fiber genus $\geq 2$) that do not
admit sections [Hil15]. Other examples of $S_{g}$-bundles over the 2-torus
with no section were constructed by Li–Litt–Salter–Srinivasan [LLSS23];
these were constructed with applications to arithmetic geometry in mind.
Both classes of examples virtually admit sections, that is, they admit
sections after pulling back to some finite cover of the base.
(2) In spite of the similarity between this question and Problem 2.22, it is
likely that substantially different techniques will be necessary.
Section
problems for surface bundles tend to be of a more group-theoretic flavor,
boiling down to obstructing a lifting of the monodromy representation
from an unpointed to a pointed mapping class group.
Available tech-
niques include cohomological considerations as well as approaches based
on the Nielsen–Thurston classification. The multisection question for Lef-
schetz fibrations is more delicate, since here it is necessary to lift the
Dehn twists in the monodromy factorization on $\operatorname{Mod}(S_{g})$ to Dehn twists
in $\operatorname{Mod}(S_{g}^{b})$, not simply to arbitrary elements in $\operatorname{Mod}(S_{g}^{b})$ projecting back
to the original twists.

References cited:
- [Kir97] R.C. Kirby. Problems in low–dimensional topology. In W. Kazez, editor, Geometric Topology. American Math. Soc./International Press, Providence, 1997.
- [Mor89] Shigeyuki Morita. Families of Jacobian manifolds and characteristic classes of surface bundles. II. Math. Proc. Cambridge Philos. Soc., 105(1):79–101, 1989. doi:10.1017/S0305004100001389.
- [Hil15] Jonathan A. Hillman. Sections of surface bundles. In Interactions between lowdimensional topology and mapping class groups, volume 19 of Geom. Topol. Monogr., pages 1–19. Geom. Topol. Publ., Coventry, 2015. doi:10.2140/gtm.2015.19.1.
- [LLSS23] Wanlin Li, Daniel Litt, Nick Salter, and Padmavathi Srinivasan. Surface bundles and the section conjecture. Math. Ann., 386(1-2):877–942, 2023. doi:10.1007/s00208-022-02421-9.

title: Kirby Problem 2.26
statement:
(Kontsevich–Zorich conjecture). Understand the homotopy types
of strata of abelian differentials. Which stratum-components are $K(\pi, 1)$ spaces?
What are the fundamental groups? For which stratum-components $\mathcal{H}$ is some ver-
sion of the monodromy map $\rho: \pi_{1}(\mathcal{H}) \to \operatorname{Mod}(S_{g})$ injective? Do the answers to
these questions change in a predictable way as one moves from the principal stra-
tum down to the minimal?
background:
Source: Kirby's Problems in Low-Dimensional Topology notes. Original problem number: KP-2.26.

Literature notes:
(1) A translation surface is a surface $T$ that admits an atlas of charts to $\mathbb{C}$
for which transition maps are translations ($z \mapsto z+c$). An abelian differ-
ential is a pair $(X, \omega)$ of a Riemann surface together with a holomorphic
differential. It is a basic but profound fact that every translation surface
corresponds to an abelian differential and vice-versa.
Fixing a genus, the space of all abelian differentials is identified with
the Hodge bundle over the moduli space of Riemann surfaces of genus $g$, the
vector bundle whose fiber over a Riemann surface $X$ is the space $H^{1,0}(X)$
of all holomorphic 1-forms on $X$. This space is stratified according to the
multiplicities of the zeroes. Every differential on a Riemann surface of
genus $g$ has $2g -2$ zeroes when counted with multiplicity; the generic case

where all zeroes are simple (the partition $1^{2g-2}$) is called the principal
stratum, and the case where there is a single zero of multiplicity $2g - 2$ is
called the minimal stratum.
In general, the stratum $\mathcal{H}_{\kappa}$ associated to the partition $\kappa = k_{1}+\cdots +k_{n}$
is a quasiprojective complex orbifold of complex dimension $2g + n - 1$,
and therefore (after passing to a finite cover to resolve the orbifold issue)
has the homotopy type of a finite CW complex. Strata are fundamental
objects in the study of Teichmüller dynamics, where they host a dynamical
system induced from a natural action of $\operatorname{GL}_{2}(\mathbb{R})$, but their topology is
quite mysterious, despite their close relationship to the moduli space of
Riemann surfaces and the mapping class group.
(2) In [KZ03], Kontsevich–Zorich compute $\pi_{0}$ for all strata. They find that
each stratum has between between one and three connected components.
For the partitions $2g - 2$ and $g - 1, g - 1$, there are special “hyperelliptic”
components that can be identified with configuration spaces of points in
$\mathbb{C}$, resolving Problem 2.26 in this case.
In [KZ97], they pose a version of Problem 2.26, conjecturing that
each stratum component should be a $K(\pi, 1)$ and that the fundamental
groups should be some flavor of mapping class group.
(3) Work of Calderon–Salter [CS23] identifies the image of $\pi_{1}(\mathcal{H})$ in the map-
ping class group under the natural monodromy homomorphism for all non-
hyperelliptic stratum components in genus $g \geq 5$. They find that these
are “framed mapping class groups”—the stabilizer of the distinguished
framing on the translation surface inherited from the standard framing
on $\mathbb{C}$. This shows that whenever the monodromy homomorphism is in-
jective, the fundamental group of the stratum component is indeed some
flavor of mapping class group, as predicted by the conjecture.
The question of monodromy injectivity appears to be subtle, how-
ever. In the hyperelliptic setting, injectivity was established in the work
of Kontsevich–Zorich. On the other hand, in genus 3, there is a stratum-
component known as $\mathcal{H}^{\mathrm{odd}}(4)$
for which injectivity is known not to hold.
Work of Looijenga–Mondello [LM14] computes the fundamental group
to be $A(E_{6})$ (the Artin group of type $E_{6}$) modulo its center. Under the
monodromy map, the Artin generators are sent to Dehn twists about sim-
ple closed curves whose intersection pattern is given by the $E_{6}$ Dynkin
diagram.
Work of Wajnryb [Waj99] shows that this homomorphism
$A(E_{6}) \to \operatorname{Mod}(\Sigma_{3})$ has a non-central element in the kernel.

References cited:
- [KZ03] Maxim Kontsevich and Anton Zorich. Connected components of the moduli spaces of Abelian differentials with prescribed singularities. Invent. Math., 153(3):631–678, 2003. doi:10.1007/s00222-003-0303-x.
- [KZ97] M. Kontsevich and A. Zorich. Lyapunov exponents and Hodge theory, 1997. arXiv: hep-th/9701164.
- [CS23] Aaron Calderon and Nick Salter. Framed mapping class groups and the monodromy of strata of abelian differentials. J. Eur. Math. Soc. (JEMS), 25(12):4719–4790, 2023. doi:10.4171/jems/1290.
- [LM14] Eduard Looijenga and Gabriele Mondello. The fine structure of the moduli space of abelian differentials in genus 3. Geom. Dedicata, 169:109–128, 2014. doi:10.1007/s10711-013-9845-2.
- [Waj99] Bronislaw Wajnryb. Artin groups and geometric monodromy. Invent. Math., 138(3):563–571, 1999. doi:10.1007/s002220050353.

title: Kirby Problem 2.27
statement:
For $n \geq 4$, does the braid group $B_{n}$ admit a finite-index sub-
group that embeds in a right-angled Artin group?
background:
Source: Kirby's Problems in Low-Dimensional Topology notes. Original problem number: KP-2.27.

Literature notes:
(1) In CAT(0) geometry, a cube complex is called special if it satisfies certain
conditions on its hyperplanes [HW08]. Groups acting by combinatorial
isometries on special cube complexes are of particular interest in geometric
group theory, and are closely related to subgroups of right-angled Artin
groups. A group is said to be virtually special if it contains a finite-index
subgroup isomorphic to the fundamental group of a special cube complex.
(2) By [BKK16], any group that embeds in a right-angled Artin group acts
by $C^{\infty}$-diffeomorphisms on $\mathbb{R}$. As braid groups do not admit such ac-
tions [FF20], they do not embed in right-angled Artin groups, so it is
necessary to pass to proper subgroups.
(3) One could go further and ask whether braid groups are virtually special.
This is strictly stronger than Question 2.27.
(4) In light of the resolution of the congruence subgroup problem for braid
groups (see [Mar19] and the references therein), to resolve Problem 2.27
in the negative, it suffices to obtain a cofinal sequence of subgroups of $B_{n}$,
none of which embed in a right-angled Artin group.

References cited:
- [HW08] Frédéric Haglund and Daniel T. Wise. Special cube complexes. Geom. Funct. Anal., 17(5):1551–1620, 2008. doi:10.1007/s00039-007-0629-4.
- [BKK16] Hyungryul Baik, Sang-hyun Kim, and Thomas Koberda. Right-angled Artin groups in the C8 diffeomorphism group of the real line. Israel J. Math., 213(1):175–182, 2016. doi:10.1007/s11856-016-1307-8.
- [FF20] Benson Farb and John Franks. Groups of homeomorphisms of one-manifolds, I: Actions of nonlinear groups. In What’s next?—the mathematical legacy of William P. Thurston, volume 205 of Ann. of Math. Stud., pages 116–140. Princeton Univ. Press, Princeton, NJ, 2020. doi:10.2307/j.ctvthhdvv.9.
- [Mar19] Dan Margalit. Problems, questions, and conjectures about mapping class groups. In Breadth in contemporary topology, volume 102 of Proc. Sympos. Pure Math., pages 157–186. Amer. Math. Soc., Providence, RI, 2019. doi:10.1090/pspum/102/12.

title: Kirby Problem 2.28
statement:
Let $\Gamma$ be a graph that is not a nontrivial join, and let $A(\Gamma)$
be the associated right-angled Artin group. Does there exist an injective map from
$A(\Gamma)$ to the mapping class group of a surface such that every loxodromic element
of $A(\Gamma)$ is sent to a pseudo-Anosov mapping class?
background:
Source: Kirby's Problems in Low-Dimensional Topology notes. Original problem number: KP-2.28.

Literature notes:
(1) There are many injective homomorphisms from right-angled Artin groups
into mapping class groups [CP01, CLM12, Kob12], and general criteria
are fairly well-understood [KK14b]. Right-angled Artin groups have a
Nielsen–Thurston classification, not unlike mapping class groups [BC12,
KK14a], wherein each element is either elliptic or loxodromic.
(2) The set of loxodromic elements of $A(\Gamma)$ is nonempty if and only if $A(\Gamma)$
does not split as a nontrivial direct product, which is true if and only if $\Gamma$
does not split as a nontrivial join.

(3) By [MT16, KMT17], the restriction of any such injective map to a sub-
group where every nontrivial element is loxodromic is necessarily a convex
cocompact subgroup of the mapping class group of $S$. However, any such
subgroup obtained in this way is free (see [KK14a]). In particular, this
does not provide a strategy to construct convex cocompact surface sub-
groups as in Problem 2.23.
(4) In light of [KMT17], the problem can be reformulated entirely in terms
of the combinatorial topology of the underlying surface. Let $\Gamma$ be fixed,
and let $\Lambda$ be the opposite graph, i.e., the one obtained by reversing the
adjacency relation in $\Gamma$. It suffices to find a surface $S$ and $\pi_{1}$-injective,
pairwise non-nested subsurfaces $\\{S_{v}\\}_{v\\in V(\\Gamma)}$ indexed by the vertices of $\Gamma$
such that the following hold:
(i) Each $S_{v}$ supports a pseudo-Anosov mapping class (in the mapping
class group of $S_{v}$). In particular, each $S_{v}$ is non-annular.
(ii) Subsurfaces $S_{v}$ and $S_{w}$ intersect essentially if and only if $v$ and $w$ are
not adjacent in $\Gamma$ (or equivalently, adjacent in $\Lambda$).
(iii) Let $Y \subset \Lambda$ be a connected subgraph such that every vertex of $\Lambda$ is
adjacent to a vertex of $Y$ . Then every essential, simple, nonperipheral
curve on $S$ essentially intersects $S_{v}$ for some vertex $v$ of $Y$ .
The difficulty of this reformulation is the non-canonical nature of $Y$ for a
general graph $\Lambda$.

References cited:
- [CP01] John Crisp and Luis Paris. The solution to a conjecture of Tits on the subgroup generated by the squares of the generators of an Artin group. Invent. Math., 145(1):19– 36, 2001. doi:10.1007/s002220100138.
- [CLM12] Matt T. Clay, Christopher J. Leininger, and Johanna Mangahas. The geometry of right-angled Artin subgroups of mapping class groups. Groups Geom. Dyn., 6(2):249–278, 2012. doi:10.4171/GGD/157.
- [Kob12] Thomas Koberda. Right-angled Artin groups and a generalized isomorphism problem for finitely generated subgroups of mapping class groups. Geom. Funct. Anal., 22(6):1541–1590, 2012. doi:10.1007/s00039-012-0198-z.
- [KK14b] Sang-Hyun Kim and Thomas Koberda. An obstruction to embedding right-angled Artin groups in mapping class groups. Int. Math. Res. Not. IMRN, 2014(14):3912– 3918, 2014. doi:10.1093/imrn/rnt064.
- [BC12] Jason Behrstock and Ruth Charney. Divergence and quasimorphisms of right-angled Artin groups. Math. Ann., 352(2):339–356, 2012. doi:10.1007/s00208-011-0641-8.
- [KK14a] Sang-Hyun Kim and Thomas Koberda. The geometry of the curve graph of a rightangled Artin group. Internat. J. Algebra Comput., 24(2):121–169, 2014. doi:10.1142/S021819671450009X.
- [MT16] Johanna Mangahas and Samuel J. Taylor. Convex cocompactness in mapping class groups via quasiconvexity in right-angled Artin groups. Proc. Lond. Math. Soc. (3), 112(5):855–881, 2016. doi:10.1112/plms/pdw009.
