title: Kirby Problem 2.29
statement:
Determine the Artin groups that can be embedded into a map-
ping class group.
background:
Source: Kirby's Problems in Low-Dimensional Topology notes. Original problem number: KP-2.29.

Literature notes:
(1) If the Artin group is simply laced and the homomorphism sends each
standard generator to a Dehn twist, then there is an almost complete
classification. It is known that the Artin groups of type $A_{n}$ (see [BH73]),
$D_{n}$ (see [PV96]) and $\widetilde{A}_{n}$ (see [Ryf23]) can be embedded into a mapping
class group in this way. It is also known that an Artin group does not
embed in this way if its Coxeter graph is connected and contains a full
subgraph isomorphic to either $\widetilde{D}_{n}$ with $n \geq 4$ (see [Lab97]), or $E_{6}$ (see
[Waj99]). These leave a finite number of possible open cases.
(2) Say a homomorphism from an Artin group to a mapping class group is
geometric if each standard generator is sent to a Dehn multi-twist. The
question is very open in the case of non-geometric embeddings. There are
by now various examples of non-geometric embeddings of Artin groups
into mapping class groups; see e.g., [CMM21] for the case of right-angled
Artin groups and [Sze10, BT12] for the case of braid groups.
(3) The question is also closely related to another folklore question on Artin
groups: which Artin groups are virtually special (possessing a finite-index
subgroup isomorphic to a subgroup of a right-angled Artin group). It is
known that every right-angled Artin group embeds into a mapping class
group, and so obstructions to embedding an Artin group into mapping

class groups also obstruct embeddability into right-angled Artin groups.
From this point of view it is also natural to consider a “virtual” version of
the above question, namely to determine which Artin groups have some
finite-index subgroup that embeds into a mapping class group.
(4) This problem is historically attributed to J. Crisp and L. Paris [CP01].

title: Kirby Problem 2.30
statement:
Which right-angled Artin groups contain closed hyperbolic sur-
face groups? Is there an algorithmic or graph-theoretic criterion to decide this?
background:
Source: Kirby's Problems in Low-Dimensional Topology notes. Original problem number: KP-2.30.

Literature notes:
All but finitely many surface groups embed in right-angled Artin
groups [CW04], and right-angled Artin groups on cycles of length at least five
contain hyperbolic surface groups [SDS89]. Right-angled Artin groups on graphs
up to eight vertices containing surface groups were classified by Crisp–Sageev–
Sapir [CSS08]; they also posed the question of whether a right-angled Artin group
contains a surface group if and only if it contains a one-ended word-hyperbolic
group. See also [Kim10].

title: Kirby Problem 2.31
statement:
Let $S$ be a closed surface of genus at least 2. Show that the
stable commutator length is rational on the commutator subgroup of $\pi_{1}(S)$.
background:
Source: Kirby's Problems in Low-Dimensional Topology notes. Original problem number: KP-2.31.

Literature notes:
(1) If $G$ is a group and $g \in [G, G]$, the commutator length of $g$, denoted cl $(g)$,
is the least number of commutators in $G$ whose product is $g$, and the
stable commutator length of $g$, denoted scl $(g)$, is the limit of cl $(g^{n})/n$ as
$n \to \infty$.
(2) Suppose $X$ is a space with $\pi_{1}(X) = G$, suppose $L$ is an oriented circle,
and suppose $f: L \to G$ takes $L$ to the conjugacy class of $g \in [G, G]$. After
replacing $f$ by inclusion, consider the the affine subspace $V$ of $H_{2}(X, L; \mathbb{R})$
that is mapped by the boundary map in homology to the fundamental
class $[L]$ of $L$ in $H_{1}(L; \mathbb{R})$. Then the stable commutator length of $g$ is $1/4$
times the infimum of the (relative) Gromov norm on the subspace $V$ .
Taking $L$ to be a 1-manifold and $f: L \to X$ to be a map for which
$f_{*}[L] = 0$ in $H_{1}(X; \mathbb{R})$ extends the definition of stable commutator length
to all homologically trivial formal chains (a purely group-theoretic defini-
tion is given in [Cal09b]).
The conjecture above may be broadened as follows.
Let $G$ be an
arbitrary word-hyperbolic group and $f: L \to X$ an arbitrary map from
an oriented 1-manifold $L$ to $X$ with $f_{*}[L] = 0$ in $H_{1}(X; \mathbb{R})$. Here are a
few related conjectures:
(a) the stable commutator length of $L$ is rational;
(b) the Gromov norm of any rational class in $H_{2}(X, L; \mathbb{Q})$ is rational;
and

(c) the Gromov norm of any rational class in $H_{2}(X; \mathbb{R})$ is rational.
For $X$ a closed surface of genus at least 2, the answer to (c) is positive,
and for every $L$ the answer to (b) is positive for all rational $\alpha \in V$ mapping
to the fundamental class of $[L]$ outside a compact interval.
(3) This is known to be true for elements represented by curves supported in
an essential proper subsurface $S' \subset S$ (see [Cal09b]).
(4) If $S$ is a compact oriented surface, possibly with boundary and every
component having negative Euler characteristic, the Gromov norm of the
fundamental class of $S$ in $H_{2}(S, \partial S; \mathbb{R})$ is $-2\chi(S)$.
If $f: L \to X$ is as above, a map $F: S \to X$ virtually bounds $f$ if there
is a degree $n$ (oriented) covering map $\pi: \partial S \to L$ for which $f\pi = F$ on $\partial S$
(we allow the possibility that $L$ is empty). Such a map is extremal if it is
an isometry for the Gromov norm. Extremal maps are $\pi_{1}$-injective.
A further conjecture: In each case of the conjecture in Remark (1),
there is an extremal map of a surface virtually bounding $L$ (or virtually
representing a given class in $H_{2}(X; \mathbb{Q})$ if $L$ is empty).
This conjecture could be thought of as bearing on Gromov’s question
of whether every one-ended hyperbolic group contains a closed surface
subgroup.
(5) The questions above have a positive answer for free groups.
See e.g.,
[Cal09b].

References cited:
- [Cal09b] Danny Calegari. scl, volume 20 of MSJ Memoirs. Mathematical Society of Japan, Tokyo, 2009. doi:10.1142/e018.

title: Kirby Problem 2.32
statement:
Does every surface bundle over a surface admit a flat connec-
tion? What about surface bundles over 3-manifolds?
background:
Source: Kirby's Problems in Low-Dimensional Topology notes. Original problem number: KP-2.32.

Literature notes:
(1) An $S_{g}$-bundle $p: E \to B$ admits a flat connection if it admits a codimen-
sion 2 foliation everywhere transverse to the fibers. Equivalently, the bun-
dle admits a flat connection if the monodromy map $\rho: \pi_{1}(B) \to \operatorname{Mod}(S_{g})$
admits a lifting $\widetilde{\rho}: \pi_{1}(B) \to \operatorname{Diff}(S_{g})$.
(2) Work of Morita [Mor87] shows that the MMM classes $e_{i} \in H^{2i}(\operatorname{Mod}(S_{g}))$
obstruct the existence of a flat connection for $i \geq 3$. In practical terms,
this means that there are surface bundles over manifolds of dimension at
least 6 that admit no flat connection. Conversely, the first MMM class is
known not to obstruct flatness; see [KM05]. New techniques, presumably
of a more dynamical flavor, will be required to obstruct the existence of
flat connections on surface bundles when the base is of lower dimension.

(3) This question can be asked for varying degrees of regularity, all the way
from lifting to the group of homeomorphisms, up to real-analytic or volume-
preserving diffeomorphisms.
In the volume-preserving case, techniques from symplectic geome-
try may be relevant. This discussion follows ideas outlined in [KM05].
Let $\omega$ be a volume form on $S_{g}$, and let $\operatorname{Diff}(S_{g}, \omega)$ denote the group of
volume-preserving diffeomorphisms; the identity component is denoted
$\operatorname{Diff}_{0}(S_{g}, \omega)$. An $S_{h}$-bundle over $S_{g}$ is determined by a set $a_{1}, b_{1},..., a_{h}, b_{h}$
of mapping classes for which the surface relation $[a_{1}, b_{1}]... [a_{h}, b_{h}]$ holds.
From this point of view, a flat volume-preserving connection consists of a
choice of lifts $\alpha_{i}, \beta_{i} \in \operatorname{Diff}(S_{g}, \omega)$ such that $[\alpha_{1}, \beta_{1}]... [\alpha_{h}, \beta_{h}] = 1$.
One possible method for obstructing such a lift proceeds as follows.
Beginning with a surface bundle specified by the mapping classes $a_{1}, b_{1},..., a_{h}, b_{h}$
as above, the set of all lifts $\alpha_{i}, \beta_{i}$ is a torsor for the group $\operatorname{Diff}_{0}(S_{g}, \omega)^{2h}$.
There is a map (not a group homomorphism)

$$
\mu: \operatorname{Diff}_{0}(S_{g}, \omega)^{2h} \to \operatorname{Diff}_{0}(S_{g}, \omega)
$$

that sends a set of lifts $\alpha_{1}, \beta_{1},..., \alpha_{h}, \beta_{h}$ to the surface word $\prod_{i=1}^{h}[\alpha_{i},\beta_{i}]$;
the fiber $\mu^{-1}(\operatorname{id})$ then describes the set of flat volume-preserving connec-
tions on the bundle.
$\operatorname{Diff}_{0}(S_{g}, \omega)$ admits a flux homomorphism Flux: $\operatorname{Diff}_{0}(S_{g}, \omega) \to H^{1}(S_{g}; \mathbb{R})$
whose kernel is the group of Hamiltonian diffeomorphisms Ham $(S_{g}, \omega)$. A
first question is whether the flux homomorphism can serve as an obstruc-
tion to admitting a flat connection, although this seems unlikely to be the
case.
Considering next the set of lifts for which $[\alpha_{1}, \beta_{1}]... [\alpha_{h}, \beta_{h}]$ is Hamil-
tonian, one is led to wonder if the Hofer metric on Ham $(S_{g}, \omega)$ could be
of use in obstructing the existence of a flat connection. Perhaps it is pos-
sible to show that the image of $\mu$ must stay far away from 0 in the Hofer
metric? (See [MS17a] for an introduction to the Hofer metric.)

References cited:
- [Mor87] Shigeyuki Morita. Characteristic classes of surface bundles. Invent. Math., 90(3):551–577, 1987. doi:10.1007/BF01389178.
- [KM05] D. Kotschick and S. Morita. Signatures of foliated surface bundles and the symplectomorphism groups of surfaces. Topology, 44(1):131–149, 2005. doi:10.1016/j.top.2004.05.002.
- [MS17a] Dusa McDuff and Dietmar Salamon. Introduction to symplectic topology, volume 27. Oxford University Press, 2017.

title: Kirby Problem 2.33
statement:
Let $S$ be a closed compact surface (without boundary).
Is
there a finitely generated, torsion-free group $G$ such that $G$ cannot act faithfully by
homeomorphisms on $S$?
background:
Source: Kirby's Problems in Low-Dimensional Topology notes. Original problem number: KP-2.33.

Literature notes:
(1) There are non-compact surfaces for which every countable group acts by
homeomorphisms [APV21].
(2) We pose the question for closed surfaces only, since the presence of bound-
ary gives access to special techniques that may be able to resolve the ques-
tion as stated without developing new methods for the closed case. On the
other hand, the question is open even for the disk, relative to the bound-
ary. Potential candidates include lattices in high rank Lie groups. For
more regular actions (i.e., smooth actions) more is known; see [BFH22],
for instance.

(3) The torsion-free hypothesis is necessary, since there are often a priori
bounds on the size of torsion in surface homeomorphism groups.
(4) In the case of the plane, Le Roux [LR11] has studied actions of the
fundamental group of the Klein bottle under the assumption that the
standard generators act freely and preserving orientation. Among other
results, he finds obstructions for the action of certain torsion-free groups
by fixed-point free orientation-preserving homeomorphisms.
(5) A more general question would be to find an algebraic characterization
of groups acting on $S$ by homeomorphisms. Such characterizations are
known for groups acting on the interval and on the circle, via orderability.
It may be difficult to find concise characterizations; see e.g., [dlNG22,
Ros13, Hyd19].

References cited:
- [APV21] Tarik Aougab, Priyam Patel, and Nicholas G. Vlamis. Isometry groups of infinite genus hyperbolic surfaces. Math. Ann., 381:459–498, 2021.
- [BFH22] Aaron Brown, David Fisher, and Sebastian Hurtado. Zimmer’s conjecture: subexponential growth, measure rigidity, and strong property (T). Ann. of Math. (2), 196(3):891–940, 2022. doi:10.4007/annals.2022.196.3.1.
- [LR11] Frédéric Le Roux. Free planar actions of the Klein bottle group. Geom. Topol., 15(3):1545–1567, 2011. doi:10.2140/gt.2011.15.1545.
- [dlNG22] Javier de la Nuez Gonzalez. Non-Roelcke precompactness of groups of surface homeomorphisms, 2022. arXiv:2202.06527.
- [Ros13] Christian Rosendal. Global and local boundedness of Polish groups. Indiana Univ. Math. J., 62(5):1621–1678, 2013. doi:10.1512/iumj.2013.62.5133.
- [Hyd19] James Hyde. The group of boundary fixing homeomorphisms of the disc is not leftorderable. Ann. of Math. (2), 190(2):657–661, 2019. doi:10.4007/annals.2019.190.2.5.

title: Kirby Problem 2.34
statement:
Let $S$ be a compact surface. For $0 \leq r < s$, does there exist a
nontrivial finitely generated subgroup $G_{r} \leq \operatorname{Diff}^{r}_{0}(S)$ such that every action of $G_{r}$
on $S$ by $C^{s}$ diffeomorphisms is trivial? Can these examples be torsion-free?
background:
Source: Kirby's Problems in Low-Dimensional Topology notes. Original problem number: KP-2.34.

Literature notes:
(1) For $0 \leq r \leq \infty$, let $\operatorname{Diff}^{r}_{0}(M)$ denote the identity component of the group
of $C^{r}$ diffeomorphisms of a manifold $M$.
For nonintegral $r$, we write
$r = k + \epsilon$ for $k \in \mathbb{N}$ and $0 \leq \epsilon < 1$, and we consider $C^{k}$ diffeomorphisms
whose $k^{th}$ order derivatives are $\epsilon$–Hölder continuous.
(2) The condition that every higher-regularity action of $G_{r}$ be trivial can be
relaxed, for instance, to ask that every such action of $G_{r}$ be non-faithful,
or abelian.
(3) Problems of this nature have been extensively investigated in dimen-
sion one, where Kim and Koberda gave a positive answer to this ques-
tion [KK20, KK21]; one obtains finitely generated groups with infinite
simple commutator subgroups such that each smoother action has abelian
image. No instances are known in dimension greater than one. Prior to
this, Plante–Thurston showed that nilpotent groups of $C^{2}$-diffeomorphisms
of the interval are abelian [PT76], but Farb–Franks showed that there can
be non-abelian nilpotent actions of regularity $C^{1}$ [FF03]. More generally,
Castro–Jorquera–Navas build nilpotent groups that can act at a certain
regularity but whose higher-regularity actions are all abelian [CJN14].
Further examples of finitely generated groups acting with critical regular-
ities on 1-manifolds are constructed in [MW23].
(4) In the case $r = 0$ and $s \geq 1$, it is possible to use Thurston’s Stability
Theorem [Thu74b] to exhibit particular groups of homeomorphisms that
cannot act faithfully by diffeomorphisms. See, for instance, [Cal06a].

References cited:
- [KK20] Sang-hyun Kim and Thomas Koberda. Diffeomorphism groups of critical regularity. Invent. Math., 221(2):421–501, 2020. doi:10.1007/s00222-020-00953-y.
- [KK21] Sang-hyun Kim and Thomas Koberda. Structure and regularity of group actions on one-manifolds. Springer Monographs in Mathematics. Springer, Cham, [2021] ©2021. doi:10.1007/978-3-030-89006-3.
- [PT76] J. F. Plante and W. P. Thurston. Polynomial growth in holonomy groups of foliations. Comment. Math. Helv., 51(4):567–584, 1976. doi:10.1007/BF02568174.
- [FF03] Benson Farb and John Franks. Groups of homeomorphisms of one-manifolds. III. Nilpotent subgroups. Ergodic Theory Dynam. Systems, 23(5):1467–1484, 2003. doi: 10.1017/S0143385702001712.
- [CJN14] Gonzalo Castro, Eduardo Jorquera, and Andrés Navas. Sharp regularity for certain nilpotent group actions on the interval. Math. Ann., 359(1-2):101–152, 2014. doi: 10.1007/s00208-013-0995-1.
- [MW23] Kathryn Mann and Maxime Wolff. Reconstructing maps out of groups. Ann. Sci. Éc. Norm. Supér. (4), 56(4):1135–1154, 2023. doi:10.24033/asens.2551.
- [Thu74b] William P. Thurston. A generalization of the Reeb stability theorem. Topology, 13:347–352, 1974. doi:10.1016/0040-9383(74)90025-1.
- [Cal06a] Danny Calegari. Dynamical forcing of circular groups. Trans. Amer. Math. Soc., 358(8):3473–3491, 2006. doi:10.1090/S0002-9947-05-03754-2.

title: Kirby Problem 2.35
statement:
Is the first-order theory of the mapping class group of a surface
decidable?
background:
Source: Kirby's Problems in Low-Dimensional Topology notes. Original problem number: KP-2.35.

Literature notes:
(1) The first order theory of a group $G$ in the language of group theory is the
formal first-order language equipped with group multiplication and the
identity element. A first-order theory is decidable if there is an algorithm
(i.e., Turing machine) that decides which sentences are true in that theory
and which are false.
(2) For homeomorphism groups of surfaces (and indeed all compact manifolds
of positive dimension), the corresponding theory is not decidable because
it interprets arithmetic [KKdlNG25].
(3) The theory of free groups is decidable; this is part of the resolution of the
Tarski problem [Sel02, KM06].

References cited:
- [KKdlNG25] Sang-hyun Kim, Thomas Koberda, and J. de la Nuez González. First order rigidity of homeomorphism groups of manifolds. Commun. Am. Math. Soc., 5:144–194, 2025. doi:10.1090/cams/47.
- [Sel02] Z. Sela. Diophantine geometry over groups and the elementary theory of free and hyperbolic groups. In Proceedings of the International Congress of Mathematicians, Vol. II (Beijing, 2002), pages 87–92. Higher Ed. Press, Beijing, 2002.
- [KM06] Olga Kharlampovich and Alexei Myasnikov. Elementary theory of free non-abelian groups. J. Algebra, 302(2):451–552, 2006. doi:10.1016/j.jalgebra.2006.03.033.

title: Kirby Problem 2.36
statement:
Are systems of equations over mapping class groups and braid
groups decidable?
background:
Source: Kirby's Problems in Low-Dimensional Topology notes. Original problem number: KP-2.36.

Literature notes:
(1) A system of equations over a group $G$ is a finite conjunction of formulae
of the form

$$
r(x_{1},..., x_{n}, a_{1},..., a_{m}) = 1
$$

and

$$
r(x_{1},..., x_{n}, a_{1},..., a_{m}) \neq 1,
$$

where $r$ is a word in a free group of $\operatorname{rank} n + m$, where $(x_{1},..., x_{n})$ is
a tuple of variables, and where $(a_{1},..., a_{m})$ (with $m \geq 0$) is a tuple of
parameters in $G$. A solution to a system of equations is a tuple of elements
of $G$ such that when the elements are substituted for variables, one obtains
a valid expression in $G$.
(2) Decidability of equations would consist of an algorithm to decide whether
or not a particular system has a solution or not. Precisely, one might fix
a finite generating set for $G$ (if it exists) and use a Gödel numbering to
encode equations with parameters as natural numbers. Then, one would
require a Turing machine to take a natural number corresponding to an
equation and decide if it admits a solution.
(3) One could allow variations on the problem; for instance, one could fix the
underlying surface or allow it to vary, pass to finite index subgroups, or
restrict the topological type of the underlying surface.
(4) Decidability of the theory of a group or class of groups has a long his-
tory, starting at least with the Tarski problem. The Tarski problem asked
whether the nonabelian free groups are elementarily equivalent to each
other and whether their first order theories are decidable; see [Sel02,
KM06]. For general hyperbolic groups (possibly with torsion), Dahmani

and Guirardel proved that equations are solvable; see [DG10]. Conjec-
turally, the full first order theory of a vast generalization of hyperbolic
groups, namely hierarchically hyperbolic groups, should be decidable. A
particularly interesting special case of such a general result would be the
decidability of the first order theory of mapping class groups and braid
groups, which in turn would give a positive answer to the proposed ques-
tion.
(5) There is a vast literature on equations over groups, including finite groups
and free groups, though for mapping class groups and braid groups the
problem appears to be open. See [Rom12] for a survey.
(6) It seems likely that equations over homeomorphism groups of surfaces
(with or without parameters) are undecidable.

References cited:
- [Sel02] Z. Sela. Diophantine geometry over groups and the elementary theory of free and hyperbolic groups. In Proceedings of the International Congress of Mathematicians, Vol. II (Beijing, 2002), pages 87–92. Higher Ed. Press, Beijing, 2002.
- [KM06] Olga Kharlampovich and Alexei Myasnikov. Elementary theory of free non-abelian groups. J. Algebra, 302(2):451–552, 2006. doi:10.1016/j.jalgebra.2006.03.033.
- [DG10] François Dahmani and Vincent Guirardel. Foliations for solving equations in groups: free, virtually free, and hyperbolic groups. J. Topol., 3(2):343–404, 2010. doi:10.1112/jtopol/jtq010.
- [Rom12] Vitaliı̆ Roman’kov. Equations over groups. Groups Complex. Cryptol., 4(2):191– 239, 2012. doi:10.1515/gcc-2012-0015.

title: Kirby Problem 2.37
statement:
Give a Nielsen–Thurston-type classification for the mapping
class groups of infinite-type surfaces. In particular, which homeomorphisms are the
appropriate generalization of pseudo-Anosov homeomorphisms in this setting?
background:
Source: Kirby's Problems in Low-Dimensional Topology notes. Original problem number: KP-2.37.

Literature notes:
(1) For finite-type surfaces $S$, there is a powerful classification due to Nielsen
and Thurston of the mapping classes of $S$: every mapping class is periodic,
reducible, or pseudo-Anosov. The most important aspect of this classifi-
cation is that if a mapping class $f$ is not periodic or reducible, it must be
pseudo-Anosov, meaning that $f$ is highly chaotic and that there exist two
transverse measured foliations $\lambda^{+}$ and $\lambda^{-}$ on $S$, where $f$ stretches along
$\lambda^{+}$ and contracts along $\lambda^{-}$. The exact analog of this classification for

infinite-type surfaces is false. For instance, the homeomorphisms called
handleshifts (introduced by Patel-Vlamis [PV18]) are neither periodic,
reducible, nor pseudo-Anosov. The classification, therefore, needs to be
modified in the infinite-type setting. First, the definition of a reducible
mapping class should be generalized, but more importantly, the third cate-
gory (the analog of pseudo-Anosov mapping classes) needs to be expanded
and likely broken into subcategories.
(2) Some work has been announced on this problem by Bestvina, Fanoni and
Tao [BFT23], who classify so-called “tame” homeomorphisms that satisfy
an additional finiteness condition. Such homeomorphisms do not exhibit
any pseudo-Anosov-like behavior.
(3) Irreducible end-periodic mapping classes should form an important class
within the third category. For end-periodic homeomorphisms of infinite-
type surfaces, Handel and Mosher outlined a theory paralleling that of
pseudo-Anosov homeomorphisms in unpublished work from the 1980s,
describing a pair of transverse geodesic laminations on the surface pre-
served by the end-periodic mapping class. This theory was further de-
veloped by Cantwell, Conlon, and Fenley [CCF21]. In addition to the
above, irreducible end-periodic mapping classes share many properties
with finite-type pseudo-Anosov mapping classes; for example, they give
rise to hyperbolic mapping tori [FKLL23] and many strongly irreducible
ones are loxodromic isometries of complexes of curves and arcs [PT25].

References cited:
- [PV18] Priyam Patel and Nicholas G. Vlamis. Algebraic and topological properties of big mapping class groups. Algebr. Geom. Topol., 18(7):4109–4142, 2018. doi:10.2140/agt.2018.18.4109.
- [BFT23] Mladen Bestvina, Federica Fanoni, and Jing Tao. Towards Nielsen-Thurston classification for surfaces of infinite type, 2023. arXiv:2303.12413.
- [CCF21] John Cantwell, Lawrence Conlon, and Sergio R. Fenley. Endperiodic automorphisms of surfaces and foliations. Ergodic Theory Dynam. Systems, 41(1):66–212, 2021. doi:10.1017/etds.2019.56.
- [FKLL23] Elizabeth Field, Heejoung Kim, Christopher Leininger, and Marissa Loving. Endperiodic homeomorphisms and volumes of mapping tori. J. Topol., 16(1):57–105, 2023. doi:10.1112/topo.12277.
- [PT25] Priyam Patel and Samuel J. Taylor. Constructing endperiodic loxodromics of infinite-type arc graphs. Math. Z., 310(4):Paper No. 82, 2025. doi:10.1007/s00209-025-03784-w.

title: Kirby Problem 2.38
statement:
Give an appropriate analogue of the curve graph for infinite-
type surfaces, and characterize the surfaces for which no such graph exists.
background:
Source: Kirby's Problems in Low-Dimensional Topology notes. Original problem number: KP-2.38.

Literature notes:
(1) A motivating philosophy in geometric group theory is that one can study
the algebra of a group $G$ via the geometry of the spaces on which $G$ acts
and the dynamics of such actions. When $G$ is the mapping class group of
a finite-type surface, one of the most fruitful actions to study is that of
the mapping class group of $S$ on the curve graph, $\mathcal{C}(S)$, associated to $S$.
Part of the reason that this action is so dynamically rich is due to a
famous result of Masur and Minsky [MM00], which shows that the curve
graph is infinite-diameter and Gromov-hyperbolic: there exists $\delta > 0$
so that, for all geodesic triangles in $\mathcal{C}(S)$, each side of the triangle is
contained in the $\delta$-neighborhood of the other two. This means that $\mathcal{C}(S)$
shares properties with hyperbolic space so that some of the key tools in
hyperbolic geometry can be used to study $\mathcal{C}(S)$ and groups acting on it.
The curve graph has played a pivotal role not only in the study of mapping
class groups, but also Teichmüller theory, Kleinian groups, and the moduli
space of Riemann surfaces.

By contrast, for infinite-type surfaces the curve graph has finite di-
ameter. This makes it much harder to study the above topics for infinite-
type surfaces via the action of groups on this graph. An analogue of the
curve graph would be an infinite-diameter hyperbolic graph associated to
an infinite-type surface $S$ on which the mapping class group of $S$ acts
coboundedly and by isometries.
(2) Vlamis showed that there are infinite-type surfaces whose mapping class
groups do not act on any metric space with unbounded orbits [Vla24b];
additional examples were announced in [Vla24a]. Thus, it is not possible
to find an analogue of the curve graph that can be associated to any
infinite-type surface.
(3) Among infinite-type surfaces whose mapping class groups do admit un-
bounded actions on metric spaces, there are several associated graphs that
have been fruitful to study thus far, for instance the ray graph (Calegari
[Cal09a]), the relative arc graph (Aramayona–Fossas–Parlier [AFP17]),
the omnipresent arc graph (Fanoni–Ghaswala–McLeay [FGM21]), and
the grand arc graph (Bar-Natan–Verberne [BNV23]).
Unfortunately,
this is a piecemeal approach, since these graphs are not defined for all
infinite-type surfaces in this class, and may fail to be infinite-diameter
and hyperbolic in general.
In light of this, one wishes to first classify
which infinite-type surfaces admit an analogue of the curve graph, and to
then find a universal graph that can be associated to any such infinite-type
surface that is both infinite-diameter and hyperbolic.
(4) This problem appeared on an AIM problem list for a workshop on surfaces
of infinite type [LPRT] and was proposed for inclusion there by P. Patel
and K. Mann.

References cited:
- [MM00] Howard A. Masur and Yair N. Minsky. Geometry of the complex of curves. II. Hierarchical structure. Geom. Funct. Anal., 10(4):902–974, 2000.
- [Vla24b] Nicholas G. Vlamis. Homeomorphism groups of self-similar 2-manifolds. In In the tradition of Thurston III. Geometry and dynamics, pages 105–167. Springer, Cham,
- [Vla24a] Nicholas G. Vlamis. Homeomorphism groups of telescoping 2–manifolds are strongly distorted, 2024. arXiv:2403.03887.
- [Cal09a] Danny Calegari. Big mapping class groups and dynamics. Geometry and the imagination, https://lamington.wordpress.com/2009/06/22/big-mapping-class-groups-and-dynamics/, 2009.
- [AFP17] Javier Aramayona, Ariadna Fossas, and Hugo Parlier. Arc and curve graphs for infinite-type surfaces. Proceedings of the American Mathematical Society, 145(11):4995–5006, 2017.

title: Kirby Problem 2.39
statement:
(a) Does the mapping class group of an infinite-genus surface with no planar
ends contain every countable group?
(b) Does the mapping class group of the one-ended infinite-genus surface have
any proper finite-index subgroups?
(c) For an infinite-type surface, describe and characterize the subgroup of
mapping classes with quasi-conformal representatives. In particular, when
is it a normal subgroup of the mapping class group?
background:
Source: Kirby's Problems in Low-Dimensional Topology notes. Original problem number: KP-2.39.

Literature notes:
(1) The work of Aougab, Patel, and Vlamis [APV21] shows every mapping
class group of an infinite-genus surface with no planar ends contains every
finite group as a subgroup. Thus the problem is really about countably
infinite groups. The same work of Aougab, Patel, and Vlamis also shows
that the above question is true for infinite-genus surfaces with no planar
ends and self-similar end space, e.g., the Loch Ness monster surface. To do

this, they realize every countable group as the isometry group of a hyper-
bolic structure, and moreover, show that the above surfaces are the only
ones in which this is possible. Therefore, to answer the above question,
it is necessary to construct countably infinite subgroups of the mapping
class group that are not subgroups of the isometry group of the surface.
(2) It was shown by G. Domat [Dom22] that the mapping class group of
the one-ended infinite genus surface has nontrivial abelianization, and
the abelianization has many copies of $\mathbb{Q}$ as direct summands. It follows
that the mapping class group of the Loch Ness monster surface has many
proper subgroups of countably infinite index. In the same work, Domat
also shows that the abelianization does contain torsion subgroups, though
they are not known to be direct summands.
(3) When $S$ is a Riemann of finite type, it is a basic fact that every mapping
class admits a representative as a quasi-conformal homeomorphism, but
this is no longer true if $S$ is of infinite type. In this setting, the group
of mapping classes with quasi-conformal representatives is sometimes re-
ferred to as the Teichmüller modular group; the reader should be aware
that this term is sometimes used to refer to the entire mapping class
group in the finite-type setting. While this usage is consistent, there is
the possibility for confusion.
(4) This problem appeared on a problem list compiled at the 2021 Nearly
Carbon Neutral Geometric Topology conference [CPV21].

References cited:
- [APV21] Tarik Aougab, Priyam Patel, and Nicholas G. Vlamis. Isometry groups of infinite genus hyperbolic surfaces. Math. Ann., 381:459–498, 2021.
- [Dom22] George Domat. Big pure mapping class groups are never perfect. Math. Res. Lett., 29(3):691–726, 2022. Appendix with Ryan Dickmann.
- [CPV21] Yassin Chandran, Priyam Patel, and Nicholas G. Vlamis. Infinite-type surfaces and mapping class groups: Open problems. Available at https://https://www.patelp.com/uploads/2/5/7/9/25792573/inftypeproblems.pdf, 2021.

title: Kirby Problem 2.40
statement:
(a) Let $S$ be an infinite-type surface and $\varphi$ a mapping class for which there is
a (marked) conformal structure $\Sigma$ on $S$ with respect to which $\varphi$ is realized
as a quasi-conformal homeomorphism.
Then for each quasi-conformal
structure in the connected component of Teichmüller space containing $\Sigma$,
there is a quasiconformal homeomorphism representing $\varphi$ which minimizes
the dilatation. If the infimum of the minimal dilatations for each structure
in this component is achieved and is greater than 1, is the minimizing
quasiconformal homeomorphism unique? What is the structure of such a
minimizer?
(b) If $\varphi$ is parabolic (see Remark (1) below) for $T$, must a sequence of con-
formal structures with dilatation converging to the infimum degenerate by
pinching along some sequence of essential simple closed curves? Is this
system unique? Can it depend on the component $T$?
(c) If $\varphi$ fixes more than one component $T, T'$ of $\operatorname{Teich}(S)$, can the type be dif-
ferent for $T$ and $T'$? In particular, can $\varphi$ be parabolic for $T$ and hyperbolic
for $T'$?
background:
Source: Kirby's Problems in Low-Dimensional Topology notes. Original problem number: KP-2.40.

Literature notes:
(1) Let $S$ be a surface of infinite type, and let $\varphi$ be a mapping class for
which there is some (marked) conformal structure $\Sigma$ on $S$ for which $\varphi$

is realized by a quasiconformal homeomorphism $f: \Sigma \to \Sigma$. Then there
is some representative homeomorphism which realizes the infimum of the
dilatation. This follows from compactness (for any finite $K$) of the space
of $K$-quasiconformal homeomorphisms of the unit disk, normalized to fix
3 points on the boundary (see, e.g., [Ahl06]).
We may then try to vary the conformal structure on $S$ in the com-
ponent $T \subset \operatorname{Teich}(S)$ containing $\Sigma$, and for each point in $T$ we get a
minimum value for the dilatation of a homeomorphism representing $\varphi$,
and thereby a function $K_{T}: T \to [1, \infty)$. Note $K_{T}$ takes the value 1 if
and only if $\varphi$ is represented by an isometry for some conformal structure
in the component $T$.
Say $\varphi$ is elliptic for $T$ if $K_{T}$ achieves the value 1, parabolic for $T$ if the
infimum is not achieved, and hyperbolic for $T$ if the infimum is achieved
and is bigger than 1. Part (a) can be restated as follows: if $\varphi$ is hyperbolic
for $T$, is the minimizer unique? What is its structure?
(2) When $\varphi$ is a mapping class on a surface $S$ of finite type, there is a (marked)
conformal structure on $S$ with respect to which $\varphi$ can be realized as a qua-
siconformal homeomorphism. Moreover, there is a unique quasiconformal
homeomorphism representing $\varphi$ that minimizes the dilatation; this is the
Teichmüller map. Note that in the finite-type setting, Teichmüller space
has a single connected component.
(3) There are elementary examples of topological surfaces of infinite type $S$
and mapping classes $\varphi$ that are not realized by quasiconformal maps for
any choice of (marked) conformal structure on $S$. Perhaps the simplest
example is: let $S$ be the infinite ladder surface, which we think of as the
infinite union of twice-punctured tori $T_{n}$ indexed by integers $n \in \mathbb{Z}$ joined
end to end, let $\alpha$ be any pseudo-Anosov diffeomorphism of a single twice-
punctured torus, and let $\varphi$ be the mapping class that does $\alpha^{n}$ on $T_{n}$. No
matter what conformal structure we choose on $S$, the restriction of $\alpha^{n}$ to
$T_{n}$ has dilatation at least as big as $|n|$ times the minimum dilatation of $\alpha$
on a twice-punctured torus. This example is (highly) reducible; it would
be nice to have a straightforward irreducible example.
(4) If $S$ is a surface of infinite type, it is possible to define the Teichmüller
space of $S$ to be the space of marked conformal surfaces $f: S \to \Sigma$ up
to equivalence; see the recently announced constructions of Basmajian–
Chandran [BC24a] and Tappu [Tap23] for details. The connected com-
ponents of this space will be contractible, but (with the hypothesis that
$S$ has infinite type) there will always be infinitely many components
[Bas97, BK08]. Some mapping classes will fix no component (as in the
previous remark), some will fix some components and not others, some
will fix every component (e.g., those supported in compact subsurfaces).
What are the possible orbit types? It was recently announced by Basma-
jian and Chandran that the subgroup that fixes every component is the
compactly supported subgroup [BC24a].
(5) Recent work of Basmajian and Chandran [BC24a] announced that there
exist mapping classes $\varphi$ that are represented by quasiconformal home-
omorphisms on some components of Teichmüller space but not others.

In particular, the function $K_{T}$ defined in Remark (1) above may not be
well-defined for every component $T \subseteq \operatorname{Teich}(S)$.
(6) A version of this problem appeared on a problem list compiled at the 2021
Nearly Carbon Neutral Geometric Topology conference [CPV21].

References cited:
- [Ahl06] Lars V. Ahlfors. Lectures on quasiconformal mappings, volume 38 of University Lecture Series. American Mathematical Society, Providence, RI, second edition, 2006. With supplemental chapters by C. J. Earle, I. Kra, M. Shishikura and J. H. Hubbard. doi:10.1090/ulect/038.
- [BC24a] A. Basmajian and Y. Chandran. A Bers type classification of big mapping class groups, 2024. arXiv:2410.05606.
- [Tap23] Chaitanya Tappu. A moduli space of marked hyperbolic structures for big surfaces, 2023. arXiv:2311.01551.
- [Bas97] Ara Basmajian. Large parameter spaces of quasiconformally distinct hyperbolic structures. J. Anal. Math., 71:75–85, 1997. doi:10.1007/BF02788023.
- [BK08] Ara Basmajian and Youngju Kim. Geometrically infinite surfaces with discrete length spectra. Geom. Dedicata, 137:219–240, 2008. doi:10.1007/s10711-008-9294-5.
- [CPV21] Yassin Chandran, Priyam Patel, and Nicholas G. Vlamis. Infinite-type surfaces and mapping class groups: Open problems. Available at https://https://www.patelp.com/uploads/2/5/7/9/25792573/inftypeproblems.pdf, 2021.

title: Kirby Problem 2.41
statement:
Give a finite list of practically computable invariants of the
mapping class group or pure mapping class group of an infinite-type surface $S$ that
determine the topology of $S$.
background:
Source: Kirby's Problems in Low-Dimensional Topology notes. Original problem number: KP-2.41.

Literature notes:
(1) Let $S$ be a surface, possibly of infinite type. When $S = S_{g,b}^{p}$ is of finite
type, the homeomorphism type of the surface is encoded in the isomor-
phism type of its mapping class group, with two pairs of exceptions for
small values of $g, b$, and $p$. Most cases can be distinguished by consid-
ering well-known group invariants: work of Birman–Lubotsky–McCarthy
[BLM $^{+}83$] computes the algebraic rank, and Harer [Har86] computes
the virtual cohomological dimension, both in terms of $g$ and $b$. Combin-
ing these formulas, it is possible to determine the topology of the surface
$S$, although note that this argument breaks down when either $g = 0$ or
$b = 0$ (see [RS11, Remark A.2]).
(2) The classification of infinite-type surfaces tells us that an infinite-type sur-
face is determined by its end space $E$, the closed subgroup of non-planar
ends $E^{g}$ of $S$, the genus, and the number of compact boundary compo-
nents of $S$.
However, the end space of an infinite-type surface can be
any closed subset of a Cantor set, and in practice, it is hard to tell when
two such subsets are homeomorphic. In addition, Bavard–Dowdall–Rafi
[BDR20] prove algebraic rigidity for mapping class groups of infinite-type
surfaces: if Map $(S)$ is isomorphic to Map $(S')$, then $S$ and $S'$ are home-
omorphic. But again, big mapping class groups are uncountable groups
and determining when two of these groups are isomorphic in general is
difficult. Thus, we pose the question above.
(3) There has been one result by Aougab–Patel–Vlamis [APV21, Theorem
8.1] in this direction for $n$-ended orientable infinite-genus surfaces with no
planar ends.

References cited:
- [BLM+83] Joan S Birman, Alex Lubotzky, John McCarthy, et al. Abelian and solvable subgroups of the mapping class groups. Duke Mathematical Journal, 50(4):1107–1120, 1983.
- [Har86] John L. Harer. The virtual cohomological dimension of the mapping class group of an orientable surface. Invent. Math., 84(1):157–176, 1986. doi:10.1007/BF01388737.
- [RS11] Kasra Rafi and Saul Schleimer. Curve complexes are rigid. Duke Math. J., 158(2):225–246, 2011. doi:10.1215/00127094-1334004.
- [BDR20] Juliette Bavard, Spencer Dowdall, and Kasra Rafi. Isomorphisms between big mapping class groups. International Mathematics Research Notices, 2020(10):3084– 3099, 2020.
- [APV21] Tarik Aougab, Priyam Patel, and Nicholas G. Vlamis. Isometry groups of infinite genus hyperbolic surfaces. Math. Ann., 381:459–498, 2021.

title: Kirby Problem 2.42
statement:
Is the geodesic flow in almost every direction on the Chamanara
surface ergodic? What about on the translation surface considered by Bruin and
Lukina, which is similar to the Chamanara surface?
background:
Source: Kirby's Problems in Low-Dimensional Topology notes. Original problem number: KP-2.42.

Literature notes:
(1) Translation surfaces have geodesic flows in every direction that preserve
Lebesgue measure. Kerckhoff, Masur, and Smillie proved that for every
finite-type translation surface, this is the only probability measure pre-
served by the flow (that is, the flow is uniquely ergodic) in almost every
direction [KMS86]. As a corollary, they obtain that the flow in almost
every direction is ergodic with respect to the Lebesgue measure.
It is
natural to ask to what extent this generalizes to infinite-type surfaces.
Fraczek and Ulcigrai produced many examples of infinite-area, infinite-
type translation surfaces where the straight line flows are not ergodic in
almost every direction [FU14]. For finite-area translation surfaces, how-
ever, this is widely open.
(2) The Chamanara surface, first described by Reza Chamanara in [Cha04],
is one of the best known translation surfaces. Chamanara defines a family
of translation surfaces with a parameter $\alpha \in [0, 1]$. For the case $\alpha = 1/2$,
called the standard Chamanara surface, consider a square with edge length
1, and divide the top and bottom sides into two halves. Identify the top
right half with the bottom left half via a translation, and then divide the
unidentified top and bottom edges in half, identify the top right half with
the bottom left half via a translation, and repeat. Do the same for the
left and right edges, always identifying the upper part of the right edge
with the lower part of the left edge. Excluding the corners of the square
and the points where we divided the edges, we obtain the Chamanara
surface, a one-ended infinite-genus translation surface of finite area. See
also [DHV24, Example 2.4.22] for another description of the surface.
The Chamanara surface has a close relationship to baker’s map and is
sometimes called the baker’s map surface; see [CGL06] for further details.
Bruin and Lukina consider a family of translation surfaces similar to
the Chamanara surfaces [BL23], but their surfaces lack certain metric
symmetries enjoyed by the Chamana surfaces, and so different techniques
may be necessary to approach this problem.
(3) Similarly to proving that there exists a billiard in a polygon where the
billiard flow is ergodic (in the 3-dimensional unit tangent bundle), one
can use a Baire Category argument to show that there exists a finite-
area, infinite-type surface where the flow in almost every direction is er-
godic with respect to Lebesgue measure. Moreover, by work of Vorobets
[Vor97], one can even find an explicit example, but these arguments do
not seem applicable in the two situations above.

References cited:
- [KMS86] Steven Kerckhoff, Howard Masur, and John Smillie. Ergodicity of billiard flows and quadratic differentials. Ann. of Math. (2), 124(2):293–311, 1986. doi:10.2307/1971280.
- [FU14] Krzysztof Fraczek and Corinna Ulcigrai. Non-ergodic Z-periodic billiards and infinite translation surfaces. Invent. Math., 197(2):241–298, 2014. doi:10.1007/s00222-013-0482-z.
- [Cha04] R. Chamanara. Affine automorphism groups of surfaces of infinite type. In In the tradition of Ahlfors and Bers, III, volume 355 of Contemp. Math., pages 123–145. Amer. Math. Soc., Providence, RI, 2004. doi:10.1090/conm/355/06449.
- [DHV24] V. Delecroix, P. Hubert, and F. Valdez. Infinite translation surfaces in the wild, 2024. arXiv:2403.05424.
- [CGL06] R. Chamanara, F. P. Gardiner, and N. Lakic. A hyperelliptic realization of the horseshoe and baker maps. Ergodic Theory Dynam. Systems, 26(6):1749–1768, 2006. doi:10.1017/S0143385706000484.
- [BL23] Henk Bruin and Olga Lukina. Rotated odometers. J. Lond. Math. Soc. (2), 107(6):1983–2024, 2023. doi:10.1112/jlms.12731.
- [Vor97] Ya.B̃. Vorobets. Ergodicity of billiards in polygons. Mat. Sb., 188(3):65–112, 1997. doi:10.1070/SM1997v188n03ABEH000211.

title: Kirby Problem 2.43
statement:
Let $X$ be a compact, totally disconnected subset of $\mathbb{R}^{2}$ with
$|X| \geq 2$, and let $\Gamma_{X}$ denote the mapping class group of $\mathbb{R}^{2} - X$.
(a) For $Y \subset X$, let $\Gamma_{X,Y}$ be the subgroup of $\Gamma_{X}$ permuting $Y$ . Classify in-
variants $q$ that are functorial.
(b) If $X \subset \mathbb{R}^{2}$ is totally disconnected and $\alpha$ is a homeomorphism of $\mathbb{R}^{2}$ fixing
$X$ as a set, let $C_{\alpha}(X)$ denote the space of $\alpha$-invariant closed subsets of

$X$, in the Hausdorff topology. Let $q$ be functorial as in part (a). Classify
those $q$ that are continuous or semi-continuous.
(c) What is the relationship between the translation length $\tau_{X}$ and topological
entropy? More precisely, is there a positive constant $C$ so that if $\alpha$ is a
homeomorphism of $\mathbb{R}^{2}$ permuting $X$ and $g$ is the class of $\alpha$ in $\Gamma_{X}$, then
the (topological) entropy of $\alpha$ is at least as big as $C \cdot \tau_{X}(g)$?
(d) Suppose $X$ is a Cantor set in the plane, and let $P\Gamma_{X}$ denote the ‘pure’
subgroup of $\Gamma_{X}$ fixing $X$ pointwise. Let $N$ be a subgroup of $P\Gamma_{X}$ that is
normal in $\Gamma_{X}$, and for each integer $n$, let $N_{n}$ be the subgroup of $P\Gamma_{n}$ that
is the image of $N$ restricted to any $n$-element subset of $X$. What possible
sequences of subgroups $N_{n}$ can arise in this way?
(e) For which $g \in \Gamma_{X}$ is there an embedding $X \to \mathbb{R}^{2}$ for which $g$ is represented
by a diffeomorphism $\alpha$ which is $C^{\infty}$? Or $C^{k}$ for fixed $k$?
background:
Source: Kirby's Problems in Low-Dimensional Topology notes. Original problem number: KP-2.43.

Literature notes:
(1) In Part (a), an invariant is functorial if for each $X$, there is a map
$q_{X}: \Gamma_{X} \to \mathbb{R}$ so that the following holds.
For each inclusion $Y \subset X$
and each $g \in \Gamma_{X,Y}$ with image $g_{Y} \in \Gamma_{Y}$ under the natural restriction map
$\Gamma_{X,Y} \to \Gamma_{Y}$ , there is an inequality $q_{X}(g) \geq q_{Y} (g_{Y})$. In part (b), an in-
variant is (semi-)continuous if the map $C_{\alpha}(X) \to \mathbb{R}$ taking $Y$ to $q_{Y} ([\alpha])$
is (semi-)continuous for all $\alpha$, where $[\alpha]$ is the class of $\alpha$ in $\Gamma_{Y}$ .
(2) The ray graph $\mathcal{R}_{X}$ is the graph whose vertices are isotopy classes of rays in
$\mathbb{R}^{2} - X$ from infinity to a point in $X$, and whose edges are pairs that may
be realized disjointly. This graph is hyperbolic, connected, and infinite
diameter, and its flag complex is contractible. The group $\Gamma_{X}$ acts on it
by isometries.
There is a cyclic order on the set of vertices of $\mathcal{R}_{X}$ according to
the cyclic order on the geodesic representatives at infinity (with respect
to any complete hyperbolic structure on $\mathbb{R}^{2} - X$) which may be order
completed to a circle $S^{1}_{X}$ on which $\Gamma_{X}$ acts by (orientation-preserving)
homeomorphisms.
Numerical invariants of elements of $\Gamma_{X}$ may be defined in terms of
these actions, including
(a) rotation number rot $_{X}(g) \in \mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}$ for $g \in \Gamma_{X}$ acting on $S^{1}_{X}$;
(b) translation length $\tau_{X}(g)$ for $g \in \Gamma_{X}$ acting on $\mathcal{R}_{X}$; and
(c) counting quasimorphisms $H_{X,\sigma}(g)$ for $g \in \Gamma_{X}$ and $\sigma$ a $\Gamma_{X}$-orbit of
path in $\mathcal{R}_{X}$.
Some of these invariants have a well-defined ‘name’ (rotation number,
translation length) independent of $X$. Others depend on choices that are
special to $X$.
Another way to express the fact that some invariants have a well-
defined name is to say that they are functorial in the sense of part (a).
For example, an inclusion $Y \to X$ induces a 1-Lipschitz map $\mathcal{R}_{X} \to \mathcal{R}_{Y}$
well defined up to bounded distance, and translation length $\tau_{X}$ in the
graph $\mathcal{R}_{X}$ is functorial.
(3) There is a partial order $<$ due to Boyland [Boy88] on the set of all
conjugacy classes in all (finite type) braid groups where $g < h$ if for every
homeomorphism $\alpha$ of the disk fixing the boundary with a finite $\alpha$-invariant
set $X$ such that $\alpha$ represents $g$ relative to $X$, there is another $\alpha$-invariant

set $Y$ such that $\alpha$ relative to $Y$ represents $h$. We say that $g$ forces $h$, and
this partial order is called braid forcing. A numerical invariant $q$ from
(finite type) braid groups to $\mathbb{R}$ is monotone if it is monotone with respect
to braid forcing partial order.
All monotone invariants arise as follows: let $G$ denote the group of all
homeomorphisms of the disk fixed on the boundary, and for each braid $g$,
let $G_{g}$ be the subset of $G$ of homeomorphisms representing $g$ relative to
some finite invariant set. Then $g < h$ if and only if $G_{g} \subset G_{h}$. For any func-
tion $f: G \to \mathbb{R}$, we obtain a monotone invariant by $f(g) = \sup_{\alpha\in Gg} f(\alpha)$.
Braid forcing makes perfect sense for mapping class groups instead of
braid groups, and one may extend this notion in the obvious way to a par-
tial order on all conjugacy classes in all $\Gamma_{X}$ simultaneously. Thus, another
natural question is: What is the relationship between (semi-)continuity
and Boyland’s braid forcing?
(4) In [CC22] the individual subgroups $N_{n}$ that can arise as in part (d) are
identified; they satisfy the so-called ‘inertia’ condition.
(5) Let $\mathcal{R}_{X}$ be the ray graph and $S^{1}_{X}$ the circle on which $\Gamma_{X}$ acts by home-
omorphisms as in Remark 2. An additional question is: Can the (non)-
realization property of part (e) be related to numerical properties of $g$ that
can be computed from the action on $\mathcal{R}_{X}$ or $S^{1}_{X}$?

References cited:
- [Boy88] Philip Boyland. An analog of Sharkovski’s theorem for twist maps. In Hamiltonian dynamical systems (Boulder, CO, 1987), volume 81 of Contemp. Math., pages 119– 133. Amer. Math. Soc., Providence, RI, 1988. doi:10.1090/conm/081/986261.
- [CC22] Danny Calegari and Lvzhou Chen. Normal subgroups of big mapping class groups. Trans. Amer. Math. Soc. Ser. B, 9:957–976, 2022. doi:10.1090/btran/108.

title: Kirby Problem 2.44
statement:
Given an infinite-type surface $S$, which homeomorphisms $f: S \to$
$S$ give rise to mapping tori $M_{f}$ that admit a hyperbolic structure? For those which
do admit a hyperbolic metric, is $M_{f}$ homeomorphic to the interior of a compact
hyperbolic manifold with totally geodesic boundary?
background:
Source: Kirby's Problems in Low-Dimensional Topology notes. Original problem number: KP-2.44.

Literature notes:
(1) Thurston’s theorem on the hyperbolization of mapping tori states that
for a finite-type surface $S$ and a homeomorphism $f$ of the surface $S$, the
mapping torus

$$
M_{f} = S \times [0, 1]/(x, 0) \sim (f(x), 1)
$$

is hyperbolic if and only if $f$ is pseudo-Anosov.
This question works
towards an analogue of the theorem for infinite-type surfaces.
A first approach to this problem could be to give a list of criteria
on $f$ that ensures certain properties necessary for the mapping torus to
be hyperbolic. For instance, to give criteria on $f$ that ensure that $M_{f}$ is
atoroidal.
(2) It is known from work of Field–Kim–Leininger–Loving [FKLL23] that for
a strongly irreducible end-periodic homeomorphism $f$ of an infinite-type
surface $S$, the mapping torus $M_{f}$ is hyperbolic and homeomorphic to the
interior of a compact hyperbolic manifold with totally geodesic boundary.
This motivates the second part of the question above.

References cited:
- [FKLL23] Elizabeth Field, Heejoung Kim, Christopher Leininger, and Marissa Loving. Endperiodic homeomorphisms and volumes of mapping tori. J. Topol., 16(1):57–105, 2023. doi:10.1112/topo.12277.

background:
Source: Kirby's Problems in Low-Dimensional Topology notes. Original problem number: KP-2.45.

Literature notes:
(1) The (oriented) cobordism group of $n$-dimensional manifolds, denoted $\Delta_{n}$,
consists of equivalence classes of pairs $(M^{n}, f)$ where $M$ is a compact
oriented manifold and $f$ is a homeomorphism. The equivalence relation
is given by $(M_{0}, f_{0}) \sim (M_{1}, f_{1})$ if there is a compact cobordism between
$M_{0}$ and $M_{1}$ with a homeomorphism extending $f_{0}$ and $f_{1}$. This group was
computed for $n \geq 4$ by Kreck [Kre84b] and for $n = 3$ by Melvin [Mel79].
Bonahon [Bon83] (see also [EE82]) showed that $\Delta_{2} \cong \mathbb{Z}^{\infty} \oplus (\mathbb{Z}/2)^{\infty}$. As in
usual cobordism theories, compactness is used to ensure that one gets a
nontrivial group.
(2) An end-periodic manifold $M$ is a noncompact manifold with finitely many
ends, such that each end $\epsilon$ has a neighborhood that is half of an infinite
cyclic cover of a compact manifold $X_{\epsilon}$. End-periodic manifolds behave
in many respects (topological, geometric, and analytic) as if they were
actually compact. An end periodic automorphism $f: M \to M$ is a home-
omorphism or homeomorphism that is a covering translation over $X_{\epsilon}$ on
some neighborhood of each end $\epsilon$. End-periodic homeomorphisms arise
naturally in the study of depth-one foliations [CCF21], with the behav-
ior in the end corresponding to the limiting behavior of a non-compact
leaf as it approaches a compact leaf. Cobordisms of end-periodic auto-
morphisms are defined as in the compact case, with the extension required
to be end-periodic, and one defines the end-periodic cobordism group $\Delta^{e}_{n}$
as above.
(3) This problem is meaningful in all dimensions; the calculation of the usual
$\Delta_{2}$ makes use of special techniques related to the Nielsen-Thurston classifi-
cation of surface automorphisms. A similar end-periodic Nielsen-Thurston
theory, originating in unpublished work of Handel-Miller, is developed in
depth in [CCF21], and it seems reasonable to approach the computation
of $\Delta^{e}_{2}$ using similar tools.

References cited:
- [Kre84b] Matthias Kreck. Bordism of diffeomorphisms and related topics. Springer-Verlag, Berlin, 1984. With an appendix by Neal W. Stoltzfus.
- [Mel79] Paul Melvin. Bordism of diffeomorphisms. Topology, 18(2):173–175, 1979. doi:10.1016/0040-9383(79)90034-X.
- [Bon83] Francis Bonahon. Cobordism of automorphisms of surfaces. Ann. Sci. École Norm. Sup. (4), 16(2):237–270, 1983. URL: http://www.numdam.org/item?id=ASENS 1983 4 16 2 237 0.
- [EE82] A. L. Edmonds and J. H. Ewing. Remarks on the cobordism group of surface diffeomorphisms. Math. Ann., 259(4):497–504, 1982. doi:10.1007/BF01466055.
- [CCF21] John Cantwell, Lawrence Conlon, and Sergio R. Fenley. Endperiodic automorphisms of surfaces and foliations. Ergodic Theory Dynam. Systems, 41(1):66–212, 2021. doi:10.1017/etds.2019.56.

title: Kirby Problem 2.46
statement:
(a) Which coarsely boundedly generated mapping class groups of infinite-type
surfaces are hyperbolic?
(b) Consider the class of surfaces with $n \geq 2$ ends, all accumulated by genus.
Are the mapping class groups of these surfaces quasi-isometric for different
values of $n$?
background:
Source: Kirby's Problems in Low-Dimensional Topology notes. Original problem number: KP-2.46.

Literature notes:
(1) Big mapping class groups are not finitely, countably, or compactly gener-
ated. There is a generalization of compactness called coarse boundedness,

defined and studied extensively by C. Rosendal [Ros13, Ros22] for Pol-
ish groups. It turns out that when the (pure) mapping class group of an
infinite-type surface admits a coarsely bounded generating set, the quasi-
isometry type of the group is well-defined. Mann–Rafi [MR23] and T.
Hill [Hil25] give a classification of those surfaces whose mapping class
groups and pure mapping class groups have this property, respectively.
This problem asks which coarsely boundedly generated mapping class
groups of infinite-type surfaces are quasi-isometric to a hyperbolic metric
space. In other words, for which infinite-type surfaces is the mapping class
group with the word metric coming from a coarsely bounded generating
set a hyperbolic metric space?
(2) The mapping class groups of some surfaces are not only coarsely bound-
edly generated, they are themselves coarsely bounded.
In particular,
they are finite diameter (when equipped with a word metric coming from
a coarsely bounded generating set), and so are elementary hyperbolic.
Schaeffer-Cohen [SC24] showed that the mapping class group of a plane
minus a Cantor set is quasi-isometric to the loop graph, which is an infi-
nite diameter hyperbolic graph associated to the surface. This is the only
known example of a mapping class group of an infinite-type surface that
is non-elementary hyperbolic.
(3) Problem 2.46.(b) is a special case of the broad (and possibly unanswerable)
problem of determining the quasi-isometry type of coarsely boundedly
generated mapping class groups of infinite-type surfaces.

References cited:
- [Ros13] Christian Rosendal. Global and local boundedness of Polish groups. Indiana Univ. Math. J., 62(5):1621–1678, 2013. doi:10.1512/iumj.2013.62.5133.
- [Ros22] Christian Rosendal. Coarse geometry of topological groups, volume 223 of Cambridge Tracts in Mathematics. Cambridge University Press, Cambridge, 2022.
- [MR23] Kathryn Mann and Kasra Rafi. Large-scale geometry of big mapping class groups. Geom. Topol., 27(6):2237–2296, 2023. doi:10.2140/gt.2023.27.2237.
- [Hil25] Thomas Hill. Large-scale geometry of pure mapping class groups of infinite-type surfaces. Proc. Amer. Math. Soc., 153(6):2667–2680, 2025. doi:10.1090/proc/17181.
- [SC24] Anschel Schaffer-Cohen. Graphs of curves and arcs quasi-isometric to big mapping class groups. Groups Geom. Dyn., 18(2):705–735, 2024. doi:10.4171/ggd/751.

title: Kirby Problem 2.47
statement:
(a) Given a mapping class $\psi$ of a based surface $S$, there is an induced endo-
morphism of the symmetric product $\operatorname{Sym}^{i}(S)$ and hence an endofunctor
$\psi_{*}$ of the partially wrapped Fukaya category $\mathcal{F}(S)$ as constructed, say, by
Auroux [Aur10]. Compute the categorical entropy of $\psi_{*}$, in the sense
of [DHKK14], for $\psi$ pseudo-Anosov.
(b) Given a fibered knot $K$ with pseudo-Anosov monodromy, what is

$$
\limsup_{n\to\infty}\left(\dim \widehat{\mathrm{HFK}}(\Sigma^{n}(K),\widetilde{K};i)\right)^{1/n},
$$

where $\widetilde{K}$ is the branch locus in the $n$-fold cyclic branched cover $\Sigma^{n}(K)$,
and $i$ denotes the Alexander grading (in $\mathbb{Z}$) with respect to the fiber surface.
Here, $\widehat{\mathrm{HFK}}$ denotes the knot Floer homology of $K$ [OS04c, Ras03].
(c) With notation as in the previous question, what is

$$
\limsup_{n\to\infty}\left(\dim \widehat{\mathrm{HF}}(\Sigma^{n}(K))\right)^{1/n}
$$

for the Heegaard Floer invariant $\widehat{\mathrm{HF}}$ [OS04e] of the closed 3-manifold
$\Sigma^{n}(K)$?
(d) Given a closed surface $S$ and a pseudo-Anosov automorphism $\psi$, let $M_{\psi}$
denote the mapping torus of $\psi$, and $\widehat{\mathrm{HF}}(M_{\psi};i)$ the summand of
$\widehat{\mathrm{HF}}(M_{\psi})$
spanned by the spin $^{c}$-structures $\mathfrak{s}$ with $\langle c_{1}(\mathfrak{s}), [F]\rangle = i$. What is

$$
\limsup_{n\to\infty}\left(\dim \widehat{\mathrm{HF}}(M_{\psi^{n}},i)\right)^{1/n}?
$$

What about

$$
\limsup_{n\to\infty}\left(\dim_{\mathbb{F}_{2}}\mathrm{HF}^{+}(M_{\psi^{n}},i)\right)^{1/n}
$$

for $i \neq 0$ (or for twisted $\mathrm{HF}^{+}$ for $i = 0$)?
background:
Source: Kirby's Problems in Low-Dimensional Topology notes. Original problem number: KP-2.47.

Literature notes:
(1) In (a), the categorical entropy is equal to

$$
\limsup_{n\to\infty}\left(\dim H_{*}(\widehat{\mathrm{CFDA}}(\psi^{n},i-g))\right)^{1/n},
$$

where $\widehat{\mathrm{CFDA}}(\psi)$ is the bordered Floer bimodule [LOT15] and $g$ is the
genus of $S$.
In the case $i = 1$, this entropy is equal to the dilatation
$\lambda(\psi)$ [LOT13, DHKK14]. For (d), see [OS04e] for the definition of
$\mathrm{HF}^{+}$, which is a Floer homology relative to a divisor; $\widehat{\mathrm{HF}}$ is Floer homology
in the complement of that divisor.
(2) Properties of bordered Floer homology imply that the categorical en-
tropy is an upper bound for the answers to the remaining questions
(perhaps up to a constant factor) [LOT15].
Also, the growth rate of
$\bigoplus_i \widehat{\mathrm{HFK}}(\Sigma^{n}(K),\widetilde{K},i)$ is an upper bound for the growth rate of
$\widehat{\mathrm{HF}}(\Sigma^{n}(K))$.
(3) The growth rate of $|H_{1}(\Sigma^{n}(K))|$ is a lower bound for the growth rate
of $\widehat{\mathrm{HF}}(\Sigma^{n}(K))$.
(4) Some results about the growth rate of Heegaard Floer homology of branched
covers were proved in [HM18], though these results are about linear, not
exponential, growth.
(5) In (d), the reason for the restriction to $\mathrm{HF} ^{+}$ with $i \neq 0$ is that $\mathrm{HF} ^{+}$ is
finitely generated over $\mathbb{F}[\operatorname{U}]$ but not over $\mathbb{F}$ for $i = 0$.
(6) Some further observations on these questions can be found in [Cor18].
(7) One can ask similar questions about the growth of knot invariants like knot
Floer homology, Khovanov homology, or symplectic Khovanov homology
when one inserts a high power of a braid.

References cited:
- [Aur10] Denis Auroux. Fukaya categories of symmetric products and bordered HeegaardFloer homology. J. Gökova Geom. Topol. GGT, 4:1–54, 2010.
- [DHKK14] G. Dimitrov, F. Haiden, L. Katzarkov, and M. Kontsevich. Dynamical systems and categories. In The influence of Solomon Lefschetz in geometry and topology, volume 621 of Contemp. Math., pages 133–170. Amer. Math. Soc., Providence, RI, 2014. doi:10.1090/conm/621/12421.
- [OS04c] Peter Ozsváth and Zoltán Szabó. Holomorphic disks and knot invariants. Adv. Math., 186(1):58–116, 2004. doi:10.1016/j.aim.2003.05.001.
- [Ras03] Jacob Rasmussen. Floer homology and knot complements. PhD thesis, Harvard University, Cambridge, MA, 2003. https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0306378.
- [OS04e] Peter Ozsváth and Zoltán Szabó. Holomorphic disks and topological invariants for closed three-manifolds. Ann. of Math. (2), 159(3):1027–1158, 2004. doi:10.4007/annals.2004.159.1027.
- [LOT15] Robert Lipshitz, Peter Ozsváth, and Dylan Thurston. Bimodules in bordered Heegaard Floer homology. Geom. Topol., 19(2):525–724, 2015. doi:10.2140/gt.2015.19.525.
- [LOT13] Robert Lipshitz, Peter Ozsváth, and Dylan Thurston. A faithful linear-categorical action of the mapping class group of a surface with boundary. J. Eur. Math. Soc. (JEMS), 15(4):1279–1307, 2013. doi:10.4171/JEMS/392.

title: Kirby Problem 2.48
statement:
The mapping class group of a closed, orientable, genus $g$ sur-
face $S$ acts by symplectomorphisms on the symmetric product $\operatorname{Sym}^{g}(S)$. In partic-
ular, it acts smoothly on $\operatorname{Sym}^{g}(S)$.
(a) What is the kernel of the map from the mapping class group of $S$ to the
smooth mapping class group of $\operatorname{Sym}^{g}(S)$? What about in the based case?
(b) Given disjoint simple closed curves $\alpha_{1},..., \alpha_{g}$ in $S$, there is a correspond-
ing torus $T_{\alpha}$ in $\operatorname{Sym}^{g}(S)$: the image of $\alpha_{1} \times \cdots \times \alpha_{g} \subset S^{g}$. These are
the tori that appear in Heegaard Floer theory. When do $\alpha_{1},..., \alpha_{g}$ and
$\beta_{1},..., \beta_{g}$ give smoothly isotopic tori? When are they Lagrangian isotopic
for an appropriate choice of symplectic form?
background:
Source: Kirby's Problems in Low-Dimensional Topology notes. Original problem number: KP-2.48.

Literature notes:
(1) The question relates to whether Heegaard Floer homology is truly a sym-
plectic invariant, or should be determined by the smooth isotopy classes
of the Heegaard tori. (Examples of the difference between smooth and
symplectic topology in other settings have received substantial interest,
though many such examples are now known; [Sei97] is particularly rele-
vant.)
(2) The fact that the mapping class group acts symplectically on $\operatorname{Sym}^{g}(S)$,
for appropriate symplectic forms, was shown by Perutz [Per08a]. (The
obvious map, where a diffeomorphism $\varphi$ of the surface $S$ sends a point
$\{x_{1},..., x_{g}\} \in \operatorname{Sym}^{g}(S)$ to $\{\varphi(x_{1}),..., \varphi(x_{g})\}$ gives a homeomorphism but
is not typically smooth; an exception is if $\varphi$ is holomorphic with respect
to some complex structure on $S$ and the smooth structure on $\operatorname{Sym}^{g}(S)$ is
induced from this complex structure, in which case the obvious induced
map of $\operatorname{Sym}^{g}(S)$ is also holomorphic.) Clarkson used Heegaard Floer ho-
mology to show that the map from the based mapping class group to
the group of symplectomorphisms of $\operatorname{Sym}^{g}(S\setminus\{z\})$ modulo the Hamilton-
ian diffeomorphisms is injective [Cla17].
(This uses the fact that, for
appropriate choices of symplectic forms [Per08b], the Heegaard tori are
exact [Hen12, HLL22a], and so Heegaard Floer homology agrees with
the usual Lagrangian intersection Floer homology.)
(3) The fundamental group of $\operatorname{Sym}^{g}(S)$ (for $g > 1$) is isomorphic to $H_{1}(\Sigma)$.
In particular, the Torelli group of $S$ acts trivially on $\pi_{1}(\operatorname{Sym}^{g}(S))$. (It also
acts trivially on the homology of $\operatorname{Sym}^{g}(S)$.) Also, by Perutz’s work, if $\alpha'_{1}$
is obtained from $\alpha_{1}$ by a handleslide, then $\alpha_{1} \times \cdots \times \alpha_{g}$ and
$\alpha'_{1} \times \cdots \times \alpha_{g}$
are smoothly isotopic (and, in fact, Hamiltonian isotopic for appropriate
symplectic forms) [Per08b].
(4) In the case $g = 2$, one might be able to use the Abel-Jacobi map (which
in this case presents $\operatorname{Sym}^{2}(S)$ as a blow-up of the Jacobian torus) to show
that the Torelli group acts trivially, since it acts trivially on the Jacobian
torus $H^{1}(S; \mathbb{R})/H^{1}(\Sigma; \mathbb{Z})$. Perhaps this suggests that the Torelli group or
the Johnson kernel acts trivially in the higher-genus case as well.

References cited:
- [Sei97] Paul Seidel. Floer homology and the symplectic isotopy problem. PhD thesis, University of Oxford, 1997.
- [Per08a] Tim Perutz. Lagrangian matching invariants for fibred four-manifolds. II. Geom. Topol., 12(3):1461–1542, 2008. doi:10.2140/gt.2008.12.1461.
- [Cla17] Corrin Clarkson. Three-manifold mutations detected by Heegaard Floer homology. Algebr. Geom. Topol., 17(1):1–16, 2017. doi:10.2140/agt.2017.17.1.
- [Per08b] Timothy Perutz. Hamiltonian handleslides for Heegaard Floer homology. In Proceedings of Gökova Geometry-Topology Conference 2007, pages 15–35. Gökova Geometry/Topology Conference (GGT), Gökova, 2008.
- [Hen12] Kristen Hendricks. A rank inequality for the knot Floer homology of double branched covers. Algebr. Geom. Topol., 12(4):2127–2178, 2012. doi:10.2140/agt.2012.12.2127.
- [HLL22a] Kristen Hendricks, Tye Lidman, and Robert Lipshitz. Rank inequalities for the Heegaard Floer homology of branched covers. Doc. Math., 27:581–612, 2022.

title: Kirby Problem 2.49
statement:
(AMU conjecture). Let $S$ be a surface with negative Euler char-
acteristic. If $\varphi \in \operatorname{Mod}(S)$ acts by a pseudo-Anosov on some subsurface (including
$S$ itself), show that there exists $p_{0}(\varphi)$ such that the Witten–Reshetikhin–Turaev
representation $\rho_{p}(\varphi)$ has infinite order for $p \geq p_{0}(\varphi)$.
background:
Source: Kirby's Problems in Low-Dimensional Topology notes. Original problem number: KP-2.49.

Literature notes:
(1) Given a compact Lie group $G$, the Witten–Reshetikhin–Turaev $G$-quantum
representations, introduced by Witten [Wit89] and rigorously defined
by Reshetikhin and Turaev [RT91], are families of representations of
$\operatorname{Mod}(S)$.
The most studied case is when $G = \operatorname{SU}(2)$ or $G = \operatorname{SO}(3)$,
in which case these representations are indexed by an integer $p \geq 3$. More
precisely we have:

$$
\rho_{p}: \operatorname{Mod}(S) \to PGL(d_{p}(S), \mathbb{C}),
$$

where $d_{p}(S)$ is given by the famous Verlinde formula and is a polynomial
in $p$ of degree $3g - 3$ (where $g$ is the genus of $S$). The representation $\rho_{p}$
sends a Dehn twist to a torsion element, and when $S$ has negative Euler
characteristic, $\rho_{p}(\operatorname{Mod}(S))$ is infinite for $p$ big enough. Moreover, Ander-
sen (see [And06]) proved that if $\varphi \in \operatorname{Mod}(S)$ is non-central, then $\rho_{p}(\varphi)$
is nontrivial for $p$ sufficiently large. This property is called asymptotic
faithfulness.
(2) Geometric properties of these representations are quite mysterious. For
instance, it is not known if the Nielsen-Thurston classification can be de-
tected by quantum representations. In [AMU06], Andersen, Masbaum,
and Ueno studied the case of the four-holed sphere. They proved that if
$\varphi$ is pseudo-Anosov in the mapping class group of the four-holed sphere,
then $\rho_{p}(\varphi)$ has infinite order for $p$ big enough. In the same paper, they
stated the above problem as a conjecture; it is now known as the AMU
conjecture.
(3) If $\varphi \in \operatorname{Mod}(S)$ does not act as a pseudo-Anosov on a subsurface, then up
to some power, it is the product of powers of commuting Dehn twists, and
so $\rho_{p}(\varphi)$ has finite order for all $p$. Also, as the quantum representations
enjoy some nice “splitting” properties regarding subsurfaces, it is enough
to prove this conjecture for pseudo-Anosov elements.
(4) The AMU conjecture is only known for two surfaces: the four-holed sphere
(proved in [AMU06]) and the one-holed torus (see [San12]). In general,
finding pseudo-Anosov elements satisfying the conjecture is already a dif-
ficult task. In [EJ16], it was proved that a certain class of “homological”
pseudo-Anosov elements on holed spheres satisfy the AMU conjecture.
Examples of point pushing mapping classes satisfying the AMU conjec-
ture have been studied in [KS16] and [MS21]. See also [DK22] where
examples were found using exponential growth of certain quantum invari-
ants; this paper shows that the Volume Conjecture (see Problem 1.27)
implies the AMU conjecture.

- [RT91] N. Reshetikhin and V. G. Turaev. Invariants of 3-manifolds via link polynomials and quantum groups. Invent. Math., 103(3):547–597, 1991. doi:10.1007/BF01239527.
- [And06] Jørgen Ellegaard Andersen. Asymptotic faithfulness of the quantum $\mathrm{SU}(n)$ representations of the mapping class groups. Ann. of Math. (2), 163(1):347–368, 2006. doi:10.4007/annals.2006.163.347.
- [AMU06] Jørgen Ellegaard Andersen, Gregor Masbaum, and Kenji Ueno. Topological quantum field theory and the Nielsen-Thurston classification of M$(0,4)$. Math. Proc. Cambridge Philos. Soc., 141(3):477–488, 2006. doi:10.1017/S0305004106009698.
- [San12] Ramanujan Santharoubane. Limits of the quantum SO(3) representations for the one-holed torus. J. Knot Theory Ramifications, 21(11):1250109, 13, 2012. doi: 10.1142/S021821651250109X.

title: Kirby Problem 2.50
statement:
(Volume conjecture for surface diffeomorphisms). Let $S$ be a
closed oriented surface, let $q=e^{2\pi i/n}$ be a root of unity, and let $\mathcal{K}^{q}(S)$ be the Kauff-
man bracket skein algebra. Let $\phi: S \to S$ be a pseudo-Anosov diffeomorphism with
mapping torus $M_{\phi}$, and let $r: \pi_{1}(S) \to \operatorname{SL}_{2}(\mathbb{C})$ be a smooth point in the charac-
ter variety that is $\phi$-invariant. Finally, let $L$ be the intertwiner realizing an iso-
morphism between the representations of $\mathcal{K}^{q}(S)$ corresponding to $[r]$ and $[r \circ \varphi_{*}]$,
normalized so that $\det(L) = 1$. Show that

$$
\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{1}{n}\log|\operatorname{Trace} L|=\frac{1}{4\pi}\operatorname{vol}_{\mathrm{hyp}} M_{\phi}.
$$
background:
Source: Kirby's Problems in Low-Dimensional Topology notes. Original problem number: KP-2.50.

Literature notes:
(1) For a closed oriented surface $S$ and a root of unity $q$, results of [BW17a,
FKBL19, GJS25, KK22, FKBL25] more or less establish a one-to-
one correspondence between irreducible representations of the Kauffman
bracket skein algebra $\mathcal{K}^{q}(S)$ and smooth points in the $\operatorname{SL}_{2}(\mathbb{C})$ character
variety of $S$. Thus in the above setup, the representations constructed
from $[r]$ and $[r \circ \varphi_{*}]$ must be isomorphic by some map $L$ called the in-
tertwiner. After normalizing $L$ so that $\det(L) = 1, |\operatorname{Trace} L|$ is dependent
only on the choice of $\varphi, r, q$, and the puncture invariants.
(2) This conjecture appears in [BWY21] and is a toy version of the Kashaev
Volume Conjecture [Kas97] (see Problem 1.27), as revisited by Baseilhac-
Benedetti [BB04]. In preprints, the conjecture has been claimed for some
examples [BWY22, Pan24, Wan25] and for torus knots. There also
exist versions of this conjecture for punctured surfaces, involving puncture
invariants on the quantum side and 3-manifolds obtained from $M_{\phi}$ by
Dehn filling on the hyperbolic side [PW24].

References cited:
- [BW17a] Francis Bonahon and Helen Wong. Representations of the Kauffman bracket skein algebra II: Punctured surfaces. Algebr. Geom. Topol., 17(6):3399–3434, 2017. doi: 10.2140/agt.2017.17.3399.
- [FKBL19] Charles Frohman, Joanna Kania-Bartoszynska, and Thang Lê. Unicity for representations of the Kauffman bracket skein algebra. Invent. Math., 215(2):609–650, 2019. doi:10.1007/s00222-018-0833-x.
- [GJS25] Iordan Ganev, David Jordan, and Pavel Safronov. The quantum Frobenius for character varieties and multiplicative quiver varieties. J. Eur. Math. Soc. (JEMS), 27(7):3023–3084, 2025. doi:10.4171/jems/1427.
- [KK22] Hiroaki Karuo and Julien Korinman. Azumaya loci of skein algebras, 2022. arXiv: 2211.13700.
- [FKBL25] Charles D. Frohman, Joanna Kania-Bartoszynska, and Thang T. Q. Lê. Sliced skein algebras and geometric Kauffman bracket. Adv. Math., 463:Paper No. 110118, 65, 2025. doi:10.1016/j.aim.2025.110118.
- [BWY21] Francis Bonahon, Helen Wong, and Tian Yang. Asymptotics of quantum invariants of surface diffeomorphisms i: conjecture and algebraic computations, 2021. arXiv: 2112.12852.
- [Kas97] Rinat M Kashaev. The hyperbolic volume of knots from the quantum dilogarithm. Letters in mathematical physics, 39(3):269–275, 1997.

title: Kirby Problem 3.1
statement:
Classify the smallest volume hyperbolic 3-manifolds of various types. In particular:

(a) Determine the nonorientable closed hyperbolic 3-manifolds of least volume.

(b) Determine the n-cusped hyperbolic 3-manifolds of least volume for each $n\geq 3$.

(c) Determine the smallest volume hyperbolic 3-manifolds with n orientable cusps for each n.

(d) Determine the n-cusped orientable hyperbolic 3-manifolds of least volume for each n.
background:
Source: Kirby's Problems in Low-Dimensional Topology notes. Original problem number: KP-3.1.

Literature notes:
(1) Parts (a)--(c) appeared in [Kir97, Problem 3.60].

(2) There has been a lot of progress in determining the hyperbolic 3-manifolds of low volume [GHM+21]. In particular, the orientable hyperbolic manifold of smallest volume was shown to be the Weeks manifold by Gabai, Meyerhoff, and Milley [GMM09, Mil09]; its volume is approximately 0.9427. Extensive evidence from SnapPy indicates that the hyperbolic 3-manifold with smallest volume is orientable (hence is the Weeks manifold). Closed nonorientable 3-manifolds appear to have larger volumes, and so the currently available techniques do not readily apply to them, which suggests why part (a) remains open.

(3) The two smallest orientable hyperbolic 3-orbifolds were identified by Gehring, Marshall, and Martin [GM09], [MM12], as was the smallest volume nonorientable 3-orbifold.

(4) The n-cusped manifolds with smallest volume are known for n = 1 and 2; in both cases, these manifolds are nonorientable. For n = 1, Adams [Ada87] showed that the Gieseking manifold is the unique smallest manifold, with volume $v_3$ $\approx$ 1.0149, the volume of a regular ideal tetrahedron. For n = 2, Adams [Ada88] proved that the least volume is $2v_3$, and showed that there is a unique 2-cusped manifold with this volume.

(5) The smallest volume orientable hyperbolic 3-manifolds with n cusps are known for n = 1, 2 and 4. For n = 1, this is due to Cao and Meyerhoff [CM01], who showed that there are two manifolds with smallest volume $2v_3$, the figure-eight knot complement and the figure-eight knot sister. For n = 2, Agol [Ago10] proved that there are two orientable 2-cusped manifolds with smallest volume, the Whitehead link complement and the $(-2,3,8)$ pretzel link complement, both of which have volume $v_8$, which is the volume of a regular ideal octahedron, approximately 3.6638. For n = 4, Yoshida [Yos13] proved that the link $8^4_2$ is the unique orientable 4-cusped manifold with smallest volume $2v_8$ $\approx$ 7.3276. For n = 3, the minimal volume is conjectured to be realized by the 3-chain link complement, which has volume approximately 5.33 (see [Zha23] for some results in this direction).

(6) Agol [Ago10] has conjectured that for $n\leq 10$, the minimal volume of an orientable n-cusped hyperbolic manifold is realized by the minimally twisted n-chain link complement. However, for larger values of $n$ ($11\leq n\leq 25$ and $n\geq 60$), it has been shown [KPR12] that these manifolds do not have minimal volume, as the $(n-1)$-fold cyclic cover over one component of the Whitehead link has smaller volume.
